w-adys-aw-ii-jagie-o: Little is known of Jogaila's early life, and even his year of birth is uncertain: historians once assumed about 1352, but some recent research suggests about 1362. He was the son of Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, and Algirdas's second wife, Uliana of Tver, and spent most of his early years in Vilnius. His father designated him heir in place of his older half-brother Fiodor, and he ascended the Lithuanian throne after Algirdas died in 1377. In his early reign his mother acted as regent, and his uncle Kęstutis, Duke of Trakai, continued to rule the north-western region.

Jogaila was raised a Lithuanian polytheist. His mother urged a marriage with Sofia, daughter of Prince Dmitri of Moscow, which would have required conversion to Orthodoxy, but that would not have stopped the crusades of the Teutonic Knights. He chose instead a Polish proposal to become a Catholic and marry the eleven-year-old Queen Jadwiga. On 14 August 1385 at Kreva Castle he confirmed his promises in the Union of Krewo, including the adoption of Christianity. He was baptised in Kraków as Ladislaus in 1386, married Jadwiga on 18 February 1386 and was crowned king, and in 1387 he converted Lithuania to Catholicism.

He ruled as co-monarch with Jadwiga, who attended to cultural and charitable activity, until her death in 1399, after which he was sole ruler. In 1402 he married Anna of Cilli, a granddaughter of Casimir III, a match that restored legitimacy to his reign. The Union of Vilnius and Radom of 1401 made his cousin Vytautas the Grand Duke under his overlordship, forging a permanent defensive alliance between the two states. His brother Švitrigaila stirred up revolts in Lithuania and won the backing of the Teutonic Knights. The allied victory over the Order at Grunwald in 1410, followed by the Peace of Thorn, secured the borders of Poland and Lithuania.

He also granted Vilnius a city charter modelled on Magdeburg Law, and in 1387 and 1413 Catholic boyars of Lithuania received privileges denied to the Orthodox. His policy of unifying the two legal systems was partial at first, but by the Union of Lublin in 1569 there was little difference between them.

Jogaila died on 1 June 1434. He was the last pagan ruler of medieval Lithuania and founded the Jagiellonian dynasty, which ruled both states until 1572. His reign extended Polish frontiers and is often considered the beginning of Poland's Golden Age. His sons Władysław III and Casimir Andrew both ruled Poland. He kept close ties with Ruthenian culture, bringing Ruthenian masters to Poland to paint frescoes, among them the king's bedroom at Wawel Castle in 1393-1394. He appears on the obverse of the 100 złoty banknote.
w-adys-aw-iv-vasa: Władysław was born on 9 June 1595 at the royal summer residence of Łobzów, near Kraków, the eldest son of Sigismund III Vasa and his first wife, Anna of Austria. His father had inherited the Swedish throne in 1592 but was deposed in 1599 by his uncle, later Charles IX, which began a long feud in which the Commonwealth's Vasa kings claimed the Swedish crown.

His mother died in 1598, and he was raised by Urszula Meierin, a former lady of her court. He studied for several years at the Kraków Academy and for two years in Rome, and spoke and wrote German, Italian and Latin.

In the Time of Troubles the Seven Boyars elected the young Władysław tsar after the overthrow of Vasily Shuysky. His father, who aimed to convert Russia to Roman Catholicism, refused the boyars' request to send him to Moscow and have him adopt Orthodoxy, and he never reigned. He mounted his own campaign in 1616, but could not take Moscow, and he kept the title of grand duke of Moscow without power until 1634.

In 1621 he was a commander at Chocim in the war with the Ottomans, where he urged the other commanders to stay and fight. In 1624 and 1625 he travelled in western Europe under the name Snopkowski, met Rubens in Antwerp and was impressed by opera in Florence.

The election sejm of 1632 chose Władysław without serious rivals, and he was crowned in Wawel Cathedral on 6 February 1633. In the Smolensk War of 1632 to 1634 he broke the Russian siege of Smolensk in September 1633 and surrounded the army of Mikhail Shein, which surrendered on 1 March 1634. He modernised the army with Western infantry and artillery and tried to found a navy, which led to the port village of Władysławowo, but the ships were gone by the 1640s.

A Catholic, he was tolerant: the Senate had 6 Protestant members when he took power and 11 when he died. The szlachta thwarted his efforts to strengthen the monarchy, and he died on 20 May 1648 without a legitimate son. His half-brother John II Casimir Vasa succeeded him, and his reign was later remembered as a golden era of stability before the Khmelnytsky Uprising and the Deluge.
w-arthur-lewis: William Arthur Lewis was born in Castries, Saint Lucia, then part of the British Windward Islands federal colony, the fourth of five sons of George Ferdinand and Ida Lewis, who had migrated from Antigua. His father died when Arthur was seven, and Ida raised the children alone. A gifted student, he finished school at 14 and worked as a clerk until he could sit the examination for a government scholarship.

He had hoped to be an engineer, but, as he later said, neither the government nor the white firms would employ a black engineer, so he turned to business administration. At 18 he won the scholarship to the London School of Economics, where he studied under John Hicks, Arnold Plant, Lionel Robbins and Friedrich Hayek.

Lewis graduated in 1937 with first-class honours and took a PhD in industrial economics under Arnold Plant. He became the first black faculty member at the school and worked there until 1948. In 1947 he became a lecturer at the Victoria University of Manchester, and in 1948 a full professor, teaching there until 1957. He advised the governments of Nigeria, Ghana, Trinidad and Tobago, Jamaica and Barbados. When Ghana became independent in 1957 he was appointed its first economic advisor and helped draw up its first Five-Year Development Plan, for 1959 to 1963.

In 1959 he became Vice Chancellor of the University of the West Indies. He was knighted in 1963 and that year joined Princeton University, where he held a full professorship and later the James Madison chair until he retired in 1983. He also served as Chancellor of the University of Guyana from 1966 to 1973 and was the first president of the Caribbean Development Bank, from 1970 to 1973. In 1979 he shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Theodore Schultz for pioneering research on economic development.

Lewis's Labour in the West Indies (1939) was an account of the Caribbean labour movement of the 1930s. His article of 1954, Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour, introduced the dual sector model. A capitalist sector grows by drawing labour from a subsistence sector, where workers can be paid above their marginal product.

Because labour is in unlimited supply, the capitalist sector can expand without raising wages, profits are reinvested, and the process becomes self-sustaining. The point at which the surplus labour is absorbed is called the Lewisian turning point. He also wrote The Theory of Economic Growth (1955) and Politics in West Africa (1965), which argues for power-sharing through proportional representation, federalism and coalition governments. He died in Bridgetown, Barbados, in 1991.
w-b-yeats: William Butler Yeats was born in Sandymount, County Dublin, on 13 June 1865, a Protestant of Anglo-Irish descent. His father, John, studied law and became a portrait painter. His mother, Susan Mary Pollexfen, came from a wealthy merchant family in Sligo, and the family soon moved to Merville in Sligo, which he came to think of as his spiritual home. He was educated in Dublin and London, and began writing at seventeen, drawing heavily on Shelley, Spenser and pre-Raphaelite verse before turning to Irish mythology, folklore and Blake.

His first collection, The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems, appeared in 1889. He had a lifelong interest in mysticism, spiritualism and the occult. In 1889 he met Maud Gonne, an ardent Irish nationalist, and his unrequited love for her had a lasting effect on his poetry. She refused his proposals in 1891, 1899, 1900 and 1901 and in 1903 married Major John MacBride. In 1899 Yeats, Lady Gregory, Edward Martyn and George Moore founded the Irish Literary Theatre, and with Lady Gregory and John Millington Synge he founded the Abbey Theatre, serving as its chief in its early years. His plays include Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902).

From 1900 his poetry became more rooted in the physical world, realistic and political. Collections of this phase include The Wild Swans at Coole (1919) and The Tower (1928). In 1922 he was appointed to the first Senate of the Irish Free State, and he served a second term from 1925. In December 1923 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature for poetry that gives expression to the spirit of a whole nation, and the money allowed him to repay his own debts and his father's. In the 1930s he composed marching songs for the Blueshirts, never used, and later distanced himself from the movement.

Yeats died of heart failure at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, France, on 28 January 1939, aged 73. He had wished to be buried quickly in France and moved to Sligo a year later. In September 1948 his body was taken to the churchyard of St Columba's Church at Drumcliff, County Sligo, aboard the Irish Naval Service corvette LÉ Macha. His epitaph comes from the last lines of Under Ben Bulben.
w-e-b-du-bois: Du Bois was born on 23 February 1868 in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, to Alfred and Mary Silvina Burghardt Du Bois. His mother's family belonged to the very small free black population of the town and had long owned land there. With money donated by neighbours Du Bois attended Fisk University in Nashville from 1885 to 1888. His residence in the South gave him his first experience of Jim Crow laws, the suppression of black voting and lynching. He then completed graduate work at Harvard.

In 1896 he took a one-year research post at the University of Pennsylvania, and his fieldwork in Philadelphia's African-American neighbourhoods led to The Philadelphia Negro (1899), the first case study of a black community in the United States. In July 1897 he became professor of history and economics at Atlanta University. At the First Pan-African Conference in London in July 1900 he delivered a speech, To the Nations of the World, asking European leaders to allow their colonies self-government and to recognise the rights of African Americans.

His collection of 14 essays, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), made him a spokesman of his race, second only to Booker T. Washington. He opposed Washington's Atlanta Compromise, which asked Southern blacks to accept segregation and disenfranchisement, and held that African Americans should fight for equal rights, to be won by an educated elite he called the talented tenth. In 1905 he and others met near Niagara Falls and wrote the principles of what became the Niagara Movement.

Du Bois attended a conference in New York in 1909 and a second in 1910, which created the NAACP; at his suggestion the word colored was used, to include dark-skinned people everywhere. In 1910 he became its Director of Publicity and Research, left Atlanta University and moved to New York to edit The Crisis, whose circulation reached 100,000 in 1920. After the First World War he attended the Pan-African Congresses, embraced socialism and held capitalism a primary cause of racism.

After the Second World War he took part in peace activism and was targeted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation. He spent the last years of his life in Ghana and died in Accra on 27 August 1963. His Black Reconstruction in America (1935) challenged the prevailing view that Black Americans were responsible for the failures of Reconstruction, and his autobiography Dusk of Dawn (1940) is regarded in part as one of the first scientific treatises in American sociology.
w-t-cosgrave: William Thomas Cosgrave was born at 174 James's Street, Dublin, to Thomas Cosgrave, a grocer, and Bridget (Nixon) Cosgrave. He attended the first Sinn Féin convention in 1905, was a Sinn Féin councillor on Dublin Corporation from 1909 and joined the Irish Volunteers in 1913.

In the Easter Rising of 1916 he served under Éamonn Ceannt as a captain at the South Dublin Union. His death sentence was commuted to penal servitude for life, and he was interned at Frongoch in Wales. He won the Kilkenny City by-election of August 1917 for Sinn Féin while still imprisoned. In 1919 de Valera's ministry named him Secretary of Local Government, charged with organising non-cooperation with the British authorities and an alternative system of government.

Cosgrave supported the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 6 December 1921, siding with Michael Collins and Arthur Griffith against Éamon de Valera. After Griffith and Collins died in August 1922, in the midst of the Civil War, the pro-Treaty leadership chose Cosgrave, in part for his democratic credentials. He became Chairman of the Provisional Government on 30 August and President of Dáil Éireann on 9 September, and on 6 December 1922 the Dáil elected him President of the Executive Council of the new Irish Free State.

He defended the state severely. His government's Public Safety Bill of October 1922 allowed execution of those captured bearing arms against it, although he disliked the death penalty in principle. By May 1923, 77 republicans had been shot after courts martial, among them Erskine Childers, Liam Mellowes and Rory O'Connor. In April 1923 he founded Cumann na nGaedheal, and the Civil War ended in May when the anti-Treaty IRA announced a ceasefire.

His ministry faced an army crisis in 1924 and the collapse of the Boundary Commission, after which he agreed with the British and Northern Irish prime ministers that the border should stay as it was and that the Free State need not pay its share of the imperial debt. Its economic policy was conservative, with low taxation and a balanced budget. Cosgrave lost the election of February 1932 to Fianna Fáil and handed over power.

Cosgrave became Leader of the Opposition and, after Cumann na nGaedheal merged with other groups to form Fine Gael in 1933, its leader in 1934. He led it through defeats in 1937, 1938 and 1943 and retired on 26 January 1944, succeeded by Richard Mulcahy. He died on 16 November 1965, aged 85, and was given a state funeral.

Historians have seen him as an effective chairman rather than a charismatic leader, who steered the state through its most turbulent years and kept it democratic when other post-war democracies turned to dictatorship.
waalo: Oral histories say that before it became a kingdom the area was ruled by a patchwork of Lamanes, a Serer title meaning the original owner of the land, and the names of places suggest rule by the Jaa'ogo dynasty of Takrur. Early Arabic writers describe an island town called Awlil near the mouth of the Senegal River. The founding is linked to Ndiadiane Ndiaye, a figure known partly through oral tradition, dated to 1287, though John Donnelly Fage placed him in the fourteenth century and Jean Boulegue around 1300.

According to some oral accounts Ndiaye was driven out by his half-brother Barka Mbodj, the first ruler to take the royal title Brak, before founding Jolof and making Waalo a vassal. The Brak went on paying symbolic tribute to the Bourba Jolof until 1715, long after the empire broke up following the Battle of Danki in 1549.

European trade on the coast from the 15th century shifted wealth towards coastal vassals such as Waalo. The French settled at the river mouth in 1638 and at Saint-Louis in 1659. The Marabout War of Nasr ad-Din overthrew Waalo's aristocracy for a time until his death in 1674, and Moroccan forces drove the Brak to move the capital to the south bank. Under Yerim Mbyanik, Njaam Aram Bakar and Naatago Aram in the 18th century Waalo dominated the Senegal estuary and Cayor and controlled river trade.

Defeat by the Damel of Cayor in 1765 was followed by a long civil war, Moorish raids and slaving: in 1775 the English took more than 8000 slaves from Waalo in less than six months. Lingeer Njembot Mbodj married the Emir of Trarza in 1833, which led Saint-Louis to attack Waalo, and the French conquered the kingdom in 1855.

The kingship passed among three matrilineal families, the Logar, the Tedyek and the Joos, the last of Serer origin, whose struggles to make one of their own Brak caused repeated civil wars. A council called the Seb Ak Baor, of three great electors, chose each king. Women held high positions, and several Lingeer, among them Njembot Mbodj and Ndaté Yalla Mbodj, ruled in their own right or as regents. Waalo took fees on every boatload of gum arabic or slaves shipped on the river, and Saint-Louis depended on its millet.
wabash-river: The Wabash drains most of Indiana and a significant part of Illinois. It rises about four miles south of Fort Recovery, Ohio, from farmland drainage, flows north and then sharply west into Indiana, crosses northern Indiana to the south-west and turns south near the Illinois border, where its southern part forms the boundary between the two states. It is the largest northern tributary of the Ohio River and the third largest overall, after the Cumberland and Tennessee. Its major tributaries are the Tippecanoe, White, Embarras and Little Wabash rivers. The name is the English form of the French Ouabache, which adopted the Miami-Illinois word waapaahšiiki, meaning water over white stones, since the river bottom in Huntington County is white limestone.

As the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated 14,000 to 15,000 years ago, meltwater formed proglacial Lake Maumee. Around 11,000 years ago it broke through the Fort Wayne Moraine and drained catastrophically, scouring a valley one to two miles wide, the Wabash-Erie Channel. For part of its course the Wabash follows the path of the pre-glacial Teays River.

French explorers first mapped the river to the Mississippi in the latter half of the 17th century. Until the mid-18th century the Ohio was considered a tributary of the Wabash, and French traders used it as a vital route between Canada and the Gulf of Mexico. In the 18th century the Miami people controlled at Kekionga the profitable 8-mile portage between the Maumee and the Wabash.

The United States fought five colonial and frontier-era battles on or near the river: Vincennes in 1779, St. Clair's Defeat in 1791, the Attack on Fort Recovery in 1794, Tippecanoe in 1811 and the Siege of Fort Harrison in 1812. In the mid-19th century the Wabash and Erie Canal, one of the longest in the world, was built along much of the river, but railroads surpassed it and most of the canal no longer exists. The river below Terre Haute was navigable by large ships during much of the 19th century, with steamships calling regularly. By the late 19th century erosion from farming and runoff had made it impassable to them, and dredging was not undertaken because railroads were preferred.

The river is about 503 miles long, or 810 kilometres, and flows freely for 411 miles from the dam near Huntington, Indiana, to the Ohio. It is the state river of Indiana and the subject of the state song, On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away, by Paul Dresser. Counties, townships, colleges and a canal bear its name, as did four US Navy warships. A 329-acre remnant of the old-growth forests that bordered it survives at Beall Woods State Park, near Mount Carmel, Illinois.
wadai-empire: The Wadai Sultanate, or Wadai Empire, lay east of Lake Chad in what is now Chad and the Central African Republic, and bordered the Sultanate of Darfur and the Sultanate of Baguirmi. It emerged in the seventeenth century under its first sultan, Abd al-Karim, who overthrew the ruling Tunjur people. Abd al-Karim, of a noble family of the Maba, was joined by the Maba and other small groups under an Islamic banner. He married Meiram Aisa, the daughter of the Tunjur king Daud, and made marriage pacts with the Masalit and Dajo. He built his capital at Wara, founded the Kolak dynasty and made Islam the state religion, although most commoners followed traditional religions.

After Abd al-Karim's death Wadai saw civil wars and hostile relations with Bornu and Darfur, and its wealth came from slave trading and raiding. It paid tribute to Darfur until the kolak Ya'qub Arus refused it late in the seventeenth century, defeating a Darfur attack. Under Muhammad Sabun (1804 to c. 1815) Wadai conquered Baguirmi in 1805, killed its ruler and sold 20,000 people into slavery. Around 1809/10 a new route to the north, linking Ennedi, Kufra and Jalu-Awjila to Benghazi, freed Wadai from dependence on Bornu and Darfur, and Sabun began minting coins.

Muhammad al-Sharif sacked Bornu's capital, Kukawa, in 1846, made Abéché the capital and allied with the Senussi, who controlled the trade route. By the late nineteenth century Wadai exported slaves, ivory and ostrich feathers, imported firearms, and controlled much of the Chad Basin.

After the sultan Yusuf died in 1898, Darfur and the Senussi backed rival candidates. The French began hostilities in 1906, backing Adam Asil, and took Abéché in 1909. Muhammad Salih, known as Dud Murra, fought on until his defeat in 1910. The sultanate was reconstituted under French suzerainty in 1935 with Muhammad Urada ibn Ibrahim as kolak, and became part of independent Chad in 1960. It continues as a non-sovereign monarchy.

Wadai's army had cavalry, some in quilted or steel armour, and in the 1870s 4,000 flintlock muskets. French observers wrote that its soldiers shot badly and disliked hand-to-hand fighting. At the siege of Massenya in 1870 the army of Sultan Ali breached the walls with a buried mine of gunpowder.
wadd: Wadd was worshipped above all by the Minaeans, the people of the Kingdom of Ma'in in South Arabia, whose inscriptions name him in the Ancient South Arabian script. He was also the national god of the Awsan kingdom, where in the Hellenistic era a king was proclaimed son of Wadd and received offerings as if he were himself a god. In the Islamic era Wadd was believed to have been worshipped by the Banu Kalb, a tribe of northern Arabia.

The formula Wd'b, read as Wadd is [my?] father, was written on amulets and buildings, often beside a symbol of a crescent moon with the small disc of Venus. Minaeans living on the Greek island of Delos raised an altar to him with two inscriptions, one in the Minaean language and one in Greek. The Minaean text opens with the symbols of three Minaean gods, Wadd's being a snake, and records that Hāni' and Zayd'il of the lineage of Hab erected the altar of Wadd and of the deities of Ma'in at Delos; the Greek text calls him Oaddos, god of the Minaeans.

Minaean colonists also worshipped Wadd at Dedan, modern Al-'Ula, during Lihyanite rule, where a temple of Wadd evidently stood. Minaean inscriptions record Levites in that temple, who according to some scholars served as priests or cult servants and could later be promoted to higher positions.

The Qur'an (71:23) names Wadd among five gods of the time of Noah, with Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr. The theophoric name Abd Wadd survived in that of Amr ibn Abd Wadd, a champion of the Quraish who challenged the Muslims to a duel during the Battle of the Trench and was killed by Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad.

According to Hisham ibn al-Kalbi's Book of Idols, the Banu Kalb worshipped Wadd in the form of a man, said to represent heaven, with an idol and temple at Dumat al-Jandal. A former devotee, Malik ibn Harithah, described the statue as a huge man clothed in two robes, with a sword at his waist, a bow on his shoulder, a spear bearing a standard and a quiver full of arrows. The temple was demolished on the orders of Muhammad during the expedition of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
wadenswil: Wädenswil lies on the Zürichsee lakeshore in the district of Horgen in the canton of Zürich, Switzerland, and is locally often called Wättischwiil, Wädischwiil or Wädi. On 1 January 2019 the former municipalities of Hütten and Schönenberg were merged into it. Before that merger it covered 17.4 square kilometres, of which 59.3 per cent was used for agriculture, 9.6 per cent was forest and 29.8 per cent was settled. Most of its people speak German, with Italian and Serbo-Croatian the next most common languages in the census of 2000.

Since the early 1500s Wädenswil and nearby Richterswil have been home to groups of Anabaptists, many of whom emigrated to Pennsylvania in the 1700s. Many of the surnames common in the area are still found plentifully in the southeastern part of that state.

The Wädenswil brewery was a brewery from 1833 until 1990. Its building was partly demolished in 2003, but brewing in the town has continued since 1992 with the Wadi-Brau-Huus AG. The Schloss Au on the Au Peninsula, with its auxiliary buildings and park, is listed in the Swiss inventory of cultural property as an object of regional importance.

Wädenswil–Vorder Au is one of the 56 Swiss sites that make up the UNESCO World Heritage Site Prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, and the settlement is listed in the Swiss inventory of cultural property as a Class A object of national significance. The town lies on the A3 motorway and on the lakeside railway line to Zürich, and ships serve it across the lake. It is the seat of the ZHAW Wädenswil, a centre for life sciences and facility management.

Natives of the town include the landscape artist Johann Gottfried Steffan, the politician Walter Hauser, a member of the Swiss Federal Council from 1888 to 1902, the architect Hans Auer, who designed the Federal Palace of Switzerland, the politician Robert Haab, a member of the Federal Council from 1917 to 1929, and the prehistorian Otto Hauser.
wadi-allaqi: Wadi Allaqi, also written Wadi Allaqui or Wadi Alalaqi, is the major dry river of the south-eastern part of Egypt's Eastern Desert. About 250 km long, it begins in Sudan below the Halaib Triangle and drains the country from the hills near the Red Sea to the valley of the Nile. Its mouth lies south of Aswan on the eastern shore of Lake Nasser, and the lower part of the wadi is now flooded by the lake.

The wadi is known for its gold and its rock inscriptions, among them a notable site at Umm Ashira. In the Middle Kingdom of Egypt a fortress was built at Quban, near the wadi's original mouth, and another at Ikkur. A stela attributed to Ramesses II of the New Kingdom, found near Quban, records the search for water for the gold workers and its discovery. That well lies 60 km into the wadi, near Umm Ashira, beyond the part now under Lake Nasser.

The gold deposits and mines lie in the upper parts of the wadi, at Hairiri, Heimur, Umm Garaiyat, Marahig, Seiga, Shoshoba and Abu Fas. Between the 9th and 13th centuries gold and emeralds were extracted there by chattel slaves. Mining in the Early Arab Period intensified under the rule of Ahmad ibn Tulun, and two forts were built at Derahib in this period.

The wadi is used by nomadic Beja of the Ababda and Bisharyn tribes, about 1,000 people in 2003, who graze livestock, make charcoal, gather medicinal plants, quarry copper and nickel and farm on a small scale. Since 1989 the area has been a nature reserve managed by the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency, and in 1993 UNESCO declared it a Biosphere Reserve.
wadi-el-hudi: The mining region covers about 100 square kilometres of the Eastern Desert and includes a large wadi and a mountain, Gebel el-Hudi; the name is thought to come from the Arabic word for guide. Here the Precambrian gneiss meets younger Cretaceous Nubian sandstone, so quartz, amethyst and gold are plentiful, with amazonite, copper, carnelian, talc, barite and galena. The main valley lies on a desert route between the Nile Valley and the Red Sea or Sudan, used for at least 7,000 years, and pastoral nomads left rock art and camped in its rock shelters before, during and after the mining.

State-sponsored amethyst expeditions began under Mentuhotep IV of the 11th Dynasty and were enlarged by Senwosret I of the 12th. Inscription WH 4, from the first year of Mentuhotep IV, records 150 hekat of amethyst, about 680 litres, and stela WH 6 counts over 1,500 people under Senwosret I, among them 1,000 labourers and 300 soldiers. Fortified settlements such as Sites 4, 5 and 9 were built, Site 9 by Nubian workers to Egyptian plans in local stone, and inscriptions show Nubians as a significant part of the workforce. The workers ate salted fish, sheep and cattle brought from the Nile Valley.

The inscriptions run to the reign of Sobekhotep IV, whose year 6 stelae mention a temple to Hathor, Lady of Amethyst, and Satet, Lady of Elephantine. Under Amenhotep II the Viceroy of Kush, Usersatet, set up a stela though the mine had been closed for 300 years. Small groups mined in the Persian period, large expeditions reopened the amethyst mine at Site 4 in the Ptolemaic period, and large groups mined gold at Sites 3 and 13 in the 9th and 10th centuries CE.

After reports that inscriptions were being taken and sold, the surveyor George W. Murray and his colleagues alerted the Antiquities Service, and 40 stelae went to the Aswan Museum and the Egyptian Museum. Ahmed Fakhry surveyed the region from 1944, made its first map and numbered its sites, and Ashraf Sadek published translations in 1980. Since 2014 the Wadi el-Hudi Expedition, led by Kate Liszka, Meredith Brand and Bryan Kraemer, has recorded over 300 inscriptions.
wadi-hammamat: The wadi lies in the Red Sea Hills about 110 kilometres east of Qena and 80 kilometres from the Nile Valley, directly east of Qift. It forms a six-kilometre gorge between Jabal el-Hammamat, Jabal Rasfah, Jabal Shahimiyyah and Jabal el-Sid, running from the well of Bir el-Hammamat in the west to Bir el-Fawakhir in the east. Its present name, taken from the well, was given by European explorers in the 19th century; local people had called the valley Wadi el-Kafr.

The valley's core is greywacke, known as Bekhen stone, while gold-bearing quartz veins lie at its eastern end and beyond, in Wadi Fawakhir and Wadi el-Sid. The wadi is only a few kilometres of a road 183 kilometres long from Coptos to the port of Myos Hormos, modern El Qoseir, a journey of about six days. About 750 inscriptions in hieroglyphs, hieratic, Demotic and Ancient Greek have been found there.

In the Old Kingdom greywacke from the valley began to be used for statues, steles and sarcophagi, and pharaohs sent large expeditions there. Under Mentuhotep III the chancellor Henenu led an expedition through the wadi to prepare a voyage to the Land of Punt, and late in the reign of Senusret I an expedition of 19,000 people brought back 60 sphinxes and 150 statues. Under the Achaemenid Persian occupation the stone for the statue of Darius the Great at the royal palace of Susa came from the valley.

The Romans built a quarrymen's village and military post there under Tiberius, and after merchants complained in 76 or 77 the prefect Lucius Julius Ursus had forts and fortified wells built along the road. Quarrying ceased in the crisis at the end of the 2nd century. The Byzantine Empire resumed gold mining nearby in the 5th century, and after the Arab conquest Muslim pilgrims used the route to reach El Qoseir and cross the Red Sea to Jeddah.

Route 256, the Qift–El Qoseir road, follows almost exactly the ancient road; its construction destroyed the remains of a Ptolemaic sanctuary of Min at Bir el-Fawakhir. The wadi marks the boundary between Qena Governorate and the Red Sea Governorate, and gold is still mined in the area, notably at Wadi el-Sid.
wadiyar-dynasty: The family belonged to the Urs clan, and its name comes from the Kannada odeya, meaning lord. The Wadiyars claimed descent from the deity Krishna and an origin in Dvārakā, but historians such as P. V. Nanjaraj Urs, Nobuhiro Ota and Aya Ikegame suggest they were local feudal lords who claimed Puranic ancestry. Their line begins with Yaduraya, a garrison leader made prefect of Mysore in 1399 by Harihara II of the Vijayanagara Empire, who took the title Raja and the surname Wadiyar.

After the Vijayanagara Empire disintegrated in 1565, Mysore became an independent kingdom. Kanthirava Narasaraja I pushed its frontiers as far as Trichy, and the kingdom reached its peak under Devaraja Wodeyar II, who divided the administration into 18 departments called chavadis and introduced a coherent system of taxation.

When the British restored the kingdom in 1799 under a subsidiary alliance with annual tribute, the capital returned to Mysore and the four-year-old Krishnaraja Wodeyar III was anointed. On a plea of non-payment the kingdom was run by the Mysore Commission from 1831 to 1881, when power passed back to his grandson Chamaraja Wadiyar X, who founded the Mysore Representative Assembly, the first of its kind in princely India. Mahatma Gandhi praised the realm of Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV as a Ramarajya. The last ruler, Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar, later served as rajapramukh of Mysore State and as governor of Mysore and of Madras; the titles were abolished in 1971.

Mysore Palace was the family's main residence for most of its recorded history, with a second palace at Bangalore by the early 1900s. The Wadiyars patronised musicians, writers and painters, making Mysore a cultural centre of Karnataka, and in 1940 Jayachamaraja Wadiyar and the industrialist Walchand Hirachand founded Hindustan Aircraft Limited in Bengaluru. Folklore tells of the curse of Alamelamma, the widow of the Vijayanagara viceroy Tirumala, who is said to have drowned herself in the Kaveri after cursing the kings of Mysore to be childless; a golden idol of her is still kept in the palace and honoured at the close of the Dasara festivities. Adoption has continued the line, most recently with Yaduveer Wadiyar in 2015.
wadjet: Wadjet, whose name means Green One, was originally the local goddess of the city of Dep or Buto in Lower Egypt, an important site in prehistoric Egypt. Her worship began in the Predynastic period and developed from that of a local goddess to a patron goddess. From about the 4th dynasty she was claimed as the patron and protector of the whole of Lower Egypt. A temple in Per-Wadjet gave the city its name, and its oracle may have been the source of the oracular tradition that spread to Greece. She also had a large temple at Imet, now Tell Nebesha, where she was worshipped as Lady of Imet.

Wadjet was usually shown as an Egyptian cobra, later also as a woman with a snake's head or a woman wearing the uraeus. The image of Wadjet with the sun disk is called the uraeus, the emblem on the crown of the rulers. She was also shown as a winged cobra, as a vulture like her sister Nekhbet, or as a lion-headed goddess, though some historians doubt that the seated lion-headed bronzes depict her rather than Sekhmet. One of her earliest depictions, from before 3100 BCE, is a cobra entwined around a papyrus stem.
She was closely associated with the Eye of Ra and the Eye of Horus, and the green and blue Wadjet eye amulets of daily life were a token of fertility and protection.

Wadjet was the protector of kings and of women in childbirth. After unification she and her sister Nekhbet, goddess of Upper Egypt, jointly protected all Egypt; the two were called the Two Ladies, and scenes of the sisters as two cobras appear in the tomb of Sety I. In myth she was Ra's daughter and his seeing eye, and she was also the nurse of the infant Horus, who was hidden with his mother Isis in the swamps of the Nile Delta from his uncle Set.

Wadjet and Nekhbet appear in the Pyramid Texts as nurses who sustain the king's divinity, and a pendant from the tomb of Tutankhamun shows Wadjet suckling the adult king. She also appears in the tomb of Nefertari, wearing the double crown.
wafd-party: The Wafd, whose name means 'delegation' in Arabic, grew out of earlier nationalist movements, among them the Urabi Revolt of the early 1880s, in which its future leader Saad Zaghloul had taken part. It took shape during the First World War and was founded in November 1918. Its original members were seven prominent figures from the landed gentry and the legal profession. They went to Reginald Wingate, the British High Commissioner in Egypt, with Zaghloul as their spokesman and asked to represent Egypt at the Paris Peace Conference, telling him that their main goal was an immediate end to the British occupation.

Zaghloul had gathered representatives of most of Egypt's political and social groups, so that the Wafd was at first more a coalition than a party. The British refused it permission to go to London or Paris, and it answered by publishing memoranda and giving speeches.

In 1919 the British arrested Zaghloul and three other leaders and exiled them to Malta. The deportations provoked a strike of law students that grew into demonstrations chanting 'Long live Saad! … Long live Independence!', and so began the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. Government and courts shut down, riots broke out and the British gradually suppressed them. They released Zaghloul and his followers, hoping to split the leadership, but the party became more unified. Its crescent and cross on a green flag, which protesters had used to show unity between Muslim and Christian Egyptians, became its symbol.

After the British protectorate ended in 1922, the Wafd became the preeminent political organisation of Egypt's liberal period and helped to shape the constitution of 1923. It won 179 of 211 seats in the election of 1924 and, in 1936, 89 percent of the vote and 157 seats.

The Wafd paid little attention to young people in the 1920s, and by the mid-1930s the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood, founded in 1928, had a more effective local system of organisation. After student demonstrations against the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 revealed cracks in the party, its leaders created a youth wing, the Blue Shirts, with uniforms, badges and the motto Obedience & Struggle, but by June 1937 they feared it was becoming too militant and restricted it.

Popular support fell, chiefly, in the view of one account, because the party did not boycott the government of King Farouk after it accepted the treaty of 1936, which alienated many nationalists. After the revolution of 1952 Gamal Abdel Nasser banned all Egyptian political parties in January 1953, and the party's newspaper Al Misri was closed in 1954.
waffen-ss: The Waffen-SS, meaning Armed SS, was the combat branch of the Nazi Party's paramilitary Schutzstaffel. Its origins lie in the selection on 17 March 1933 of 120 SS men by Sepp Dietrich to form the Sonderkommando Berlin. By November 1933 it had 800 men and swore allegiance to Adolf Hitler alone, and it became the Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler on 13 April 1934. At the outbreak of the war Heinrich Himmler's military formations included this regiment, the Verfügungstruppe under Paul Hausser, and the Death's Head units of Theodor Eicke, made up of concentration camp guards.

In August 1939 Hitler placed the Leibstandarte and the Verfügungstruppe under the operational control of the Army High Command, while Himmler kept the Death's Head regiments for what were called special tasks of a police nature behind the advancing armies. By spring 1941 the force equalled six or seven divisions. In keeping with Nazi racial policy, membership was at first open only to people of Germanic origin, but after the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 propaganda called the war a European crusade against Bolshevism, and units of foreign volunteers and conscripts were raised. Ethnic Poles, regarded as subhumans, were barred.

From 1942 growing numbers of foreigners, many not volunteers, entered the ranks. The 7th SS Division Prinz Eugen was drafted from ethnic Germans under threat of punishment and used in anti-partisan operations in the Balkans. In 1943 came the 13th Waffen Mountain Division Handschar, a Bosnian Muslim unit and the first non-Germanic division, and the 14th Galician division. The 15th Latvian, 19th Latvian and 20th Estonian divisions followed, the last formed by general conscription in February 1944. Late-formed divisions were often small battle groups in name only. The Waffen-SS was disbanded in May 1945.

The Waffen-SS took part in numerous atrocities. As an integral part of the SS it was declared a criminal organisation by the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg in 1946, because of its involvement in the Holocaust, the Porajmos and war crimes, including executions of prisoners of war and mass killings of civilians, often during anti-partisan operations. Members, except conscripts, who made up about a third of the membership, were denied many of the rights given to military veterans.
wagri: Wagria was laid waste in the Slavic uprisings of 983 and of about 1040 under Gottschalk, when many German towns and churches were destroyed and the region was largely depopulated. In 1066 the Wagri joined the Wilzi in storming the line of Saxon burgwarden from Mecklenburg to Schwerin and raided German territory as deep as Hamburg.

Around 1090 the still pagan Wagri and Liutizi came under the sway of the Rani-born Kruto, each tribe electing its own chief subordinate to him. In 1093 the Christian Obodrites under Henry, aided by some Saxons and the local Low German population, defeated Kruto at the Battle of Schmilau near Ratzeburg, and the Wagri were reduced once more to paying tribute.

The Christianisation of Wagria began under Unwan, Archbishop of Bremen, in the 1020s, and around 1126 the priest Vicelin of Oldenburg began to preach to the Wagri and Wilzi with the permission of Henry, then reigning from Lübeck. In the following years the Emperor Lothair II built castles across Wagria, and Canute Lavard and the Holsteiners invaded it and carried off the Wagrian leaders Pribislav and Niklot in chains.

In 1142 Henry the Lion and Adolf II of Holstein divided the conquered Slav lands along the Trave: Wagria with its castle of Sigberg went to Adolf, and Polabia with Ratzeburg to Henry. A great influx of German colonists followed. During the Wendish Crusade of 1147 the Wagri attacked recent settlements of Flemings and Frisians, the last recorded act of their resistance to Germanisation.
wagria: In the Middle Ages, and still on early modern maps, Wagria was bounded on the north and east by the Baltic Sea from the Kiel Fjord to Lübeck Bay, and inland by the rivers Schwentine and Trave. It corresponds roughly to the present districts of Plön and Ostholstein in Schleswig-Holstein, though the name now usually means only the Oldenburg Peninsula, whose highest point is the Bungsberg at 168 metres.

The name comes from the Wagri, a Slavic Lechitic tribe, and a region so called existed at least as early as the 8th century, covering the land between the Kiel Fjord and the middle and lower Trave. Its chief stronghold stood at the centre of Starigard, the Old Castle, now Oldenburg in Holstein, where the ramparts survive. Other important settlements were Old Lübeck, or Liubice, and Plön, or Plune.

The chronicler Helmold of Bosau gives a vivid contemporary account of how, in 1143, Count Adolf II of Schauenburg and Holstein brought settlers from Holstein and Stormarn and from Westphalia and Holland to make Wagria a profitable land, as part of the German eastward expansion of the High Middle Ages. According to Helmold, those from Holstein received the most sheltered land west of Segeberg on the Trave, the Westphalians the country around Dargun, the Dutch the area of Eutin and the Frisians Suesel, while the Plön area remained uninhabited. The count let Slavs settle Oldenburg, Lütjenburg and other coastal districts in return for taxes, so the local Slavs also took part in the new settlement of the region.
wahhabism: Wahhabism takes its name from the Hanbali scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703 to 1792), who was inspired by the earlier Hanbali scholars Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim. The name is primarily an exonym. It was probably first used by his brother Sulayman ibn Abd al-Wahhab, a staunch opponent of his views until 1776, and the movement's political opponents widely used it. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab and his early followers called themselves Muwahhidun, the monotheists, from tawhid, the oneness of God. Present-day followers reject the term and often call themselves Salafi.

The movement began as a revivalist effort in central Arabia in the early eighteenth century. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab called on his disciples to denounce practices associated with Sufi orders as idolatrous impurities and innovations, and to turn to the Quran and hadith. Historians have called the movement puritanical, while its adherents describe it as a reform movement to restore pure monotheistic worship. It also represented the first major Arab-led revolt against the foreign empires that had dominated the Islamic world since the Mongol invasions and the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate.

In theology Wahhabism is closely aligned with the Athari school, which relies on the literal meaning of the Quran and hadith and opposes the rational argument favoured by Ash'arite and Maturidite theologies. Its central emphasis is tawhid al-ibada, the doctrine that worship belongs to God alone. The intercession of prophets and saints, widespread among other Muslims, is therefore considered a violation of tawhid. The dispute with other Muslims is not over tawhid itself but over what counts as tawhid.

In law, Ibn Abd al-Wahhab emphasised the Quran and the Sunna, accepted consensus only where it confirmed them, and rejected deference to past juristic opinion, taqlid, in favour of independent reasoning, ijtihad. This set the movement against the Ottoman Sufi ulema, who upheld taqlid. He defined armed jihad as an endeavour that needs a religious justification and can be declared only by an imam, and the soldiers of the Emirate of Diriyah were forbidden to attack women, children and non-combatants.

Ibn Abd al-Wahhab's teachings were the official creed of the three Saudi states for more than two centuries. Wahhabism was also one of several Islamic revivalist currents of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, which included Uthman dan Fodio's movement in Nigeria, the Padri movement in Indonesia and the Mahdist movement in Sudan. From the nineteenth century Arab Salafiyya reformers corresponded with Wahhabis and defended them against Sufi attacks.

Scholars distinguish Wahhabism from Salafism in different ways. Some call Wahhabism a conservative creed centred on Saudi Arabia and Salafism a broader movement that arose independently in many places, while others see Wahhabism as the Salafism native to Arabia. Critics, including other Sunnis, have compared its doctrines to those of the Kharijites.
waikato: The Waikato stretches from the Coromandel Peninsula in the north to the north-eastern slopes of Mount Ruapehu in the south and from the west coast to the east coast of the North Island. Broadly it follows the catchment of the Waikato River, whose name the region takes; waikato is a Māori word traditionally translated as flowing water.

The west coast is rough hill country with three large natural harbours, Raglan, Aotea and Kāwhia. Inland lies the broad alluvial plain of the river, now largely pastoral land created by European settlers who drained the natural swamps, and to the east rise the forested Kaimai and Mamaku Ranges. The river flows out of Lake Taupō and is used for hydroelectricity.

Before Europeans arrived, the Waikato held the third most densely populated part of New Zealand, after Northland and Auckland and the Bay of Plenty. It was inhabited by iwi of the Tainui confederation, and between about 1750 and 1842 it was subject to many invasions and migrations by other Māori groups. In 1840 forty-four Waikato chiefs travelled to the Manukau Harbour to sign the Treaty of Waitangi. From 1840 to 1860 Anglican missionaries helped Waikato Māori build a trade in crops such as peaches, maize and wheat, with eight flour mills supplying the Auckland market until the boom ended in 1856 to 1857.

In the late 1850s Māori grew dissatisfied with the price the government paid for land: an average of 6d an acre, sold to settlers for 10 shillings. Some Waikato hapū formed a separate kingdom, the King Movement or Kīngitanga, and Waikato Māori had helped Taranaki Māori in the First Taranaki War. In 1863 and 1864 the colonial government, with troops from Britain and Māori loyal to the Crown, invaded the Waikato. Fighting at Rangiriri, Ngāruawāhia, Rangiaowhia and Ōrākau among other places ended in defeat for the Kīngitanga, whose forces withdrew south of the Puniu River to the area still known as the King Country.

The Waikato is governed by the Waikato Regional Council, established in 1989, and covers about 23,900 square kilometres. Its largest city is Hamilton, home to the University of Waikato, and its population was 498,771 at the 2023 census. The economy rests largely on dairy farming, which has been the main agricultural activity since the late 19th century. The headquarters of the Māori King Movement are at Tūrangawaewae Marae at Ngāruawāhia.
waikiki: The Hawaiian name Waikīkī means spouting fresh water, likely a reference to the springs and streams that fed the wetlands which once separated it from the interior of the island. The neighbourhood now extends from the Ala Wai Canal, a channel dug to drain those wetlands, on the west and north, to Diamond Head (Lēʻahi, tuna brow) on the east. The beach is noted for its views of the Diamond Head tuff cone, its usually warm and cloud-free climate and its surf break. Before 1950 it was continuous and known simply as Waikīkī Beach; seawalls and other developments have since divided the coast into eight beaches.

After the founding of the Kingdom of Hawaii, Waikīkī was its first capital, from 1795 to 1796. In the 1800s it was a retreat for Hawaiian royalty, who surfed there on early forms of longboards. A few small hotels opened in the 1880s. In 1893 the Greek-American George Lycurgus leased a guest house and renamed it Sans Souci, creating one of the first beach resorts; Robert Louis Stevenson stayed there that year, and the place became popular with tourists from the mainland.

In the early 1900s developers dug the Ala Wai Canal, then called the Waikīkī Drainage Canal, to get rid of the wetlands, which were claimed to harbour disease-carrying mosquitoes. A Hawaiian dredging company run by Walter F. Dillingham carried out the project between 1921 and 1928. The surfer Duke Kahanamoku, who competed in the Olympics, made the beach a surfing centre. The first high-rise hotels were built in 1955, including the Waikiki Biltmore and the Sheraton Princess Kaiulani Hotel, and large resort hotels filled the area, alongside early 20th-century hotels such as the Moana Surfrider and the Royal Hawaiian.

The beach is almost entirely man-made. Hotels and homes built too close to the natural shoreline, and seawalls and groins that blocked the movement of sand, caused erosion from the late 1800s; by 1950 more than 80 structures occupied the shoreline. Sand was imported from California in the 1920s and 1930s and again until the 1970s, and restoration projects have been carried out since, including a partial one completed in 2012.

Waikīkī includes Kapiʻolani Park, Fort DeRussy and Kūhiō Beach Park. Its main thoroughfare is Kalākaua Avenue, named after King Kalākaua, and Kūhiō Avenue is named after Prince Kūhiō. A bronze statue of Duke Kahanamoku, installed in 1990, stands at the beach.
wailuku: Wailuku lies at the mouth of the ʻĪao Valley, 249 feet (76 m) above sea level at the base of West Maui Volcano, on the northern edge of the isthmus between East Maui (Haleakalā) and West Maui. It is just west of Kahului. The name means destroying water. Wailuku is also known as Pūʻalikomohana or Nā Wai ʻEhā, the four waters, which are the land divisions of Waikapū, Wailuku, Waiʻehu and Waiheʻe. It is one of the three moku, or districts, of west Maui, with Lāhaina and Kāʻanapali.

The area was a centre of power and population in prehistoric Hawaii and the home of some of Maui's rulers. Tradition names Wakalana as a leading Wailuku chief, and holds that Kapawa, king of Hawaiʻi before Pili, was buried here. In the late 15th century Maui's ruler Kakaʻe designated the ʻĪao Valley as a burial ground for aliʻi, whose remains were buried in secret places. In 1790 Kamehameha the Great defeated Kalanikūpule and the Maui army there at the Battle of Kepaniwai, during his campaign to unify the islands. The fighting was said to be so bloody that bodies blocked ʻĪao Stream, giving the site its name, the damming of the waters.

New England missionaries arrived in the mid-1800s and brought their religion, skills, implements and agricultural methods. By the 1860s the Wailuku Sugar Company, owned by C. Brewer & Co., and other plantations were growing and milling sugarcane, with irrigation ditches carrying water from the mountains. The industry flourished to the detriment of the native people. Thousands of workers came from China, Japan, Okinawa, Korea, the Philippines, Europe and America, and many settled in Wailuku. In 1905 it became the county seat of Maui, a centre of government and business, and growth continued until the late 1960s, when the sugar industry reduced its operations.

Historic sites include Kaʻahumanu Church, dating to 1876 and named after Queen Kaʻahumanu, wife of Kamehameha I, the Wailuku Civic Center Historic District, and the Bailey House, a 19th-century former seminary and home that now holds a history museum and the Maui Historical Society. Two ancient temples near the town, the Halekiʻi Heiau and the Pihanakalani Heiau, date back hundreds of years and were used for religious purposes by native Hawaiians. In the 1990s the former C. Brewer land was developed as the Kehalani neighbourhood. The population was 17,697 at the 2020 census.
wainganga-river: The Wainganga rises in the Mahadeo Hills near the village of Gopalganj in Seoni District, on the southern slopes of the Satpura Range, where the land stands at an average of 625 m above sea level. It winds south through Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra across wide floodplains of sweeping meanders and low alluvial flats, between banks 10 to 15 m high. Its forested valley is thinly populated. The united stream it forms with the Wardha River empties into the Godavari at Kaleshwaram in Telangana.

The river drains Balaghat District of Madhya Pradesh and the Chandrapur, Gadchiroli, Bhandara, Gondia and Nagpur districts of Maharashtra. Its main tributaries are the Thel, Thanwar, Bagh, Chulband, Garhavi, Khobragadi and Kathani from the right, and the Hirri, Chandan, Bawanthari, Kanhan and Mul from the left. The longest is the Kanhan, at 275 km. The Thanwar valley lay on the Hindu pilgrimage route from South to North India, and the village of Jhulpur on its bank was a halting place and temple town.

Balaghat, Bhandara, Seoni and Gadchiroli are the main cities on its banks, with Pauni, Tirora and Bramhapuri among the smaller towns, and the river is their chief source of water. By 2012 about 149 dams had been built in its basin, among them the Bheemgarh Dam in Seoni District, described as the biggest mud dam in Asia. The river carries goods and passengers under the National Waterways Project.

Rudyard Kipling set his Mowgli stories in The Jungle Book of 1894 and The Second Jungle Book of 1895 on the Wainganga, the water source of the jungle's people and the site of the Peace Rock. The forests of the Kanha National Park, which grew around the river, hold tigers, leopards and bears.
waiofar: Waiofar succeeded his father, Hunald I, peacefully in 745 when Hunald entered a monastery, and with the duchy he inherited the conflict with the rising Carolingian family. Pepin the Short, king of the Franks from 751, was his nominal overlord. Open conflict can be dated to 753, when Waiofar gave asylum to Pepin's brother Grifo, who had fled Francia after a failed attempt to seize the Duchy of Bavaria; Grifo was killed the same year near the River Arc on his way to Lombardy. According to local sources Waiofar also attacked Pepin's forces as they besieged Narbonne between 752 and 759.

Little is known of Waiofar's government beyond his wars. He used counts to rule Bourges, Poitiers and the Auvergne in the Frankish manner, and one charter survives, drawn up around 756–57, in which he and Hunald are styled princes. He confiscated church lands and gave them to his followers, and his army had a professional core of Gascons. In 760 Pepin denounced the seizure of church lands and invaded Berry and the Auvergne. Waiofar's counts struck back at Chalon-sur-Saône in 761, but Pepin took Bourbon, Chantelle and Clermont, then Bourges and Thouars in 762, when Waiofar's cousin Count Mantio was also killed in an ambush near Narbonne.

In 763 Waiofar offered to submit in return for Bourges and other cities, but nothing came of it, and in 764 he attended Pepin's assembly at Worms. Between 763 and 766 he withdrew his garrisons from Poitiers, Limoges, Saintes, Périgueux and Angoulême; Bernard Bachrach holds that he destroyed their walls first, while Archibald Lewis thinks Pepin did so.

The last phase of the war was fought with growing brutality, the chroniclers recording that Pepin burnt villas, despoiled vineyards and laid the land waste. By 766 most of Waiofar's followers had left him; in 768 most of his family was captured and executed in the forest of Périgord, and on 2 June he was killed by his own men, allegedly at Pepin's instigation. A kinsman, perhaps his son, Hunald II, took up his claims against Pepin's successor, Charles.
waipio-valley: Waipiʻo means curved water in the Hawaiian language. The valley was formed by stream erosion in the weak basalt lava of the Kohala volcano, and its floor at sea level lies almost 2,000 ft (610 m) below the surrounding land. Several large waterfalls drop into it and feed the river that runs from the foot of the largest falls, at the back of the valley, out to the ocean, where the shore is a black sand beach. In Hawaiian folklore the valley is the place where the gateway to Lua-o-Milu, the underworld, lay hidden from view by sand.

The valley was the capital and permanent residence of many early Hawaiian aliʻi, chiefs or kings, until the time of King ʻUmi. The first chief to hold a court there is named as Kahaimoelea. It was the site of the ancient grass palace of the kings, with its stands of nioi trees, and was known for the nioi known as the Nioi wela o Pakaʻalana, the burning nioi of Pakaʻalana. At its peak the valley probably supported 10,000 people on 800 acres (320 ha) of taro. In the 18th century Kahekili II, king of Maui, raided Waipiʻo and burned the four sacred trees to the ground.

A few taro farms still work the valley floor. The 2006 Kiholo Bay earthquake brought down a cliff at the valley's entrance into the ocean and caused rock falls on the access road. That road, paved but open only to four-wheel-drive vehicles, descends from a lookout on the southern wall, rising 800 feet (240 m) in 0.6 miles (1.0 km); access to the valley floor is allowed to Big Island residents, permitted tour operators and those practising Native Hawaiian traditional or customary rights. A foot trail, the Waimanu or Muliwai Trail, leads on to the Waimanu Valley.
waitangi-northland: Waitangi lies on the north side of the Waitangi River in the Bay of Islands, 60 kilometres north of Whangārei on the North Island, and is joined by a bridge near the river mouth to the town of Paihia. Its Māori name means noisy waters or weeping waters, probably after the Haruru Falls on the river. The Waitangi Wharf at the estuary mouth serves passenger ferries between Russell and Paihia.

The Declaration of Independence of New Zealand, He Whakaputanga, was signed here on 28 October 1835. On 5 February 1840 Lieutenant Governor William Hobson read the proposed treaty to some 300 European and Māori people gathered in front of James Busby's residence. Many chiefs, among them Te Kemara, Rewa and Moka Te Kainga-mataa, spoke against accepting the Crown's rule, while others, including Te Wharerahi, Pumuka and the Hokianga chiefs Tāmati Wāka Nene and Eruera Maihi Patuone, came to support it.

The meeting was due to resume on 7 February, but a number of chiefs pressed to sign earlier, and the treaty was first signed on 6 February in a marquee in the grounds of Busby's house, by representatives of the Crown, chiefs of the Confederation of the United Tribes and other leaders. Other chiefs signed later elsewhere, while some delayed or refused. In 2007 the researcher Brent Kerehona questioned whether Moka actually signed, since no mark stands beside his name. The treaty followed the Declaration of Independence without making it void.

The Waitangi Treaty Grounds have been open to the public since 1934. The Treaty House, first occupied by Busby, British resident from 1832, and his wife Agnes, was restored in the 1930s for the centenary of 1940. The carved meeting house Te Whare Rūnanga opened on 6 February 1940, and the grounds hold Te Kōngahu Museum of Waitangi, opened in 2016, and Te Rau Aroha Museum of the Price of Citizenship, opened in 2020.
wajid-ali-shah: Mirza Wajid Ali Shah became the eleventh king of Awadh on 13 February 1847, when the kingdom was in decline. Under a treaty of 1801 the British East India Company had taken much of it, charged it the cost of maintaining the Bengal Army and repeatedly demanded loans, but it kept the rest as a buffer. As king he took a close interest in justice, introduced reforms and reorganised the army. The Resident at Lucknow, General William Sleeman, reported maladministration and lawlessness, though he himself opposed outright annexation. Later studies have suggested that Awadh was neither as bankrupt nor as lawless as the British claimed.

Trained in singing by Basit Khan, Pyar Khan and Jafar Khan, he wrote over forty works as Akhtarpiya and was the most prominent of the composers who enriched the thumri; James Kippen argued that the thumri already existed as a vocal form by 1800. Under his patronage Kathak became the court dance and the Lucknow Gharana took shape, with Thakur Prasadji as his guru. He staged the Rahas, his dance-dramas, and his Radha Kanhaiyya Ka Qissa has been called the first play of the Hindustani theatre. He wrote in Persian and Urdu as Akhtar, and in 1854 granted Mirza Ghalib a pension of five hundred rupees a year.

After the annexation on 11 February 1856 he went by Kanpur to Calcutta, landing near Metiabruz on 13 May 1856. His mother, his brother and his eldest son went to England to plead his case. When the rebellion of 1857 reached Lucknow and the sepoys installed one of his sons, he was held in Fort William with his prime minister, while his wife Begum Hazrat Mahal led the resistance as regent. At Matiya Burj he spent his income of 12 lakh rupees a year on a second Lucknow, and his verse Huzn-i-Akhtar records his journey into exile. He died on 1 September 1887.
wakayama-prefecture: Wakayama Prefecture lies in the Kansai region of Honshu and has an area of 4,724 square kilometres. It borders Osaka Prefecture to the north and Mie Prefecture and Nara Prefecture to the north-east. It occupies the south-western coast of the Kii Peninsula on the Kii Channel, which connects the Pacific Ocean with the Seto Inland Sea, across from Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku. Present-day Wakayama is mostly the western part of the old province of Kii. The city of Wakayama is its capital and largest city, with Tanabe, Hashimoto and Kinokawa among the other major cities.

On 17 and 18 July 1953 torrential rain was followed by the collapse of levees, river flooding and landslides over a wide area of the prefecture. Many bridges and houses were destroyed. The Government of Japan officially confirmed that 1,015 people died, 5,709 were injured and 7,115 houses were lost.

Mount Kōya, in the Ito District, is the headquarters of the Shingon sect of Japanese Buddhism. It has one of the first Japanese style Buddhist temples in Japan and remains a pilgrimage site, its ancient temples standing among tall cedars. The Sacred sites and pilgrimage routes in the Kii Mountain Range, which extend for miles through the prefecture, are recognised as Japan's 11th UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Kumano Shrines stand on its southern tip.

The prefecture has been growing oranges for centuries: in the Arida District they have been produced for more than 400 years. It is also known for ume, the Chinese flowering plum, and has hot springs such as Nanki-Shirahama Onsen, Kawayu Onsen and Yunomine Onsen.
walafrid-strabo: Walafrid, nicknamed Strabo or Strabus, meaning squint-eyed, was an Alemannic Benedictine monk and theological writer who lived on Reichenau Island in southern Germany. He was born in Swabia and educated at Reichenau Abbey, where his teachers were Tatto and Wetti, to whose visions he devoted one of his poems. He then studied for some time at the monastery of Fulda under Rabanus Maurus before returning to Reichenau, of which he was made abbot in 838.

For unclear reasons he was expelled from his house and went to Speyer. His own verses suggest the cause was that, although he had been tutor to Charles the Bald, he took the side of Charles's elder brother Lothair I after the death of Louis the Pious in 840. He was restored to his monastery in 842.

His theological works include an exposition of the first twenty psalms and an epitome of Rabanus Maurus's commentary on Leviticus. De exordiis et incrementis quarundam in observationibus ecclesiasticis rerum, written between 840 and 842 for Reginbert the Librarian, deals in 32 chapters with churches, altars, prayers, bells, pictures, baptism and communion. It uses current German words for the things described, and its last chapter pictures a body of lay and ecclesiastical officers as an organic unity, a view of public office seen from the court.

His historical works include the rhymed Life of Saint Gall, still the primary authority for that saint's life though written nearly two centuries after his death, and a shorter life of Saint Othmar. The Liber de visionibus Wettini, in hexameters, was written at the age of eighteen and tells how Wetti saw Charlemagne suffering in Purgatory. His best-known poem, the Liber de cultura hortorum, later published as the Hortulus, describes the garden he tended on Reichenau, with the medicinal and other uses of its herbs, from sage to rue, melons, poppies and the rose. De Imagine Tetrici is a dialogue inspired by an equestrian statue at Charlemagne's palace at Aachen.

Walafrid died on 18 August 849 on an embassy to his former pupil, Charles. Rabanus Maurus wrote his epitaph, praising him as the faithful guardian of his monastery. Johannes Trithemius credited him with the Glossa Ordinaria on the Bible, an error that remained current well into the 20th century, since the work dates from the 12th century and is now attributed to Anselm of Laon and his followers.
walata: Oualata, also written Walata, is a small oasis town at the eastern end of the Aoukar basin in south-eastern Mauritania. The chronicles of the 17th century call it Biru. The whole commune covers 93,092 square kilometres, mostly desert, and the main town lies in its south. The area is believed to have been settled first by an agro-pastoral people akin to the Mandé Soninke, who lived along the rocky promontories of the Tichitt-Oualata and Tagant cliffs facing the basin and built some of the oldest stone settlements on the African continent.

The town formed part of the Ghana Empire and grew wealthy through trade. At the beginning of the thirteenth century it replaced Aoudaghost as the principal southern terminus of the trans-Saharan trade and became an important commercial and religious centre; by the fourteenth century it belonged to the Mali Empire. A route from Sijilmasa through the salt mines of Taghaza ended there. Raymond Mauny estimated that in the Middle Ages the town held between 2,000 and 3,000 people.

Ibn Battuta found its people Muslim and mainly Massufa, a section of the Sanhaja, and was surprised by the respect and independence that women enjoyed. He stayed about fifty days and noted the heat, a few small date palms shading watermelons, underground water and plenty of mutton.

From the second half of the 14th century Timbuktu gradually replaced Oualata as the terminus of the route, and the town declined. In 1433 the Mali Empire lost control of it, and in 1480 it was besieged for a month and sacked by the Mossi; the inhabitants regrouped, pursued the invaders and rescued many of the captives.

Leo Africanus, visiting in 1509-1510, described a small kingdom of three large villages and some huts among the palm groves, with a large Songhai-speaking population, and tributary to the king of Timbuktu. In the early 17th century Hassaniya Arabs arrived, and their influence produced the present name. For a century and a half the Lemhajib, three Soninke families, dominated local politics before being absorbed into the Berber and Arab milieu.

The old town covers about 600 by 300 metres, some of it in ruins. Its sandstone buildings are coated with banco, and some are decorated with geometric designs; the town is known for its highly decorative vernacular architecture. The mosque now lies on the eastern edge, and a museum holds manuscripts. Oualata was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, together with Ouadane, Chinguetti and Tichitt.
walcheren: Walcheren is a region and former island in Zeeland at the mouth of the Scheldt estuary, between the Eastern Scheldt in the north and the Western Scheldt in the south, roughly rhombus-shaped. Its two sides facing the North Sea are dunes and the rest of its coast is dykes. Middelburg, the provincial capital, lies at its centre, Vlissingen is the main harbour 9 kilometres to the south, and Veere is the third municipality in the north.

The island was joined to its neighbours by later works: the Sloedam, built in 1871 for a railway, and polders made after the Second World War connected it to Zuid-Beveland, and the Veerse Gatdam, completed in 1961, linked it to Noord-Beveland. The name is first attested in Latin spellings such as villam Walichrum about 790, and probably combines a word for moist with one for a sandy ridge.

In Roman times the island was a point of departure for ships going to Britain and had a temple of the goddess Nehalennia, popular with those crossing the North Sea. In the ninth century it was the seat of the Danish Viking Harald, who conquered part of what became the Netherlands with his brother Rorik. In 1588 Dutch rebels and English fighters held Walcheren, which blocked access to Antwerp and denied the Spanish Armada a deep-water port for supplies and shelter. Under the Secret Treaty of Dover of 1670 England was to receive Walcheren, but the plan failed when Dutch resistance repulsed the French and English attack.

On 30 July 1809 a British expeditionary force landed to attack the French fleet at Flushing and to assist the Austrians against Napoleon. British troops captured Flushing, but the Austrians had been defeated at Wagram in early July and the French fleet had moved to Antwerp. The force lost over 4,000 men to Walcheren Fever, thought to be a combination of malaria and typhus, against 106 killed by enemy action, and withdrew in December.

Walcheren was fought over in 1940 and again in 1944, in the final stage of the Battle of the Scheldt, because it commanded the route to Antwerp. On 3 October 1944 the RAF bombed the sea wall at Westkapelle, flooding the island. Canadian troops fought along the narrow Walcheren Causeway from 31 October, and British Commandos landed at Westkapelle on 1 November in Operation Infatuate to silence the German coastal batteries. All German resistance on the island had ceased by 8 November 1944.
waldemar-margrave-of-brandenburg: Waldemar was a son of Margrave Conrad of Brandenburg-Stendal and of Constance, eldest daughter of the Piast duke Przemysł I of Greater Poland. He belonged to the line of Ascanian margraves that began with Albert the Bear in 1157. He was co-regent from 1302 and succeeded his uncle Otto IV as margrave in 1308. In 1309 he married his cousin Agnes, daughter of Margrave Hermann of Brandenburg-Salzwedel; the marriage remained childless.

In 1307 an agreement with the Swienca family ceded him Pomerelia, and Brandenburg troops occupied Świecie, Tczew and the strategic places up to Gdańsk. King Władysław I of Poland called in the Teutonic Knights, who took Danzig, and by the Treaty of Soldin of 1309 Waldemar gave up his claims east of the Łeba to the Teutonic Order for 10,000 silver marks. The same year Rostock shut its gates against him. In 1312 he captured Margrave Frederick I of Meissen, who had to cede the March of Lusatia, Torgau and Großenhain and pay a ransom of 32,000 silver marks. In the imperial election of 1314 Waldemar voted for Louis IV against Frederick the Fair.

His support for Stralsund against Prince Henry II of Mecklenburg and his occupation of the Lordship of Stargard provoked a coalition of Mecklenburg, Werle and Denmark. His troops were defeated near Gransee in August 1316, and by the Treaty of Templin of 1317 he gave up Stargard and Neubrandenburg, while Schlawe and Stolp passed to Duke Wartislaw IV of Pomerania. On the death of his cousin John V in 1317 he became sole ruler of Brandenburg, and in 1319 he acquired Züllichau and Schwiebus in Silesia.

Waldemar died on 14 August 1319. When his ward Henry II died in 1320, the margraviate fell as a vacant fief to King Louis IV, who in 1323 granted it to his eldest son Louis, ignoring the claims of the Ascanian princes of Anhalt. In 1348 an impostor in the Archbishopric of Magdeburg claimed to be Waldemar returning from a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. Exploiting the rivalry of the Wittelsbach and Luxembourg dynasties, he was invested by King Charles IV for about two years before he was unmasked and fled to Dessau.
waleran-iii-duke-of-limburg: Waleran, also called Walram, was born around 1165, a son of Henry III of Limburg and Sophia of Saarbrücken. As a younger son he did not expect to inherit and was at first Lord of Montjoie. He led an adventurous youth and took part in the Third Crusade in 1192. His first wife was Cunigunda, a daughter of Frederick I, Duke of Lorraine, with whom he had Sophie, who married Frederick of Isenberg, Matilda, who married William III, Count of Jülich, the future Duke Henry IV and a younger Waleran.

He supported the imperial candidate Philip of Swabia, but after Philip's death in 1208 he went over to his rival, Otto of Brunswick. In 1212 he went with his first cousin Henry I, Duke of Brabant, to Liège, then at war with Guelders. Cunigunda died in 1214, and in May of that year he married Ermesinde of Luxembourg, becoming by right of his wife Count of Luxembourg and Count of Arlon. Their children were Catherine, who married Matthias II, Duke of Lorraine, Henry, later Count of Luxembourg, and Gerhard, Count of Durbuy.

He inherited Limburg on his father's death in 1221. Two years later he tried once more to take Namur from the Margrave Philip II, failed, and made peace at Dinant on 13 February 1223. He then attended several imperial diets and went with Emperor Frederick II into Italy. On his way back he died at Rolduc on 2 July 1226.
wales: Wales is a generally mountainous country on the western side of central southern Great Britain, about 270 kilometres from north to south. It is bordered by England to the east and by sea in all other directions, with about 2,700 kilometres of coastline. The highest mountains are in Snowdonia, where Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) rises to 1,085 metres. The English words Wales and Welsh derive from an Old English word, Wealh, which the Anglo-Saxons used for the Britons; the Welsh name for themselves, Cymry, descends from a Brythonic word meaning 'fellow-countrymen'.

The territory was permanently settled from the end of the last ice age. In the Bronze Age the Great Orme in North Wales became Britain's premier producer of copper. After the Roman withdrawal, Britain fractured into kingdoms, and Anglo-Saxon settlers gradually displaced the culture and language of the Britons, leaving one group isolated in the western peninsula, whom their English neighbours called Welsh. Medieval Wales stayed divided into kingdoms that fought each other as much as the English.

In the 10th century Hywel ap Cadell, later Hywel Dda, gained control of Gwynedd and Powys in 942 and so of nearly all of Wales, and codified Welsh law. Wales was briefly united under Gruffudd ap Llywelyn in 1055. Owain Glyndŵr led the Welsh Revolt in the early 15th century and briefly re-established an independent state with its own parliament. In the 19th century mining and metallurgy transformed Wales into an industrial society, and the population rose from 587,000 in 1801 to 2,421,000 by 1911.

Both Welsh and English are official languages, and Welsh is dominant in parts of the north and west. Wales has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward I in Gwynedd, the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct and Canal, the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape and the Slate Landscape of Northwest Wales. Medieval Welsh manuscripts such as the Red Book of Hergest preserve the Mabinogion and the earliest forms of the Arthurian legend.
wali-songo: The name joins the Arabic wali, used of Muslim saints, with the Javanese sanga, nine. Each of the nine is usually given the Javanese title sunan, which may come from susuhunan, here meaning honoured, and most were also called raden in their lifetimes as members of royal houses. The term was created later by historians, and there was never an official group with members: the lists of the nine vary between sources, and their chronology suggests that nine may never have been alive at the same time.

Islam was present on Java before them. Tang records mention merchants from the Middle East in Srivijaya and in Kalingga on Java in 674, and when the Chinese Muslim admiral Zheng He came to Java in 1405 he found 1,000 Chinese Muslim families each in Tuban, Gresik and Surabaya. His scribe Ma Huan, on the last voyage of 1433, reported that the Chinese and Arab townspeople of the north coast were Muslim while most of the indigenous population were not.

The most generally accepted history, supported by a reading of the inscription on his grave, places the origin of the first of them, Malik Ibrahim, in Kashan in Iran, and he is linked with the Kubrawi Sufi tradition; a theory first published in 1968 gave several of the early saints Chinese ancestry. Malik Ibrahim, known as Sunan Gresik, is said to have arrived on Java in 1404 and died in 1419; his work included commerce, healing and better farming methods.

His son Sunan Ampel, born in Champa and dead at Demak in 1481, is the focal figure: father of Sunan Bonang and Sunan Drajat, father-in-law of Sunan Giri, grandfather of Sunan Kudus and teacher of Raden Patah. Sunan Bonang taught Sunan Kalijaga, whose son was Sunan Muria. Sunan Gunung Jati founded and first ruled the Cirebon Sultanate, and his son Maulana Hasanudin became the first sultan of Banten. Some of these family ties are well documented, others less so.
