Sources agree that the nine helped spread Islam on Java, though not that they introduced it, and the extent of their influence is hard to measure. Their methods are remembered through the arts: Sunan Bonang and Sunan Drajat composed for the gamelan, Sunan Kalijaga used wayang kulit shadow puppets and gamelan music to teach, and Sunan Kudus may have originated wayang golek puppetry. Their graves, called pundhen in Javanese, are venerated as places of ziarah, local pilgrimage, and many Javanese families and public figures claim descent from them.
wallia: Wallia was elected king of the Visigoths in 415, after the assassinations of Athaulf and Sigeric. Athaulf, who had married Galla Placidia in 414, was murdered by followers who believed him a puppet of Roman interests. Sigeric ignored Visigothic rights of procedure for military leadership and seemed likewise to acquiesce to the Romans, and he died seven days after taking power. Wallia was chosen because the Visigoths were convinced he would end any peace negotiations with Rome. At the time the main antagonist of the Goths was Constantius, the magister militum of Emperor Honorius.

Like his predecessor Alaric, Wallia tried to take his forces to northern Africa but foundered in the Sea of Gibraltar, a failure that led him to sue for peace. He accepted a treaty offered by Honorius. The writer Orosius reported that the terms agreed in 416 and 418 were very favourable to the Romans and included the return of Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. The historian Michael Kulikowski described her recovery by Constantius as a route into the imperial family.

As Roman federates, Wallia's Goths marched against the Alans and Vandals in Baetica and Lusitania, at the behest of Constantius. Between 417 and 418 they inflicted considerable defeats on both and killed the Alan ruler Addax. Hydatius recorded that Wallia, in the name of Rome, inflicted a vast slaughter on the barbarians in Spain. Constantius then recalled the Goths, perhaps, as the historian Randers-Pehrson suggests, out of fear at their success, and settled them in southern Gaul, in the Garonne valley from Toulouse to Bordeaux and along the Atlantic coast from Les Landes to the Loire.

Wallia died before he was able to leave Spain, and Theodoric I succeeded him. His daughter was the mother of Ricimer and the mother-in-law of Gundowech, King of the Burgundians. He is sometimes assumed to have been the historical model for Walter of Aquitaine, a figure of legend.
wallis-island: Wallis, called ʻUvea in Wallisian, is a Polynesian island and atoll in the Pacific Ocean belonging to the French overseas collectivity of Wallis and Futuna. It lies north of Tonga, northeast of Fiji and west of Samoa, and is of volcanic origin, with fertile soil that allows subsistence farming. Its highest point is Mount Lulu Fakahega, 131 metres. Several crater lakes, among them Lalolalo, are almost perfect circles with straight vertical walls.

Together with some fifteen smaller islands on a large barrier reef, Wallis forms the Wallis archipelago, 240 kilometres northeast of Futuna and Alofi. The climate is hot and humid, with an average temperature around 26 °C and a rainy season from November to April, which is also the season of tropical cyclones. The island is divided into three districts: Hihifo in the north, Hahake and Muʻa in the south.

Archaeological excavations have identified sites on Wallis dating from about 1400. The island was part of the Tongan maritime empire, but the influence of the Tuʻi Tonga declined until ʻUvea became important in itself. Several high-ranking Tongan titles, such as Halaevalu, trace their descent from ʻUvea, and the large canoe Lomipeau, according to legend, was built there as a gift to the Tuʻi Tonga. The fortress of Talietumu, near Lotoalahi in Muʻa, was the last holdout of the Tongans until they were defeated.

The island was named after Captain Samuel Wallis, who saw it on 16 August 1767 from HMS Dolphin, after he had found Tahiti. In 1835 armed missionaries from Tonga attacked, trying to convert the island to Protestantism by force. In October 1837 Jean-Baptiste Pompallier visited and left a priest and a brother, and four years later Wallis was reported to be a Catholic community. On 5 April 1842 its authorities requested French protection, and a protectorate treaty was signed in April 1887.

In 1942 the island's administration, pro-Vichy until then, was deposed on 26 May by a Free French corvette from New Caledonia, and US Marine Corps units landed on 29 May. After a referendum in 1959, Wallis became a French overseas territory in 1961. The population was 8,333 in 2018, about 72 per cent of the territory, and most people speak ʻUvean as their mother tongue. Almost all are Roman Catholic, and the chief church is the Cathedral of Mata Utu, the capital.
wallonia: Wallonia is one of the three regions of Belgium, with Flanders and Brussels. It is landlocked, covers 16,901 square kilometres, 55 per cent of the country's area, and holds about 31 per cent of its people. Most of its major cities and two thirds of its population lie in the east to west valley of the Sambre and Meuse, the former industrial backbone of Belgium. To the north of the valley lies the fertile Central Belgian Plateau, and the south and south-east form the forested highlands of the Ardennes. Its largest city is Charleroi and its capital is Namur.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul in 57 BCE, and the Low Countries became part of the province of Gallia Belgica. Its people were Celtic with a Germanic influence that was stronger in the north. They became Gallo-Romans, whom their Germanic neighbours called Walha, and they gave up their Celtic dialects for Vulgar Latin. The Sambre and Meuse valley was already an important industrial area in the Roman Empire.

In the Middle Ages the region was a centre of brass and bronze working, with Huy, Dinant and Chimay as important towns, and Mosan art, a regional Romanesque style, flourished in the Meuse valley in the 11th to 13th centuries. In the 12th and 13th centuries the iron masters of Liège developed a way of refining iron ore with a blast furnace, called the Walloon Method.

Wallonia was the first fully industrialised area in continental Europe, in the 19th century, and was second only to the United Kingdom in industrialisation. The coal and iron valley from Liège to Charleroi became known as the sillon industriel. Strikes and general strikes took place there, among them the Walloon jacquerie of 1886 and the general strikes of 1893, 1902 and 1913, the last for universal suffrage. After the Second World War a general strike of 1950 was directed against Leopold III and the winter general strike of 1960 to 1961 demanded autonomy for Wallonia.

Belgium is a federal state, and the Walloon Region is governed by the Parliament of Wallonia and the Government of Wallonia. The first regional council sat on 15 October 1980, and a directly elected parliament was created in June 1995. French is the official language, and German also in the eastern cantons annexed from the German Empire at the end of the First World War. Traditional regional Romance languages such as Walloon and Picard are in decline. In 1995 Walloon Brabant became the youngest of its five provinces.
walloon-brabant: Walloon Brabant lies in Belgium's French-speaking region of Wallonia and borders Flemish Brabant to the north and the provinces of Liège, Namur and Hainaut. It covers 1,097 square kilometres and has about 414,000 inhabitants. Its capital is Wavre, although the municipality of Braine-l'Alleud is slightly more populous. Its only administrative district, the arrondissement of Nivelles, has 27 municipalities. The word Walloon descends from an old West Germanic word meaning foreigner or speaker of Celtic or Latin, and Brabant comes from Old Dutch words meaning fallow district.

The names Walloon and Brabant are much older than the political entity. In 1628 Louis de Haynin described Belgium as divided into two roughly equal regions, Walloon and Flemish, according to whether people spoke French or a Low German that foreigners called Flemish. He contrasted Lothier, or Walloon Brabant, with the larger German or Flemish part of Brabant, which then stretched into what is now the Netherlands.

The Battle of Waterloo took place in this province in June 1815. The province itself was created in 1995 when the former province of Brabant was split into three parts: Walloon Brabant, Flemish Brabant and the Brussels Capital Region, which belongs to no province. The split accommodated the federalisation of Belgium into the three regions of Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels.

Nivelles is the most important town and has the Collegiate Church of Saint Gertrude with its westwork. The towns include Waterloo, Wavre and Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve, where the University of Louvain (UCLouvain) is located, alongside a science park of 231 hectares with life sciences, fine chemistry, information technology and engineering. Industrial steel production at Clabecq continues, and the Ronquières inclined plane on the Brussels-Charleroi Canal links canal traffic between Charleroi and Brussels. Many residents work in neighbouring Brussels. The Piétrain breed of pig takes its name from a village in Jodoigne. The castle of Corroy-le-Château is among the best-preserved castles of its period in northern Europe.
walloons: The term Walloon derives from the Proto-Germanic *walha, used for Celtic and Latin speakers. Its oldest written trace is in Jean de Haynin's memoirs of 1465, where it refers to the Roman populations of the Burgundian Netherlands. From the 16th century to the Belgian revolution the terms provinces wallonnes and pays wallon named a territory, and at Belgian independence the word came to mean Belgians who spoke a Romance language such as French, Walloon or Picard. The area now called Wallonia was settled by Celtic tribes and later by Roman and Frankish settlers, and from the early Middle Ages to the early modern period it was divided among many city-states and external powers.

Walloons are historically credited with pioneering the Industrial Revolution on the Continent in the early 19th century, and the Walloon region, a major coal and steel area, became the economic centre of Belgium. Between the 1930s and the 1970s the decline of steel and coal shifted the balance towards Flanders.

The Walloon Movement began at the end of the 19th century to assert the identity of Walloons as French speakers, and the concept of Wallonia as their heartland was invented in 1886. The Walloon language, widespread until the Second World War, has been dying out, in part because the public schools prohibited it in favour of French. The heartland of Walloon culture is the Meuse and Sambre valleys, with Charleroi, Dinant, Namur, Huy, Verviers and Liège.

Walloons are primarily Roman Catholic, with a historical Protestant minority dating from the Reformation. Walloon migrants settled widely. From the 11th century the Meuse towns of Dinant, Huy and Liège traded with Germany, where Wallengassen, Walloons' quarters, were founded; in Cologne they were the most important foreign community. Walloons settled in Wrocław in Poland probably from the 12th century, and numerous Walloons took part in the German colonisation of Transylvania in the 13th century.

From the 1620s Walloon miners and ironworkers, led by the entrepreneur Louis de Geer, came to Sweden, and later to Finland. Between 5,000 and 7,500 emigrants described as Brabantines and Hesbignons went to Wisconsin from 1852 to 1856.
walls-of-constantinople: Byzantium, according to tradition, was founded by Greek colonists from Megara led by Byzas around 658 BCE, and it was enclosed by a small wall of twenty-seven towers. The researcher Raymond Janin thinks the wall known from late sources reflects the city as rebuilt by the Spartan general Pausanias after 479 BCE. Tombstones were used to repair it in 340 BCE against an attack by Philip II of Macedon.

Constantine the Great rebuilt the city from 324 to 336 and inaugurated it on 11 May 330 as New Rome. His wall, a single line reinforced with towers, ran about 2.8 kilometres west of the earlier Severan wall. It was begun in 324 and completed under his son Constantius II (r. 337-361). By the early 5th century the city had already spread beyond it.

The Theodosian walls lie about 2 kilometres west of the Constantinian wall and take their name from Emperor Theodosius II (r. 402-450). The work was done in two phases, the first under Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East, and a law in the Codex Theodosianus shows it finished in 413. An inscription found in 1993 records nine years of work, which suggests that building began around 404 or 405.

Earthquakes on 25 September 437 and 6 November 447 damaged the walls, the second destroying 57 towers. With Attila the Hun in the Balkans, Theodosius II had them restored in 60 days, using the chariot-racing factions as labour. Most scholars date the outer wall and the wide moat to this repair, though the outer wall may have been part of the original plan.

The Blachernae walls join the Theodosian line to the sea wall at the Golden Horn. They are 12 to 15 metres high and thicker than the Theodosian walls. The Golden Horn wall ran 5,600 metres, and the Propontis wall almost 8,460 metres, with thirteen gates and 188 towers.

The garrison was small: the imperial guards and the city watch under the urban prefect. Threats were met by the field armies in the provinces, and in emergencies such as the earthquake of 447 the guilds and hippodrome factions were conscripted. The walls saved the city during sieges by the Avar-Sassanian coalition, Arabs, Rus' and Bulgars, among others.

Further defences stood beyond the city, including the 56-kilometre Anastasian Wall, built in the mid-5th century about 65 kilometres to the west and abandoned in the 7th. Before the last Ottoman assault, Sultan Mehmed II built Rumelihisarı on the Bosphorus in just over four months in 1452. Restoration began in the 1980s with UNESCO support, but it was criticised, and the World Monuments Fund placed the walls on its 2008 Watch List.
walrad-prince-of-nassau-usingen: Walrad was born at Roermond on 25 February 1635, the youngest son of Count William Louis of Nassau-Saarbrücken and Anna Amalia of Baden-Durlach, a daughter of Margrave George Frederick of Baden-Durlach. On 31 March 1659 the three brothers divided their father's lands: John Louis received Ottweiler, Gustav Adolph kept Saarbrücken and Walrad took Usingen, founding a new branch of the House of Nassau.

Walrad spent most of his career in the Dutch States Army under William III of Orange, and at different times was field marshal of both the Holy Roman Empire and the United Provinces. In 1664 he reached Szentgotthárd too late for the Battle of Saint Gotthard, but in 1683 he fought in the battle that lifted the Ottoman siege of Vienna, for which King John III Sobieski of Poland gave him the Order of the White Eagle.

In the War of the Palatine Succession he fought at Fleurus on 1 July 1690 and at Steenkerke on 3 August 1692, and he commanded the allied left wing at the Battle of Landen in 1693. In the War of the Spanish Succession he was charged with enforcing the imperial ban on Elector Joseph Clemens of Cologne, who had sided with France, and in 1702 commanded the allied troops at the Siege of Kaiserswerth.

Usingen, in the Taunus, gained in standing as the seat of the new line. Between 1660 and 1663 Walrad replaced its old castle with a new palace. After a fire destroyed much of the town in 1692 he rebuilt the upper town on a plan of symmetrical streets that still shapes it, with representative buildings along the high street. To repopulate a district left thin by the Thirty Years' War he welcomed Huguenot refugees from France and granted them freedom of religion; the Huguenot Church in Usingen recalls them.

He died at Usingen on 17 October 1702 and was succeeded by his son William Henry, one of three surviving children of his first marriage to Catherine Françoise de Croÿ-Roeulx. The town erected a monument to him in the palace gardens in 1905.
walram-ii-count-of-nassau: Walram was the second son of Count Henry II of Nassau and Matilda of Guelders and Zutphen, youngest daughter of Count Otto I of Guelders and Zutphen and Richardis of Bavaria, herself a daughter of Otto I Wittelsbach, Duke of Bavaria. He first appears in a charter of 20 July 1245. Before 1250 he married Adelheid of Katzenelnbogen, daughter of Count Diether IV of Katzenelnbogen.

Walram and his brother Otto I succeeded their father before 1251, and in that year received town privileges for Herborn from the German King William. The division of 16 December 1255, known today as the Prima divisio, gave Walram the lordships of Wiesbaden and Idstein and the districts of Weilburg and Bleidenstadt. Nassau Castle, Laurenburg Castle, the Esterau, shared with the counts of Diez, the fiefs in Hesse and several other districts stayed in joint ownership.

Perhaps soon after the treaty Walram challenged some of its terms. He suffered from a mental illness, and whether it already influenced him then is unknown; what is certain is that in an attack of insanity he burned his copy of the treaty. He served King Rudolf I of Germany as Hofmarschall and Geheimrat. He lost several towns, among them Niederlahnstein, Pfaffenhofen and Vallendar, to the Archbishop of Trier, and he carried on the Dernbacher Feud against Hesse.

Walram died, allegedly in mental derangement, on 24 January 1276, and his son Adolf succeeded him as count; Adolf was King of Germany from 1292 to 1298 and died at Göllheim. Another son, Diether, was Archbishop of Trier from 1300 to 1307. His widow Adelheid became a Clarissan nun, living in Wiesbaden in summer and Mainz in winter, and was buried in the St. Clara monastery in Mainz, where their daughter Richardis was also a nun.
walter-bagehot: Walter Bagehot was born in Langport, Somerset, on 3 February 1826. His father, Thomas Watson Bagehot, was managing director and vice-chairman of Stuckey's Bank. He studied mathematics at University College London and in 1848 earned a master's degree in moral philosophy. Called to the Bar by Lincoln's Inn, he preferred to join his father in 1852 in the family's shipping and banking business. In 1858 he married Elizabeth Wilson, whose father, James Wilson, was the founder and owner of The Economist; the couple had no children.

In 1855 Bagehot founded the National Review with his friend Richard Holt Hutton, and in 1861 he became editor-in-chief of The Economist. During his 16 years as editor he expanded its reporting of politics and increased its influence among policy-makers. He was widely accepted by the British establishment and was elected to the Athenaeum in 1875.

The English Constitution (1867) explores the constitution of the United Kingdom, in particular its Parliament and monarchy. It appeared as Parliament enacted the Reform Act 1867, so Bagehot wrote an extended introduction for the second edition of 1872. In Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market (1873) he sought to explain the world of finance and banking; Bagehot's dictum holds that in a crisis central banks should lend freely to solvent institutions, but only against sound collateral and at interest rates high enough to deter borrowers not genuinely in need.

In Physics and Politics (1872) he examined how civilisations sustain themselves, arguing that in their earliest phase they are sustained by conformism and military success, and that once secure they can mature into systems allowing greater diversity and freedom. His view rested on a distinction between the accomplished man and the rude man, which he thought the result of inheritance through the generations, and he used the same reasoning to develop a form of pseudoscientific racism. He cited John Lubbock and Edward Tylor, though neither accepted innate hereditary differences, and Tylor rejected his emphasis on physical heredity.

Bagehot never fully recovered from a bout of pneumonia in 1867 and died on 24 March 1877 from complications of what was said to be a cold. Collections of his literary, political and economic essays were published after his death, on subjects from Shakespeare and Disraeli to the price of silver. His collected works were issued in 15 volumes by The Economist between 1965 and 1986. The minor planet 2901 Bagehot is named in his honour.
walter-burley-griffin: Walter Burley Griffin was born on 24 November 1876 in Maywood, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, the eldest of four children. He completed a degree in architecture at the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign in 1899, also taking courses in horticulture and forestry. In Chicago he worked for progressive architects in the Prairie School style, then from 1901 for Frank Lloyd Wright, overseeing the construction of several of Wright's houses. The two quarrelled after Wright's trip to Japan in 1905, and Griffin set up his own practice in 1906. On 29 June 1911 he married Marion Lucy Mahony, an architect who had worked in Wright's office.

In April 1911 the Australian Commonwealth Government held an international competition for its new federal capital. On 23 May 1912 Griffin's design, with renderings by his wife, was chosen from 137 entries. He went to Australia in 1913 and became Federal Capital Director of Design and Construction. The First World War forced cuts to his plans, funds were short, and he struggled with political and bureaucratic opposition. A Royal Commission in 1917 found that officials had supplied him with false data. He resigned in December 1920, and the only permanent structure of his design built in Canberra was the grave of General Bridges.

The Griffins also designed the New South Wales towns of Leeton and Griffith, Newman College at the University of Melbourne and the Capitol Theatre in Melbourne, which opened in 1924. From 1919 they developed the Sydney suburb of Castlecrag, with small flat-roofed houses set in native bushland. Griffin also devised a modular concrete system called Knitlock. In the 1930s he designed incinerators, twelve between 1930 and 1938.

Through contacts in the anthroposophy movement Griffin won a commission in 1935 to design the library of the University of Lucknow in India, and he then received more than 40 further commissions there. He died of peritonitis in early 1937, five days after gall bladder surgery, and was buried in Lucknow. Marion Mahony Griffin completed the Pioneer Building he had been working on.

Griffin was largely under-appreciated in Australia during his lifetime. In 1964, when Canberra's central lake was filled as he had intended, Prime Minister Robert Menzies named it Lake Burley Griffin. In 1988 the Royal Australian Institute of Architects named its national Civic Design Award after him.
walter-devereux-1st-earl-of-essex: He was born at Carmarthen Castle in Wales, the eldest son of Sir Richard Devereux, who died in 1547 in the lifetime of his own father, the 1st Viscount Hereford, and of Lady Dorothy Hastings, daughter of the 1st Earl of Huntingdon. Through his father's line he was related to the Bourchier family, earlier holders of the earldom of Essex. In 1561 or 1562 he married Lettice Knollys, daughter of Sir Francis Knollys and Catherine Carey; their children included Robert, Penelope, Dorothy and Sir Walter Devereux, who was killed at the siege of Rouen in 1591.

On his grandfather's death on 27 September 1558 he became 2nd Viscount Hereford. He shared the custody of Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1568, became Lord Lieutenant of Staffordshire in 1569 and served as high marshal of the field against the Northern Rebellion that year. He was created Earl of Essex on 4 May 1572 and made a Knight of the Garter on 17 June. He then offered to subdue or colonise part of Ulster at his own cost, and in August 1573 sailed from Liverpool with about 1,200 men.

A storm scattered his fleet, and wintering at Belfast his force shrank through sickness, famine and desertion to little more than 200 men. Quarrelling with the deputy Fitzwilliam and with the Queen, he turned to raids and massacres among the O'Neills. In October 1574 he seized Sir Brian MacPhelim O'Neill at a feast in Belfast Castle, killed his attendants and had him, his wife and his brother executed in Dublin. Ordered to break off the enterprise, he used the discretion left to him to defeat Sir Turlough Luineach O'Neill, and his men massacred several hundred of Sorley Boy MacDonnell's followers, chiefly women and children, hiding in the caves of Rathlin Island.

He returned to England at the end of 1575 but accepted the post of Earl Marshal of Ireland and reached Dublin in September 1576. Taken ill at a banquet at Dublin Castle, he died on 22 September 1576, probably of dysentery. Rumour said he had been poisoned at the behest of the 1st Earl of Leicester, who married his widow two years later, but a post-mortem found natural causes. His son Robert succeeded him.
walter-gropius: Walter Adolph Georg Gropius was born in Berlin on 18 May 1883, the third child of Walter Adolph Gropius and Manon Auguste Pauline Scharnweber. His great-uncle Martin Gropius designed the Kunstgewerbemuseum in Berlin as a follower of Karl Friedrich Schinkel. After studying architecture in Munich and Berlin for four semesters, he joined the office of Peter Behrens in 1908, where his colleagues included Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier.

In 1910 he set up a practice in Berlin with Adolf Meyer. The glass curtain walls of their Faguswerk shoe-last factory at Alfeld-an-der-Leine became a founding monument of European modernism. In 1914 he was drafted and served on the Western front, was wounded, and received the Iron Cross twice.

In 1919 Gropius became master of the Grand-Ducal Saxon School of Arts and Crafts in Weimar, on the recommendation of Henry van de Velde, and transformed it into the Bauhaus. The faculty included Paul Klee, Johannes Itten, Josef Albers, László Moholy-Nagy and Wassily Kandinsky. The school aimed to extend beauty and quality to every home through well-designed industrial objects.

Its first major commission, the Sommerfeld House of 1921, was designed with Meyer. Facing political and financial difficulties, Gropius and the Bauhaus moved to Dessau in 1925, where he designed the school building, the Master Houses and the Törten housing estate. He left the Bauhaus in 1928, and Hannes Meyer took over.

In 1934 Gropius left Nazi Germany with the help of Maxwell Fry, on the pretext of a visit to Italy, and lived in London with the Isokon group. He moved to the United States in February 1937 and taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, where he chaired the Department of Architecture from 1938 until 1952. With Marcel Breuer he designed projects such as the Aluminum City Terrace housing in Pennsylvania, and in 1938 he built his own house in Lincoln, Massachusetts. In 1945 he became senior partner of The Architects Collaborative, and in 1959 he won the AIA Gold Medal.

Gropius died in Boston on 5 July 1969, aged 86, after an operation in June. His widow, Ise Gropius, gave the Gropius House in Lincoln to Historic New England in 1980, and it is now a house museum. In 1996 the Bauhaus Building and the Master Houses in Dessau were added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Berlin district of Gropiusstadt is named after him. The Gropius-Bau in Berlin, by contrast, is named for his great-uncle Martin.
walter-lini: Walter Hadye Lin̄i was born at Agatoa village on Pentecost Island. He went to the Australian Missionary Sunday School at Lamalanga, Nazareth School at Agatoa and Vureas School on Aoba, then worked in the Anglican diocesan office at Lolowai before training for the priesthood at St Peter's College in Siota, in the Solomon Islands, and St John's College, Auckland. As a deacon in the Solomon Islands he helped found the forerunner of the football club Real Kakamora and started a newspaper, The Kakamora Reporter.

Back home, with Donald Kalpokas and John Bani, he formed the New Hebrides Cultural Association and its paper, New Hebrides Viewpoint, at a time when the islands were a condominium ruled by the United Kingdom and France. They then founded the New Hebrides National Party, which elected him its full-time president in 1974. In May 1974 he asked the United Nations Committee of 24 on decolonisation for independence by 1977.

He led the party's change of name to the Vanua'aku Pati. After it boycotted the 1977 elections he headed the Vanuaaku People's Provisional Government, and in December 1978 he joined the government of national unity as minister for social affairs. He became Chief Minister after the party won the 1979 election and Prime Minister at independence on 30 July 1980, winning again in 1983 and 1987. His government's ties with the Eastern Bloc and Libya and its opposition to nuclear testing in the region drew criticism in the West. A leading advocate of Melanesian socialism, he kept Vanuatu in the Non-Aligned Movement and backed the Kanak independence movement in New Caledonia and self-determination for East Timor.

He suffered a stroke in 1987 but stayed active in politics. In 1988 President Ati George Sokomanu tried without success to remove him. Factional strife in his party ended his term in 1991, and he joined the National United Party, which he led at his death, later serving as deputy prime minister and minister of justice and of the interior. He died of an illness in Port Vila on 21 February 1999. His sister Hilda Lin̄i and brother Ham Lin̄i also became politicians.
walter-nash: Nash was born on 12 February 1882 in Kidderminster, Worcestershire, into a poor family with an alcoholic father, and won a scholarship to King Charles I Grammar School that the family could not afford to take up. He worked as a clerk and kept a shop after marrying Lottie May Eaton in 1906, but illness, the death of a daughter at birth and a recession led the family to leave for New Zealand, where he arrived in Wellington in 1909.

There his Christian faith merged with socialism, and through friends such as Michael Joseph Savage, Bob Semple and Harry Holland he became a Christian socialist and a pacifist. During the First World War his open pacifism led police to scrutinise his mail for evidence of sedition.

Nash helped found the New Plymouth branch of the Labour Party in 1918, was fined in 1921 for importing seditious literature after a tour of European socialist conferences, and became the party's national secretary in 1922. He won the Hutt seat at a by-election in 1929 and held it for 13 consecutive terms, over 38 years. As minister of finance he reintroduced a graduated land tax, oversaw the nationalisation of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and negotiated trade terms in England and in Berlin and Moscow, holding the post for 14 years, through the whole of the Second World War.

Elected leader after Peter Fraser's death, he was ridiculed for saying of the 1951 waterfront dispute, "We are not for the waterside workers, and we are not against them." As prime minister he also took foreign affairs and Māori affairs. The Black Budget, presented by Arnold Nordmeyer, angered the public, though economists praised its financial discipline.

Nash resisted calls to retire, partly to keep Nordmeyer from succeeding him, and stepped down as leader only in February 1963, the first Labour leader not to die in office. He died on 4 June 1968, aged 86 and still a member of Parliament. His state funeral, the first since Fraser's in 1950, was the first in New Zealand to be televised. He had been made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1965, but twice declined a life peerage.
walter-raleigh: Raleigh was born into a landed gentry family of Protestant faith at Hayes Barton, in East Devon, the youngest of five sons of Walter Raleigh of Fardel Manor. His mother, Katherine Champernowne, was the third wife of his father. His half-brothers included Humphrey Gilbert and Adrian Gilbert, and through the Champernowne connection the Raleigh and Gilbert brothers all became prominent under Elizabeth I and James I. Little is known of his early life, though in his late teens he spent some time in France taking part in the religious civil wars.

From 1579 to late 1580 Raleigh took part in suppressing the Desmond Rebellions in Ireland and was present at the siege of Smerwick. In 1585 he received 40,000 acres in the Munster Plantation, including Youghal, where he was mayor in 1588 and 1589. A royal charter of 25 March 1584 authorised him to explore and colonise lands not held by any Christian prince, and the region reached by the first expedition was named Virginia for Elizabeth. He was knighted in 1585. In 1591 he secretly married Elizabeth Throckmorton, one of the queen's ladies-in-waiting, and the couple were imprisoned in the Tower of London in 1592.

Raleigh heard of a city of gold in South America and explored what is now Guyana and eastern Venezuela in search of Lake Parime and Manoa. His Discovery of Guiana, published in 1596, made exaggerated claims and contributed to the El Dorado legend. He took part in the capture of Cádiz in 1596 and in the Islands Voyage of 1597, and from 1600 to 1603 as governor of Jersey he modernised its defences, including the building of Elizabeth Castle.

Arrested on 19 July 1603 for involvement in the Main Plot against James I, Raleigh defended himself at his trial at Winchester. The chief evidence was the sworn confession of Henry Brooke, 11th Baron Cobham, whom the tribunal refused to call as a witness. He was convicted, but the king spared his life. Pardoned in 1617, he led a second expedition to Venezuela, during which men under Lawrence Kemys attacked the Spanish outpost of Santo Tomé de Guayana, and his son Walter was killed. On his return the Spanish ambassador demanded that the sentence be reinstated, and Raleigh was beheaded at the Old Palace Yard on 29 October 1618. His poetry, in the plain style, includes The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd.
walter-reed: Walter Reed was born on the outskirts of Gloucester, Virginia, the fifth child of Lemuel Sutton Reed, a travelling Methodist minister, and his first wife, Pharaba White. He enrolled at the University of Virginia and completed his M.D. in 1869, two months before he turned eighteen, the youngest person ever to receive that degree there. He took a second M.D. at the Bellevue Hospital Medical College in New York in 1870, interned at several New York hospitals and worked for the New York Board of Health until 1875. That year he passed a thirty-hour examination and joined the U.S. Army Medical Corps as an assistant surgeon.

For the next sixteen years the army posted Reed to outposts in the American West, where he cared for soldiers, their dependents and several Native American tribes, at one point several hundred Apaches, among them Geronimo. In 1893 he joined the faculty of George Washington University and the newly opened Army Medical School in Washington, where he held the professorship of bacteriology and clinical microscopy and became curator of the Army Medical Museum. In 1896 he showed that yellow fever among soldiers stationed near the Potomac did not come from the river water: the men who fell ill had taken trails through swampy woods at night. In 1898 he chaired a panel that found flies spreading an epidemic of typhoid fever in army camps.

In May 1900 Major Reed went to Cuba to head a board that the Surgeon General, George Miller Sternberg, had charged with studying yellow fever. Under his leadership the U.S. Army Yellow Fever Commission showed that mosquitoes transmit the disease and disproved the belief that it passed by clothing and bedding soiled by victims. Experiments at Camp Lazear, named in November 1900 for his assistant Jesse William Lazear, who died of yellow fever during the work, used human volunteers, among them medical personnel, who let themselves be bitten by infected mosquitoes.

Reed himself credited the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay with identifying the mosquito as the vector, and he often cited him. Mosquito eradication then largely stemmed yellow fever in Panama during the building of the Panama Canal, under William C. Gorgas. Reed received honorary degrees from Harvard and the University of Michigan. In 1902 he suffered a ruptured appendix and died on 23 November of peritonitis, aged 51, and he was buried in Arlington National Cemetery. The Walter Reed General Hospital in Washington opened in 1909, and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research is the successor to the Army Medical School.
walter-rodney: Walter Anthony Rodney was born on 23 March 1942 into a working-class family in Georgetown, Guyana. He attended the University College of the West Indies from 1960 and took a first-class honours degree in history in 1963. In 1966, at 24, he earned a PhD in African History at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. His dissertation on the slave trade on the Upper Guinea Coast was published by Oxford University Press in 1970 as A History of the Upper Guinea Coast 1545–1800 and was acclaimed for its originality in challenging the conventional view.

He taught at the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania in 1966–67 and from 1969 to 1974, and in 1968 at the University of the West Indies at Mona, Jamaica. He argued that Africa could break from imperialism only under the banner of socialism and the leadership of the working classes. On 15 October 1968 the government of Prime Minister Hugh Shearer of Jamaica declared him persona non grata and the university dismissed him. Protests by students and the poor of West Kingston escalated into the Rodney riots, which began on 16 October and left six dead and heavy damage.

Back in Dar es Salaam he rose to associate professor in 1973, supported Julius Nyerere’s socialist government and spoke to villagers in Kiswahili. How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) described how Africa had been exploited by European imperialists, which he argued led directly to the modern underdevelopment of most of the continent. It became influential and controversial.

In 1974 Rodney returned to Guyana, but the government of Forbes Burnham rescinded the promised professorship at the University of Guyana. He joined the Working People’s Alliance, which sought to replace ethnic politics with class solidarity. In 1979 he was arrested and charged with arson after two government offices burned; the charges were dropped for lack of evidence.

On 13 June 1980 he was killed in Georgetown, aged 38, by an explosive device in his car. His brother Donald, injured in the blast, said a Guyana Defence Force sergeant, Gregory Smith, had given Walter the device. A Commission of Inquiry concluded that it was a state-ordered killing and that Burnham must have known of the plot. Donald, convicted in 1982 of possessing explosives, was exonerated on appeal on 14 April 2021.

Guyana awarded Rodney its Order of Excellence in 1993 and set up a Walter Rodney Chair in History. The American Historical Association gave him the Albert J. Beveridge Award in 1982 for A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905.
walter-v-of-brienne: Walter was the only son of Hugh of Brienne, who held the county of Brienne in France and the counties of Lecce and Conversano in southern Italy, and of Isabella de la Roche, younger daughter of Duke Guy I of Athens, who brought estates in the Peloponnese. The historian Guy Perry calls him a child of the War of the Sicilian Vespers.

After his father, a commander of King Charles II of Naples, was captured at the Battle of the Counts on 23 June 1287, Walter was handed to the Aragonese admiral Roger of Lauria as a hostage for the ransom and held for years in the fortress of Augusta in Sicily, where he probably learnt Catalan.

His father fell fighting Lauria at Brindisi in the summer of 1296, and Walter, once released, was invested with Brienne before May 1297. To avenge his father he and two French nobles hired 300 horsemen, the Knights of Death, and joined the invasion of Sicily led by Robert, Duke of Calabria. Lured by a false report that the castellan of Gagliano Castelferrato would surrender, he refused to withdraw and was captured. He was freed after the Treaty of Caltabellotta of 1302, returned to France and married Joanna of Châtillon, daughter of the constable of France.

When Guy II of Athens died without heirs on 5 October 1308, the High Court of Achaea preferred Walter's claim over that of his cousin Eschiva of Ibelin, ruling that among relatives of equal degree the male came first. He landed at Glarentza in the summer of 1309. John II Doukas of Thessaly, backed by Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos and Anna Palaiologina Kantakouzene of Epirus, had thrown off Athenian overlordship, and Walter hired the Catalan Company and its Turkish allies, who forced John to sue for peace after six months.

Walter still owed the mercenaries four months' pay. He kept 200 horsemen and 300 almogàvars, ordered the rest to leave and threatened death for disobedience, and the whole company rose against him. On 15 March 1311, on the marshy plain of Halmyros, the Catalans, though ready to make peace, destroyed his army; a Turkish soldier cut off his head. His son Walter VI of Brienne tried in vain to recover the duchy and in 1348 buried the head at Lecce.
walter-vi-of-brienne: Walter was the son of Walter V of Brienne and Joanna of Châtillon, daughter of the constable of King Philip IV of France, and heir to lands all around the Mediterranean. When his father died at the Battle of Halmyros on 15 March 1311 he became count of Brienne, Lecce and Conversano, but of the Duchy of Athens only Argos and Nauplia remained. In December 1325 he married Beatrice, niece of King Robert of Naples, and served for a few months as vicar in Florence for Robert's son Charles, Duke of Calabria.

In June 1330 Pope John XXII issued a crusading bull for Walter against the Catalans, and he sailed from Brindisi in August 1331. He forced the County of Cephalonia and Zakynthos and the Despotate of Epirus to recognise King Robert's overlordship and seized Leucas and Vonitsa for himself, but in Boeotia the Catalans avoided battle behind the walls of Thebes and Athens. Without the troops or money for a long war, and finding no support among the native Greek population, he returned to Brindisi by summer 1332, more deeply in debt.

In 1342 he was called to Florence, then in a severe economic crisis caused by English debts to its banks and by the cost of trying to obtain Lucca from Mastino della Scala. The ruling merchants meant him to rule for a limited time, but the lower classes proclaimed him signore for life. He imposed harsh measures, including the flat tax estimo and postponed repayment of forced loans, which angered the city though they eased its finances, and after ten months a conspiracy drove him out.

In 1344 he married Jeanne, daughter of Ralph III, Count of Eu; their two daughters died young. Appointed constable of France in 1356, he was killed at the Battle of Poitiers on 19 September 1356, and his titles passed to his sister Isabella and her sons, Sohier of Enghien taking the title of duke of Athens. The Duke of Athens in the seventh tale of the second day of the Decameron, written less than ten years after his rule in Florence, is probably a satirical allusion to him.
walter-von-cronberg: Walter von Cronberg came from a rather poor family of knights from Kronberg Castle near Frankfurt. He joined the Teutonic Order in 1497, was a tax collector in the Komturei of Mergentheim from 1499 and became Komtur of Frankfurt in 1504. Under Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach he served as the order's legate to King Sigismund I the Old of Poland, and in 1517 he founded the Brotherhood of St. Sebastian. In 1526 he was chosen Deutschmeister, master of the order's German branch.

When Albert converted to Lutheranism and was excommunicated, von Cronberg declared himself the next Grand Master. He based his claim on a 14th-century statute of Werner von Orseln, which provided that if the Grand Master was absent, the master of one of the other branches would take the position. Wolter von Plettenberg, master of the Livonian branch, also claimed the office. Emperor Charles V averted the conflict in 1527 by deciding in von Cronberg's favour and naming him Administrator of the Office of Grand Master.

At the same time the Grand Master's claim to Albert's Duchy of Prussia was renewed. Because no control could be exercised there, the Grand Master's seat moved from Königsberg to Mergentheim, near Würzburg, which had been the seat of the Deutschmeister in southern Germany.

From 1530 von Cronberg devoted himself to preserving the Catholic character of the order. He could not stop its further secularisation within the Holy Roman Empire, as more and more knights broke their oaths by turning Protestant or by refusing obedience to the Catholic Grand Masters. He died on 4 April 1543, having led the order from 1527, and is counted as its 38th Grand Master.
walther-von-der-vogelweide: Little is known of Walther's life. His name appears in no contemporary record except one entry in the travel accounts of Bishop Wolfger von Erla of Passau, which notes five shillings paid to Walther the singer for a fur coat. He was a knight, but probably not a wealthy or landed one, and the surname von der Vogelweide, meaning bird-pasture, seems to point to a general geographic feature rather than a specific estate. His birthplace is unknown. Some scholars have argued for the Waldviertel in Lower Austria and others for the Wipptal in South Tyrol. He learned his craft at the court of Vienna under Duke Frederick I of the house of Babenberg, from the master Reinmar von Hagenau.

Duke Frederick's death in 1198 ended the period in which Walther produced most of his love lyrics, and he became a wanderer from court to court, singing for his lodging and bread. He left the court of Duke Bernhard of Carinthia and spent three years with Dietrich I of Meissen, complaining that he received neither money nor praise. Around 1214 he received a diamond from Diether III von Katzenelnbogen.

His political poems began in 1198 with an appeal to Germany against the ambitions of the princes. He attended the coronation of Philip at Mainz that year and supported him, backed Otto of Brunswick after Philip's murder in 1208, and turned to Frederick II after the Battle of Bouvines in 1214. Frederick gave him a small fief in Franconia. He opposed the extreme claims of the popes, though his religious poems show his sincere Catholicism.

Walther seems to have settled on his fief near Würzburg about 1224, and he died about 1230. He was buried at Würzburg, and a new monument, the Lusamgärtchen, was erected over the spot in 1843. His work survives in over 30 manuscripts, far more than that of his contemporaries. The Codex Manesse holds the largest collection, 440 strophes, and only a handful of his melodies survive, among them that of the Palästinalied. In the first decade of the 13th century Gottfried von Strassburg named him the leader of the Minnesänger after Reinmar's death. He is one of the competitors in the tale of the Wartburg song contest, which appears in Richard Wagner's Tannhäuser.
waltzing-matilda: The tune goes back to Scotland. Robert Tannahill wrote a poem, Thou Bonnie Wood of Craigielea, before 1806, and his friend James Barr set it to music, published in 1818. Thomas Bulch, an English expatriate in Australia, wrote a quick march for brass band called Craigielee, most likely in 1891. Christina Macpherson, who played the tune that Paterson set his words to, based it on her memory of that march. She played by ear and had little ability to write down note lengths, so her drafts contain mistakes, though the melody she recalled can be inferred with fair accuracy.

The words arose amid a bitter labour dispute. In 1894 striking shearers burned shearing sheds in central Queensland, and on 2 September the shed at Dagworth was set alight. The same day Samuel Hoffmeister, a leader of the strikers known as Frenchy, was found dead at a camp by a billabong near Kynuna. The inquest found suicide. Some historians, among them Ross Fitzgerald, see the strike and Hoffmeister's death behind the song, while others stress Paterson's relationship with Sarah Riley.

The song tells of a swagman, an itinerant worker, who boils his billy at a bush camp near a billabong and catches a stray jumbuck, or sheep. When the squatter who owns it and three troopers come to arrest him for theft, he cries that they will never catch him alive and drowns himself in the billabong, and his ghost haunts the place. The title is slang for travelling on foot with a swag, or bundle, slung on the back; Matilda is a romantic term for the swag. Coolibah is a kind of eucalyptus that grows near billabongs.

There are no official lyrics. Harry Nathan published the first setting on 20 December 1902, changing the melody and some words. On 12 January 1903 Paterson sold the rights, with some other pieces, to Angus & Robertson for five pounds. The tea trader James Inglis bought them for five guineas and asked Marie Cowan to turn the song into a jingle for Billy Tea. Her version, published in 1903, remains the best known.

The song was first recorded in 1926 by John Collinson and Russell Callow, and by 1995 at least 500 artists had recorded it. It has never been the official anthem of Australia, but from 1976 to 1984 it was one of three national songs that could replace God Save the Queen. In the plebiscite of 1977 it took 28 percent of the vote, against 43 for Advance Australia Fair. It is the quick march of the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and the official song of the US 1st Marine Division. Waltzing Matilda Day has been marked on 6 April since 2012, and the Waltzing Matilda Centre stands in Winton.
walvis-bay: Walvis Bay lies just north of the Tropic of Capricorn in the delta of the Kuiseb River. The bay is protected by the Pelican Point sand spit and is the only natural deep-water harbour on the country's coast. Its waters are rich in plankton and marine life and draw large numbers of southern right whales, which attracted whalers and fishing vessels. The Dutch called it Walvisch Baye and the English Whale Bay, and the Herero people called it Ezorongondo. The climate is a rare mild form of cold desert, with about 13 millimetres of rain a year and high humidity.

The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão reached Cape Cross, north of the bay, in 1485, and Bartolomeu Dias anchored his flagship São Cristóvão in the bay on 8 December 1487, naming it O Golfo de Santa Maria da Conceição. The Portuguese made no formal claim. At the end of the 18th century the Dutch East India Company used it as a stopover between Cape Town and the Netherlands, but no year-round settlement was attempted and little commercial development took place until the late 19th century.

During the Scramble for Africa the British claimed the bay, and the Cape Colony completed its annexation in 1884, together with the Penguin Islands, after initial steps in 1878, while Germany annexed the surrounding land as German South West Africa. In 1910 the bay became part of the Union of South Africa as an exclave of the Cape. A boundary dispute with Germany was settled in 1911, with a confirmed area of 1,124 square kilometres. The Germans overran it early in the First World War, and South African forces ousted them in 1915.

South Africa held South West Africa under a League of Nations mandate, and in 1922 an Act placed Walvis Bay's administration under the mandated territory. In 1977 South Africa repealed it and returned control to the Cape Province, making the bay an exclave. The United Nations Security Council in Resolution 432 of 1978 called for its reintegration into Namibia. It stayed under South African sovereignty after Namibian independence in 1990. In 1992 the two countries set up a Joint Administrative Authority, and South Africa transferred sovereignty of Walvis Bay and the Penguin Islands to Namibia on 1 March 1994.

Walvis Bay is the second largest city in Namibia and its largest coastal city, with 102,704 people at the 2023 census. It lies at the end of the TransNamib Railway to Windhoek. Under South African administration it was developed as a segregated town, with Black residents in Kuisebmond, Coloured residents in Narraville and Whites in the centre. Fishing and the port form a major part of its economy, and tourists come for Dune 7, the salt works, birdlife and Bird Island.
wanderer-above-the-sea-of-fog: Caspar David Friedrich painted Wanderer above the Sea of Fog in 1818, though some sources indicate 1817. Its provenance in the 19th century is unclear. By 1939 it belonged to the gallery of Wilhelm August Luz in Berlin, and it was then apparently sold to the German lawyer Ernst Henke before returning to the Luz gallery. After passing between private collections it was acquired by the Hamburger Kunsthalle in 1970. In 1817 Friedrich had struck up a friendship with the scientist Carl Gustav Carus and the Norwegian painter Johan Christian Dahl, and in January 1818 he married Caroline Brommer.

A man in a dark green overcoat stands on a rocky precipice with his back to the viewer, gripping a walking stick in his right hand, his hair caught in the wind. Ridges and forested escarpments jut from the sea of fog in the middle ground, and faded mountains rise on the left and level into lowland plains on the right. The landscape is composed of elements of the Elbe Sandstone Mountains in Saxony and Bohemia, sketched in the field and rearranged by Friedrich in the studio. The Zirkelstein stands in the background on the right, and the rocks under the traveller are a group on the Kaiserkrone.

Friedrich used the Rückenfigur, a figure turned away from the viewer, considerably more often than other artists, and it is generally thought to invite viewers inside the painting. Helmut Börsch-Supan wrote that it is harder to imagine this landscape without a figure than in any other painting.

Some suggest the man is a self-portrait, pointing to his red hair, and the painting has been read as an emblem of self-reflection and as an evocation of the sublime. Friedrich wrote that the artist should paint not only what he has in front of him but also what he sees inside himself. He was an outspoken supporter of German liberal and nationalist feeling, and the art historian Norbert Wolf holds that the figure wears an Altdeutsch outfit, a political statement in that era; other scholars describe the clothing as a Jäger infantry uniform.

The painting and Friedrich's work were not at first regarded as masterpieces, though he was respected in German and Russian circles. His reputation improved in the 20th century, and the painting has since appeared on book covers and other objects. Robert Macfarlane calls it the archetypical image of the mountain-climbing visionary.
wang-anshi: Wang Anshi was born on 8 December 1021 in Linchuan, in present-day Jiangxi province, into a family of holders of the jinshi degree. He placed fourth in the palace examination and obtained his own jinshi degree in 1042. As a district magistrate at Yinxian he reorganised hydrological projects for irrigation and gave credits to the peasants. He observed a mourning period for his mother from 1063 to 1066 and in 1067 became governor of Jiangning. In 1058 he had sent Emperor Renzong a letter of ten thousand characters proposing administrative reforms, which went unanswered until Emperor Shenzong took the throne.

Shenzong faced declining taxes and a growing burden on commoners, since owners of large estates evaded their share. He sought Wang's advice in 1069 and made him vice counsellor, and a year later chancellor. Wang's New Policies aimed to cut government expenditure and strengthen the military in the north. They sought to relieve the peasantry and to check the monopolists of land and wealth, whom he called engrossers.

The measures included the equal tax law, a land survey meant to reveal hidden land, the green sprouts law, which lent money or seed to peasants, and the labour recruitment law, which replaced corvée labour with hired labour. The market exchange law set up bureaux to fix prices and buy surplus goods, and the baojia system organised households into security groups with police powers. A three college law reorganised the National University. Officials abused the loan scheme, and within months the government was charging 20 to 30 per cent annual interest.

The reforms divided the court into the Reformers and a Conservative faction led by Sima Guang, who argued that the elite families rather than the state should be the pillars of society. The poet Su Shi was jailed and exiled for criticising the reforms. After a famine in 1074 and the debts of farmers, Wang resigned in 1076. Shenzong died in 1085, Sima Guang returned, and the New Policies were abolished, though supporters regained power from 1093 and the policies largely continued under Emperor Huizong. Wang died on 21 May 1086.

Wang was also a major poet, writing in the shi form modelled on Du Fu, and was counted among the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song. Chinese politicians and historians have looked back on his reforms as either principled and measured or misguided and disastrous.
wang-chongyang: Wang was born Wang Zhongfu into a wealthy family that had been a prominent local clan for generations, and was educated in the Chinese classics and in martial arts. He entered the prefectural school and passed the imperial examination, and early in the Tianjuan era of Emperor Xizong of Jin, between 1138 and 1140, he came first in the military examination, after which he took the name Dewei. Despite these honours he long served only as a minor official in charge of collecting wine, then resigned and withdrew home, where he spent his days drinking.

According to tradition, in the summer of 1159 he met the immortals Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin in a tavern in Ganhe Town, near Zhongnan in Shaanxi, and they taught him the secrets of Taoist cultivation. He took the name Zhe and the Taoist name Chongyang, and dug a tomb at the edge of his village near Mount Zhongnan, which he called the Tomb of the Living Dead and marked with a plaque reading Lunatic Wang; he lived there for three years.

In 1167 he burnt his thatched hut and went east to Shandong. At Ninghai he met Ma Danyang, who built him a hut in the garden of his mansion; Wang named it the Quanzhen Hut, which gave the school its name. Ma's wife Sun Bu'er, Qiu Chuji, who arrived aged nineteen in the ninth month of 1167, Tan Chuduan, Liu Chuxuan, Wang Chuyi and Hao Datong followed. Between 1168 and 1169 he founded five congregations in Shandong, each named for the Three Teachings, since he taught the unity of Taoism, Buddhism and Confucianism.

In 1169 he set out west with Ma, Tan, Liu and Qiu and died at Daliang, now Kaifeng, on 22 January 1170. The four carried his coffin to his old home in Liujiang Village below Mount Zhongnan, the site Quanzhen revered as the Ancestral Hut, now Chongyang Palace.

His teaching joined internal alchemy, in which the practitioner's own body is the cauldron, with study of the Tao Te Ching, the Classic of Filial Piety and the Heart Sutra, good deeds, the curbing of desire and monastic life. His writings include the Fifteen Essays to Establish the Teaching and over a thousand poems. The Yuan dynasty gave him posthumous titles, and each of his seven disciples founded a lineage, among them Qiu Chuji's Longmen.
wang-dao: Wang Dao's grandfather Wang Lan and father Wang Cai were mid-level Jin officials, and from them he inherited the title Viscount of Jiqiu; he was a grandnephew of Wang Xiang. In the late reign of Emperor Hui he served on the staff of Sima Yue, Prince of Donghai, and there befriended Sima Rui, Prince of Langye. On his advice Sima Rui slipped out of Luoyang and spent most of the War of the Eight Princes safe in his principality. When Sima Rui was posted to Jianye, Wang joined his staff as chief adviser.

On Wang's counsel Sima Rui personally visited the respected local gentlemen He Xun and Gu Rong and invited them into his government, winning the trust of the south. After Luoyang fell to Han-Zhao in July 311, Wang helped settle the refugees who poured in, and he urged Sima Rui to take the throne, first as Prince of Jin in 317 and then as emperor in 318.

When his cousin Wang Dun rebelled in 322, Wang Dao and his clan begged at the palace for their lives. The official Zhou Yi interceded for him in secret, but Wang, unaware of it, stayed silent when Wang Dun asked about Zhou, who was then executed. On finding Zhou's petitions in the archives Wang said, “Although I did not kill Boren, Boren died because of me!”, words that became a Chinese idiom.

Emperor Ming made him prime minister, and in 324 Wang helped defeat Wang Dun's forces by spreading word that his cousin was dead. During the rebellion of Su Jun, who took Jiankang in early 328, Wang stayed in the capital, secretly ordered the provinces to resist, then fled to join the loyalist armies of Tao Kan and Wen Jiao. Wen declined the regency and gave it to Wang.

Wang governed largely unchallenged for his last years, though Yu Liang tried in 338 to have him removed. He died regent on 7 September 339 and was buried with honours usually reserved for emperors. His lenient rule, with few punishments, steadied the Jin regime but also allowed corruption and incompetence that made it hard for Jin armies to retake the north. Under the Southern Dynasties his line was counted with that of Xie An as the two most honoured noble houses.
wang-jian-former-shu: Wang Jian, courtesy name Guangtu, came from Wuyang, in modern Luohe in Henan. He was described as ambitious and alert in youth but also as a hoodlum, who gave up his family's craft of baking for butchering cattle, stealing donkeys and smuggling salt. Jailed at Xuchang for his misdeeds, he was released in secret by the jailers and stayed for a time with the monk Chuhong in the Wudang Mountains, who urged him to change his ways and foretold great deeds. He then joined the army of Zhongwu Circuit.

In 881, after the rebel Huang Chao took Chang'an, the eunuch general Yang Fuguang formed 8,000 Zhongwu troops into eight corps, one of them under Wang Jian. When Yang died in 883, the corps followed Lu Yanhong in pillaging the region, but in 884 Wang Jian and his friend Han Jian deserted to the eunuch Tian Lingzi at Chengdu, who adopted them as his sons. During Emperor Xizong's flight from Chang'an in 885, Wang Jian cleared the road through crowds of refugees, bore the imperial seal, and let the emperor sleep on his knees.

He later took Lang Prefecture and allied with Gu Yanlang of Dongchuan Circuit. Summoned to Chengdu in 887 and then opposed by its governor Chen Jingxuan, he made war on Xichuan Circuit, whose 12 prefectures his army is said to have pillaged. As military governor of Xichuan he was described as diligent, frugal and open to advice, but also as suspicious, so that many able subordinates were put to death. In 900 Emperor Zhaozong made him Prince of Langye.

Though illiterate, he liked the company of learned men and kept members of Tang aristocratic families at his court to pass on their knowledge. In 908 he made Lady Zhou empress, and after his adopted son Wang Zongji, a chancellor, challenged him to name an heir, he had Zongji put to death and named his second son Wang Zongyi crown prince. That year his forces joined Qi and Jin in an attack on Chang'an, but withdrew after the Later Liang defeated the Qi army. He died on 11 July 918.
wang-jian-qin: Wang Jian was born in Dongxiang, Pinyang, in Guanzhong, north-east of present-day Fuping County in Shaanxi. According to the New Book of Tang his family's original surname was Ji, and his 16th-generation ancestor in the male line was Prince Qiao, a son of King Ling of Zhou, who was reduced to commoner status for remonstrating with his father; because people still saw his family as royal, they called it the Wang, the king's family, and his descendants took that surname.

In 236 BCE Wang Jian led the Qin army that attacked Zhao and took nine cities, the start of King Ying Zheng's wars of unification. Zhao ceased to exist in 228 BCE, after Qin spies at the Zhao court had its leading general Li Mu replaced and Wang Jian captured its king. According to the Shiji, after Jing Ke's failed attempt to assassinate the king, Wang Jian conquered Jing Ke's home state of Yan in 226 BCE.

Against Chu, Wang Jian asked for 600,000 men, while the general Li Xin said 200,000 would do. The king chose Li Xin, and Wang Jian retired, pleading ill health. Li Xin's army was destroyed at the Battle of Chengfu by Chu forces under Xiang Yan and Lord Changping, and the king recalled Wang Jian with the army he had asked for. At the send-off, and several times during the campaign, he demanded lavish rewards; he later told his men that the distrustful king would think a general with such petty wants had no designs on the throne.

From 224 BCE Wang Jian kept his troops inside their fortifications, training them in secret, until after a year Chu disbanded most of its army. He then overran Huaiyang, defeated Xiang Yan at Shouchun, and Xiang Yan died at Qinan, killed in battle or by his own hand. Lord Changping was killed by Wang Jian's deputy Meng Wu, and Chu fell in 223 BCE. Letters home from two Qin soldiers, Hei Fu and Jin, asking for clothing and money, record the long campaign.

Wang Jian later retired because of old age. His son Wang Ben, himself an important general, finished the conquests against Yan, Dai and Qi, ending the Warring States period in 221 BCE. The Wang clans of Langya and Taiyuan counted Wang Jian among their ancestors, and modern Chinese folklore ranks him with Bai Qi, Lian Po and Li Mu as one of the four foremost generals of the late Warring States.
wang-jingwei: Wang Zhaoming was born in Sanshui, Guangdong, of Zhejiang origin, and passed the county-level imperial examination for the xiucai degree in 1902. In 1903 he went to study at Hosei University in Japan on a Qing government scholarship. In 1905 he met the exiled revolutionary Sun Yat-sen and joined the Tongmenghui in Tokyo. He gained attention as a polemicist for its journal People's News, notably in debates with Liang Qichao, who advocated constitutional monarchy. His pen name Wang Jingwei, adopted in 1905, came from the mythical jingwei bird that tries to fill the ocean with twigs and pebbles.

In 1910 Wang and others in a Tongmenghui cell planted a bomb meant for the regent, Prince Chun. It was discovered, and he was arrested and sentenced to life imprisonment, but was released after the Wuchang Uprising. After Sun's death in 1925 he became the first president of the Nationalist government, then controlling only Guangdong, and adhered to Sun's policy of cooperation with the Soviet Union and the Chinese Communist Party. He became Chiang Kai-shek's principal rival in the Kuomintang.

In 1927 he led the left-wing government at Wuhan against Chiang's at Nanjing, but in the July 15 Incident he followed Chiang in purging the Communists. In 1930 he joined a coalition against Chiang that was defeated in the Central Plains War. After the Mukden Incident the two reached an accommodation, and Wang served as premier while Chiang commanded the army.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War Wang at first advocated resistance while negotiating, and from 1937 held secret talks with Konoe Fumimaro. In December 1938 he left the wartime capital Chongqing for Hanoi and called for a peace settlement with Japan, for which the Kuomintang expelled him. On 30 March 1940 he became head of the Reorganized National Government at Nanjing, which nominally governed Japanese-occupied China outside Manchuria. It copied the structure of the Republic of China's government and used its blue sky and white sun flag.

In March 1944 Wang went to Japan for treatment of a wound from an assassination attempt in 1935, and he died at the Nagoya Imperial University Hospital on 10 November 1944, less than a year before Japan's surrender. A testament attributed to him, published in the 1960s, claims to record his deathbed wishes; its authenticity remains disputed. Both the Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party denounced him as hanjian, a traitor to the Chinese people. He also wrote poetry, and his poems and a literary column on the South Society have been published.
wang-mang: Wang Mang, whose courtesy name was Jujun, was born in 45 BCE, a son of Wang Man, a younger brother of Empress Wang Zhengjun. His father died young, and unlike most of his brothers Wang Mang was not made a marquess. He became known for self-discipline and for promoting capable men, which began to reverse the general view of the Wang clan as arrogant and wasteful. He held the highest post in the government, commander of the armed forces, and after Emperor Cheng died in 7 BCE he remained powerful. He later retired, and in 5 BCE Emperor Ai sent him back to his march in Xindu.

Emperor Ai died in 1 BCE without an heir. Grand Empress Dowager Wang summoned Wang Mang back and placed him in charge of the armed forces and the government. The child Emperor Ping was enthroned and Wang Mang became his regent. He moved against his enemies, demoting and exiling the relatives of Emperor Ai and the Fu and Ding families. When Emperor Ping left no heir, Wang Mang passed over the 53 adult great-grandsons of Emperor Xuan and examined the 23 great-great-grandsons, all of them children, because he wanted a ruler he could control. He seized the throne in 9 CE and founded the Xin dynasty.

Wang Mang sought to restore the golden age of the early Zhou dynasty as described in the Book of Rites. He changed the structure of government and renamed places, including Chang'an. In 9 CE he declared all land the property of the empire under the wangtian system and abolished slavery, but landowners and officials resisted and he repealed the measures in 12 CE. The Yellow River flooded in 11 CE, and famine led to prophecies that he had lost the Mandate of Heaven. From about 17 CE rebellions arose, notably those of the Lülin and the Chimei, and relations with the Xiongnu broke down. Officials left counties without magistrates for years.

In spring 23 CE a Xin army of some 430,000 men failed to crush the new Han regime under the Gengshi Emperor. Rebel armies sacked Chang'an in October of that year, and Wang Mang was killed in the fighting at the palace. The Han dynasty was restored, and his rule marks the division between the Western and Eastern Han. Traditional Chinese historiography saw him as a tyrant and usurper, while some recent historians portray him as a visionary and selfless reformer.
wang-shenzhi: Wang Shenzhi was born in 862 at Gushi in modern Henan, where an ancestor, Wang Ye, had served as county magistrate and settled the family. His father was Wang Nin and his mother a Lady Dong; his two older brothers were Wang Chao and Wang Shengui. In 881 the bandit leader Wang Xu seized Guāng Prefecture and made Wang Chao his discipline officer, and when Qin Zongquan attacked him, Wang Xu led 5,000 soldiers and the people south across the Yangtze, reaching Fujian by 885.

On the march Wang Xu ordered the old and weak abandoned and threatened to kill Lady Dong, whom the brothers kept with them; growing paranoid, he put to death officers he thought more able than himself. At Na'an Wang Chao and the forward commander ambushed and arrested him, and the army chose Wang Chao as its leader. He took Quan Prefecture and, after the governor Chen Yan died in 891, sent Wang Yanfu with Wang Shenzhi as his deputy against Fu Prefecture, which fell in summer 893.

Wang Shenzhi then served as deputy military governor. In 897 the ailing Wang Chao entrusted the circuit to him rather than to his own sons, and after Wang Chao's death Wang Shengui declined the succession, judging his younger brother more accomplished. Emperor Zhaozong of Tang confirmed Wang Shenzhi as military governor of Weiwu, later created him Prince of Langya in 904, and in 907 Wang recognised Zhu Quanzhong's new Later Liang dynasty.

As Prince of Min, Wang was said to be frugal, often wearing hemp shoes and keeping his mansion small; punishments were relaxed and taxes low. He sent yearly tribute to the Later Liang by a sea route so dangerous that losses of 40 to 50 per cent were common. In 916 he married a daughter to Qian Chuanxiang, son of Qian Liu of Wuyue, and began to issue lead coins alongside copper ones. He removed his nephew Wang Yanbin from Quan Prefecture in 920 for plotting with the Later Liang, recognised the Later Tang in 923 and repelled a Southern Han attack in 924. Falling ill in 925, he placed his eldest son Wang Yanhan in charge and died later that year.
wang-shichong: Wang Shichong was born in 567. His family descended from the Zhi clan of the Western Regions, presumably Yuezhi, and took the name Wang when his widowed grandmother remarried. Studious in military strategy and the law, he rose through the army and by 610 supervised Emperor Yang's palace at Jiangdu. In 613 he defeated and killed the rebel Liu Yuanjin south of the Yangtze, then slaughtered his men after promising to spare them if they surrendered. In 615 he marched north to relieve the emperor, besieged by the Turks at Yanmen, and was made acting governor of Jiangdu in 616.

In 617 Emperor Yang sent him to defend Luoyang against the rebel Li Mi. After the emperor was killed in 618, Wang joined the officials who proclaimed Yang Tong emperor and became one of the seven nobles who ruled in his name. When his colleagues made peace with Li Mi, Wang struck first: he killed Lu Chu, had Yuan Wendu handed over and executed, and took all power. In the autumn of 618 he defeated Li Mi at the Battle of Yanshi, and most of Li's territory submitted to Luoyang.

After taking the throne Wang created his son Wang Xuanying crown prince and nineteen relatives princes. When a plot to restore Yang Tong was uncovered, Wang Shichong had the former emperor forced to drink poison and, when that failed, strangled. A Tang army under Li Shimin, son of Emperor Gaozu, attacked in the autumn of 620 and besieged Luoyang in the spring of 621. Wang's catapults and crossbows inflicted heavy losses, but after Dou Jiande was captured at Hulao, Wang left the city and surrendered.

Taken to Chang'an, Wang told Emperor Gaozu that the Prince of Qin had promised to spare him. Gaozu reduced him to a commoner and ordered him and his clan into exile in modern Sichuan, while Dou Jiande was executed. Dugu Xiude, whose father Dugu Ji had been executed by Wang, then killed him and his brother Wang Shiyun to avenge his father, and was punished only with the loss of his post. The rest of the clan were executed after plotting rebellion on the way into exile. Traditional historians reviled Wang; Liu Xu, editor of the Old Book of Tang, called him a wicked man who happened to encounter an incompetent ruler.
wang-shifu: Wang Shifu, whose personal name was Wang Dexin, was born in Dadu, present-day Beijing, the capital of the Yuan dynasty; his family's ancestral home was at Baoding in Hebei. He came of a noble family, and his father was a general in the service of Genghis Khan. Following the example of his elders, Wang began an official career as a county official and was later promoted to investigating censor of Shanxi Province for his talent and achievements. His character and disposition, however, led him to leave official life in the end and devote himself to writing.

Fourteen plays are attributed to Wang, of which only three survive: The Romance of the Western Chamber (Xi Xiang Ji), Li Chun Hall and Po Yao Ji. He is counted a representative of the Wencaipai, the literary talent group, in the literature of Chinese opera.

The Romance of the Western Chamber is an amplified zaju, the theatrical form popular in his day. Set against the orthodox repertoire of Yuan zaju, Wang developed a new format of his own. The play dramatises and reworks a love story already popular in the 12th century, and shares its plot with other zaju.

Wang's way of writing is marked by a delicate, indirect portrayal of his characters' changing feelings, through which he shapes them, and by foreshadowing, which gives his plots unexpected turns and lets him show the complexity of life. Because the play achieved popular success with a form of his own invention, it has been suggested that Wang may have been an experienced professional of the theatre in the first age of Chinese drama.
wang-xizhi: Wang Xizhi was born around 303 in Linyi, in Langya Commandery, into the aristocratic Wang clan of Langya. His father, Wang Kuang, was governor of Huainan. After the Western Jin collapsed the family fled to southern China and helped establish the Eastern Jin in 317. He studied calligraphy under Wei Shuo, his father's cousin, and under his uncle Wang Yi, and after his parents died he lived in the household of his uncle Wang Dao. Around 323 he became engaged to Xi Xuan, daughter of the general Xi Jian. They had eight recorded children, among them Wang Xianzhi, who also became a skilled calligrapher; the two were later called the Two Wangs.

Between 324 and 354 Wang held various government posts, beginning as an assistant in the Palace Library. He served as a military aide to the general Yu Liang, became governor of Linchuan in 336, and was administrator of Kuaiji from 347, the year he received his highest title, General of the Right Army. He disliked war and never took part in fighting.

On 22 April 353 he hosted 41 friends, relatives and pupils at the Orchid Pavilion on Mount Kuaiji for the Double Third Festival. They played a winding stream party, composing poems as cups of rice wine floated towards them, and wrote 41 poems. Wang composed the Lantingji xu as a preface to the collection. In 355 he resigned, citing ill health, after a rival, Wang Shu, gained oversight of Kuaiji and investigated its finances. He moved to Jinting, devoted himself to Taoist practice, and died around 361.

Wang was skilled in regular, semi-cursive and cursive script, and is best known for his semi-cursive work, the style of the Lantingji xu. Apart from that preface and his letters, he mainly produced copies of existing texts. Emperor Taizong of Tang gathered over 2,000 of his works, had court scholars study his technique, and had tracing copies and ink rubbings made, which set Wang and his style as the standard of Chinese calligraphy. No original work by him is known to survive, only rubbings and a few tracing copies.

The authenticity of the Lantingji xu has been debated since the Song dynasty, and in 1965 Guo Moruo rejected Wang's authorship. The discovery of an Eastern Jin tomb inscribed in regular script in 1988 weakened one of his arguments. Wang was named the Sage of Calligraphy around the Tang dynasty, and his style was passed to Japan in the Nara and Heian periods.
wang-yangming: Wang Shouren was born in Yuyao, Zhejiang, on 26 October 1472, into a scholarly family with a tradition of bureaucratic service. His father, Wang Hua, placed first in the imperial examination of 1481 and rose to vice-minister of the Ministry of Rites, but was later demoted and expelled from government service for offending the eunuch Liu Jin. Wang earned the juren degree in 1492 and the jinshi degree in 1499.
