He served as an executive assistant in various departments until he was banished in 1506 for offending a eunuch, and his career then resumed when he became Governor of Jiangxi.

Wang was a successful general, known for the strict discipline he imposed on his troops. In 1517 and 1518 he was sent to suppress peasant revolts in Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong; concerned with the destruction of war, he petitioned the court to allow amnesty. In 1519 he faced the rebellion of Zhu Chenhao, the fourth Prince of Ning, whose base at Nanchang allowed him to sail down the Yangtze and capture Nanjing. Wang prepared for battle and deceived the prince into believing that armies were moving to surround him. The prince hesitated, giving time for Nanjing to be reinforced, and was defeated and captured.

As governor Wang also built schools and rehabilitated rebels. He was made an earl but was ostracized for opposing Zhu Xi. Thirty-eight years after his death he was given the titles Marquis and Completion of Culture, and in 1584 he was offered sacrifice in the Confucian Temple, the highest honour for a scholar.

Wang was the leading figure of the School of the Mind, founded by Lu Jiuyuan of the Southern Song, which unified knowledge with action; its rival, the School of Principle, treated gaining knowledge as a preparation for action. From the Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism of his time he developed the idea of innate knowing: every person knows from birth the difference between good and evil, intuitively and not rationally. He held that knowledge and action are one, and that the mind alone is the source of all reason. To clear away selfish desires he practised sitting still, which resembles Chan meditation.

His school became one of the dominant Confucian schools of the mid and late Ming and of the Qing. In Japan, where it is called Ōyōmei-gaku, it influenced the samurai ethic; Nakae Tōju is regarded as its founder there, and Kumazawa Banzan, Saigō Takamori and Takasugi Shinsaku came from it.
wang-zhengjun: Born in Yuancheng, modern Handan in Hebei, Wang was the second daughter of Wang Jin, then minister of justice, and Lady Li. Two men to whom she was promised, among them the Prince of Dongping, died before the marriages took place. At 18 she entered the palace as a palace woman. When the crown prince Liu Shi fell ill with grief after the death of his favourite, Consort Sima, she was one of the palace women presented to him, and he chose her, allegedly only because she sat closest to him. She bore him a son, Ao, and on 12 April 48 BCE, after Liu Shi had become Emperor Yuan, she was made empress.

Emperor Yuan came to favour Prince Liu Kang, son of Consort Fu, over the crown prince, and only the intercession of the official Shi Dan kept Ao as heir. When Ao succeeded in 33 BCE as Emperor Cheng, Wang as empress dowager raised her brothers to marquessates against the rule laid down by Emperor Gao, and Wang Feng, Wang Yin, Wang Shang, Wang Gen and then Wang Mang successively commanded the armed forces and controlled the administration.

Under Emperor Ai, who took the throne in 7 BCE, she yielded power to the Fu and Ding clans of his grandmother and mother. When Ai died without an heir in 1 BCE, she went at once to the palace, seized the imperial seal and transferred command from his favourite Dong Xian to Wang Mang. As regent for Emperor Ping, Wang Mang flattered her while purging his enemies; in 5 CE he poisoned the emperor and forced her to make him acting emperor.

After Wang Mang took the throne he gave her the additional title Wenmu, but she never acknowledged his dynasty and had her ladies keep the Han calendar and uniforms. When around 12 CE he destroyed the temple of Emperor Yuan, she cursed him and refused his invitations. She died on 3 February 13 CE and was buried in Emperor Yuan's tomb, though Wang Mang dug a trench between them. Historians largely view her with sympathy, as a benevolent but over-doting woman whose dependence on her clan led to the fall of the Western Han.
wangen-im-allgau: Wangen im Allgäu lies in south-east Baden-Württemberg, north-east of Lake Constance, in the Westallgäu, on the north bank of the Obere Argen. The Untere Argen flows past the north-west of the city and unites with the Obere Argen to its south-west. The city is second in size in the Ravensburg district and a centre for the surrounding communities. Its name was officially given as Wangen in Allgäu in 1936.

The place was first mentioned in 815 as Wangun in a monastery document. In 1217 a royal document declared that Wangen should remain in royal hands, and in 1286 King Rudolph I granted it the status of a free imperial city. In the late Middle Ages its growth was helped by its position at the crossroads between Ravensburg, Lindau, Leutkirch and Isny and by the growing trade through the Alps. Scythes and canvas were its main manufactured exports, and they gave the city a large trade surplus, which it used to buy lands beyond its walls as a safeguard against economic swings.

During the German Mediatisation of 1802 Wangen lost its free status and was incorporated into the Kingdom of Bavaria; in 1810 it changed hands to the Kingdom of Württemberg. From 1938 to 1972 it was the seat of the Wangen rural district, and in 1973 the state government designated it a Große Kreisstadt, a large district town, because its population had passed 20,000.

Despite major fires in 1539, 1793 and 1858, the old town still joins architecture from the Early Middle Ages to the late Baroque. The Oberstadtkirche St. Martin, one of the oldest buildings, was already present in the 9th century and contains Romanesque and Gothic work. The Ravensburg Gate, the city's main landmark, was first mentioned in 1472 and probably took its present appearance in 1608, with Renaissance decoration; the Lindau Gate and the Pfaffenturm tower are of similar age. A local history museum, opened in 1974 in a former mill, shows the original mill mechanisms.
wanli-emperor: Zhu Yijun was born on 4 September 1563, during the reign of his grandfather, the Jiajing Emperor. His father, Zhu Zaiji, was the heir to the throne, and his mother, Lady Li, was one of his concubines. His father became the Longqing Emperor in 1567 and named him heir in 1568. When the Longqing Emperor died on 5 July 1572, Zhu Yijun succeeded two weeks later, on 19 July, at the age of nine, and adopted the era name Wanli, meaning "ten thousand years (of rule)".

For the first ten years Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng effectively led the government, supported by the Emperor's mother and the eunuch Feng Bao. He centralized government, streamlined administration and strengthened the military, and the efficiency of administration improved markedly between 1572 and 1582. After Zhang died in 1582 the Emperor changed his administrative arrangements. From 1586 a dispute over the succession divided the bureaucracy: the Emperor favoured his third son, Zhu Changxun, the son of his consort Lady Zheng, while many officials upheld the claim of his eldest son, Zhu Changluo, who was named heir only in 1601.

In the 1590s the Ming put down a rebellion at Ningxia in 1592, drove the Japanese out of most of Korea by 1593 and thwarted a second Japanese invasion in 1597. In 1596 a shortage of silver after the costly rebuilding of palaces burnt in a fire led the Emperor to send eunuchs and officers to open mines, which local authorities opposed. In 1596 he also tried to set up a parallel administration of eunuchs, abandoned in 1606. The Donglin Academy, founded in 1604, became an intellectual centre critical of the court. In 1619 the Jurchens defeated Ming armies at the Battle of Sarhu and took part of Liaodong. After 1588 the Emperor no longer left Beijing.

The Emperor's health failed in 1620, and he died on 18 August. An edict the next day sent a million liang of silver to the frontier troops and ordered an end to mining and trade dues. His eldest son, Zhu Changluo, took the throne on 28 August as the Taichang Emperor. Traditional Chinese historiography portrays the Wanli Emperor as a main cause of the dynasty's decline, citing greed, misuse of eunuch power and seclusion. Confucian scholars' hostility came partly from his protection of military officers against complaints from civilian officials.
wannsee-conference: Discrimination against Jews was codified in Germany immediately after the Nazi seizure of power on 30 January 1933, and the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 stripped Jews of citizenship. After the invasion of Poland in September 1939 the extermination of European Jews began, first through mobile death squads, the Einsatzgruppen, and it accelerated after the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941.

On 31 July 1941 Hermann Göring gave Reinhard Heydrich written authorisation to prepare a plan for a total solution of the Jewish question in territories under German control. Heydrich sent invitations on 29 November 1941 for a meeting on 9 December, but it was postponed, and on 8 January 1942 he sent new invitations for 20 January.

The meeting took place at a villa at Am Großen Wannsee 56 to 58, bought by the Security Service in 1940 as a conference centre. Fifteen officials attended, mostly state secretaries and undersecretaries of the ministries together with SS officials; eight were lawyers. Heydrich spoke for nearly an hour. He reported that about 537,000 Jews had emigrated by 31 October 1941 and that there were about eleven million Jews in Europe.

Since emigration had been prohibited, Jews were to be evacuated to the east and allocated to labour, in the course of which a large portion would be eliminated by natural causes. Europe would be combed through from west to east, with Jews first sent to transit ghettos in the General Government. He also discussed who counted as a Jew and how people of mixed descent and Jews in mixed marriages would be treated.

Questions and comments followed for about thirty minutes. Wilhelm Stuckart and Otto Hofmann pointed to the legal difficulties over mixed marriages, and Josef Bühler, State Secretary of the General Government, hoped the killings would begin as soon as possible. Adolf Eichmann later said that after cognac was served the participants spoke bluntly of methods of killing and extermination. Eichmann wrote the minutes, the Wannsee Protocol, at Heydrich's instruction in office language rather than verbatim.

The conference lasted only about ninety minutes. Historians such as Peter Longerich and Laurence Rees hold that the decision to exterminate the Jews had already been made and that Heydrich met the officials to secure the cooperation of the ministries and to assert SS control over the deportees' fate. Copies of the minutes were destroyed at the end of the war.

Copy number 16 of 30 was found in 1947 by the US prosecutor Robert Kempner among files seized from the German Foreign Office, and it was used in the Nuremberg trials. On 20 January 1992, the fiftieth anniversary, the villa was opened as the Haus der Wannsee-Konferenz, a Holocaust memorial and museum.
wanyan-chenglin: Wanyan Chenglin was born in 1202, a descendant of Helibo, the father of Aguda, the founder and first emperor of the Jin dynasty. He served the dynasty as a military general, and Emperor Aizong valued him for his courage and talent. His elder brother, Wanyan Chengyi, was chancellor and was killed fighting the Mongols at Pucheng around 1232.

When the Mongol Empire attacked the Jin in 1232, Aizong abandoned the capital, Bianjing, present-day Kaifeng, and fled to Caizhou, present-day Runan County in Henan. Many ministers and officers deserted the emperor along the way, but Chenglin stayed with him throughout the journey. At Caizhou he advised Aizong to set up a central command and to prepare the city's defences against a Mongol attack.

In the first month of 1234 the Mongols, now allied with the Southern Song dynasty, besieged Caizhou. Aizong, not wishing to be remembered as the last emperor of the Jin, announced that he would abdicate in Chenglin's favour. Chenglin refused, but the emperor insisted, saying that he himself was too fat to ride into battle, while Chenglin was fit, strong and a talented commander who might escape and keep the dynasty alive. Chenglin reluctantly accepted.

On 9 February 1234, shortly after the abdication ceremony began, news came that the enemy had breached the walls. Aizong hanged himself in the Youlan Room, while Chenglin rallied his soldiers and fought in the streets and alleys until he was forced back into the inner city. On hearing of Aizong's death he gathered his remaining followers, held a ceremony of mourning and gave the dead emperor the temple name Aizong. He was killed when the enemy overran the city later that day. Historians call him Emperor Mo, meaning last emperor.
wanyan-liang: Wanyan Liang, whose Jurchen name was Digunai, was born on 24 February 1122, the second son of Wanyan Zonggan, also called Woben, the eldest son of the dynasty's founder Wanyan Aguda (Emperor Taizu). His mother, Lady Da, came from a prominent family of Balhae descent. Under Emperor Xizong his father was described as the most influential man at the Jin court, and Digunai served as an army marshal. In 1150 he overthrew Emperor Xizong in a coup d'état. Distrusting the Jurchen aristocracy after taking the throne by illegitimate means, he ordered the massacre of the descendants of Emperor Taizong, so securing the line of Emperor Taizu to which he belonged.

After the Jin victory over the Song in 1141, Digunai sought to make the Jin the sole Chinese empire and to present himself as a sinicised ruler. In 1150 he lifted Emperor Taizong's ban on Han Chinese dress and introduced the imperial examination system, founding an Imperial Academy the next year. He adopted Chinese court practices, among them the imperial carriage in 1151, a system of feudal rights in 1156 and the Song style of court ceremony in 1157. Seeking the Mandate of Heaven, he moved his court from Shangjing, in present-day Harbin, and in 1157 ordered the palaces there destroyed.

Where the Tang and Song had rarely imposed corporal punishment on the educated elite, he kept the Khitan and Jurchen custom of flogging, and at times watched in person as chancellors, censors and a princess were beaten with poles or whips.

His attempt to conquer the Southern Song and unify China failed when his fleet was defeated at the battles of Tangdao and Caishi in 1161. Many officers deserted and in places the people rose against him. He decreed that the superior of any deserter be executed, rank by rank up to the army commander, and ordered the army to cross the Yangtze at Guazhou within three days on pain of death. Subordinates led by Yelü Yuanyi, commander of the West Zhejiang Front, killed him in a camp near the river on 15 December 1161.

His cousin Wulu, who had led a rebellion against him, was proclaimed emperor. As Emperor Shizong he posthumously demoted Digunai to Prince Yang of Hailing in 1162, and in 1181 reduced him further to the status of a commoner, so that he is also known as the Commoner of Hailing.
wanyan-yongji: Wanyan Yongji, whose childhood name was Xingsheng, was born Wanyan Yunji; his given name was changed to avoid a naming taboo, since the father of Emperor Zhangzong was Wanyan Yungong. He was the seventh son of Emperor Shizong and of Lady Li, a Balhae concubine, and so an uncle of Zhangzong. In 1171 he was made Prince of Xue, and his title was later changed in turn to Prince of Sui, Prince of Lu, Prince of Han and Prince of Wei. When Zhangzong died without a male heir in 1208, he was chosen as the new emperor, the seventh of the Jin dynasty.

Under Genghis Khan the Mongols were then preparing to attack the Jin. They first struck Western Xia, a vassal of the Jin; Wanyan Yongji ignored its request for help, and it surrendered. In 1211 the Mongols launched a full-scale invasion and in the ninth month besieged the central capital, Zhongdu, in present-day Beijing, but withdrew before its strong defences. In 1212 they besieged the western capital, Datong, while the Khitan Yelü Liuge led a rebellion, submitted to the Mongols and defeated a 600,000-strong Jin army at Dijinao'er. The emperor was known as indecisive and weak.

In the eighth month of 1213, as the Mongols again attacked Zhongdu, the general Heshilie Zhizhong, also known as Hushahu, rebelled and killed him; he died on 11 September 1213. Hushahu placed Wanyan Xun, Emperor Xuanzong, on the throne and, backed by about 300 officials, urged that the dead ruler be demoted to a commoner. As a compromise Xuanzong made him Marquis of Donghai Commandery. A month later Hushahu was himself killed by the general Zhuhu Gaoqi. In 1216 Xuanzong restored the title Prince of Wei with the posthumous name Shao. One of his daughters, the Princess of Qi State, married Genghis Khan.
waqf: There is no direct Quranic injunction about awqāf, but one is inferred from Surah Al Imran (3:92), which says that righteousness is not reached until a person gives some of what they cherish. The institution rests on hadiths. One tradition says that after the Hijrah the first waqf was a grove of 600 date palms whose proceeds fed the poor of Medina.

The two oldest known deeds, or waqfiyas, are from the 9th century and a third from the early 10th, all within the Abbasid Caliphate. In Egypt the earliest known waqf was a pond called Birkat Ḥabash with its orchards, founded in 919 to run a hydraulic complex and feed the poor. In India the 14th-century Insha-i-Mahru records that Muhammad of Ghor gave two villages to a congregational mosque in Multan.

A waqf is a contract, so the founder, the waqif, must be an adult of sound mind who can handle financial affairs. Being a Muslim is not required, and dhimmis may found one. The founder must name a specific beneficiary, may not reserve a right to sell or revoke, and must own the property outright. The founder appoints an administrator, a nāẓir or mutawallī, and sets the rules for successors.

A waqf is meant to last forever, but Islamic law admits conditions under which it ends: if its goods are destroyed or no longer used as the founder intended, or if a judge, the ḳāḍī, declares it void for an illegal act or purpose. It is also void if the founder converts to another religion.

Waqf revenue paid for mosques, madrasas, public kitchens, caravanserais and libraries. After waqf law and madrasa foundations were firmly established by the 10th century, the number of hospitals multiplied, and by the 11th century many Islamic cities had several. Waqfs paid doctors, surgeons and pharmacists, bought food, medicines and equipment, kept buildings in repair and supported medical schools. The institution was not popular everywhere: in West Africa very few examples are found, and they were limited to the area around Timbuktu and Djenné.
war-elephant: It is uncertain when elephant warfare began, but it is widely accepted that it began in ancient India. Elephants were widely used in warfare by the later Vedic period, by the 6th century BCE. From India the practice spread west to the Achaemenid Empire. At the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE the Persians placed fifteen elephants at the centre of their line, and Alexander the Great, deeply impressed, took the first fifteen into his own army and added to their number. Kush also kept war elephants, perhaps in the Great Enclosure at Musawwarat al-Sufa, and supplied them to the Egyptians, the Ptolemies and the Syrians.

In battle elephants were usually placed in the centre of the line, to prevent a charge or to make one, and their size and appearance made them valued heavy cavalry. Rome brought back many elephants at the end of the Punic Wars and used them in Greece. At Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE their quick charge shattered the Macedonian left wing. The Gupta Empire formed local squads of one elephant, one chariot, three cavalrymen and five foot soldiers.

China used them sparingly: the Southern Han is the only state in Chinese history known to have kept a permanent corps, which Song crossbowmen defeated at Shao on 23 January 971. The Khmer Empire mounted double crossbows on elephants. Elephants were trained by mahouts using chains and a hook called an ankus.

Elephants could fail. In the Sack of Delhi, Timur's army, though three times the size of its opponents, almost lost for fear of the elephants, and is said to have won by tying flaming straw to its camels, which ran forward and frightened the elephants into crushing their own troops. With the arrival of gunpowder in the late 15th century the balance changed: elephants could withstand muskets, but a single cannon shot could knock one down. Nevertheless they remained in use in Southeast Asia until the end of the 19th century, and the Siamese army used them until 1893. The bishop in chess is called an elephant in many languages, including Sanskrit, Arabic and Russian.
war-in-afghanistan-2001-2021: The Taliban emerged from religious students who sought to end warlordism in Afghanistan through stricter adherence to Sharia. In 1996 they seized Kabul, with military support from Pakistan and financial support from Saudi Arabia, and founded the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. They issued edicts forbidding women to work outside the home or attend school. The United Nations reported 15 massacres of civilians between 1996 and 2001, many targeting Shias and Hazaras. Under the Taliban, al-Qaeda trained fighters in Afghanistan, and an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 men passed through the camps before 11 September 2001.

On that day 19 al-Qaeda members hijacked four airliners and carried out coordinated attacks in the United States, in which 2,996 people died, including the hijackers. President George W. Bush demanded that the Taliban hand over Osama bin Laden and close the camps. The Taliban leader Mullah Omar refused, and the Taliban said bin Laden was protected by Pashtun laws of hospitality.

The United States officially invaded on 7 October 2001 with Operation Enduring Freedom, though CIA teams had entered the country weeks earlier to link up with the Northern Alliance in the Panjshir Valley. With American air support the Northern Alliance took several key cities within weeks, and by November the Taliban had lost most of the country. The coalition formed the International Security Assistance Force, and an Afghan Interim Administration was set up. By 2003 the Taliban had reorganised and begun an insurgency of guerrilla warfare, suicide attacks and reprisals against perceived collaborators.

Troop numbers grew, with a surge from late 2009 to September 2012. An American covert operation in Pakistan killed bin Laden in 2011. NATO formally ended ISAF combat operations in 2014 and handed security to the Afghan government, while a new NATO mission, Resolute Support, and the American Operation Freedom's Sentinel continued. The United States and the Taliban concluded a deal for the withdrawal of all American troops. In the summer of that withdrawal the Taliban launched an offensive and took Kabul on 15 August, the day President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.

The last American military aircraft left on 30 August. The war is estimated to have killed between 176,000 and 212,000 people, including 46,319 civilians, and a further 66,650 people died in the related war in north-west Pakistan. Although more than 5.7 million former refugees returned after 2001, 2.6 million Afghans were still refugees at the fall of Kabul and about 4 million were internally displaced. It was the longest war in American military history, surpassing the Vietnam War by seven months.
war-of-1812: The causes of the war have long been debated. The United States objected to the British orders in council of 1807, which restricted trade with Napoleonic France, and to the Royal Navy's impressment of seamen from American vessels, men whom Britain claimed as British subjects. Britain also supported Indigenous confederacies resisting American expansion in the Northwest Territory, and some Americans may have wished to annex part or all of Canada.

On 1 June 1812 President James Madison sent Congress a message setting out American grievances. The House voted 79 to 49 and the Senate 19 to 13 for war, divided on party lines, with no Federalist in favour. Madison signed the declaration on 18 June 1812, the first formal declaration of war by the United States, passed by the smallest margin of any in American history.

Neither side was ready. Britain was engaged against Napoleon, most of its army was in the Peninsular War, and it had officially 6,034 regular troops in Canada in July 1812. Its aims were defensive. American forces under William Hull crossed into Upper Canada on 12 July 1812 and reached Sandwich, but all the invasions of Canada failed. At sea the Royal Navy blockaded the American coast and raided the Chesapeake Bay, while American privateers inflicted limited damage on British commerce. About 4,000 African Americans escaped slavery aboard British ships.

After Napoleon's exile in April 1814 Britain reinforced North America, and in August 1814 it captured and burned Washington. American victories at Baltimore and Plattsburgh in September helped end major fighting in the north. In the south, American forces and their Indigenous allies defeated the Red Stick faction of the Muscogee, and Andrew Jackson's army repulsed a British attack on New Orleans in January 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent had been signed. The treaty was agreed in December 1814 and ratified by the Senate on 17 February 1815.

The treaty restored the pre-war territorial status quo and did not settle the maritime issues, though impressment largely ceased once the Napoleonic Wars ended. American losses were 2,260 killed in action and about 15,000 dead from all causes related to the war, while British losses were about 1,160 killed in action. At least 10,000 Indigenous people are estimated to have died.

The Indigenous allies of Britain lost their cause, since the proposed barrier state was rejected at Ghent, and the United States went on to negotiate over two hundred treaties for Indigenous land. In the United States the war was called a second war of independence and the Federalist Party collapsed. Britain remembers it little. Canadians later used its memory to help build a national identity after 1867.
war-of-canudos: Canudos, which its inhabitants called Belo Monte, lay in the semi-arid sertão of Bahia, a poor region of subsistence farming and cattle raising that suffered severe droughts. For the sertanejos the republic proclaimed on 15 November 1889 brought chiefly higher taxes, and the deposed emperor Pedro II was still loved by the common people. Antônio Vicente Mendes Maciel, known as Antônio Conselheiro, was one of many itinerant preachers of the backcountry. He held that monarchs ruled by God-given right and predicted the return of the Portuguese king Sebastian, and local landowners and the Church hierarchy saw him as a threat.

In 1893 he settled with his followers at Canudos on the Vaza-Barris River, a site that was hard to reach. Within two years it had become the second-largest urban centre in Bahia, living from crops and the export of leather. The press branded its people monarchists who planned to restore the monarchy.

The conflict began over lumber ordered from Juazeiro for a new church. The judge Arlindo Leoni blocked the delivery and asked Governor Luis Viana for police, claiming the town faced an invasion. In November 1896 a force of about 100 men under Pires Ferreira was surprised at Uauá by between 1,000 and 3,000 followers armed with old muskets, pikes and scythes, and withdrew to Juazeiro. President Prudente de Morais then sent federal troops. A force that left Juazeiro on 12 January 1897 was surrounded and fell back to Monte Santo, while the settlement grew to over 30,000 residents.

Colonel Antônio Moreira César followed with 1,300 men, but they lost their way among the huts, he was mortally wounded, and the retreat of 6 March 1897 became a rout. In Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo rioters destroyed four monarchist newspaper offices. General Arthur Oscar de Andrade Guimarães then led the final campaign, in which more than 8,000 soldiers besieged and starved the settlement until the fighting ended on 5 October 1897.

Antônio Conselheiro had probably died of dysentery on 22 September. His body was exhumed and his head displayed on a pike. Men who surrendered on the promise of their lives were hacked to death, the soldiers burned the settlement, and about 150 survivors remained. Estimates of the dead range from about 30,000, given by Euclides da Cunha, to some 15,000 according to Robert M. Levine and 5,000 according to Joel Singer.

Walnice Nogueira Galvão sees the war's main result as the consolidation of the republic, though public opinion later recognised that the peasants had no tie to real monarchists. The town's site now lies under the reservoir of the Cocorobó Dam, built in the 1960s, and the Canudos State Park, established in 1986, preserves many places of the war.
war-of-chioggia: Genoa and Venice had long competed for the trade of the Levant and the eastern Mediterranean and had fought several wars over it. Genoa sought a monopoly of the Black Sea trade in grain, timber, fur and slaves, all the more after the collapse of Mongol hegemony over the Central Asian trade route made that trade riskier. The immediate quarrel was over the Aegean island of Tenedos, which Venice had acquired from the Byzantine Empire in 1377, and the two republics backed rival claimants to the Byzantine throne. Venice's allies included Bernabò Visconti of Milan; Genoa's included Leopold III, Duke of Austria, besides Hungary, Padua and Aquileia.

On 30 May 1378 Vettor Pisani defeated a Genoese squadron off Cape d'Anzio, capturing its admiral Luigi de' Fieschi, while Carlo Zeno raided Genoese stations in the Levant. On 7 May 1379, however, Luciano Doria's fleet destroyed Pisani's off Pola in Istria, leaving him only six galleys; Doria fell in the battle and Pisani was imprisoned on his return. Under Pietro Doria the Genoese, with Paduan and Hungarian allies, took Chioggia on 16 August 1379, and Venice was encircled. When the Venetian senate asked for peace, the Genoese answered that they would bit and bridle the Horses of Saint Mark.

Pisani was released by popular demand, and on the night of 22 December 1379 he and the doge Andrea Contarini sank stone-laden vessels in the channels, shutting the Genoese fleet in at Chioggia. Zeno's galleys arrived off Brondolo on 1 January 1380. A Genoese relief force under Matteo Maruffo came only on 12 May and could do nothing, and on 24 June 1380 the starving garrison surrendered.

The Treaty of Turin, made on 8 August 1381 through the mediation of Amadeus VI of Savoy, the Green Count, gave neither side a formal advantage, and Venice ceded Tenedos to Savoy. Both republics had suffered enormous economic damage, but Genoa lost its naval ascendancy and its shipping was not seen in the Adriatic again. The war saw the first use of shipborne cannon in support of amphibious assaults, and its events are still recalled in the Palio della Marciliana held each year at Chioggia.
war-of-devolution: The 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees ended the Franco-Spanish War, and Louis XIV married Maria Theresa, eldest daughter of Philip IV of Spain. To prevent France from inheriting the Spanish Empire, she renounced her inheritance rights, and in return Louis was promised a dowry of 500,000 gold écus, which was never paid. After Cardinal Mazarin died in 1661, Louis began an expansionist policy, and Jean-Baptiste Colbert argued that control of the Spanish Netherlands was essential to French economic growth.

Philip's death in September 1665 left his four-year-old son Charles as king, with his widow Mariana of Austria as regent. French lawyers argued that the unpaid dowry made the renunciation invalid. The Spanish and imperial courts rejected the claim, since the law applied only in Brabant, Namur and Hainault and concerned private property, but it gave Louis a legal justification.

The French crossed the border on 24 May 1667 with Louis in attendance. Turenne, the supreme commander, took Charleroi, which the Spanish governor Castelo Rodrigo abandoned after destroying its fortifications, and by the end of July Tournai, Kortrijk and Oudenaarde had fallen. Turenne besieged Lille on 10 August, and its garrison surrendered on 28 August. Sickness proved a bigger problem for his troops than battle.

The Treaty of Breda of 31 July 1667 ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War and opened talks on a common front against France. England and the Dutch Republic signed the Triple Alliance on 23 January 1668, and Sweden joined on 5 May. In February 1668 the Prince de Condé invaded Franche-Comté, which had fewer than 2,000 defenders. Besançon surrendered on 7 February, Dole on 14 February and Gray on 19 February.

Turenne, Condé and Philippe of Orléans argued for continuing the war, while Lionne, Colbert and Le Tellier recommended peace, mainly on financial grounds. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was signed by Spain and France on 2 May 1668. France withdrew from Franche-Comté and from the Spanish Netherlands except for eleven towns, among them Lille, Douai, Tournai and Charleroi, and Vauban began work on the defence line known as the Ceinture de fer.

The invasion ended the long-standing Franco-Dutch alliance. Louis concluded that the best way to win Dutch agreement to his demands was to defeat the Republic first, and he began planning the Franco-Dutch War.
war-of-jenkins-ear: The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave British merchants access to Spanish American markets through the Asiento de Negros, a monopoly to supply 5,000 slaves a year, and the Navío de Permiso, which allowed two ships a year to sell goods at Porto Bello and Veracruz. Both were held by the South Sea Company. Smuggling was too profitable to stop, and Spain tried either to manage the illegal trade or to use it as an instrument of policy.

The war is often portrayed as a trade dispute, but modern historians argue that Spanish concern over British colonial expansion in North America mattered equally. The Tory opposition, seeking to unseat Robert Walpole's Whig government, also campaigned for war. In April 1731 the Spanish guarda costa captain was alleged to have severed the ear of the British captain Robert Jenkins, and in 1738 opposition politicians used the incident to rouse support.

Admiral Edward Vernon captured Portobelo on 22 November 1739 with six ships of the line. Its fall was greeted with enthusiasm in Britain, and Rule Britannia was written in 1740 to mark it. Vernon then tried Cartagena de Indias, the Spanish gold-trading port in New Granada, three times. His largest attack, with an amphibious force from 13 March to 20 May 1741, failed against the fortifications and the strategy of the Spanish commander Blas de Lezo. Heavy British losses came mostly from disease, chiefly yellow fever, which took more lives than the fighting.

Commodore George Anson sailed for the Pacific in September 1740. Most of his men died of disease, but on 20 June 1743 he captured a Manila galleon carrying more than a million gold coins and returned to London having circled the globe. In North America, James Oglethorpe besieged St. Augustine in 1740 without success, and in 1742 he defeated a Spanish landing from 2,000 troops at Bloody Marsh. Privateers on both sides were active, and Spanish ones seized hundreds of British ships.

By mid-1742 the War of the Austrian Succession had broken out in Europe, and its scale drew attention away from the Americas. Vernon's return that year ended major offensive operations. France entered the war in 1744, and fear of a French invasion persuaded British policymakers against sending large forces overseas. Fighting formally ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle of 1748, under which Britain largely failed to achieve its territorial and economic aims in the Americas.
war-of-saint-sabas: The war began when the Venetians were evicted from Tyre in 1256, and grew out of a dispute over land in Acre owned by the monastery of Mar Saba but claimed by both Genoa and Venice. Genoa was aided by Philip of Montfort, Lord of Tyre, by John of Arsuf and by the Knights Hospitaller; Venice by John of Ibelin, Count of Jaffa and Ascalon, and the Knights Templar. The Genoese navy at first had the upper hand, until the Republic of Pisa, a former ally, signed a ten-year military alliance with Venice.

In 1257 the Venetian admiral Lorenzo Tiepolo broke through Acre's harbour chain, destroyed several Genoese ships, took the disputed property and razed its fortifications. He could not drive the Genoese, 800 men with 50 to 60 ballistae, from their quarter, and his blockade lasted perhaps twelve to fourteen months, while food reached them through the nearby Hospitaller complex. In August 1257 the regent John of Arsuf made a treaty with Ancona, an ally of Genoa, but John of Ibelin and John II of Beirut brought the kingdom's feudatories over to Venice, with the support of Plaisance of Cyprus, Bohemond VI of Antioch and the Knights Templar.

In June 1258 Philip of Montfort marched on Acre with a band of Hospitallers while a Genoese fleet of some 48 galleys and four sailing ships under Rosso della Turca attacked by sea. The Venetians quickly overran the fleet, and the Genoese abandoned their quarter and withdrew with Philip to Tyre. A fragile peace held by 1261, and Pope Urban IV called a council to restore order. Genoa then turned to Michael VIII Palaiologos, who after the Treaty of Nymphaeum funded fifty ships against Venice. In 1266 the Genoese allied with the Mamluk sultan Baibars, though their promised fleet never sailed, and on 16 August 1267 they took the Tower of Flies and blockaded Acre's harbour for twelve days.

Both sides employed Muslim soldiers, mostly Turcopoles, against Christian foes. Apart from the religious buildings, most fortified structures in Acre were destroyed at one time or another, and the Rothelin continuation of William of Tyre's History counts 20,000 dead in all, a heavy loss for states short of soldiers. The Peace of Cremona ended the hostilities in 1270, but the Genoese did not regain their quarter in Acre until 1288.
war-of-the-austrian-succession: The Mutual Pact of Succession of 1703 provided that if the Habsburgs died out in the male line, their possessions would pass first to the daughters of Emperor Joseph I and then to those of his younger brother Charles. Since Salic law excluded women, the agreement needed the approval of the Habsburg territories and the Imperial Diet. Emperor Charles VI died on 20 October 1740.

Frederick II had become king of Prussia on 31 May 1740, aged 28, and wished to overcome the limits that his scattered territories set on Prussian power. The death gave him a chance to take resource-rich Silesia before Augustus of Saxony and Poland could act. Prussia's army of 80,000 was better trained than the Austrian one, and France had agreed to attack from the west.

Prussia occupied Silesia in December 1740. At Mollwitz on 10 April 1741 Frederick made mistakes and left the field, and his deputy von Schwerin won a narrow victory. A Franco-Bavarian force marched along the Danube and took Linz on 14 September 1741, and with a Saxon force of 20,000 advanced on Prague. On 12 February 1742 Charles Albert of Bavaria was crowned Emperor Charles VII, the first non-Habsburg emperor in 300 years, but Austrian troops captured Munich that day. Maria Theresa ended a secret truce with Frederick by publishing its terms, damaging his bond with his allies.

In 1743 the allied Pragmatic Army beat French troops at Dettingen, the last time a British monarch personally led troops in battle. After Charles VII died on 20 January 1745, his son Maximilian III Joseph signed the Treaty of Füssen on 22 April, agreeing to vote for Maria Theresa's husband Francis Stephen as emperor. In the Low Countries the French took Tournai after Fontenoy, then Ghent, Bruges and Antwerp, and won at Rocoux in October 1746. Elsewhere Britain and Spain fought at sea, in the war's North American theatre King George's War, and in India, where the French took Madras in September 1746.

By early 1748 France was close to bankruptcy, and a British naval blockade had collapsed its customs receipts and caused food shortages. Louis XV agreed to return the Austrian Netherlands, a decision that few of his countrymen understood and that gave rise to the phrase as stupid as the Peace. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, signed in October, confirmed Maria Theresa in her titles, but many signatories were unhappy. Britain's insistence that Austria cede Silesia undermined the Anglo-Austrian Alliance, since Austria felt it had gained little from large British subsidies. This led to the Diplomatic Revolution and, in 1756, the outbreak of the Seven Years' War.
war-of-the-breton-succession: Duke John III of Brittany disliked the children of his father's second marriage and tried in vain to have his half-siblings declared illegitimate. Being childless, he chose as heir Joan of Penthièvre, daughter of his brother Guy, who in 1337 married Charles of Blois, a nephew of King Philip VI of France. In 1340 John III reconciled with his half-brother John of Montfort and named him heir, and he died on 30 April 1341.

Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois. John of Montfort acted quickly, taking Nantes and the ducal treasury at Limoges, and by mid-August held most of the duchy, including Nantes, Rennes and Vannes. The rival kings backed opposite sides: the French supported Blois, the female heir, and the English supported the male heir, Montfort.

After John of Montfort surrendered at Nantes in November 1341 and was imprisoned, his wife Joan of Flanders led his cause from Hennebont and Brest. The siege of Brest was broken on 18 August 1342 by an English army under the Earl of Northampton. The Truce of Malestroit of 19 January 1343 did little to stop the fighting, since Charles of Blois claimed to fight a separate war. His forces took Quimper by assault on 1 May 1344, and civilians were slaughtered, estimated at between 1,400 and 2,000. John of Montfort died on 16 September 1345, leaving a five-year-old son, John.

The French defeats at Crécy in 1346 and Calais in 1347 weakened Charles, and he was captured at La Roche-Derrien in 1347 and spent five years in the Tower of London. In 1351 thirty knights on each side fought the Combat of the Thirty between Josselin and Ploërmel, a chivalric episode that had no effect on the outcome. The war resumed in 1363. At the Battle of Auray on 29 September 1364, John de Montfort and the English commander John Chandos defeated Charles of Blois, who was killed, and Bertrand du Guesclin, who was captured.

The First Treaty of Guérande of 12 April 1365 made John of Montfort Duke of Brittany. It provided that the duchy would pass from male to male in the Montfort family and failing that to the male line of Penthièvre, and Joan of Penthièvre kept her titles and a rent of 10,000 livres.

King Charles V of France, depleted by the Hundred Years' War, recognized John and so won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366 the new duke surprisingly took an oath of allegiance to Charles V and not to Edward III of England, who had supported him. The Montfortists later repudiated the succession terms after the Penthièvres kidnapped John V in 1420, which mattered in 1488 when the duchy passed to Anne of Brittany.
war-of-the-castilian-succession: Joanna, born in 1462, was Henry IV's only child, but a rumour that her father was Beltrán de la Cueva earned her the mocking name la Beltraneja. Nobles forced Henry to name his half-brother Alfonso heir in 1465, and after Alfonso's death in 1468 the Treaty of the Bulls of Guisando gave Isabella the right of succession. In 1469 she secretly married Ferdinand, heir to the Crown of Aragon, against Henry's wishes. When Henry died in December 1474 both women were proclaimed queen, and Joanna's weaker party arranged her marriage to her uncle, the 43-year-old Afonso V of Portugal. Louis XI of France, a rival of Aragon in Roussillon and Italy, sided with them.

Afonso entered Castile on 10 May 1475 and was proclaimed king with Joanna at Plasencia on 25 May, but he found fewer supporters than he had expected and avoided battle, and his caution weakened Joanna's alliance. Zamora rose against him in December. On 1 March 1476 Ferdinand caught the retreating Portuguese near Toro; Afonso fled while his son John held his ground, and both sides claimed victory. Politically the battle was decisive, as most Portuguese troops and Joanna withdrew to Portugal and her noble supporters gradually submitted, while a French attack at Fuenterrabía was repelled.

The struggle shifted to the Atlantic, over the gold and slaves of Guinea. Castilian sailors from Palos raided its coast and sold captured Africans as slaves. In 1478 a Portuguese fleet defeated the Castilians at Elmina and took them prisoner to Lisbon, and in February 1479 a Portuguese army entered Extremadura but was beaten near Albuera by Alonso de Cárdenas, Master of the Order of Santiago. Pope Sixtus IV then annulled the dispensation for Afonso's marriage to his niece.

The Treaty of Alcáçovas was signed on 4 September 1479 and ratified by the Castilian and Aragonese monarchs at Toledo on 6 March 1480. Afonso V gave up his claim to Castile, and Isabella and Ferdinand any claim to Portugal. Portugal received most of the Atlantic territories, while Castile kept the Canary Islands. Joanna renounced her Castilian titles and chose a convent rather than marriage to Prince John, though she stayed active in politics. Isabella's daughter Isabella married Prince Afonso of Portugal, her large dowry serving in practice as war compensation.
war-of-the-confederation: The confederation created by Marshal Andrés de Santa Cruz in 1836 alarmed its neighbours. In Chile Diego Portales, the power behind President José Joaquín Prieto, feared it would upset the balance of power and threaten Chilean independence, and the rivalry between the ports of Callao and Valparaíso sharpened the quarrel. A tariff war followed, Peru raising its duty on Chilean wheat and Chile its duty on Peruvian sugar. In 1836 the exiled former president Ramón Freire sailed from Lima with Confederate help to overthrow Prieto and was captured, and on the night of 21 August 1836 a Chilean raid under Victorino Garrido seized three Confederate ships at Callao.

Santa Cruz accepted every Chilean demand except the dissolution of the confederation, and Chile declared war on 28 December 1836. The Argentine Confederation of Juan Manuel de Rosas declared war on 9 May 1837, but the two allies fought separately throughout.

On 6 June 1837 Portales was shot by mutinous officers at Quillota, a murder blamed on Santa Cruz that rallied Chilean opinion behind the war. A first expedition of about 2,800 men under Admiral Manuel Blanco Encalada landed at Islay and occupied Arequipa, but Santa Cruz surrounded it, and on 17 November 1837 Blanco Encalada signed the Treaty of Paucarpata, which Chile repudiated. In 1838 General Manuel Bulnes led a second army, which won at Portada de Guías outside Lima on 21 August. On 12 January 1839 the Chilean fleet defeated the Confederate squadron at Casma, and at Yungay on 20 January the Confederates lost over 2,400 casualties and more than 1,600 prisoners, against about 1,300 Chilean dead.

Santa Cruz had already been overthrown as president of Bolivia by General José Miguel de Velasco, and he fled to Ecuador and later to Europe. On 25 August 1839 General Agustín Gamarra, president of Peru, declared the confederation dissolved, and the Chilean troops left on 19 October. Gamarra then invaded Bolivia himself and was killed at the Battle of Ingaví on 18 November 1841; peace came in 1842. In Chile the army tripled in size during the war, and historians see in it the consolidation of Peruvian and Chilean ideas of nationality.
war-of-the-eight-princes: Sima Yi seized control of the state of Cao Wei in 249, and in February 266 his grandson Sima Yan, Emperor Wu of Jin, forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty. In late 289 Emperor Wu fell gravely ill, and his father-in-law Yang Jun hid the decree naming him and Sima Liang, Prince of Ru’nan, as co-regents, while the empress Yang Zhi issued another making her father sole regent.

The name of the conflict comes from the biographies of eight Sima princes collected in Chapter 59 of the Book of Jin. It was not one continuous war but intervals of peace broken by short and intense periods of fighting.

Empress Jia, wife of the new Emperor Hui, enlisted Sima Liang and Sima Wei, Prince of Chu, and on the night of 23 April 291 had Yang Jun overthrown. Wei, armed with a forged edict, then had Liang executed, and the empress turned her troops on Wei, who was captured and executed in turn. For nine years she ruled in the emperor’s name, until in 300 she had the Crown Prince, Sima Yu, who was not her son, arrested. Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, then took the regency and usurped the throne.

A coalition of three princes, Sima Jiong, Sima Ying and Sima Yong, with some 200,000 troops, overthrew him, and Jiong became regent on 11 August 301. Further rivalries brought fighting in and around Luoyang, where Sima Ai, Prince of Changsha, held the capital until 303 against armies sent by Yong and Ying. Ying then made himself Crown Prince in May 304, and Sima Yue, a second cousin of Emperor Wu, fought him with allies who brought many Xianbei and Wuhuan soldiers. In 305 Yue led the eastern governors against Yong, who held the emperor at Chang’an, and took control of the court. Ying was caught at Ye, and Yong was strangled in his carriage at Xin’an.

The wars devastated the Jin heartland in northern China and opened the empire to rebellion, above all by tribal peoples who had resettled in the Central Plains. Yue’s victory was short-lived. Emperor Hui died on 8 January 307 after eating poisoned bread. Ji Sang and Shi Le sacked Ye in 307, killing Sima Teng, and Wang Mi ravaged the North China Plain and laid siege to Luoyang in 308.

Shi Le and Wang Mi then joined Liu Yuan’s state of Han, and together they overran most of the lands north of the Yellow River, while in Sichuan the Jin failed to destroy Li Xiong’s state of Cheng. The war ushered in the Sixteen Kingdoms era, more than a century of warfare between short-lived dynasties in the north and the Eastern Jin dynasty in the south.
war-of-the-fifth-coalition: Austria had been defeated in 1805 and spent three years reforming its army. Encouraged by events in Spain, where much of the French army was committed to the Peninsular War, it sought a new confrontation to avenge its defeats and regain lost territory. Its ally Russia had made peace with Napoleon at Tilsit, and at the Congress of Erfurt in 1808 agreed to support France if Austria attacked. Austria built the largest army in its history, conscripted from across the empire, but its quality was hampered by incomplete training and the army's multinational nature. The Austrians hoped Prussia would join them, but it stayed neutral.

On 10 April 1809 Austrian forces under Archduke Charles crossed the Inn into Bavaria, a French client state, without a formal declaration of war. The attack came about a week before Napoleon expected it, and the first French response under Louis-Alexandre Berthier was disorganised until Napoleon arrived on 17 April. After fighting around Regensburg and Landshut, Charles retreated eastwards but failed to reach Vienna before the French. A French crossing of the Danube was repulsed on 21–22 May at the Battle of Aspern-Essling. After more than six weeks of preparation the French crossed again, and on 5–6 July Napoleon won the Battle of Wagram, a close battle in which the Austrians withdrew in good order.

Elsewhere Archduke John defeated Eugène de Beauharnais at Caldiero on 30 April but was beaten at the Piave on 8 May and driven from Italy. The Austrians invaded the Duchy of Warsaw, and in July a British force of over 39,000 landed at Walcheren in the Netherlands, the largest British expedition of the Napoleonic Wars.

The Treaty of Schönbrunn, signed on 14 October 1809, took Carinthia, Carniola and the Adriatic ports from Austria, ending its access to the Mediterranean. West Galicia went to the Duchy of Warsaw, Salzburg to Bavaria and the district of Tarnopol to Russia. Austria lost over three million subjects, about 20 per cent of its population, and agreed to pay an indemnity of almost 85 million francs. After the war Napoleon married Marie Louise, the daughter of Emperor Francis.

Aspern-Essling showed that Napoleon could be beaten on the battlefield. The war also saw risings against French rule, among them Andreas Hofer's rebellion in Tyrol, the Gottscheer rebellion and revolts in Italy, which were suppressed but foreshadowed later nationalist risings.
war-of-the-first-coalition: Other European monarchies watched developments in France with alarm from 1791. Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor and brother of Queen Marie Antoinette, at first looked on calmly but grew concerned as the Revolution radicalised. On 27 August 1791 he and King Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening vague but severe consequences if harm came to Louis XVI. Paris saw this as a serious threat. France declared war on Austria on 20 April 1792, after the Assembly voted for it. The coalition was only loosely allied and fought with little coordination, since each power wanted to annex a different part of France.

The French army was disorganised and its first invasion of the Austrian Netherlands failed. In July 1792 an army under the Duke of Brunswick, mostly Prussians, invaded France and took Longwy and Verdun. At Valmy on 20 September a tactical draw boosted French morale and the Prussians chose to retreat. Two days later the National Convention proclaimed the French Republic. Dumouriez won at Jemappes on 6 November and occupied the Austrian Netherlands. After the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793 France declared war on Britain and the Netherlands, and the First Coalition took shape.

France met reverses at Neerwinden and in the Vendée. It formed the Committee of Public Safety and introduced the levée en masse. In 1794 victory at Fleurus won the Austrian Netherlands and the Rhineland. France seized the Low Countries and set up the Batavian Republic. Prussia withdrew and signed the Peace of Basel, and Spain made peace later in 1795.

In 1796 Napoleon Bonaparte separated the armies of Sardinia and Austria in Italy, forced peace on Sardinia, captured Milan and besieged Mantua. Archduke Charles defeated Jourdan on the Rhine. Mantua fell on 2 February 1797 with 18,000 Austrians surrendering.

Austria sued for peace in April 1797 and the Peace of Leoben led to the Treaty of Campo Formio in October. Austria ceded the Austrian Netherlands to France, and northern Italy became several French sister republics. The coalition collapsed, leaving only Britain at war with France.
war-of-the-flemish-succession: The dispute concerned two counties held by one ruler: Flanders, a fief of the king of France, and Hainault, a fief of the king of Germany. When Baldwin IX left on the Fourth Crusade in 1202 he placed them under his elder daughter Joan, who inherited them and died without heirs in 1244. Her sister Margaret had married Bouchard of Avesnes, a marriage annulled in 1221 on Joan's orders, but not before three children were born, among them John I of Avesnes. In 1223 Margaret married William II of Dampierre and had three more children, among them William III and Guy of Dampierre.

The half-brothers John I of Avesnes and William of Dampierre fought from Margaret's accession in 1244 until King Louis IX intervened in 1246, giving Flanders to William and Hainault, which was technically not his to give, to John. Margaret handed the government of Flanders to William in 1247 but kept Hainault for herself. William died in 1251 and Flanders passed to Guy.

With Louis away on the Seventh Crusade from 1248, John revolted against his mother and attacked Guy, and persuaded the German anti-king William of Holland to seize Hainault and the Flemish lands within the Empire. At the Battle of West-Capelle on 4 July 1253 Guy was defeated, and he and his mother were forced to respect Louis's division.

Margaret would not accept defeat and granted Hainault to Charles of Anjou, the king's brother, newly back from the crusade. Charles took up her cause against John I of Avesnes but failed to take Valenciennes and narrowly escaped death in a skirmish. When Louis returned in 1254 he confirmed his earlier arbitration and ordered his brother out of the conflict, and Charles went back to Provence. The king's second ruling closed the war and left John secure in Hainault, while Flanders stayed with Guy of Dampierre.
war-of-the-fourth-coalition: The Fourth Coalition formed within months of the collapse of the Third. After the victory at Austerlitz, Napoleon sought a general peace with Britain and Russia while trying to isolate Prussia. Several quarrels pushed Prussia towards war. Hanover, a German state in personal union with the British monarchy, had been secretly promised to Britain by Napoleon in the course of peace overtures, although it had earlier been offered to Prussia. In July 1806 Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine under his protection, which ended the Holy Roman Empire. Prussia took offence at this interference in German affairs, and on 9 October 1806 it declared war.

Napoleon marched the Grande Armée in three parallel columns through the Franconian Forest in his bataillon-carré formation. After skirmishes at Schleiz and Saalfeld, he defeated the Prussians at the double Battle of Jena–Auerstedt on 14 October 1806. At Auerstedt a single corps under Marshal Davout defeated the bulk of the Prussian army. The Prussians sustained 65,000 casualties and lost a further 150,000 prisoners, while the French suffered about 15,000 casualties. Napoleon entered Berlin on 27 October and issued the Berlin Decree on 21 November, beginning the Continental System.

The French then entered Poland, where Napoleon created the Duchy of Warsaw. The inconclusive and bloody Battle of Eylau on 7–8 February 1807 forced the Russians to withdraw north, and on 14 June Napoleon routed them at Friedland. Alexander I sued for peace at Tilsit. In Swedish Pomerania the French took Stralsund on 24 August 1807 after a siege.

In the Treaties of Tilsit of July 1807 Russia agreed to join the Continental System. Napoleon demanded much Prussian territory, from the lower Rhine west of the Elbe, which went to the new Kingdom of Westphalia under his brother Jérôme Bonaparte, and from the former Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which went to the Duchy of Warsaw, ruled by the king of Saxony. Napoleon was then master of almost all western and central Europe except Spain, Portugal and Austria. Britain remained at war, and Napoleon's invasion of Portugal began the Peninsular War.
war-of-the-golden-stool: After several earlier wars, British troops occupied Ashanti again in January 1896 and sent the Asantehene, Prempeh I, into exile. On 25 March 1900 the governor, Frederick Hodgson, reached Kumasi with a small force. In a speech known through an Ashanti translator he told the assembled leaders that Prempeh would not return, that they owed £160,000 a year with interest under the Treaty of Fomena of 1874, and that the Queen was entitled to the Golden Stool. The chiefs heard him in silence and began preparing for war on their return home. The anthropologist Edwin W. Smith later called it a singularly foolish speech, and Gaurav Desai notes that the Ashanti held the stool to embody the soul of the whole people.

Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, rallied the hesitant chiefs, saying that if the men would not fight, the women would. When Hodgson's deputy, Captain Cecil Armitage, searched the bush for the stool, his force was ambushed, and the survivors fell back to the Kumasi Fort, held by 18 Europeans and 500 Hausa troops with Maxim guns. The Ashanti besieged it, cut the telegraph and blocked the roads with 21 log barricades, making only one assault, on 29 April. On 23 June Hodgson, his wife and more than a hundred Hausas broke out.

A relief force of 1,000 men under Major James Willcocks, repulsed with heavy losses at the stockade of Kokofu on its way, attacked from Bekwai on 14 July and relieved the fort on the evening of 15 July, when its defenders were two days from surrender. Lieutenant Colonel Morland routed the Ashanti at Kokofu on 22 July, and in September flying columns defeated an Ashanti force at Obassa on 30 September and destroyed Kokofu.

The war cost the British and their allies about 1,000 dead. In 1901 the British exiled numerous chiefs, among them Yaa Asantewaa, to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921. In Parliament David Lloyd George attacked the government's policy over the stool, which the British went on seeking until 1921. Labourers who later found it and stripped its gold ornaments were sentenced to death by an Ashanti court, but British officials arranged their exile instead. Prempeh I was allowed to return in 1924, and Ashanti became part of Ghana in 1957.
war-of-the-julich-succession: By the early 17th century the spread of Lutheran and Calvinist teaching had met the Catholic resurgence of the Counter-Reformation, and conflicts such as the Cologne War and the Strasbourg Bishops' War had produced two armed camps, the Catholic League and the Protestant Union. The United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg covered some 14,000 km², lay close to the Spanish Road and had a booming economy, fed by refugees from the Eighty Years' War. Duke John William, who suffered from serious mental illness, died without heirs on 25 March 1609.

The Protestant claimants were Johann Sigismund, Elector of Brandenburg, and Wolfgang Wilhelm of Palatinate-Neuburg, whose small principality, hemmed in by Bavaria and the Electoral Palatinate, saw the rich duchies as a major prize. The Catholic Archduke Leopold V occupied Jülich.

The first phase ran from 10 June 1609 to 24 October 1610. Leopold was left without Habsburg money or troops, apart from 6,000 escudos sent secretly by the Spanish ambassador Baltasar de Zúñiga. Henry IV of France backed the claimants, perhaps moved also by the flight of the Prince and Princess of Condé to Brussels. At Schwäbisch Hall, from 10 January 1610, the Protestant Union agreed that the claimants would raise 5,000 infantry and 1,300 cavalry, the Union 4,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, and Henry 8,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry. Leopold was defeated, and the Treaty of Dortmund set up a temporary joint rule.

The two possessors then fell out. Wolfgang Wilhelm became a Catholic, Johann Sigismund announced his conversion to Calvinism on Christmas Day 1613, and Brandenburg's new viceroy, George William, proved popular with the Jülich nobility. In Aachen, Protestants had expelled the Catholic council in a riot on 5 July 1611. In May 1614 300 Dutch troops ejected the Neuburg garrison from Jülich, and Wolfgang Wilhelm answered by seizing Düsseldorf. Ambrogio Spinola led about 20,000 men to Aachen, besieged it from 24 August 1614 and restored the old council.

Spinola and Maurice of Nassau opened peace talks on 13 October 1614, with Spanish and Dutch envoys standing for Neuburg and Brandenburg and mediators from Cologne, France and England. The resulting Treaty of Xanten favoured Spain but did not settle the matter. In the Thirty Years' War the duchies saw the Siege of Jülich of 1621-1622 and were burdened by Swedish, Imperial and Hessian troops, and the rivalry of Neuburg and Brandenburg flared again in the Düsseldorf Cow War. The crisis drew in Spain, the Dutch Republic, France and England and is counted among the European wars of religion.
war-of-the-league-of-cambrai: By the end of 1503 the Venetian Senate had taken Rimini, Faenza and other cities of the Romagna from the dispossessed lords who offered to submit. In the spring of 1508 Venice provoked Pope Julius II by appointing its own candidate to the bishopric of Vicenza. Julius called on Christian nations to subdue Venice, and on 10 December 1508 the Papacy, France, the Holy Roman Empire and Ferdinand II of Aragon concluded the League of Cambrai, which provided for the partition of Venice's territory in Italy.

In April 1509 France declared war on Venice, and on 27 April Julius imposed an interdict on the Venetians. On 14 May Bartolomeo d'Alviano confronted the French at the Battle of Agnadello. Outnumbered, he asked his cousin Niccolò di Pitigliano for reinforcements; Pitigliano ordered him to break off and went on his way, but Alviano fought on, and his army was surrounded and destroyed. Venice recovered Padua, which withstood a siege in September 1509.

In 1510 Julius, alarmed by the French presence in Italy, made peace with Venice, and the League of Cambrai fell apart. On 4 October 1511 he proclaimed the Holy League of the Papal States, Venice and Spain, later joined by England and the Swiss. The French won at Ravenna on 11 April 1512 but were driven from Milan. After Julius's death Venice turned to France, and on 23 March 1513 the two agreed at Blois to divide northern Italy between them.

The Swiss routed the French at Novara on 6 June 1513, and the English won the Battle of the Spurs on 16 August. Francis I, who had succeeded Louis XII, renewed the Venetian alliance in 1515 and won a decisive victory over the Swiss and Milan at Marignano on 13 and 14 September 1515.

Ferdinand II died in January 1516 and was succeeded by his grandson, the future Emperor Charles V. In August 1516 the Treaty of Noyon between Charles and Francis recognised French claims to Milan and Spanish claims to Naples.

Maximilian made one more attempt to invade Lombardy, then negotiated, and the Treaty of Brussels, concluded on 6 December 1516, accepted French occupation of Milan and confirmed Venetian claims to the remaining imperial possessions in Lombardy, except for Cremona. By January 1517 Verona had been surrendered to the Venetians, and celebrations in Venice ran from January to March 1517. The treaties essentially returned the map of Italy to the situation of 1508. The peace lasted only four years: the rivalry of the Valois and the Habsburgs and the election of Charles V as emperor in 1519 led to the Italian War of 1521-26.
war-of-the-league-of-cognac: Alarmed by the French defeat in the Italian War of 1521, Pope Clement VII and the Republic of Venice set about building an alliance to drive Charles V from Italy. Francis I of France had been captured at Pavia and had signed the Treaty of Madrid, leaving his two eldest sons in Spain as surety. Once released he repudiated the treaty as signed under duress and promised to help the pope.

The League of Cognac was formed on 22 May 1526 in the French town. Its members were Francis, who wanted revenge for his defeat, the pope, whose authority had been challenged over benefices in Spain and Naples, the republics of Venice and Florence, which feared a larger imperial invasion, and Francesco II Sforza, Duke of Milan, whose duchy was under imperial occupation. Henry VIII of England refused to join.

A month after its formation the League seized Lodi, but imperial troops marched into Lombardy and forced Sforza to leave Milan. In September 1526 the Viceroy of Naples and Cardinal Pompeo Colonna defeated the papal forces and briefly held Rome. Charles V then gathered 14,000 German landsknechte under Georg Frundsberg and 6,000 Spanish soldiers under the Duke of Bourbon, who advanced on Rome. When Bourbon fell in the assault, the underpaid imperial troops mutinied and sacked the city. The pope took refuge in the Castel Sant'Angelo, his flight made possible by the Swiss Guards' last stand.

In August 1527 a French army under the Viscount of Lautrec entered Italy, took Genoa with the help of Andrea Doria, and besieged Naples on 29 April 1528. Doria then defected to Charles V, plague broke out in the French camps, killing Lautrec, and the remnant of the army capitulated at Aversa in August 1528. A second French army under the Count of Saint-Pol was defeated at Landriano on 21 June 1529.

Negotiations at Cambrai were conducted mainly by Francis's mother, Louise of Savoy, and Charles's aunt, Margaret of Austria, so the treaty was called the Peace of the Ladies. Signed on 3 August 1529, it required Francis to renounce his claims to Artois, Flanders and Tournai and to pay a ransom of two million gold écus for his sons.

At Bologna Clement VII gave absolution to those who had sacked Rome and promised to crown Charles King of Naples and Holy Roman Emperor, and Francesco Sforza was allowed to return to Milan on payment of 900,000 scudi. Florence alone kept resisting. In 1530 imperial forces won the battle of Gavinana, in which the Prince of Orange was killed, and the republic capitulated ten days later. The pope installed Alessandro de' Medici as Duke of Florence.
war-of-the-mantuan-succession: The House of Gonzaga had ruled Mantua since 1308 and acquired Montferrat by marriage in 1574. Both territories were part of the Holy Roman Empire and lay beside the Spanish-governed Duchy of Milan, guarding the supply route known as the Spanish Road. When Vincenzo II died in December 1627, the strongest claimant was his cousin Charles Gonzaga, Duke of Nevers, a French peer, whose son Charles had married Vincenzo's niece Maria Gonzaga, heiress of Montferrat, three days before. The Spanish commander Gonzalo de Córdoba and Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy, had already agreed to partition Montferrat, Spain taking the fortress of Casale Monferrato.

The siege of Casale began in March 1628, while Savoyard forces took Trino and Nizza Monferrato. After the surrender of La Rochelle in October 1628, Louis XIII stormed the barricades of the Pas de Suse in March 1629, lifted the siege and took Pinerolo. Emperor Ferdinand II, freed by the Treaty of Lübeck of June 1629, sent 30,000 troops from Germany under Ramboldo, Count of Collalto, and Ambrogio Spinola replaced Córdoba and renewed the siege of Casale.

Bubonic plague struck both sides, and about 35% of the population of Northern Italy died between 1629 and 1631. At Ostiglia in April 1630 Imperial troops killed around 600 civilians, by contemporary estimates. Reduced to 700 effectives, the garrison of Mantua surrendered to Gallas and Aldringen on 18 July 1630, and the sack reportedly yielded booty worth over 18 million ducats. Casale held out, and on 29 October the Spanish withdrew under a truce negotiated by the papal representative Mazarin.

Ferdinand needed his troops against Gustavus Adolphus, who had landed in Pomerania with 18,000 men. Louis XIII refused to ratify the Treaty of Ratisbonne signed by his envoy Father Joseph on 13 October 1630, and the Treaty of Cherasco of 19 June 1631 confirmed Nevers in return for minor concessions to Savoy. French garrisons stayed in Casale and Pinerolo, so Spain gained nothing for its outlay of 10 million escudos.

Plague and the sack cut the population of Mantua by over 70% between 1628 and 1631, and it took decades to recover. The diversion of Imperial resources helped the Swedes establish themselves in the Empire until 1648, and the split the war opened between the Habsburgs and the papacy made it acceptable for France to employ Protestant allies against fellow Catholics.
war-of-the-pacific: After independence, the frontiers of the Atacama coast were uncertain. The Boundary Treaty of 1866 set the border at 24° S and shared the tax on mineral exports between 23° and 25° S, and the arrangement caused discontent. In February 1873 Peru and Bolivia signed a secret treaty of alliance against Chile, revealed only in 1879. In 1874 a new boundary treaty kept the border at 24° S, gave Bolivia the tax revenue between 23° and 24° S and guaranteed Chilean enterprises against tax increases for 25 years.

In February 1878 Bolivia nevertheless raised taxes on the Chilean company Compañía de Salitres y Ferrocarril de Antofagasta, a ten-centavo tax that gave the conflict the name Ten Cents War. Chile asked for arbitration, but the Bolivian president Hilarión Daza treated it as a domestic matter, cancelled the company's licence and seized its property.

On the day of the planned auction in February 1879, about 200 Chilean soldiers landed at Antofagasta and seized it without resistance, supported by a local population that was 93 to 95 per cent Chilean. Peru tried to mediate while preparing for war. None of the three states had a general staff or medical corps, and Chile's army had shrunk to 2,400 men. Control of the sea was decisive, because supply by sea was faster than moving it through the Atacama Desert. For the first five months the war was naval, and Peruvian raiding delayed the Chilean invasion by six months until the capture of the ironclad Huáscar at the Battle of Angamos gave Chile naval supremacy. Chile then occupied the Peruvian province of Tarapacá.

Bolivia withdrew after the Battle of Tacna on 26 May 1880, leaving Peru to fight alone. Chilean forces occupied Lima in January 1881. Remnants of the Peruvian army and irregulars under Cáceres waged a guerrilla war, and in Peru's highlands there were also uprisings of indigenous peasants and Chinese labourers.

Chile and Peru signed the Treaty of Ancón on 20 October 1883. Peru ceded Tarapacá, and Chile was to occupy Tacna and Arica for ten years before a plebiscite, which the two countries failed to agree on for decades. In 1929 a settlement mediated under President Herbert Hoover gave Arica to Chile and Tacna to Peru. Bolivia signed a truce in 1884, and the Treaty of Peace and Friendship of 1904 ceded the whole Antofagasta region to Chile, in return for a railway from Arica to La Paz and freedom of transit for Bolivian trade. Authors have called the war a national trauma for Peru and Bolivia, and Bolivians commemorate the lost coast each year on 23 March.
war-of-the-polish-succession: Since 1572 the king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania had been elected by the nobility, and the Sejm, the legislature, was often paralysed by the liberum veto. By the early 18th century neighbours, especially Russia, interfered increasingly. Augustus II died on 1 February 1733. In the secret Treaty of the Three Black Eagles of 1732, Russia, Austria and Prussia had agreed to oppose both Stanisław Leszczyński and Augustus II's son, and to support Manuel of Portugal. France's chief minister Cardinal Fleury backed Stanisław, whose daughter Marie Leszczyńska was married to Louis XV, hoping to weaken Austria and secure Lorraine. Philip V of Spain wanted to regain Italian territories, and the two Bourbon courts signed a Pacte de Famille in 1733.

On 12 September 1733 a sejm of 12,000 delegates elected Leszczyński, but about 3,000 nobles under Russian protection elected Frederick August II of Saxony as Augustus III on 5 October. Russian troops under Peter Lacy took Warsaw, and Stanisław fled to Danzig, which capitulated in June 1734; he escaped to France. France declared war on Austria and Saxony on 10 October 1733 and soon took Lorraine and the fortress of Kehl. Prince Eugene of Savoy could not relieve Philippsburg, which fell in July 1734, and the Duke of Berwick was killed there.

In northern Italy, Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia and the French took Milan, but the allies quarrelled and made little progress against Mantua. In the south Don Carlos led a largely Spanish army into Naples, defeated the Austrians at Bitonto in May 1734 and subdued Sicily. Austria was left isolated: Britain and the Dutch Republic stayed neutral, and Robert Walpole argued that the Anglo-Austrian alliance was purely defensive.

A preliminary peace was made in October 1735 and ratified in the Treaty of Vienna in November 1738. Augustus III was confirmed as king of Poland. Stanisław received Lorraine, which passed to France on his death in 1766, and Francis Stephen of Lorraine became heir to Tuscany. Don Carlos gave up Parma, which went to Austria, and was confirmed as king of Naples and Sicily, while Charles Emmanuel gained territory west of the Ticino including Novara and Tortona. France recognised the Pragmatic Sanction. The war reaffirmed that Poland-Lithuania's affairs, including the election of its ruler, were controlled by the great powers.
war-of-the-portuguese-succession: King Sebastian I of Portugal died at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578 and was succeeded by his great-uncle, Cardinal Henry, who had been his regent after 1557. Henry renounced his clerical offices to marry and continue the Aviz dynasty, but Pope Gregory XIII, aligned with the Habsburgs, would not release him from his vows, and he died without naming a council of regency to choose a successor.

Several claimants came forward. By feudal custom the nearest heir was the boy Ranuccio Farnese, but his father was an ally and subject of Philip II of Spain, so his claim was not pressed. His aunt Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, had a strong claim, but Portugal had never had a recognised reigning queen.

Philip II descended from Manuel I through his mother, Infanta Isabella of Portugal, and had the support of the high nobility and clergy. António, Prior of Crato, a grandson of Manuel I through an illegitimate line, had wider popular support.

António proclaimed himself King of Portugal and of the Algarves at Santarém on 24 July 1580 and was acclaimed in several towns, but he governed on the mainland for only 33 days. On 25 August the Spanish army under Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, Duke of Alba, defeated him at the Battle of Alcântara, and two days later Alba took Lisbon.

In early 1581 António fled to France and then sailed for the Azores, which Spain had not yet occupied, with French adventurers under the Florentine exile Filippo Strozzi. A Spanish fleet under Álvaro de Bazán, Marquis of Santa Cruz, defeated them off Terceira and São Miguel on 26 and 27 July 1582. António's attempt to rule from Terceira, where he even minted coins, ended in 1583.

The Cortes of Tomar recognised Philip II as King Philip I of Portugal in 1581. In 1589 António tried again for Lisbon with English forces under Sir Francis Drake and Sir John Norreys, but the people did not rise and the attempt was abandoned. Portugal and Spain stayed united in the Iberian Union, formally separate and with their own administrations, until 1640, when the Braganza line took the throne in John IV.
war-of-the-quadruple-alliance: Under the Peace of Utrecht of 1713, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, Spain ceded Sardinia to Austria and Sicily to Savoy. Recovering them was a priority for Philip V of Spain, a priority reinforced by his chief minister Cardinal Giulio Alberoni and by his second wife Elisabeth Farnese, both natives of Parma.

Utrecht barred Spain from ever uniting with France or Austria, and Philip gave up any claim to the French throne. After deaths in the French royal family in 1711 and 1712 made him heir presumptive to the young Louis XV, he cast doubt on that renunciation. Britain and France agreed an alliance in 1716 and formed the Triple Alliance with the Dutch in January 1717 to enforce the terms.

Spanish forces landed on Sardinia in August 1717 and held it by November, meeting little opposition. In July 1718 the Spanish landed 30,000 men on Sicily. By then Austria had signed a treaty with the Ottoman Empire and joined the Quadruple Alliance.
