On 11 August a British squadron under Sir George Byng destroyed the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Cape Passaro. An Austrian force was defeated at the First Battle of Milazzo on 15 October. After the discovery of the Cellamare conspiracy, Alberoni's plot to replace the regent of France with Philip V, France declared war, and by 17 December 1718 France, Britain and Austria were all at war with Spain; the Dutch joined in August 1719.

In April 1719 a French army under the Duke of Berwick invaded the Basque districts and besieged San Sebastián. An expedition under the Duke of Ormonde to put James Stuart on the British throne was scattered by a storm in March 1719, and a small force of Spanish marines was defeated with its Highland allies at Glen Shiel in June. A British raid took Vigo in October. In Sicily the Austrians under Count de Mercy lost at Francavilla on 20 June 1719 but won the second Battle of Milazzo, took Messina in October and besieged Palermo.

Philip dismissed Alberoni in December 1719 and made peace by the Treaty of The Hague on 17 February 1720. He relinquished all territory captured in the war, but his third surviving son's right to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza was recognised. France returned Pensacola and its conquests in northern Spain in exchange for commercial benefits, and Victor Amadeus II of Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia. The war was unusual in the 18th century in having Britain and France on the same side.
war-of-the-second-coalition: The war followed the War of the First Coalition (1792–97), which ended with the Treaty of Leoben on 18 April 1797 and the Treaty of Campo Formio in October 1797, leaving Britain to fight on alone. Peace between France and Austria was uneasy: the French demanded territory the treaty did not name, the Habsburgs were reluctant to hand over what it did, and in 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte's seizure of Malta angered Emperor Paul I of Russia, the honorary head of the order of knights that ruled the island.

The coalition took months to form. Naples allied with Austria on 19 May 1798 and with Russia on 29 November, and Russia allied with the Ottoman Empire on 23 December and with Britain on 26 December. Prussia declined to join.

Britain and Russia aimed to stop the French Republic's expansion and restore the monarchy, while Austria, weakened and deep in debt, sought chiefly to recover its position. In 1799 the Russian general Alexander Suvorov won a series of victories in Italy and drove the French back to the Alps. The Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland failed, and in Switzerland an Austro-Russian army was routed at the Second Battle of Zurich. These reverses, and British searches of shipping in the Baltic, led Russia to leave the coalition. Napoleon returned from Egypt in October 1799 and a coup made him First Consul.

In 1800 Napoleon led an army across the Great St. Bernard Pass and narrowly defeated the Austrians at the Battle of Marengo, after which Austria agreed to evacuate Piedmont, Liguria and Lombardy. Moreau invaded Bavaria and won the Battle of Hohenlinden, and the Armistice of Steyr followed on 25 December. In 1801 the British navy attacked the Danish fleet at the Battle of Copenhagen, after the Second League of Armed Neutrality had formed against searches of neutral ships, and the Ottomans and British forced the French in Egypt to surrender.

Austria signed the Armistice of Treviso on 16 January 1801 and, on 9 February, the Treaty of Lunéville for the whole Holy Roman Empire, in effect accepting the terms of Campo Formio. France kept all its earlier gains and obtained new lands in Tuscany, while Austria was granted Venetia and the former Venetian Dalmatia. Most other allies signed separate peaces in 1801. Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens in March 1802, followed by the Ottomans in June 1802. The peace lasted several months, until Britain declared war on France in May 1803 and began the Napoleonic Wars. The coalition had failed to overthrow the revolutionary government, largely because of differences of strategy among its three major powers.
war-of-the-sixth-coalition: Napoleon invaded Russia in June 1812 to compel Emperor Alexander I to remain in the Continental System. The Grande Armée numbered as many as 650,000 men, about half of them French. After the inconclusive Battle of Borodino and the French occupation of Moscow, which Alexander refused to bargain over, Napoleon was forced to withdraw. The Prussian corps that had been compelled to serve with him was neutralised by the Convention of Tauroggen, signed on 30 December 1812 without the consent of the Prussian king, and the Treaty of Kalisch on 28 February 1813 ranged Prussia on the Allied side.

Napoleon raised new forces and inflicted 40,000 casualties on the Allies at Lützen on 2 May and at Bautzen on 20 and 21 May 1813, though he lost about as many men. An armistice ran from 4 June to 13 August, during which Austria joined the Allies. Napoleon won at Dresden on 26 and 27 August, but at the Battle of Leipzig, the Battle of Nations, from 16 to 19 October, a French army reinforced to 191,000 faced more than 430,000 Allied troops. He retreated in fairly good order, though the bridge over the White Elster was blown early and 30,000 men were left to be captured.

Meanwhile Wellington routed Joseph Bonaparte's army at Vitoria on 21 June 1813. In France, Napoleon won several battles in the Six Days' Campaign in early 1814 with fewer than 80,000 men against a Coalition force of 370,000 to 405,000. At the Treaty of Chaumont on 9 March the Allies agreed to keep the Coalition until Napoleon's total defeat. Their armies entered Paris on 31 March.

On 2 April the French Senate declared Napoleon deposed. He wished to fight on, but on 4 April his marshals, led by Ney, refused to march. Napoleon abdicated on 11 April 1814, and the Treaty of Paris followed on 30 May. He was exiled to Elba and the Bourbon monarchy was restored under Louis XVIII. The Congress of Vienna, from September 1814 to June 1815, was held to redraw the map of Europe. Norway declared independence on 17 May 1814, and Bernadotte invaded it in July.
war-of-the-spanish-succession: Charles II of Spain became king in 1665 at the age of four, and his poor health and lack of children made the succession a long-standing European diplomatic issue. Louis XIV of France and the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I were both grandsons of Philip III of Spain, through his daughters, and the Spanish throne could pass through women. Spain remained a global power supported by silver from the Americas, yet most of that income was already committed to creditors, and the Bourbons later found the empire bankrupt and almost defenceless, with fewer than 15,000 troops in Spain itself and a navy of 20 ships.

Charles II died in November 1700 and named Philip of Anjou his universal heir, with the support of Louis XIV. Philip was proclaimed king on 16 November 1700, which triggered the war. Britain and the Dutch Republic were driven largely by access to Spanish markets in the Americas, and they feared that France or Austria would acquire an undivided Spanish monarchy.

The Second Grand Alliance backed Charles of Austria. In Italy, Prince Eugene of Savoy led an Imperial army against the French from May 1701, and by February 1702 victories at Carpi, Chiari and Cremona forced them behind the Adda. In the Low Countries the Allies took Kaiserswerth, Venlo, Roermond, Liège and, in 1703, Bonn, but failed to take Antwerp. Britain's interest lay in protecting its Mediterranean trade routes, and by 1708 it held permanent bases at Gibraltar and Menorca. The fighting spread to North America, where it is known as Queen Anne's War, and to the West Indies.

By 1709 the Allies had put France on the defensive, but Philip had secured his position in Spain, and the Great Frost of that year caused famine in France and Spain. Talks at Geertruidenberg in 1710 broke down. The pro-peace Tories won the British election of October 1710, and when Charles of Austria became Holy Roman emperor in 1711 the British government began negotiating its withdrawal.

The Peace of Utrecht of 1713 was followed by the treaties of Rastatt and Baden in 1714. Philip was confirmed as king of Spain but renounced his rights in the French line, and Spain ceded the Spanish Netherlands, most of its Italian possessions, Gibraltar and Menorca. Austria gained the bulk of the Spanish Netherlands, together with Milan, Mantua, Naples and Sardinia, and Britain became the leading naval and commercial power while the Dutch were left bankrupt. Catalonia fought on until the fall of Barcelona in September 1714. Philip's Bourbon successors have held the Spanish throne ever since. Louis XIV died on 1 September 1715.
war-of-the-third-coalition: The Peace of Amiens broke down in 1803, and Britain declared war on France on 18 May 1803. Tensions had grown as Napoleon made himself president of the Italian Republic, annexed Piedmont and kept French troops in the Netherlands. After he crowned himself Emperor on 2 December 1804, the annexation of Genoa, Parma and Piacenza and his coronation as King of Italy left little doubt about his intentions. On 21 January 1805 William Pitt the Younger proposed an alliance with Russia and Austria. Sweden joined Britain in December 1804, Russia on 11 April 1805 and Austria on 9 August; Naples and Sicily completed the coalition on 11 September. Prussia stayed neutral.

Napoleon turned the army he had gathered at Boulogne for an invasion of England towards the Rhine. In the Ulm campaign, 210,000 French troops marched east to envelop the Austrian army of General Mack, who had made Ulm the centre of his defence while waiting for the Russians under Mikhail Kutuzov. When Mack heard that Bernadotte's corps had crossed Prussian Ansbach, he chose to stay at Ulm instead of retreating south. Murat forced General Werneck to surrender with 8,000 men at Trochtelfingten on 19 October. Two days later the Royal Navy under Horatio Nelson defeated the combined Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar.

At Austerlitz, Napoleon gave the Allies the impression that his army was weak and deliberately thinned his right flank, expecting them to weaken their own centre in attacking it. He ordered Davout's corps to march 110 km in 48 hours to support that flank, then sent Soult's IV Corps against the centre, saying, "One sharp blow and the war is over." In Italy, the French defeated the Austrians at Caldiero between 29 and 31 October. In February 1806 Masséna invaded Naples, and King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily under British naval protection.

On 26 December 1805 Austria and France signed the Treaty of Pressburg, which confirmed Austrian cessions in Italy and Germany and imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs. After Austerlitz Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, whose German states pledged to raise an army of 63,000 men. In 1806 Francis II abdicated the imperial throne and the Holy Roman Empire ceased to exist. The French lost 12,000 killed, 22,200 wounded and 5,000 captured in 1805. Peace was not lasting: neither Russia nor Britain stopped fighting, and Prussian worries about French influence led to the War of the Fourth Coalition in 1806.
war-of-the-two-peters: At the start of the second half of the fourteenth century Castile was torn by the civil war between its king, Peter of Castile, and his half-brother Henry of Trastámara. Peter of Castile sought the Kingdom of Valencia, with parts of Murcia, Elche, Alicante and Orihuela, while Peter IV of Aragon wished to dominate the Mediterranean against Castile and its ally Genoa. A naval incident raised tension: Catalan galleys under Mossèn Francesc de Perellós, sailing with letters of marque from the King of Aragon, seized two Genoese ships at Sanlúcar de Barrameda, and Peter of Castile chased him as far as Tavira without catching him.

England backed Peter of Castile and France backed Peter IV of Aragon, who also supported Henry of Trastámara, and the kingdoms of Navarre and Portugal were drawn in as well. The war can thus be seen as an extension of the wider Hundred Years' War and also of the First Castilian Civil War.

The fighting lay mostly along the border. Castile took Tarazona on 9 March 1357, and a truce followed on 8 May. After Castilian gains early in 1361 the peace of Terrer of 18 May 1361 returned all conquered places to their lords. In June 1362 Peter of Castile allied with Charles II of Navarre at Soria and with Edward III of England and the Black Prince, then invaded Aragon without a declaration of war while Peter IV was at Perpignan without troops; he failed, however, to take Calatayud.

In 1363 Castile took Tarazona again, then Cariñena, Teruel, Segorbe and Morvedre, and pressed into Valencia, taking Alicante, Elda and Gandia; the peace of Morvedre arranged by the papal nuncio Jean de la Grange on 2 July 1363 was never ratified. With Moorish allies from Granada the Castilians ravaged southern Valencia and besieged Orihuela without success in 1364. From 1366 Peter of Castile was fighting for his own throne against Henry, who had the help of Bertrand du Guesclin and his free companies, until Henry killed him at Montiel in 1369.

Castile recovered districts that had passed to Aragon, among them the lordship of Molina, and Peter IV's daughter Eleanor married John I of Castile. Though Aragon gained the upper hand, the war, with the Black Death, drought and locusts, ruined its economy and reduced its population, and the Cathedral of Tarazona was destroyed. The war is also believed to have built up the administrative and military forces that led to the union of Castile and Aragon in the next century.
warangal: Warangal lies at an average elevation of 266 metres on the eastern Deccan Plateau, a landscape of granite rocks and hills. No major river flows near it, so the city relies on the Kakatiya Canal for water. During the 160 years of Kakatiya rule between 1163 and 1323 it was known by names such as Orugallu, Ekashila Nagaram and Omatikonda, all meaning a single stone, in reference to a huge granite boulder in the Warangal fort. Three lakes, Bhadrakali, Dharmasagar and Waddepally, lie around it, with several hills carrying temples.

Beta Raja I founded the Kakatiya dynasty, and his son Prola Raja I shifted the capital to Hanamkonda. Under Ganapathideva it moved from Hanamkonda to Warangal. Later rulers included Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Prataparudra and Rani Rudrama Devi, the only woman to rule the Telugu region. Kakatiya inscriptions praised Warangal as the best city in the Telugu region, up to the shores of the ocean, and Marco Polo mentioned the dynasty's cultural and administrative distinction. The Kakatiyas left a fortress, four massive stone gateways, the Swayambhu temple of Shiva and the Ramappa temple near Ramappa Lake.

In 1323 the Delhi Sultanate defeated the Kakatiya dynasty, and Juna Khan, crown prince of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, conquered the city and renamed it Sultanpur. In 1336 the Musunuri Nayaks, who united 72 Nayak chieftains, recaptured it, restored the name Orugallu and ruled for fifty years. Warangal then belonged to the Bahmani Sultanate and the Sultanate of Golconda. Aurangzeb conquered Golconda in 1687, and in 1724 the southern provinces split away as the state of Hyderabad, which was annexed to India in 1948. Telangana state, including Warangal, was formed on 2 June 2014.

Together with Kazipet and Hanamkonda, Warangal forms the Warangal Tri-City. The Warangal Fort, the Thousand Pillar Temple and the Ramappa Temple are listed among the World Heritage Sites recognised by UNESCO. The Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, the gateway of the fort, appears in the emblem of Telangana. The Greater Warangal Municipal Corporation, established in 1899, is one of the oldest urban local bodies in India. The women of the city celebrate the floral festival of Bathukamma, honouring the goddess with flowers for nine days.
waren-muritz: Waren lies at the northern end of Lake Müritz, which has an area of 117 square kilometres and is the largest inland lake lying entirely within Germany, about 40 kilometres west of Neubrandenburg. It also lies on several smaller lakes, and the Herrensee is in the middle of the town. Waren was the capital of the former district of Müritz until the district reform of 2011. Its name may come from a Slavic word for a place of crows or ravens, or from the Germanic Warini; the lake's name derives from a Wend word for sea.

Claudius Ptolemy mentioned a place called Virunum around 150 CE that is identified with Waren. The medieval town was founded around 1260 by settlers from Westphalia, on the trade route from Stargard Land to Wismar, near a castle and a Slavic village. It grew up around St George's Church, first mentioned in 1273, with a New Town around St Mary's Church, which was merged with it in 1325. Waren is called a civitas in 1292 and an oppidum from 1331, and received fishing rights on the Müritz in 1306. From 1347 to 1425 it was the residence of a branch of the House of Werle.

Fires in 1568, 1637, 1671, 1673 and 1699, and the Thirty Years' War, repeatedly devastated the town. The present town hall dates from 1791 to 1797. The canalisation of the Elde and the Bolter Canal brought an economic boom in the 19th century, and railways opened in 1879, 1885 and 1886 made Waren a transport hub. During the Kapp Putsch in March 1920 a Freikorps group under Stephan von le Fort fired on the town from Gallows Hill, killing five people; a bullet hole at the town hall recalls it.

Under the Nazis the Jewish community, some 150 in the mid-19th century, dwindled to nine by April 1938, and none remained in 1942. From 1936 a metal works supplying military aircraft used thousands of prisoners of war and forced labourers. The Red Army occupied the town without a fight on 1 May 1945. Large parts of the old town were demolished in the 1970s, which prompted a citizens' movement to save it, and the centre was renovated from 1991.

Waren has been a state-approved health resort since 1 May 1999. Its two brick churches, St George's from the early 14th century and St Mary's, a town hall on the New Market and a harbour with old warehouses stand in the historic centre. The Müritzeum is a freshwater aquarium and an information centre for the Müritz National Park, and the town lies beside the park and the Nossentiner/Schwinzer Heath Nature Park.
wareru: Wareru was born Ma Gadu on 20 March 1253 to poor peasants in the village of Tagaw Wun, near present-day Thaton, about 100 km north of Martaban; his background was Mon, Shan or both. Around 1272 he took over his father's trade with the Siamese kingdom of Sukhothai, found work in its royal elephant stables and rose to captain of the stables by the start of King Ram Khamhaeng's reign. Mon and Thai chronicles say he then eloped with the king's daughter, though George Cœdès called the story a legend and Michael Aung-Thwin a probable trope.

Back home Gadu made his village into a fortified town, Donwun. When the governor of Martaban, Aleimma, planned a rebellion against Pagan, Gadu offered him his sister in marriage, lured him to a wedding at Donwun and had him killed. Gadu took Martaban, conquered Kampalani and, through his minister Laik-Gi, won recognition from Ram Khamhaeng as a vassal king. He declared himself king of Martaban on 30 January 1287.

Around 1290 he commissioned a law book in Mon, the Wareru Dhammathat. Allied by marriage with Tarabya of Pegu, he broke the siege of Pegu by a large Pagan army, in the dry season of 1295 to 1296 by one reckoning, and drove the invaders from the Irrawaddy delta; neither Pagan nor its successors tried a major invasion of the south again until 1385. Late in 1296 he beat Tarabya in single combat on war elephants and later executed him for plotting against him. Ruling the three Mon-speaking provinces, he gained recognition from Yuan China in 1298.

In January 1307 the two sons of Tarabya, whom he had raised, stabbed him to death in revenge for their father; they were caught and executed. Having no son, he was succeeded by his brother Gada as Hkun Law. His kingdom became the only Mon-speaking polity left after the 1290s and the wealthiest of the post-Pagan states into the 16th century, helping the Mons emerge as a coherent ethnicity. His code was adopted by the First Toungoo Empire, translated into Burmese, Pali and Siamese, and shaped the later law books of Ayutthaya and Restored Toungoo Burma.
warka-vase: German archaeologists found the vase as 15 fragments during their sixth excavation season at Uruk, in 1933 and 1934. The expedition's field book records it as find number W14873 under 2 January 1934, a large alabaster container about 96 cm high with flat reliefs. It lay in level III of the Eanna district, of the Jemdat Nasr period, also called Uruk III, together with other objects, among them fragments of a second vase, which the excavators took for votive offerings. As it was not found in its original place, the level gives only its latest possible date.

The vase had already been broken and repaired in antiquity with copper bands. Because the reconstruction of its base is uncertain, its full height is estimated at 105 to 110 cm, of which the relief occupies 92 cm. The mouth measures 38 cm across, and the wall is 2 cm thick at the top and thickens towards the bottom.

The reliefs run in three registers of 25, 17.5 and 20.5 cm from top to bottom; a band divides the lowest, so the vase is sometimes said to have four. At the bottom are the plants of the Tigris and Euphrates delta, natural reeds and cultivated grain such as date palm, barley and wheat, and above them rams and ewes walk in single file in strict profile. In the middle register nude men carry bowls and jars of fruit and grain.

The top register is a single scene at a temple. A female deity stands before two bundles of reeds and is offered a bowl of fruit and grain by a nude figure, while a ruler-figure in a ceremonial kilt and long belt faces her at the head of the procession. The scene may represent the ritual marriage of the goddess and her consort, which ensured the continued vitality of Uruk.

A plaster cast of the vase stood for many decades in room 5 of the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin. During the 2003 invasion of Iraq, in April, looters wrenched the original from its case in the National Museum of Iraq, snapping it at the base. On 12 June 2003 three unidentified men brought it back to the museum during an amnesty, broken into 14 pieces. It was restored and is displayed in the Iraq Museum as number IM19606.
warli: Until the 1870s the Warli were the primary owners of all land in the Umbergaon, Dhanu and Palghar talukas of the Thane district. In that decade the British colonial administration brought their territories under direct control, and outsiders, among them Mahajans and petty officers, used the Warlis' illiteracy to take their lands. The Warli became labourers on land they had owned. Under the begar system they cultivated the landlords' holdings without pay; as sharecroppers on small plots of inferior land they surrendered at least half the produce. Records of the period document public whippings, torture and the sexual oppression of Warli women.

In 1939 an inquiry by the British magistrate David Symington found that their living conditions had reached an abysmal depth. Organised resistance followed, led by Shamrao and Godavari Parulekar. In May 1945 about 5,000 Warlis gathered at Zari and pledged to end the begar system. In October 1945 police fired on a rally of 7,000 people at Talwada, killing five activists, among them the leader Jethya Gangad. The begar system was abolished and minimum wages were established, and by the early 1950s most of the feudal exactions had ended.

The Warli speak Varli, an unwritten language of the southern zone of the Indo-Aryan languages. They have animistic beliefs of their own and have also adopted many Hindu beliefs. Traditionally semi-nomadic, living in small groups led by a headman, they are today mainly agriculturists who grow rice and wheat among other crops. Married women wear toe rings and necklaces, and some Warli practise polygyny.

Their ritual paintings are made inside the huts, for occasions such as weddings and harvests, in white rice paste on walls of branches, earth and cow dung, with a bamboo stick chewed at the end as a brush. At the centre stands a square, the chauk, which in one type encloses the mother goddess Palaghata, symbol of fertility; around it are scenes of hunting, fishing, farming and dancing. Human and animal bodies are drawn as two triangles joined at the tip.

Painting was the preserve of Warli women until the late 1970s. In that decade Jivya Soma Mashe and his son Balu Mashe began to paint outside any ritual, as an artistic pursuit of their own. The writer Yashodhara Dalmia, in The Painted World of the Warlis, claimed that the tradition reaches back to 2500 or 3000 BCE.
warren-hastings: Warren Hastings was born at Churchill, Oxfordshire, on 6 December 1732; his mother died soon after, and he was raised by his grandfather and then by an uncle, who sent him to Westminster School. He left at sixteen when his uncle died, and joined the East India Company as a writer in 1750. He learned Urdu and Persian, and in 1752 was sent to the trading post at Kasimbazar. In 1756 he was imprisoned by Siraj ud-Daulah, escaped, and served as a volunteer in Robert Clive's force that retook Calcutta in January 1757.

In 1758 he became the British resident at Murshidabad. Back on the Calcutta council from 1761, he protested against abuses of private trade, was overruled, and resigned in December 1764. He returned to India in 1769 as deputy ruler at Madras, and in 1772 became governor at Calcutta.

The Regulating Act 1773 put Madras and Bombay under Bengal and made Hastings the first Governor-General, as one member of a five-man Supreme Council. According to William Dalrymple, he moved government from Murshidabad to Calcutta, unified currency systems, ordered the codification of Hindu and Muslim law, reformed the tax and customs system, backed James Rennell's survey of India and built granaries to guard against a repeat of the famine of 1770-71. In 1774 he sent troops to help the wazir of Oudh against the Rohillas, the first of several wars that harmed his reputation.

From 1779 to 1784 he faced a coalition of Hyder Ali of Mysore, the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Marathas, with a French fleet under Admiral Suffren also in the field. He made peace with the Marathas in 1782 and broke up the coalition. He raised funds from local treasuries, which later became the main line of attack against him. In 1781 he founded the Madrasa 'Aliya at Calcutta.

Hastings resigned in 1785 and was replaced by Lord Cornwallis. Impeached by the House of Commons in 1787 over embezzlement, extortion and coercion, he was tried before the House of Lords from 13 February 1788, with Edmund Burke among the prosecutors. The trial took 148 days over seven years, and he was acquitted on 24 April 1795, though he complained of being bankrupted by its cost. He was made a privy councillor in 1814 and died on 22 August 1818.

His introduction to Charles Wilkins's translation of the Bhagavad Gita, dated 4 October 1784, argued that knowledge of a conquered people was useful to the state. Historians note that his reliance on Brahmin advisers to interpret Hindu law helped solidify caste privileges.
warring-states-period: The Warring States period covers the final centuries of the Zhou dynasty, after the Spring and Autumn period. Several dates have been proposed for its beginning, but Sima Qian's choice of 475 BCE is the most often cited. The king of Zhou still formally ruled as sovereign but had lost political power and functioned in practice as a figurehead. The name comes from the Record of the Warring States, a history compiled in the early Han dynasty, and also reflects how the scale of warfare grew. In 403 BCE the Zhou court recognised the rulers of Zhao, Wei and Han as marquises after they conquered Jin, and in 376 BCE the three divided the last Jin territory between them.

As Qin grew disproportionately powerful, the policies of many states became oriented towards dealing with it. The Vertical Alliances, led by Su Qin, tried to stop Qin's advance, while Qin pressed neighbours into the Horizontal Alliances led by Zhang Yi; the Zhan Guo Ce records their dealings. A cycle of abortive alliances followed, and Qin invaded Zhou and ended its line of monarchs in 256 BCE.

The last stage began under Zheng, who succeeded King Zhuangxiang of Qin at the age of 13. In 230 BCE Qin ordered Neishi Teng to conquer Han, and over about ten years Zheng's armies annexed each of the other contender states. By 221 BCE Qin had founded the Qin dynasty, the first imperial dynastic state in East Asian history.

Warfare changed in scale. Near the start of the period chariots gave way to massed infantry with swords and crossbows, battles could last months or even years, and iron weapons began to replace bronze. The first native Chinese cavalry unit was formed in 307 BCE under King Wuling of Zhao. Reported casualties, such as 240,000 killed at the Battle of Yique, are thought exaggerated by scholars including Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy, but warfare clearly became excessive.

Wandering scholars offered advice to competing rulers, and the Hundred Schools of Thought arose, among them Mohism, Confucianism, Legalism and Taoism. Four of the Seven Military Classics, including the Art of War, belong to the period. Linzi, the capital of Qi, was a centre of trade in salt, silk and iron.
warrior-of-hirschlanden: The figure's pointed hat may have been made of birchbark, like the real hat found in the princely grave of Hochdorf. Its legs are modelled with some realism, but the upper body is schematic. Masks of the kind it may wear are known from burials at Klein-Klein in Styria and Trebeništa in North Macedonia, and much earlier from the shaft graves of Mycenae of about 1500 BCE. Heavy weathering suggests that the statue stood in the open for a long time before it was buried.

Other human figures of the early Iron Age have been found at Rottenburg, Tübingen, Stammheim and Stockach in Baden-Württemberg, but they are far more stylised, more carving than statue. Greek influence from the kouroi has been discussed: black-figure vessels from fortified settlements of the period show trade with the Mediterranean, probably along the Rhône and through the Greek colony of Massilia. Much closer in style are the far more elaborate statues of Capestrano in Italy, of about 550 BCE, and of Casale Marittimo in Etruria, from the middle of the 7th century BCE.

The statue came to light when the barrow was excavated in 1963. The mound was ringed by a stone circle and a dry stone wall, and its burials range from the very start of the Iron Age, Hallstatt D1 of about 600 BCE, to the beginning of the La Tène period, about 450 BCE. In the La Tène period that followed, statues of people remained very rare; examples include the finds from Glauberg in Hesse, the Holzgerlingen figure, the Mšecké Žehrovice Head in the Czech Republic and the sculptures of Roquepertuse.
wars-in-lombardy: The first campaign against the ambitions of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan, grew out of a dispute over Forlì. Its lord Giorgio Ordelaffi had named Visconti guardian of his young heir, but the boy's mother took the regency, and on 14 May 1423 the people of Forlì called in the Milanese condottiero Agnolo della Pergola. Florence declared war and was beaten repeatedly, at Zagonara in July 1424 and later at Anghiari. On 4 December 1425 it allied with Venice: conquests in Lombardy would go to the Venetians, those in Romagna and Tuscany to the Florentines.

Under Carmagnola, Captain General of the League, the allies took Brescia on 26 November 1426 after a long siege with heavy use of artillery, and the peace of 30 December 1426 gave it to Venice. Visconti refused to ratify it, but after Carmagnola crushed his army at Maclodio on 4 October 1427 the peace of Ferrara of 18 April 1428 added Bergamo and Crema. In a third war from 1431, Carmagnola's caution raised suspicion that Visconti had bought him; recalled by the Council of Ten, he was tried for treason and beheaded, and the peace of Ferrara of May 1433 restored an unsteady status quo.

In the fourth war Gattamelata and later Francesco Sforza fought for Venice against Niccolò Piccinino, who besieged Brescia in September 1438. Sforza then mediated the Peace of Cremona of 20 November 1441, entered Visconti's service and married his daughter, Bianca Maria Visconti. After Visconti died in 1447, Sforza entered Milan in May 1450. Venice declared war on him in April 1452; Sforza, joined by René of Anjou's French army, took Pontevico and Orzinuovi in 1453, leaving Venice only Brescia, Bergamo and Crema in Lombardy, until the French left early in 1454.

The Treaty of Lodi of April 1454 was a compromise peace that became the basis for an accord among Venice, Milan, Florence and Naples, blessed by Pope Nicholas V. Out of a crowd of communes and city-states the wars had produced five territorial powers, the fifth being the Papal States, while Siena, Pisa, Urbino, Mantua and Ferrara were pushed to the margins. Their pledge of non-aggression, sometimes called the Italic League, held for about forty years until the Italian Wars began in 1494, and Lodi is often marked as the emergence of the principle of the balance of power.
wars-of-alexander-the-great: Alexander became king of Macedon in 336 BCE, after his father Philip II was assassinated by Pausanias of Orestis, the captain of his bodyguards. He also succeeded Philip as head of the League of Corinth, the confederation of Greek states under Macedonian hegemony that had been formed to oppose the Achaemenid Empire. The news of Philip's death roused Thebes, Athens, Thessaly and the Thracian tribes to revolt, and Alexander acted quickly, riding south with 3,000 Macedonian cavalry and going round the Thessalians by crossing Mount Ossa.

In the spring of 335 BCE Alexander marched into Thrace and defeated the Triballi and the Illyrian kings Cleitus and Glaukias. While he was in the north, Thebes rebelled again; the city was razed and its territory divided among the other Boeotian cities, which cowed Athens into submission. In 334 BCE he crossed the Hellespont into Asia. He won at the Granicus River in May 334 BCE, at Issus in November 333 BCE, where Darius III fled the field, and at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. In 332 BCE he took Tyre, the last Persian port to hold out, which held about 40,000 people.

From 329 BCE he fought in Bactria and Sogdiana, against Spitamenes and the Sakas, and in 327 BCE his men took the Sogdian Rock by night. There he met Roxana, whom he later married. In 327 and 326 BCE he fought the hill clans of Gandhara, and Curtius reports that the whole population of Massaga was killed. He defeated the king Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, the most costly battle the Macedonians fought. At the Hyphasis River his exhausted army refused to go further east, and the river marks the limit of his conquests.

Alexander sent part of his army to Carmania under Craterus and a fleet under Nearchus along the Persian Gulf, and led the rest back to Persia through the Gedrosian Desert. According to Plutarch, he lost three quarters of his army on the sixty-day march. He had also planned an expedition into Arabia and then a campaign westward against Carthage, but after his death his generals, the Diadochi, abandoned these plans. His empire proved unstable. It broke up in the Wars of the Diadochi, which lasted about forty years and belong to the Hellenistic period.
wars-of-castro: Relations between the Farnese and other Italian nobles had long been poor. In 1612 Ranuccio I Farnese, Duke of Parma, had 100 nobles accused of a plot against him tortured and executed in Parma's main square, though the charges were likely untrue. In 1639 his son Odoardo Farnese visited Rome and refused due deference to Taddeo Barberini, nephew of Pope Urban VIII. The pope's nephews persuaded him to ban grain from Castro from Rome, cutting off a source of the duke's income, and Odoardo's Roman creditors, unpaid, turned to the pope, who chose force.

A truce negotiated by Cardinal Bernardino Spada was disowned by Urban VIII. On 12 October 1641 Luigi Mattei led 12,000 infantry and up to 4,000 cavalry against Castro, which surrendered after a brief cannonade that killed one man. On 13 January 1642 Urban excommunicated Odoardo and took away his fiefs. Odoardo marched on the Papal States and came close enough to threaten Rome, but faltered, and a new papal army of 30,000 drove him back. His allies said their quarrel was with the Barberini, not the papacy; Spain, busy with the Thirty Years' War, gave the pope little help.

Antonio Barberini had successes against the Venetians and Modenese, but the Tuscans defeated papal forces near Lake Trasimeno at the Battle of Mongiovino. After a crucial defeat at Lagoscuro on 17 March 1644 the papacy made peace at Ferrara on 31 March. Odoardo was readmitted to the Church, his fiefs and grain trade restored, and he was to resume paying his creditors.

Odoardo's son Ranuccio II Farnese refused in 1649 to pay the creditors or accept the new bishop of Castro, Cristoforo Giarda, appointed by Pope Innocent X. When Giarda was killed near Monterosi, Innocent blamed the duke. Papal forces routed Ranuccio and on 2 September 1649 destroyed Castro, its churches and the Palazzo Farnese, raising a column reading Qui fu Castro, here stood Castro.

The first war was widely seen as a disgrace to the papacy and is estimated to have cost it 12 million scudi. Urban VIII died on 29 July 1644, and his nephews Antonio, Taddeo and Francesco Barberini fled to France with Cardinal Mazarin's help. Ranuccio II had to cede the lands around Castro to the pope, and the city was never rebuilt.
wars-of-the-diadochi: Alexander the Great died on 10 June 323 BCE, leaving an empire from Macedon and Greece to the Indus valley and no clear successor. The Argead family consisted of his mentally disabled half-brother Arrhidaeus, his unborn son Alexander IV, his reputed illegitimate son Heracles, his mother Olympias, his sister Cleopatra and his half-sisters Thessalonike and Cynane.

Two factions formed, one led by Meleager, who supported Arrhidaeus, and one by the cavalry commander Perdiccas, who wished to wait for the birth of Roxana's child. They agreed that Arrhidaeus would rule as Philip III jointly with the child if it were male. Perdiccas became regent, then had Meleager and other opponents murdered, and in the partition at Babylon his supporters became satraps: Ptolemy received Egypt, Antigonus Phrygia, Lycia and Pamphylia, and Lysimachus Thrace.

News of Alexander's death inspired the Lamian War, in which Athens and other cities besieged Antipater at Lamia until Craterus defeated the Athenians at Crannon on 5 September 322 BCE. In the First War, from 321 to 319 BCE, Antipater, Craterus and Antigonus formed a coalition against Perdiccas, who was assassinated by his own generals, Peithon, Seleucus and Antigenes, after a failed attempt to cross the Nile.

At the Treaty of Triparadisus Antipater became regent and Antigonus strategos of Asia. In the Second War, from 318 to 316 BCE, Cassander made himself dominant in Macedon and Greece, and Antigonus defeated Eumenes of Cardia, who was executed after the battle of Gabiene.

In the Third War Antigonus faced an alliance of Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander. Seleucus secured Babylon after the Battle of Gaza, and Cassander had the young Alexander IV and his mother Roxane murdered, ending the Argead dynasty. By the Fourth War, Antigonus and Demetrius had taken the crown, followed by Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander. At the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE Seleucus arrived in time to crush Antigonus, who was killed.

Ipsus established the Ptolemies and the Seleucids as the two major dynasties of the Hellenistic world. Cassander died in 298 BCE, and Macedon passed through the hands of Demetrius, Lysimachus and Pyrrhus. Seleucus defeated and killed Lysimachus at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BCE, leaving himself the only living successor among the original Diadochi, and was assassinated soon afterwards by Ptolemy Ceraunus. Gallic tribes then rampaged through Macedon and Greece, and Demetrius's son Antigonus Gonatas emerged as ruler of Macedon in 277 BCE. Fifty years after Alexander's death Ptolemy II ruled Egypt, Antiochus I the Asian territories and Antigonus Macedon and most of Greece.
wars-of-the-roses: The wars were known at the time and for long afterwards as the Civil Wars. The name Wars of the Roses refers to the white rose of York and the red rose of Lancaster, which was the Lancastrian emblem by 1485. Historians disagree over the main causes. They point to the economic and social troubles that followed the Hundred Years' War with France, and to the powerful duchies Edward III created for his sons, which fed a bastard feudalism in which great lords kept private forces. The succession after Edward III's death in 1377 is held by the historian Ian Mortimer to be the root cause.

Henry IV took the throne in 1399 from Richard II, basing his right on descent in the male line from John of Gaunt, though Edmund Mortimer, descended through Lionel, Duke of Clarence, could be argued to be the heir presumptive. The mental instability of Henry VI revived the interest of his cousin Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, in a claim of his own.

Fighting began on 22 May 1455 at the First Battle of St Albans, where York captured the king and several of his rivals were killed, among them Edmund Beaufort, 2nd Duke of Somerset. After Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, took Henry again at Northampton, York was killed at Wakefield, and his 18-year-old son Edward inherited the claim. Edward defeated the Lancastrians at Towton and was crowned on 28 June 1461.

Edward IV's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville, discovered by Warwick in October 1464, and his refusal to follow Warwick's policy of closeness to France led to Warwick's rebellion. With Margaret of Anjou, Warwick invaded in September 1470 and Henry VI was restored, while Edward fled to Flanders. Edward returned with Burgundian aid, killed Warwick at Barnet, and on 4 May 1471 defeated Margaret's army at Tewkesbury, where Henry's only son Edward of Westminster was killed.

Edward IV ruled for twelve more years. After his death in 1483 his twelve-year-old son Edward V reigned for 78 days before his uncle Richard of Gloucester took the throne as Richard III, amid controversy over the disappearance of Edward IV's two sons. Henry Tudor, in exile in Brittany and then France, returned and killed Richard at Bosworth Field in 1485.

Henry was crowned Henry VII on 30 October 1485 and married Elizabeth of York, Edward IV's eldest daughter, on 18 January 1486, uniting the two claims. Challengers remained, and the wars ended in 1487 with his defeat of the Yorkist opposition at Stoke Field. The Tudors ruled until 1603. Some historians, such as K. B. McFarlane, hold that the effects of the conflict on English society were exaggerated: many parts of England, East Anglia above all, were largely unaffected.
wars-of-the-three-kingdoms: England, Ireland and Scotland were separate kingdoms joined in a personal union when James VI of Scotland succeeded Elizabeth I in 1603. His son Charles I faced disputes with the English Parliament over taxation, military expenditure and the limits of its role, and he held to the divine right of kings. Religion deepened the quarrel. English Puritans and Scottish Covenanters opposed his changes to the state churches, while in Ireland, the one kingdom with a Catholic majority, Catholics wanted an end to discrimination, more self-government and a reversal of land grants to Protestant settlers. The name itself appears first in a 1662 chronicle by James Heath, and historians use other labels as well.

The Bishops' Wars of 1639 and 1640 began when Scottish Covenanters, who had signed the National Covenant of 1638 against religious innovations, took control of Scotland and briefly occupied northern England. An Irish Catholic rebellion followed in 1641, with widespread assaults on Protestant communities, and the Irish Catholic Confederation came to hold most of Ireland. Because Parliament and the king each distrusted the other with an army, the English Civil War began in 1642. The Covenanters joined Parliament in late 1643, and Charles surrendered to the Scottish army on 5 May 1646.

Fighting resumed in 1648 in the Second English Civil War, in which the New Model Army defeated the Royalists and the Scottish Engagers. After the army purged Parliament, the Rump Parliament approved the trial of Charles, who was executed on 30 January 1649, and declared England a republic. Oliver Cromwell landed in Ireland in August 1649 and defeated the Covenanters at Dunbar on 3 September 1650. The last Royalist army, under Charles II, was beaten at Worcester on 3 September 1651.

Ireland and Scotland were ruled by military governors, their parliaments were abolished, and in Ireland almost all land held by Catholics was confiscated, with Penal Laws restricting them further. After Cromwell died in 1658, George Monck marched from Scotland to London in early 1660, and the Convention Parliament invited Charles II to return on 1 May 1660. The Restoration brought back the prewar constitutional position and the parliaments of Scotland and Ireland, and those held responsible for the regicide were executed or imprisoned. The issues of religion, the powers of Parliament and the relations between the kingdoms remained unresolved and re-emerged in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.
warsaw: Warsaw lies in east-central Poland on both banks of the Vistula, in the heartland of the Masovian Plain, about 260 km from the Baltic Sea and 523 km east of Berlin. The name in Polish is Warszawa, and its origin is uncertain. One hypothesis reads it as belonging to Warsz, a short form of the Old Polish name Warcisław, and the original Warszawa was a small fishing settlement on the river bank. Folk etymology tells of the fisherman Wars and the mermaid Sawa, who lived in the Vistula.

The first fortified settlements on the site were at Bródno in the 9th or 10th century and at Jazdów in the 12th or 13th century. Bolesław II of Masovia, Prince of Płock, established the town in about 1300, and in 1413 it was officially made capital of the Masovian Duchy, when it had about 4,500 inhabitants. The city rose to prominence after 1596, when Sigismund III moved the Polish capital and royal court from Kraków. By the 18th century Warsaw had passed Gdańsk as the most populous city of Poland. It was the capital of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795 and afterwards the seat of Napoleon's Duchy of Warsaw.

The 19th century and the Industrial Revolution made it one of the largest and most densely populated cities in Europe. Before the Second World War it held the world's second-largest Jewish population after New York, about 30 percent of its people in the late 1930s. The city was bombed and besieged in 1939. Much of the historic city was destroyed and its diverse population decimated by the Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Warsaw Uprising of 1944 and systematic razing.

Warsaw is the capital and most populous city of Poland, with about 1.87 million residents, and the seat of both houses of the Polish Parliament. The reconstructed Old Town was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1980. Other landmarks are the Royal Castle, Sigismund's Column and Wilanów Palace.
warsaw-confederation: Toleration had a long history in Poland and Lithuania: Casimir III the Great had guaranteed the rites of Orthodox Christians in 1341 and the privileges of the Armenians in 1356, and Lipka Tatars, Ashkenazi Jews and Crimean Karaites also lived there under tolerance. In 1570 Lutherans, Calvinists and the Bohemian Brethren agreed at Sandomierz to recognise one another and proposed to the Sejm that everyone might believe according to conscience, but the draft was not accepted. When Sigismund II Augustus, the last Jagiellonian king, died childless on 7 July 1572, the Protestants faced the election of a new king with no legal guarantees for their faith.

The Convocation Sejm of about 200 nobles met in Warsaw as a confederation from 6 to 29 January 1573 to keep the legal order during the interregnum. It decided that every nobleman could vote in the royal election, chose Warsaw as its place and recognised the primate Jakub Uchański as interrex. On 28 January representatives of all the main religions pledged mutual support and tolerance. The St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 moved the nobles to ensure that no monarch could do the same in Poland. Mikołaj Sienicki, Jan Firlej and Jan Zborowski did most to prepare the articles, which most Catholic bishops opposed; only Bishop Franciszek Krasiński signed. The text was written in Latin and Old Polish, with translations in Ruthenian, German and French.

The articles became part of the Henrician Articles that every elected king had to swear, and Zborowski told Henry of Valois in Paris, in Latin, that if he did not swear he would not reign. Stephen Báthory, a devout Catholic, upheld the confederation and acted against rioters who attacked dissenters. Yet it had no means of enforcement, the bishops withheld their consent, and with the Counter-Reformation non-Catholics were again gradually oppressed; after the Union of Brest of 1596 the Orthodox Church was outlawed by the Crown. Historians debate whether its freedom was meant for the nobility alone. Norman Davies called its wording extraordinary for the Europe of the time. In 2003 the text was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Programme.
warsaw-pact: The formal name of the pact was the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Before it, the Czechoslovak leadership, fearful of a re-militarised West Germany, sought a security pact with East Germany and Poland. In 1954 the Soviet Union proposed German reunification under neutrality and a General European Treaty on Collective Security, and then asked to join NATO, but the United States, the United Kingdom and France rejected all of these.

On 23 October 1954 the admission of the Federal Republic of Germany to NATO was decided, and it joined on 9 May 1955. On 14 May 1955 the Soviet Union and seven other Eastern European states established the pact in response. NATO officials, noting that the Soviet Union already had troops and political dominance in these states, called it a cardboard castle.

The founding members were the Soviet Union, Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Poland and Romania. In November 1956, after the government of Imre Nagy declared Hungary's withdrawal, Soviet troops entered and crushed the revolt, which killed an estimated 2,500 Hungarian citizens. The Soviet Union then made twenty-year bilateral treaties with Poland, East Germany, Romania and Hungary to keep its troops there. The pact's one joint action was the invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, in which every member took part except Romania and Albania, and East Germany gave only minimal support. Albania, which had withheld support since 1961, withdrew formally on 13 September 1968.

In 1989 popular discontent toppled the communist governments of Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Romania and Bulgaria. East Germany left the pact on 24 September 1990, before German reunification. On 25 February 1991 the defence and foreign ministers of the remaining members declared the pact disbanded at a meeting in Hungary, and on 1 July 1991 in Prague the Czechoslovak president Václav Havel formally ended the treaty. The Soviet Union dissolved itself in December of that year.

The organisation had two parts: the Political Consultative Committee, for political matters, and the Combined Command of Pact Armed Forces, with its headquarters in Warsaw. On paper, members pledged mutual defence and non-intervention in each other's internal affairs. In practice the commanders were always senior Soviet officers, and the Supreme Commander was also a First Deputy Minister of Defence of the Soviet Union. The Soviet Ground Forces shaped the Eastern European armies in their own image for a possible confrontation with NATO. The pact was the military counterpart of Comecon, the economic organisation of the Eastern Bloc.
warsaw-pact-invasion-of-czechoslovakia: De-Stalinization in Czechoslovakia began under Antonín Novotný in the late 1950s and early 1960s but progressed more slowly than in most Eastern Bloc states. An economic downturn in the early 1960s, and the New Economic Model of 1965, increased demand for political reform. On 5 January 1968 Alexander Dubček was elected First Secretary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia (KSČ), beginning the Prague Spring. His reforms partly decentralised the economy and loosened restrictions on the media, speech and travel, and censorship was abolished on 4 March 1968.

Leonid Brezhnev and the leaders of other Warsaw Pact countries feared that the liberalisation would harm their interests. They worried that Czechoslovakia might defect from the Eastern Bloc, leaving the Soviet Union without strategic depth or Czechoslovakia's industrial base in a war with NATO, although Czechoslovak leaders had no intention of leaving the Warsaw Pact. Negotiations in July 1968 at Čierna nad Tisou ended in a compromise.

At about 11 pm on 20 August 1968 the armies of the Soviet Union, Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary invaded. That night 250,000 troops and 2,000 tanks entered the country, and the total eventually reached about 500,000. Romania and Albania refused to take part, and Moscow ordered East German forces not to cross the border, because of the public memory of the German occupation three decades earlier. Brezhnev wanted the operation to appear multilateral, but Soviet troops outnumbered the others five to one, and the Soviet High Command was in charge throughout.

The Dubček government had taken no steps to forestall an invasion. By the morning of 21 August Dubček and other prominent reformists had been arrested and flown to Moscow. Popular opposition took the form of spontaneous nonviolent resistance, as Czechs and Slovaks met the soldiers with arguments and reproaches. During the occupation 137 Czechoslovaks were killed and 500 seriously wounded.

Reactions were divided. Most Warsaw Pact states supported the invasion, while Western nations, Romania, China and Albania condemned it, and many communist parties outside the bloc split or lost influence. Albania formally withdrew from the Warsaw Pact in September 1968. When Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček as leader of the KSČ in April 1969, his regime began normalisation, restoring firm party rule and removing the reformers. In 1989 Hungary, Poland, East Germany and Bulgaria each condemned or apologised for their part in the invasion.
wartburg: The Wartburg stands on a precipice 410 metres high, overlooking the town of Eisenach, on an extension of the Thuringian Forest above the valley of the Hörsel, through which ran the historical Via Regia. Its name probably comes from Warte, a watchtower, in spite of a tradition that its founder exclaimed, Wait, mountain, you shall bear my castle. The foundation was laid about 1067 by a Thuringian count, who with the larger sister castle Neuenburg secured the borders of his territories. The castle is first mentioned in writing in 1080, as Wartberg, by Bruno, Bishop of Merseburg, in his account of the Saxon War.

In 1131 the founder's son Louis I was raised to landgrave of Thuringia by King Lothair of Supplinburg. From 1172 to 1211 the Wartburg was one of the most important princely courts in the German Reich. Hermann I supported poets such as Walther von der Vogelweide and Wolfram von Eschenbach, who wrote part of Parzival there in 1203. The Sängerkrieg, or Minstrels' Contest, is set at the castle in 1206 or 1207 and was later used by Richard Wagner in Tannhäuser. Elisabeth of Hungary was sent there at the age of four to be raised as consort of Landgrave Ludwig IV, and lived there from 1211 to 1228 known for her charitable work.

The Wartburg remained the seat of the Thuringian landgraves until 1440. Martin Luther stayed there from May 1521 to March 1522 as Junker Jörg, taken there for his safety at the request of Frederick the Wise after the Diet of Worms, and translated the New Testament from Greek into German in ten weeks. On 18 October 1817 about 500 students of the new Burschenschaften met there, celebrating the victory over Napoleon and the 300th anniversary of the Reformation and calling for German unity under the motto Honour, Freedom, Fatherland.

Grand Duke Karl Alexander ordered a reconstruction in 1838, in Neo-Romanesque style under the architect Hugo von Ritgen, as a national cultural monument. The Wartburg Foundation was established in 1922, and the castle was restored again in 1952–54. It contains substantial original structures from the 12th to the 15th centuries, though much of the interior dates only from the 19th century. It inspired Ludwig II when he decided to build Neuschwanstein, and in 1999 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for its medieval architecture and its historical and religious significance.
wartburg-festival: After the Wars of Liberation against Napoleon, many people were bitter that hopes of national unity had been dashed by the Congress of Vienna in 1815, while democratic reform stalled and governments curbed the press and the right of association. On 12 June 1815 students at the University of Jena founded the Urburschenschaft to promote German unity. Many had fought as volunteers against Napoleon, some in the Lützow Free Corps, whose black, red and gold colours were later adopted for the Flag of Germany.

The Burschenschaft fraternities of Jena and Halle chose the Wartburg because Martin Luther had found refuge there after Emperor Charles V declared him an outlaw in 1521, and had translated the Bible there, which made the castle a symbol of German nationalism.

Students came from Berlin, Breslau, Erlangen, Göttingen, Heidelberg, Kiel, Königsberg, Leipzig, Marburg, Rostock, Tübingen and other universities, joined by Jena professors such as Lorenz Oken, Heinrich Luden and Jakob Friedrich Fries. In the knights' hall speakers presented Luther as a fighter for freedom and spoke of the way to national unity. The singing of Now Thank We All Our God and a closing blessing gave the gathering the air of a Protestant service, and at the festive meal toasts were raised to the fallen of the Liberation Wars, to Scharnhorst, Schill and Körner.

After the official programme, followers of Friedrich Ludwig Jahn staged a book burning in imitation of Luther's burning of the papal bull in 1520. Mock books stood for works such as Karl Ludwig von Haller's Restoration of Political Science, August von Kotzebue's History of the German Realm, Saul Ascher's Germanomanie and the Napoleonic Code, and a corporal's cane was burned as a symbol of foreign rule.

Metternich's government had already kept Austrian universities from taking part, and the festival was used to justify further measures against liberal forces. The Hambacher Fest of 1832 was held in a similar manner, and a second Wartburg festival took place during the Revolutions of 1848. In 1933 the students' book burning was invoked to justify the Nazi book burnings.
wartislaw-i-duke-of-pomerania: Most of what is known of Wartislaw comes from the lives of Otto of Bamberg. He was of Slavic origin. Early in life he was probably a crypto-Christian: baptised while a prisoner of the Saxons, he is thought to have hidden his new religion from his still pagan subjects.

In 1109 Wartislaw was defeated by Bolesław III Wrymouth, Duke of Poland, at the Battle of Nakło. By 1112 he had broken faith with Bolesław, who besieged Nakło, and Wartislaw swore fealty again; a year later he broke the agreement once more and faced a further campaign. Against overwhelming odds he agreed to pay tribute and to Christianize Pomerania, and together with Bolesław he backed Otto of Bamberg in the conversion of Pomerania. By 1124 his residence was at Kamień Pomorski (Kammin).

The last explicit mention of him is by Saxo Grammaticus, who describes a joint Polish-Danish expedition against him around 1129 or 1130, aimed at the islands of Wolin and Uznam. The Danish King Niels is said to have taken him prisoner and released him after Canute Lavard, called King of the Obotrites, intervened.

Otto's biographer says only that his wife was a Christian, and that Otto made Wartislaw send home 24 earlier wives and concubines before the marriage. The chronicler Thomas Kantzow, writing almost four hundred years later, named a Heila from Saxony and then Ida, a Danish princess, but later historians question both; Edward Rymar argues that his wife probably came from the Ruthenian Rurik dynasty.

Wartislaw is said to have been killed by pagans near Stolpe, in the present district of Vorpommern-Greifswald. The place is marked by a rock, the Wartislawstein, engraved with a Christian cross in remembrance of his missionary work. His brother Ratibor I succeeded him, and his sons Bogusław I and Casimir I later ruled as dukes of Pomerania; his daughter Woizlava married Pribislav of Mecklenburg.
wartislaw-iii-duke-of-pomerania: Wartislaw was the son of Casimir II of Pomerania-Demmin and Ingardis of Denmark. After Casimir's death in 1219 his mother ruled Pomerania-Demmin in place of the young duke until 1226. At that time both part duchies, Pomerania-Demmin and Pomerania-Stettin, were under Danish overlordship. That overlordship weakened after the Battle of Bornhöved in 1227 and was ended when Wartislaw, with allies from Lübeck, countered a Danish expedition in 1234. He married a Sophia whose family is not known.

The year 1236 brought heavy losses. An expedition led by Henry Borwin III of Mecklenburg-Rostock annexed most of Circipania, the western part of the duchy with the terrae Gnoien, Altkalen and Demmin, leaving Wartislaw only the residential burgh of Demmin. In the Treaty of Kremmen of the same year he had to recognise the overlordship of the Margraviate of Brandenburg over the rest of his duchy and cede the terrae Stargard, Wustrow and Beseritz, which Mecklenburg soon took over and which became known as Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

In the north he extended his influence up to the Ryck river, into the territory of Hilda, where the princes of Rügen had set up Eldena Abbey. Together with the Rugian prince he granted market rights to the coastal settlement of Greifswald, and in 1248 he received the town as a fief from Eldena. Like Barnim I, he brought German nobles to his court and settlers to the countryside, and gave Lübeck law to Demmin, Kolberg (now Kołobrzeg) in 1255, Greifenberg (now Gryfice) in 1262, and, jointly with Barnim, to Stavenhagen, Wolgast and Wollin (now Wolin).

Wartislaw died on 17 May 1264 without a son, and Pomerania-Demmin ceased to exist as a separate duchy. It would have passed to Brandenburg had Barnim I not been accepted as co-ruler in the Treaty of Landin of 1250, which allowed him to join what remained of Pomerania-Demmin after the losses of 1236 to his duchy based at Stettin. Wartislaw and his mother Ingardis were buried at Eldena Abbey near Greifswald.
wartislaw-ix-duke-of-pomerania: Wartislaw IX was the eldest son of Duke Barnim VI of Pomerania and Veronica of Hohenzollern, daughter of Frederick V, Burgrave of Nuremberg. In 1420 he married Sophia of Saxe-Lauenburg-Ratzeburg, daughter of Eric IV, Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg; they had four children, Eric II, Wartislaw X, Elizabeth and Christopher, who died young.

In his youth he saw the High Marshal of Pomerania-Wolgast, Degener Buggenhagen, killed before his eyes in 1417 or 1419 by Henneke von Behr, the favourite of Duchess Agnes, widow of his uncle Wartislaw VIII; Buggenhagen had earlier killed another of her favourites, Curdt Bonow. Accounts of Behr's end differ: some say he drowned escaping from Usedom Castle, others that he was executed in Stralsund.

Probably influenced by these events, Wartislaw agreed with the towns and nobility on a Quatember Court to secure the rule of law. From 1425 he shared power in Western Pomerania north of the Peene with his brother Barnim VII and his cousins Barnim VIII and Swantibor IV, but he outlived them all and ended his life as sole ruler of Pomerania-Wolgast west of the Swine.

Like his cousins in Stettin he faced the ambitions of the House of Hohenzollern, rulers of Brandenburg from 1411. His concern was the Brandenburg estates of Torgelow and Pasewalk, held by the dukes of Wolgast since 1369 as security for a loan; a peace treaty of 1448 transferred them to Pomerania. In the Golden Privilege of 1452 he granted wide concessions to the towns, above all to Stralsund, then led by its mayor Otto Voge.

Wartislaw died at Wolgast on 17 April 1457, six months after the formal opening of the University of Greifswald. He had arranged numerous grants for it, so that the new university was financially secure, and it remained his most lasting legacy.
warwick: Warwick is a market town adjacent to the River Avon, 14 kilometres south of Coventry and 31 kilometres south-east of Birmingham. Human activity on the hilltop goes back to the Neolithic, when a sizeable settlement stood there, and the footings of a large Roman barn of the 2nd century have been found. The town has been continuously inhabited from the 5th century. Its Old English name, Wæringwīc, may mean a settlement of a clan called the Wæring, or a fortification, or a place by a weir on the Avon.

Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, built a burh on the hilltop in 914, one of ten to defend Mercia from the Vikings, on a sandstone outcrop beside the river crossing. In the early 10th century a shire was founded with Warwick as its county town, and a royal mint was established under Æthelstan (924–939) that continued to the mid-12th century. The Danes burned much of the town in 1016. William the Conqueror founded the castle in 1068, and a town wall was built close to the burh ramparts. The Earls of Warwick, mostly of the Beauchamp family, controlled the medieval town, whose prosperity rested on its role as an administrative and military centre rather than on trade. It was incorporated as a borough in 1545.

In 1642, during the Civil War, Royalists besieged the castle, which was held for Parliament, for two weeks without cannon strong enough to damage it. The Great Fire of Warwick on 5 September 1694 destroyed 460 buildings in five hours and left 250 families homeless. Most of the centre was rebuilt in the Georgian style by architects including Francis Smith and later William and David Hiorne.

Warwick was largely bypassed by the Industrial Revolution, partly because it did not lie on important roads and the Avon was not navigable as far as the town. Its Collegiate Church of St Mary, rebuilt after the fire, keeps the Beauchamp Chapel of 1443–1464, with a copper-gilt effigy of Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, cast in 1459. The Lord Leycester Hospital on the High Street has parts dating from 1383, and the east and west gatehouses are the only remains of the town wall. Warwick adjoins Leamington Spa and Whitnash, and it is the county town of Warwickshire.
warwick-rhode-island: Warwick lies in Kent County, Rhode Island, about 12 miles south of downtown Providence and 63 miles south-west of Boston. Its entire eastern edge is waterfront. The Providence River marks its northern border with Cranston, and the shore turns into Narragansett Bay at Conimicut Point. Two southern peninsulas, Warwick Neck and Potowomut, enclose Greenwich Bay. The city has a total area of 49.6 square miles, of which 35.5 are land, and includes many villages, among them Apponaug, Conimicut, Pawtuxet Village and Shawomet.

Samuel Gorton settled the area in 1642. The Narragansett sachem Miantonomi sold him the Shawhomett Purchase for 144 fathoms of wampum, but the sachems Sacononoco and Pumham claimed he had sold the land without their approval and took their case to Boston, placing their lands under Massachusetts rule. In 1643 the Massachusetts Bay Colony sent a militia force to arrest Gorton and his followers, and all but three of them surrendered.

Gorton sailed to England and sought a charter from the king, helped by Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, after whom the settlers renamed their colony Warwick. Continuing harassment from Massachusetts led the other three Narragansett Bay colonies, Providence Plantations, Portsmouth and Newport, to unite with Warwick under a royal charter as the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations.

Warwick was badly damaged in King Philip's War of 1675 to 1676. In 1772 local patriots boarded the Gaspee, a revenue cutter enforcing the Stamp Act 1765 and the Townshend Acts in Narragansett Bay. Its commanding officer was shot and seriously wounded, and the ship was stripped of its guns and burned. This is described as the first violent act against the British Crown before the American Revolution. Warwick was also the home of General Nathanael Greene, George Washington's second-in-command, and of the Civil War general George S. Greene.

Warwick had 82,823 inhabitants at the 2020 census and is part of the Providence metropolitan area. It is home to Rhode Island's main airport, T. F. Green Airport, which also serves as a reliever for Boston's Logan International Airport. Rocky Point, which closed in 1995, is now a state park.
warwickshire: Warwickshire is a flat, lowland county, about 1,975 km2 (760 sq mi) in area, running some 56 miles (90 km) from north to south. Its far south contains a small part of the Cotswolds, and its highest point, at 261 m (856 ft), is Ebrington Hill on the border with Gloucestershire. The River Avon, a major tributary of the Severn, flows through the south.

Much of the west was covered by the ancient Forest of Arden, most of which was cut down to provide fuel for industrialisation, and many places there end in the phrase in-Arden, such as Henley-in-Arden. The remaining area, the Felden, is an undulating agricultural landscape crossed by the Avon and the Leam. The plain between the outlying Cotswolds and the Edgehill escarpment is known as the Vale of Red Horse.

The region was part of Roman Britain, and the Roman road called Watling Street later became the boundary between the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia and the Danelaw. Warwickshire came into being as a division of Mercia in the early eleventh century, and its first mention, in 1001, calls it Wæringscīr, after Warwick. In the Middle Ages the county was dominated by Coventry, one of the most important cities of England because of its textile trade.

The county played a part in the English Civil War, with the Battle of Edgehill and other skirmishes fought there. The playwright William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, and the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was planned near Snitterfield. During the Industrial Revolution the Warwickshire coalfield was exploited, Coventry and the west became manufacturing centres, and Leamington Spa developed as a resort. The novelist Mary Ann Evans, known as George Eliot, was born just outside Nuneaton in 1819.

Coventry was administered separately from the rest of the county as a county corporate from 1451 to 1842. Under the Local Government Act 1972, Birmingham, Coventry, Solihull and Sutton Coldfield were transferred in 1974 to the new West Midlands county, so that the county has no cities today.

Warwickshire is a largely rural ceremonial county with its county town at Warwick. Its largest town is Nuneaton, and it also contains Rugby, the birthplace of rugby football, Leamington Spa and Stratford-upon-Avon. Warwick Castle and Kenilworth Castle stand in the county, and the Forest of Arden gives its name to many villages. Some bodies, such as Warwickshire County Cricket Club in Birmingham, still follow the historic county boundaries.
washington-dc: Washington, D.C., lies in the Mid-Atlantic region of the East Coast, on the northeast bank of the Potomac River, across from Virginia and surrounded by Maryland to the north, east and south. The south bank of the Potomac forms the border with Virginia, and the Anacostia River and Rock Creek are its two major tributaries. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal starts in Georgetown and was used in the 19th century to bypass the Little Falls of the Potomac. The district was named for Columbia, the female personification of the American nation, and the name Washington was added later, from George Washington, the first president.

The Algonquian-speaking Piscataway people inhabited the area when Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, and the Nacotchtank maintained settlements around the Anacostia River. Conflicts with colonists and neighbouring tribes displaced the Piscataway, some of whom founded a new settlement near Point of Rocks, Maryland, in 1699. The Constitution of 1789 called for a federal district under the exclusive jurisdiction of Congress. The Residence Act, adopted on 16 July 1790, approved a capital district along the Potomac and is considered the city's founding date. In 1800 the capital moved from Philadelphia, Congress began meeting in the unfinished Capitol, and President John Adams moved into the White House.

In 1791 President George Washington commissioned the French-born military engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant to design the capital. His plan featured broad avenues radiating out from rectangles, with a grand garden-lined avenue on the site of the National Mall, inspired by Versailles and the Tuileries. Washington dismissed L'Enfant in March 1792 after conflicts with the commissioners overseeing construction, and Andrew Ellicott completed the design. In 1846 Congress returned to Virginia the land it had ceded, including Alexandria, and in 1871 it made the entire district a single municipality.

Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States and its only federal district, not part of any state. It houses the White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court Building, and its National Mall holds the Jefferson Memorial, the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument. Since the 1973 Home Rule Act it has had an elected mayor and a 13-member council, though Congress retains the power to overturn local laws. Its residents elect one non-voting delegate to the House of Representatives. Ford's Theatre, where Abraham Lincoln was shot on 14 April 1865, is both a theatre and a museum.
washington-luis: Washington Luís was born in Macaé, in Rio de Janeiro, on 26 October 1869. He moved to São Paulo and graduated from the University of São Paulo Law School in 1891. After a short spell as prosecutor in Barra Mansa he practised law in Batatais, where he began his political career as an alderman and served as mayor from 1898 to 1899. He was elected a congressman in 1900 and was a state representative for the Republican Party of São Paulo between 1904 and 1906, then Secretary of State of Justice and Public Safety from 1906 to 1912.

He was mayor of São Paulo from 1914 to 1919, during which he faced the general strike of 1917, and governor of the state from 1920 to 1924. In 1924 he led the 3rd Battalion organized in Batatais against the rebels of São Paulo, and from 1925 to 1926 he served as a senator.

Washington Luís took office as president through direct election on 15 November 1926. The Old Republic had been worn down in the 1920s by opposition from the urban middle class, the lieutenants' and workers' movements and dissident oligarchies. Early in his term the Prestes Column ended after entering Bolivian territory with 620 men. In 1927 he created the Celerada Act, which imposed press censorship and restricted the right of assembly, and which drove the Brazilian Communist Party underground.

The crash of 24 October 1929 hit Brazilian coffee, which accounted for 70 per cent of exports, and overturned the valuation policy begun in 1906 with the Taubaté Agreement. Washington Luís refused the new currency devaluation that farmers asked for. Under the system of coffee with milk politics, a man from Minas Gerais should have succeeded him, but he backed another paulista, his friend Júlio Prestes, whose victory in the election of 1 March 1930 was questioned on suspicion of fraud.

The assassination of João Pessoa on 26 July 1930 worsened opposition, and Getúlio Vargas and Osvaldo Aranha began the conspiracy that led to the Revolution of 1930. Washington Luís was deposed on 24 October by the heads of the armed forces, and a junta of generals Tasso Fragoso and Mena Barreto and admiral Isaías de Noronha took power.

Washington Luís went into exile in Europe and the United States and returned to Brazil after seventeen years, in 1947. He settled in São Paulo and devoted himself to historical studies, and he was a member of the Academia Paulista de Letras and of historical and geographic institutes. He died in São Paulo on 4 August 1957. The Rodovia Washington Luís in the state of São Paulo is named in his honour.
washington-naval-conference: At the end of the First World War the British still had the largest navy afloat, but its big ships were becoming obsolete, while the Americans and the Japanese were rapidly building expensive new warships. Britain and Japan were allies in a treaty due to expire in 1922. Observers increasingly pointed to American-Japanese rivalry for control of the Pacific as a long-term threat to peace, and the British decided that, given their colonial interests in Asia, it was better to side with Washington than with Tokyo.

Popular demand for disarmament was strong. Women's organisations and the major Protestant denominations in the United States campaigned for peace, arguing that an end to the arms race would save money and avoid future wars. The conference was called by the United States and held outside the League of Nations.

The conference met in Washington, D.C., from 12 November 1921 to 6 February 1922 at Memorial Continental Hall. Nine nations attended: the United States, Japan, China, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Portugal. Germany and Soviet Russia were not invited. The American delegation was led by Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes and included Elihu Root, Henry Cabot Lodge and Oscar Underwood. Its main aim was to restrain Japanese naval expansion in the western Pacific.

Japan sought a naval treaty with Britain and the United States and recognition of its special interests in Manchuria and Mongolia. The British brought general aims: stability in the western Pacific, no naval race with the United States, and the security of Singapore, Hong Kong and dominion countries. The American side had intercepted and decrypted secret Japanese instructions that revealed the lowest naval ratio Tokyo would accept, and used the knowledge to press the Japanese delegation, which was headed by Prince Iyesato Tokugawa.

The conference produced three major treaties: the Four-Power Treaty, the Five-Power Treaty, known as the Washington Naval Treaty, and the Nine-Power Treaty, along with smaller agreements. A ten-year agreement fixed the ratio of battleships at 5:5:3, with 525,000 tons each for the United States and Britain and 315,000 tons for Japan, and smaller limits for France and Italy.
