No battleship could exceed 35,000 tons, and the three main powers were allowed 135,000, 135,000 and 81,000 tons of aircraft carriers. Japan agreed on 4 February 1922 to return Shandong to Chinese control.

The treaty largely ended the building of new battleship fleets, and some ships under construction became aircraft carriers. The powers raced to build heavy cruisers from 1927 to 1930, until the London Naval Treaty of 1930 set a 10:10:7 ratio for cruisers and destroyers. Japan ended its participation in 1936.
washington-naval-treaty: After the First World War Britain still had the world's largest navy, followed by the United States and, more distantly, Japan, France and Italy. With the German threat seemingly over, a naval arms race among the allies seemed likely. American plans of 1916 to 1919 called for 50 modern battleships, and in 1920 the Japanese Diet authorised an eight-eight programme of eight battleships and eight battlecruisers. The American public and Congress disliked the new race, and Britain could ill afford the cost of capital ships. In November 1921 the administration of Warren Harding called the Washington Naval Conference, partly to forestall a British plan for a conference on the Pacific and Far East.

At the opening session on 21 November 1921 Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes declared that the way to disarm is to disarm, and proposed a ten-year pause in capital ship construction and the scrapping of existing or planned ships to a ratio of 5:5:3 for Britain, the United States and Japan. The treaty, finalised on 6 February 1922, set tonnage ratios of approximately 5:5:3:1.75:1.75 for the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, Italy and France. Capital ships were limited to 35,000 tons and 16-inch guns, aircraft carriers to 27,000 tons, and all other warships to 10,000 tons and 8-inch guns. The United States had to scrap 30 existing or planned capital ships, Britain 23 and Japan 17.

Article XIX barred Britain, Japan and the United States from building new fortifications or naval bases in the Pacific, though existing ones at Singapore, the Philippines and Hawaii could stay. That provision helped win Japanese acceptance of the limits. Attempts to cap cruisers and submarines failed.

The treaty ended a long period of rising battleship construction, and many ships under construction were scrapped or converted into aircraft carriers. The London Naval Treaty of 1930 extended its limits, but the Second London Naval Treaty of 1936 was largely ineffective without Japan or Italy. The American delegates had also made it clear that they would not agree unless Britain ended its alliance with Japan, which the Imperial Conference of 1921 had already decided not to renew.

In Japan the treaty split the navy between the Treaty Faction and the Fleet Faction. The delegation's director, Katō Tomosaburō, accepted the lower ratio rather than an arms race the country would lose, while Katō Kanji opposed it. Isoroku Yamamoto argued for remaining in the treaty. On 29 December 1934 Japan gave formal notice of termination, and the provisions stayed in force until the end of 1936. American cryptographers had read Japanese delegation communications during the conference.
washington-on-the-brazos: The community lies on Farm to Market Road 912 off Texas State Highway 105 in the upper north-eastern corner of Washington County, 18 miles east of Brenham and 10 miles west of Navasota, near where the Navasota River joins the Brazos. It is named after Washington, Georgia, itself named for George Washington. Officially it is simply Washington; after the Civil War it came to be called Washington-on-the-Brazos to set it apart from Washington, D.C.

John W. Hall, one of the Old Three Hundred settlers, founded the town in 1833 on land given to him by his father-in-law Andrew Robinson, at a ferry crossing of the Brazos on La Bahia Road that dated from 1821. Most settlers came from the Southern United States into what was then Mexican Texas, and the town grew into a commercial centre. Sam Houston made his headquarters there in December 1835, after the Texas Revolution broke out.

The delegates of the Convention of 1836 met there from 1 March, signed the declaration on the day after its adoption, adopted a constitution on 16 March and formed an interim government. On 17 March they fled with the townspeople before the advancing Mexican Army, and the residents returned after the Mexican defeat at San Jacinto on 21 April. Town leaders lobbied in vain for Washington to become the permanent capital: the Republic's leaders favoured Waterloo, later renamed Austin.

Washington became the seat of Washington County in 1837, but the seat moved to Brenham in 1844. The town remained a centre of the cotton trade on the river until the mid-1850s, when railroads bypassed it, and after the Civil War it declined until by the turn of the 20th century it was virtually abandoned.

The Washington-on-the-Brazos State Historic Site holds the Star of the Republic Museum, a replica of Independence Hall, where the declaration was signed, and Barrington Plantation, home of Anson Jones, the last president of the Republic of Texas. The town is also home to Blessed Virgin Mary Catholic Church, founded in 1849 as the oldest Black Catholic church in Texas.
washukanni: Waššukanni, also written Aššukanni in Middle Assyrian texts, was the capital of the Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni from around 1500 BCE to the 13th century BCE. Its name may be of Old Indo-Aryan origin, from an original *Vasukanni built on the Indic word vasu, good, with an Indic suffix -ka- and the Hurrian suffix -nni.

Its site is unknown. Most proposals lie between the Khabur River, a tributary of the Euphrates, and the Jaghjagh River in the upper Jezirah of Syria. Dietrich Opitz placed it under the largely unexcavated mound of Tell el Fakhariya near Tell Halaf; a neutron activation comparison with clay of the Amarna tablets seemed to rule this out, and Edward Lipinski rejected it, but recent German excavations led Stefano de Martino, Mirko Novák and Dominik Bonatz to support it again. No text naming the capital has yet been found there. Tell Farfara, Üçtepe Höyük in Diyarbakır Province, Koçlu Tepe and Tell al-Hawa have also been proposed, and the route of Suppiluliuma I's campaign suggests a place near Mardin.

Suppiluliuma I, who reigned c. 1344–1322 BCE, sacked the city early in his reign. In his own account he passed through Alse, captured Kutmar, ransacked Suta and reached Waššukanni, while Tusratta, the king of Mitanni, withdrew and would not meet him in battle; the Hittite king then recrossed the Euphrates and defeated Halba and Mukis. His treaty inscription records that he installed a Hurrian vassal king, Shattiwaza. Around 1290 BCE the Assyrian king Adad-nirari I sacked the city again, and it served for a time as an Assyrian provincial capital before disappearing from history. Its name survives in the Waşokanî refugee camp near Hesekê in north-eastern Syria, built for people of Serê Kaniyê and Zirgan displaced by the Turkish offensive of 2019.
wasit: Wasit stood on the west bank of the Tigris, across the river from the older city of Kashkar. Its name, meaning middle, came from its position halfway between Kufa and Basra, the two traditional administrative centres and garrisons of Iraq. The ancient city measured 16 kilometres around, and its ruins lie southeast of Kut, in the governorate that bears its name.

Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the Umayyad viceroy of Iraq, built the city as the seat of the governor and the garrison of the troops who enforced Umayyad rule in the region. He is said to have taken the doors for its citadel and main mosque from Zanzaward, and he died in Wasit in 714. When Ibn Battuta visited centuries later, he noted its fine quarters, its abundance of orchards and fruit trees, and its notable men, whose living teachers furnished lessons for meditation. The city was abandoned in the 16th century, after the Tigris changed its course.

Because the site lay away from building and farming, its remains, mostly of brick, survived. Surveys were carried out from 1936 to 1942 and again in 1985. Excavators cleared the large mosque through four stages, from the 7th back to the 1st century of the Hijri calendar, together with part of the governor's house beside it, a building known as the minaret with a tomb and a school of the 7th Hijri century, and a residential district in the late 1930s.
Some conservation has been carried out on the minaret, whose walls had worn away. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 7 September 2000, in the cultural category.
wassily-kandinsky: Kandinsky was born in Moscow, the son of Lidia Tikheeva and Vassily Silvestrovich Kandinsky, a tea merchant. He studied law and economics, and later recalled being fascinated as a child by colour. In 1889 he joined an ethnographic research group that travelled to the Vologda region north of Moscow, where houses and churches were decorated in such shimmering colours that he felt he was entering a painting. His study of the region's folk art, with its bright colours on a dark background, shaped much of his early work.

In 1896 he gave up a promising career teaching law and economics, at the age of 30, and enrolled at the Munich Academy, where his teachers eventually included Franz von Stuck. Before leaving Moscow he had seen an exhibition of paintings by Monet. He found he could not recognise the subject of Haystacks, yet the picture stayed in his memory, and this convinced him that colour could work almost independently of objects.

From 1896 Kandinsky lived in Munich, where he was first the teacher and then the partner of Gabriele Münter. He helped found the Neue Künstlervereinigung München and became its president in 1909, but the group could not reconcile his radical approach with conventional ideas and dissolved in late 1911. He then formed The Blue Rider with artists including August Macke, Franz Marc, Albert Bloch and Münter. The group issued an almanac and held two exhibitions, and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 ended its plans and sent him back to Russia.

From 1918 to 1921 he took part in Russia's cultural politics, collaborated in art education and museum reform, and was the first director of the Institute of Artistic Culture in Moscow, whose radical members rejected his spiritual view of art as too individualistic. In 1921 Walter Gropius invited him to the Bauhaus. He taught basic design and advanced theory there from 1922 until the Nazis closed the school in 1933, then moved to France and became a French citizen in 1939.

Kandinsky likened painting to music, writing that colour is the keyboard and the artist the hand that plays. He called his most spontaneous paintings improvisations and his more elaborate ones compositions. His text Concerning the Spiritual in Art, published in Munich in 1911, defines three types of painting: impressions, improvisations and compositions. Point and Line to Plane followed in 1926. His influence on Western art stems perhaps more from his theory than from his paintings. Works of his were confiscated in the Nazi campaign against "degenerate art", and the first three Compositions were destroyed during the Second World War. He died in Neuilly-sur-Seine on 13 December 1944.
wassoulou: Wassoulou, also spelled Wassulu, Wassalou or Ouassalou, is a cultural area and historical region around the point where the borders of Mali, Ivory Coast and Guinea meet, bordered by the Niger River to the north-west and the Sankarani River to the east. Its people are called Wassulu, Wassulunka or Wassulunke. The Fulani among them are believed to have come from the Fouta Djallon highlands and to have merged with the indigenous Mandé peoples before the 18th century, taking up local customs as Islam spread.

Before the 19th century the region is poorly attested, but it appears to have been a fairly decentralised and egalitarian society of jamana, alliances of small walled villages. In the 18th and early 19th centuries it was in some respects tributary to the Segou Empire, yet it still suffered regular slave raids. In 1870 Samori Ture overthrew an older Wassoulou state whose faama, or ruler, was Dyanabufarina Modi, and imposed a hierarchical government, appointing the local Muslim convert Farbalay Jakite as his representative in 1882.

The Wassoulunke rebelled several times. A rising in 1885 against the institution of Islam and the suppression of animist practices was brutally put down by Samori's brother Keme Brema, and another after his failure at the siege of Sikasso was also crushed. His war with Kenedougou left thousands of refugees, many sold into slavery or selling themselves to avoid starving. In 1891 he forced much of the population east with him and massacred the town of N'Tentou when its people refused to leave, so that his years left the region almost entirely depopulated.

Instability, including predation by colonial troops, continued under French rule. As slavery slowly died out in the French Sudan, tens of thousands of freed slaves returned to Wassoulou in the decades before the First World War.

About 160,000 people live in Wassoulou. It is the birthplace of Wassoulou music, a style that joins traditional and modern influences, with strong female singers and a pentatonic hunter's harp; Oumou Sangare, Ramata Diakite and Coumba Sidibe are among its singers.
wat-arun: A Buddhist temple stood on the site in the Ayutthaya period, before the reign of King Narai, and was known as Wat Bang Makok, later shortened to Wat Makok after the village in which it was built. According to the historian Prince Damrong Rajanubhab, French maps drawn during Narai's reign (1656-88) show it. After the fall of Ayutthaya, Taksin (1767-82) founded his new capital at Thonburi beside the temple and renamed it Wat Chaeng. He is believed to have vowed to restore it after passing it at dawn.

The temple stood within the grounds of Taksin's royal palace and enshrined the Emerald Buddha until the image was moved to Wat Phra Kaew on the eastern bank of the river in 1785. Rama I (1782-1809) moved the palace across the river, and the temple was abandoned until Rama II (1809-24) had it restored and began plans to raise the main pagoda to 70 metres. Work began under Rama III (1824-51), and the main prang was finished in 1851 after nine years of construction.

The name comes from the Hindu god Aruna, the charioteer of the sun god Surya. The central prang is encrusted with coloured porcelain and with shells of Mauritia mauritiana. The porcelain had earlier served as ballast in boats coming to Bangkok from China. Four smaller satellite prang stand at the corners, and the satellite prang is devoted to the wind god Phra Phai. The central prang is topped with a seven-pronged trident, and statues of the Hindu god Indra riding on Erawan stand over its second terrace.

The central prang stands for Mount Meru in Hindu cosmology, and in Buddhist iconography it has three symbolic levels, the base for the Traiphum, the middle for Tavatimsa and the top for Devaphum. Beside it is the ordination hall, whose Buddha image was supposedly designed by Rama II, whose murals were made under Rama V and whose entrance is guarded by two demons from the Ramakien, the white Sahassa Deja and the green Thotsakan, who is Ravana. The prang was restored in 1980 and again from 2013 to 2017, when lime plaster replaced the cement of earlier work.
wat-chaiwatthanaram: Prasat Thong built the temple as the first of his reign, on the west bank of the Chao Phraya south-west of the old city, as a memorial of his mother's residence in that area. Its name means the Temple of long reign and glorious era. It was designed in Khmer style to gain Buddhist merit and to honour his mother, though Prince Damrong believed it was built to celebrate the Ayutthaya Kingdom's victory over Longvek.

A central prang 35 metres high, with four smaller prangs, stands on a rectangular platform, with steep stairs leading to hidden entrances about halfway up. Around it stand eight chedi-shaped chapels joined by a cross-shaped gallery that was once roofed and lined with 120 seated Buddha statues, probably painted black and gold. The chapels held further seated Buddha statues under wooden ceilings with golden stars on black lacquer, and their outer walls bore twelve reliefs of scenes from the life of the Buddha, read clockwise, of which only fragments survive. East of the galleries, near the river, stood the ordination hall, flanked by two chedis in which the ashes of the king's mother were laid.

The plan follows the Buddhist world view described in the 14th-century Traiphum Phra Ruang. The central prang is Mount Meru, the axis of the world; the four small prangs are the continents in the world sea, humans living on one of them, Chomphutawip; and the rectangular gallery is the outer border of the world, the Iron Mountains.

It was a royal temple where the king and his successors held religious ceremonies, and princes and princesses were cremated there, among them Chaofa Thammathibet, son of King Boromakot. Deserted after the Burmese destruction of the capital, it suffered theft, the sale of its bricks and the beheading of its Buddha statues. The Thai Department of Fine Arts began restoring it in 1987 and opened it to the public in 1992. In the 2011 Thai floods it stood under 2 metres of water and was badly damaged, and it was restored again with a budget of 200 million baht.
wat-chedi-luang: Its name means temple of the grand stupa, and its grounds were formed from three temples: Wat Chedi Luang, Wat Ho Tham and Wat Sukmin. Building began when Saenmueangma planned to bury his father's ashes there. After ten years the work was left unfinished, continued by his widow after the king's death, and, probably because of problems of stability, completed only under Tilokaraj. The finished chedi stood 82 metres high on a base 54 metres across.

The Emerald Buddha was installed in the chedi's eastern niche in 1468, and after the earthquake of 1545 brought down its upper 30 metres the statue was moved to Luang Prabang in 1551. The grounds also hold the city pillar of Chiang Mai, Sao Inthakin, which Kawila moved there from Wat Sadeu Muang in 1800 and beside which he planted three trees believed to help it protect the town; a festival in its honour is held every May for six to eight days. A wihan near the entrance houses Phra Chao Attarot, the Eighteen-cubit Buddha cast in the late 14th century, and a pavilion on the far side of the chedi a reclining Buddha.

In the early 1990s the chedi was reconstructed with money from UNESCO and the Japanese government. The work remains controversial, some holding that the new elements are in Central Thai rather than Lanna style. For the chedi's 600th anniversary in 1995 a black jade copy of the Emerald Buddha, officially named Phra Phut Chaloem Sirirat and commonly called Phra Yok, was placed in the rebuilt eastern niche. The temple also holds daily monk chats, at which visitors may ask monks, usually novices, about Buddhism and Thailand.
wat-chet-yot: Its official name, Wat Photharam Maha Wihan, comes from the Sanskrit Bōdh Rāma Mahā Vihāra. Before building, King Tilokarat sent monks to Bagan in Burma to study the design of the Mahabodhi temple there, itself a copy of the temple at Bodh Gaya in Bihar. According to the Jinakālamālī chronicle he planted a bodhi tree on the spot in 1455, and in 1476 established a large sanctuary in the monastery, probably for the ceremony marking 2,000 years of Buddhism. The council held there the next year met to renew the Tripitaka, the Pali Canon.

The central sanctuary, the Maha Pho wihan or Maha Chedi, is a rectangular, windowless building with clearly Indian influences. On its flat roof stand the seven spires that give the temple its name: a pyramid-like spire on a square base surrounded by four smaller ones, and two bell-shaped chedis on the building's two annexes. Inside, a barrel-vaulted corridor leads to a Buddha statue, beside which narrow stairs climb to the roof, open only to men. A bodhi tree that once grew on the roof was removed in 1910 so that the structure would not collapse. The outer walls carry 70 weathered stucco reliefs of devas, whose faces are said to be modelled on King Tilokarat's relatives.

The grounds hold several more Lanna-style chedis with Buddha statues in alcoves on four sides; the largest contains the ashes of King Tilokarat. A small ubosot in the north-east corner has a carved wooden gable and double boundary stones, and at the southern end a mondop shelters a statue of the Buddha protected by the nāga Mucalinda. The temple lies north-west of the city centre and is a place of pilgrimage for those born in the year of the Snake.
wat-pho: Wat Pho is one of the oldest temples in Bangkok and existed before King Rama I made Bangkok the capital. Its first name, Wat Photaram, refers to the monastery of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. The date of the old temple and its founder are not known; it was built in the Ayutthaya period and is said to have been built or expanded under King Phetracha (1688 to 1703). After Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, King Taksin built his palace in Thonburi beside Wat Arun, across the Chao Phraya river, and the proximity raised Wat Pho to a royal monastery.

In 1788 Rama I ordered the dilapidated temple rebuilt, and had Buddha images brought from abandoned temples in Ayutthaya, Sukhothai and elsewhere, including the remnants of a huge image from Wat Phra Si Sanphet, which were enclosed in a chedi. In 1801 the new complex was renamed Wat Phra Chetuphon Vimolmangklavas and became his main temple. Rama III began to renovate and enlarge it in 1832, a work of 16 years and seven months, and Rama IV added a fourth great chedi.

The complex has two walled compounds divided by Chetuphon Road. The northern one, the phutthawat, contains the buildings dedicated to the Buddha, and the southern one, the sankhawat, holds the monks' quarters and a school. The grounds hold four great chedis of 42 metres, dedicated to the first four Chakri kings, 91 small chedis, a bot dedicated in 1791 and about 400 Buddha images in a double cloister, chosen from 1,200 that Rama I had brought.

The Buddha in the viharn built under Rama III lies in the posture of a reclining lion and represents the Buddha's passing into Nirvana. It is 15 m high and 46 m long, made of a brick core modelled in plaster and gilded, and the soles of its feet, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, are divided into 108 panels showing auspicious symbols.

Wat Pho was meant as a place of public education. A pictorial encyclopedia was engraved on granite slabs on history, medicine, health, custom, literature, proverbs, lexicography and the Buddhist religion, with texts written by about 50 people from the court of Rama III and learned monks led by Supreme Patriarch Prince Paramanuchitchinorot. UNESCO registered the marble illustrations and inscriptions in its Memory of the World Programme on 21 February 2008. Wat Pho is regarded as the first university of Thailand. Plaques show the pressure points used in traditional Thai massage, the temple still has a school of Thai medicine, and Thai massage has been included in UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
wat-phra-kaew: When King Rama I made Bangkok the capital of the Rattanakosin Kingdom on 6 April 1782, the new Chakri dynasty needed a royal palace and temple to legitimise it. He wished to distance himself from the regime of King Taksin, whom he had replaced, and the old palace at Thonburi was small and hemmed in between Wat Arun and Wat Tai Talat. The temple stands within the Grand Palace precincts. Each later king has added to, restored or embellished it as a way of making religious merit and glorifying the dynasty, and has donated sacred objects to its treasury.

The Emerald Buddha, the temple's namesake, is a meditating Buddha in the lotus position, about 66 centimetres tall, of a green semi-precious stone usually described as jade and clothed in gold. It sits on a pedestal at the western end of the ordination hall, the Ubosot, which is ringed by forty-eight columns covered in glass mosaic and by eight pavilions with gilded boundary stones. Its murals depict the life of the Buddha, the Buddha's victory over Mara and Buddhist cosmology.

A raised terrace carries the Phra Mondop, a library for the Tripitaka that Rama I had revised in 1788 after the sack of Ayutthaya in 1767; the Phra Si Rattana Chedi, a gilded stupa holding relics from Sri Lanka; and the Royal Pantheon, rebuilt under Rama VI after a fire in 1903 and opened each year on 6 April, Chakri Memorial Day. Rama IV had a scale model of Angkor Wat made after that temple was rediscovered.

Important state and royal ceremonies are held in the temple each year, presided over by the king in person and attended by government officials, which makes it a national shrine for the monarchy and the state. A covered gallery around the complex carries murals of the Ramakien, the Thai version of the Ramayana, in 178 scenes; Rama I had the epic recomposed in Thai verse around 1797. The murals were repainted under Rama III and have been restored often. Twelve guardian giants, each about 5 metres tall and drawn from the Ramakien, stand at the gates.
wat-phra-mahathat-woramahawihan: According to a legend told alike in Thailand and Sri Lanka, Prince Thanakuman and Princess Hem Chala brought a relic of the Buddha to Hat Sai Kaew and built a small pagoda there in 291 CE. The monastery was founded in the 8th century on the site of a Hindu shrine, and an earlier temple there, Wat Phra Borom That, was built in the Mahayana style of the Srivijaya empire, of which the city was part until the early 13th century. In the early 13th century, when, historians believe, epidemics and war had almost emptied the city, King Sri Dhammasokaraja built the larger bell-shaped stupa with public participation, as a symbol of Theravada Buddhism and a means of reviving the town.
His name means Ashoka the great, and the Sri Lankan form of the stupa reflects the belief that Ashoka carried the tradition of the stupa from India to Sri Lanka.

The complex covers 5.14 hectares within brick walls and four gates, divided into a sacred area for worship and a residential area for monks. Twenty-two stucco elephants stand around the base of the main stupa, standing for the 22 spiritual faculties, and its spire of 52 rings, for the 52 mental factors, is 10.89 metres high and covered with about 600 kilograms of gold leaf; the whole structure rises 78 metres.

Around it are four smaller stupas, 158 minor chedis holding the ashes of devotees, a gallery of Buddha images whose oldest is a Sukhothai-style figure of the 13th–14th century, the assembly hall Wihan Luang of the 15th and 16th centuries, and a cloister round a bodhi tree believed to come from the tree at Bodh Gaya.

Inscriptions of the Sukhothai Kingdom speak of the city and its stupa spreading Theravada Buddhism, and the temple was patronised by the Ayutthaya Kingdom. It has been restored many times, from 1612–1616 to 2009. Each year at Magha Puja, in February, the Hae Pha Khuen That procession carries a single long robe to wrap the stupa, a festival believed to date from 1230. The temple appears on the 25 satang coin, and on 25 July 2026 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.
wat-phra-si-sanphet: The temple stands where U-thong, King Ramathibodi I, ordered a royal palace built in 1350; on its completion in 1351 he made Ayutthaya the capital of his kingdom. The palace held three wooden buildings, the Phaithun Maha Prasat, Phaichayon Maha Prasat and Aisawan Maha Prasat. In 1448 King Borommatrailokkanat built a new palace to the north and turned the old grounds into a holy site. His son King Ramathibodi II built two chedis in 1492 for the ashes of his father and of his brother, King Borommaracha III, and King Borommaracha IV added a third in 1529 for the ashes of Ramathibodi II.

In 1499 a hall of worship, the Vihara Luang or Royal Chapel, was built. Ramathibodi II had a Buddha image cast for it, the Phra Si Sanphetdayan, 16 metres high on a pedestal 8 metres long, with a bronze core of about 64 tons covered in about 343 kilograms of gold. It took more than three years to complete.

The three chedis stand on a raised platform, with small chapels topped by miniature chedis leading to steep stairs. A cloister surrounded the terrace, with a hall at each end: to the west four viharn set in a cross around a mondop, to the east the Vihara Luang with its great image. Four further halls were grouped around it, among them one to the north for the statue of Phra Phuttha Lokanat, more than 10 metres high. A high wall with gates in the four directions enclosed the whole, lined inside with small chedis and low pavilions, some of which survive.

The temple was used only by members of the royal family. King Narai later added a cross-shaped vihara west of the platform, now known as Prasat Phra Narai, European in shape, with pointed-arch windows, and the temple was renovated again in 1742 under King Borommakot. When the Burmese took Ayutthaya in 1767 they looted the temple, set it on fire and melted its gold. The chedis were restored by the Fine Arts Department in 1956, and the foundations of the other buildings are preserved.
wat-phra-singh: The temple stands in the western part of Chiang Mai's old city, inside the walls and moat. Phayu, fifth king of Lan Na of the Mangrai dynasty, built it to inter in a stupa the ashes of his father Khamfu, brought from Chiang Saen. It was first called Wat Lee Chiang Phra, after the marketplace in front of it. In 1400 King Saenmueangma of Lan Na received the Phra Phuttha Sihing image from Maha Phrom, ruler of Chiang Rai, who had obtained it from Kamphaeng Phet; once it was enshrined there, people called the temple Wat Phra Singh.

From 1558 until 1775 Chiang Mai was part of a Burmese empire, and when the Burmese were driven out most of its temples lay in ruins. Kawila, who in 1782 became the first king of a new dynasty of Chiang Mai, began to restore the temple. The monk Khruba Siwichai renovated it again in the early 1920s as part of his wider effort to revive Buddhism in the Lan Na region, and in 1935 King Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII) made it a royal temple of the first grade.

The main hall, the Viharn Luang, was built in 1924 after Khruba Siwichai took down the old four-sided vihara, which was beyond repair. It is 56 metres long and 24 metres wide, in Lanna style, with a teak roof on concrete walls and pillars, swan-tail tiles and finials, and it houses the Phra Sri Sanphet statue.

The Phra Buddha Sihing is kept in the smaller Viharn Lai Kham, 30 metres long and 8 metres wide, built between 1815 and 1821 under Thammalangka, the second prince of Chiang Mai. Its pillars, timberwork and the wall behind the main image carry intricate gold-leaf and lacquer decoration, and its murals tell the tales of Sang Thong and Suwannahongse. It was later restored several times, by Kawilorot Suriyawong, Inthawichayanon and Khruba Siwichai among others.
wat-phu: Vat Phou is a ruined Khmer-Hindu temple complex in southern Laos. A sanctuary stood there from prehistoric times, centred on a spring and an offering place for a tutelary spirit. The first megalithic stone structures were probably built as early as the second century BCE, with two stone cells, a carving of a crocodile, serpent stairs and offering platforms. One of the pre-Angkor brick buildings was erected in the 7th century and became the focus of later building.

The site was first associated with the city of Shrestapura, on the Mekong directly east of Lingaparvata Mountain, later called Phou Khao. By the later part of the fifth century the city was the capital of a kingdom that texts and inscriptions connect with Chenla and Champa, and the first structure on the mountain was built about then. A lingam-shaped protuberance on the summit made the mountain the home of Shiva, with the river representing the ocean or the Ganges.

The earliest inscription found there, K.365, names Devanika, who established a sacred tīrtha in the area; it records that he had won countless victories, came from afar to found a kingdom and gave thousands of cattle to a temple foundation. The site museum holds standing Buddhas in Gupta and post-Gupta style, which Pierre-Yves Manguin groups with statues from Thailand and from Cham sites in central Vietnam as evidence of an artistic vocabulary shared across the region between the 5th and the late 7th or early 8th century.

After its first scientific description in the 19th and 20th centuries there was little scientific work until the 1990s. Lao-UNESCO projects began in 1987, and the site became a World Heritage Site in 2001. Conservation has included Italian work on the hall of Nandin from 2006, an Indian survey of the northern quadrangle in 2009 and French work on the southern palace. The site is open for religious activities and visits, and a festival is held there each February.
wat-xieng-thong: The name means Temple of the Golden City. It stands on the northern tip of the peninsula of Luang Prabang, between the Mekong and Nam Khan rivers. King Setthathirath, who built it, moved the capital of Lan Xang from Xieng Thong, later renamed Luang Prabang, to Vientiane, saying he disliked its lack of flat land. Luang Prabang nevertheless remained a royal capital until the Lao People's Democratic Republic was established in 1975, and the temple, founded alongside Vat Keo and Vat That Luang, stayed under royal patronage until then. Kings were crowned there, and it served as a place of worship, a shrine for relics, a festival ground and a library of ancient scripts.

The central shrine hall, or sim, has nine cascading roofs decorated with gold stencilling. Along the ridge runs the dok so fa, small gilded pagodas hooking upwards, whose number and detail mark a Laotian temple's standing. Inside, red and black walls carry gold stencils of mythological scenes and geometric designs, the ceiling shows dharma wheels, and the rear gable bears a glass mosaic of the tree of life.

Behind the sim, a small chapel decorated with mosaics holds a rare reclining Buddha that dates from the temple's construction. It was shown at the Paris Exhibition in 1931 and kept in Vientiane until its return in 1964. By the eastern gate the royal funerary carriage house holds a funeral carriage 12 metres high and urns for members of the royal family. Other buildings include the monks' living quarters and a boat house.

When the Black Flag Haw sacked Luang Phrabang in 1887, the temple was spared, with Wat Suwannaphumaham, because their leader Đèo Văn Trị had studied there as a monk and used it as his headquarters. The Tripiṭaka library was added in 1880 and the drum tower in 1961. In 1928 King Sisavangvong persuaded the French Governor General to share the cost of restoration, and in 2012 and 2013 the gold stencils, tiles, doors and windows were restored. Luang Prabang became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.
water-clock: The word clepsydra comes from the Greek for water thief. Two types of water clock exist. In an outflow clock a container is filled with water and drains slowly and evenly, and markings on the container show how much time has passed as the level falls. An inflow clock works the same way, except that a marked container fills.

The flow follows Torricelli's law if viscosity is neglected. Because water becomes less viscous as it warms, a clock with a long, thin nozzle would gain or lose about half an hour a day for each degree Celsius of change. Ancient clocks were probably reset daily from a sundial, so the cumulative error would not have been great.

Egyptian outflow clocks were stone vessels with sloping sides and a small hole near the bottom. Twelve columns of markings, one for each month, allowed for the changing length of seasonal hours, and priests used the clocks to find the time at night so that temple rites could be performed at the correct hour.

In Babylon the clocks were cylindrical and measured time by the weight of water flowing out, and clay tablets record their use to pay the night and day watches. In Greek and Roman courts a small earthenware clepsydra allocated time to speakers; in important cases it was filled completely, and its hole was stopped with wax if proceedings were interrupted. In Persia, water clocks timed the share of water that each farmer could take from a qanat.

Between 270 BCE and 500 CE Hellenistic and Roman engineers, among them Ctesibius, Hero of Alexandria and Archimedes, built more elaborate clocks that rang bells, opened doors to show figurines or moved pointers and dials. Ctesibius added gears and a dial indicator to show the changing length of the days automatically, and Philo of Byzantium mentioned clocks fitted with an escapement.

In China, Zhang Heng used a clepsydra in 117 to drive a model of the heavens, and in 1088 Su Song powered an astronomical clock tower, over 30 feet tall, in the same way. Al-Jazari described his elephant clock and castle clock in 1206. Water clocks stayed the common timekeeper for millennia, until verge escapement mechanical clocks replaced them in Europe around 1300.
water-wheel: A water wheel is a machine that turns the kinetic energy of flowing or falling water into useful power, often in a watermill. It is a large wheel, usually of wood or metal, with blades or buckets on its rim, fed from a mill pond formed by damming a stream. The water reaches it along a headrace and leaves by a tailrace.

There are two basic designs: a horizontal wheel on a vertical axle, often called a tub wheel, Norse mill or Greek mill, and a vertical wheel on a horizontal axle. The vertical type is divided into stream, undershot, breastshot, overshot and backshot wheels according to where the water strikes. An overshot wheel can reach 90 per cent efficiency, while a flat-board undershot wheel used about 20 per cent of the energy, as John Smeaton measured in the 18th century.

Water wheels served two main purposes: lifting water for irrigation and milling, particularly of grain. The wheel first appeared in the ancient Near East, specifically Egypt, in the 4th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE it was used there to move millstones, and the sāqiya spread rapidly across the Near East in the Hellenistic period.

The Roman architect Vitruvius, in the late 1st century BCE, gave the first clear description of a geared watermill, a combination of the Greek toothed gear and the water wheel. A poem by Antipater of Thessalonica praised the wheel for freeing women from the labour of grinding. In China the Xin Lun, written by Huan Tan about 20 CE, suggests that water wheels were used for pounding machinery in grain mills, and by the 1st century CE the wheel was in widespread use there.

After the spread of Islam, engineers continued the technology of the ancient Near East. Hama in Syria preserves large wheels on the Orontes, one with a diameter of about 20 metres and 120 compartments, and some medieval compartmented wheels lifted water as high as 30 metres. In Ireland the oldest known horizontal wheels, at Ballykilleen, date to about 636. Smeaton's investigation in the mid to late 18th century raised efficiency and supplied power for the Industrial Revolution.

Water wheels were in commercial use well into the 20th century. Their main limitation is their dependence on flowing water, which restricts where they can stand. The turbine, developed by Benoît Fourneyron beginning with his first model in 1827, was smaller, cheaper and more efficient, and it handles high heads that wheels of practical size cannot. Modern hydroelectric dams can be viewed as the descendants of the water wheel.
waterford: Waterford lies in the province of Munster at the head of Waterford Harbour, on the River Suir. Downriver the Nore and the Barrow join the Suir at a place the Irish call Cumar na dTrí Uisce, the confluence of the three waters. Its name comes from the Old Norse Veðrafjǫrðr, meaning ram or wether fjord, while the Irish name, Port Láirge, means Lárag's port.

Waterford Port has been one of Ireland's major ports for over a millennium, and in the 19th century shipbuilding was a major industry. The Malcomson family of the Neptune Shipyard operated the largest fleet of iron steamers in the world between the mid-1850s and the late 1860s.

Viking raiders first established a settlement near Waterford in 853. It and the other longphorts were vacated about 902, when the native Irish drove the Vikings out. The Vikings re-established themselves at Waterford in 914, led first by Jarl Ottar until 917, then by Ragnall ua Ímair and the Uí Ímair dynasty, and built what would be Ireland's first city.

Among its most prominent rulers was Ivar of Waterford. The medieval city was attacked several times and earned the motto Urbs Intacta Manet, the Untaken City, after repelling a siege in the 15th century. The office of Mayor of Waterford was established in 1377. In the 15th century the city was enlarged with an outer wall on the west side.

The population grew from 1,555 in 1653 to about 28,000 in the early 19th century, then declined to just over 20,000 at the end of the century before rising to more than 40,000 in the 20th. Waterford Crystal, the city's best-known export, was made there from 1783 to 1851, from 1947 to 2009 and again from 2010.

Waterford is the county town of County Waterford, with 60,079 people at the 2022 census, and the main city of Ireland's South-East Region. The Viking Triangle, the oldest quarter, lies within the original tenth-century fortifications and is triangular, with its apex at Reginald's Tower. The tower is the oldest urban civic building in Ireland and the oldest monument to keep its Viking name. Waterford keeps more of its city walls than any other Irish city except Derry. The Theatre Royal dates from 1785, and the Waterford Greenway, opened in 2017, links the city with Dungarvan. Ryanair's first flight ran between Waterford and Gatwick.
watergate-scandal: Richard Nixon, elected the 37th president of the United States in 1968, secretly expanded the bombing of the Vietnam War to Cambodia. When The New York Times exposed the bombing in May 1969, he ordered the wiretapping of reporters and suspected leakers, and his domestic policy chief John Ehrlichman directly arranged some of it after the Federal Bureau of Investigation could not bug certain targets. Of the leaks Nixon said that the government could not function if anyone could run out and leak.

In December 1971 G. Gordon Liddy became general counsel of the Committee for the Re-Election of the President, which also recruited a retired CIA officer, James McCord, as its security chief. Nixon had also had the Secret Service install microphones in the Oval Office. From 16 February 1971 to 12 July 1973 the system recorded 3,432 hours of conversation, and it was kept secret even from his secretary, Rose Mary Woods.

Two attempts in May 1972 to break into the Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex failed. On the night of 17 June 1972 the burglars, mostly Cuban exiles led by the former intelligence agents E. Howard Hunt and Liddy, were caught planting listening devices. The break-in was an implementation of Operation Gemstone. The next morning Liddy destroyed Gemstone files, and investigators found that McCord worked for the committee and that the White House had run a background check on Hunt.

Nixon denied involvement, but his administration destroyed evidence, obstructed investigators and bribed the burglars. The Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, guided by the source called Deep Throat, exposed an illegally funded political espionage programme. The cover-up helped Nixon to a landslide re-election, until revelations at the burglars' 1973 trial led to a Senate investigation.

Special prosecutor Archibald Cox subpoenaed the Oval Office tapes, and Nixon invoked executive privilege, then fired Cox in the Saturday Night Massacre, which forced the resignations of the attorney general and his deputy. In July 1974 the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released, and the House Judiciary Committee recommended impeachment for obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress. The Smoking Gun tape showed that Nixon had ordered the CIA to stop the FBI's investigation. On 9 August 1974 he became the first United States president to resign, and 69 people were charged in all.

The motive for the break-in, and who ordered it, has never been established, and no one was charged for ordering it. The scandal brought heavy Republican losses in the 1974 midterm elections and Gerald Ford's failed re-election bid in 1976, and the suffix -gate entered the language to denote scandals.
watling-street: The Romans found a broad, grassy trackway that the Britons had used for centuries, mainly between the areas of modern Canterbury and St Albans, crossing the Thames by a natural ford near Westminster. They began building paved roads soon after their invasion in 43 CE, and excavations date the London stretch to the winter of 47 to 48. Around London it was 7.5 to 8.7 metres wide and surfaced with gravel, and it was relaid at least twice before Boudica's forces sacked the city in 60 or 61. Most historians place the defeat of Boudica's Iceni by G. Suetonius Paulinus somewhere along its middle section.

The road linked the Kent ports of Dubris, Rutupiae, Lemanis and Regulbium with the Roman bridge at Londinium, then ran north-west through Verulamium to Viroconium Cornoviorum. The 2nd-century Antonine Itinerary lists its stations as part of a longer route from Richborough to Hadrian's Wall. Its Celtic and Roman name is unknown. The modern name comes from the Old English Wæcelinga Stræt, after the Waeclingas, a people of the St Albans area, at a time when street meant any paved road; the stretch between Canterbury and London was first called Casingc Stræt.

The Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum used the road as a boundary, and it is often inferred that it thus marked the south-western edge of the Danelaw; it still divides Leicestershire from Warwickshire. In the Laws of Edward the Confessor it was one of four roads under the king's peace. England's first turnpike trust was set up over it north-west of London on 4 March 1707, and in the early 19th century Thomas Telford repaved it for mail coaches from Ireland and extended it to Holyhead. Its course is followed by the A2 from Dover to London and largely by the A5 north of London.
waxaklajuun-ubaah-kawiil: His name means Eighteen are the Faces (or Images) of K'awiil, after the many forms of the Maya god K'awiil, a god of power, creation and lightning. He ruled the polity of Copán, in modern Honduras, whose Classic Maya name was probably Oxwitik, from 2 January 695 to 3 May 738, succeeding the 12th ruler, Smoke Imix. He began by building the Esmeralda Structure to entomb Smoke Imix, which ritually closed the adjacent Papagayo temple, raised some 250 years earlier by Ruler 2, son of K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo'. He later built the original hieroglyphic stairway on its east side.

Measured by the number of buildings and monuments of his reign, he is regarded as the chief patron of the arts in Copán's history, and its deep, florid relief marks the height of the city's sculpture. Some of his buildings were lost to erosion by the Copán River.

Structure 10L-22 represents a sacred man-made mountain, its entrance carved as an arching Celestial Monster, the mouth of a cave; its inner chamber was likely used for bloodletting rituals. Between 711 and 736 he raised Stelas C, F, 4, H, A, B and D, each showing him in ritual pose with a two-headed centipede bar, and Stela A ranks Copán with Calakmul, Palenque and Tikal as the four great polities of the Maya world. His last work, Ballcourt A-III, with six macaw markers, was dedicated 113 days before his death.

Quiriguá, a vassal founded in 426 that controlled the Motagua River trade route and was about one-tenth the size of Copán, had seen its ruler K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat installed under his authority. In 734, on Altar M, K'ak' Tiliw took the title k'uhul ajaw, declaring independence. Quiriguá's monuments record the beheading of Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil as an ax event; Copán's Hieroglyphic Stairway records only his death by flint and shield, and the lack of evidence for a large battle near Copán suggests he was captured abroad.

Stela I at Quiriguá records that in 736 K'ak' Tiliw hosted a delegation from Calakmul, including its ruler Wamaw K'awiil, which suggests that Calakmul, rival of Copán's ally Tikal, had a part in the defeat. No new buildings or monuments were raised at Copán for 18 years afterwards, and his successor, K'ak' Joplaj Chan K'awiil, probably ruled under Quiriguá's jurisdiction.
way-of-the-five-pecks-of-rice: In 142 CE Zhang Daoling announced that Laozi had appeared to him and ordered him to rid the world of decadence and found a new state of chosen people. As the first Celestial Master he spread the movement through Sichuan, and it grew fast under his son Zhang Heng and grandson Zhang Lu, winning over groups such as the Bandun Man of the Ba people. In 191 Zhang Lu and Zhang Xiu were sent to conquer the Hanzhong valley; Zhang Xiu was killed, and Zhang Lu founded an independent theocratic state.

When the warlord Cao Cao attacked in 215, Zhang Lu fled and later surrendered, receiving a title and land and moving to Cao Cao's headquarters at Ye, where he lent the Wei court religious legitimacy. His followers were resettled around Chang'an and Luoyang, and the fall of Wei in 266 and of northern China in 317 scattered them further.

Its followers held that qi, born from the Dao, pervades everything and that the body's spirits must be nourished by its right balance. Sin made qi leave the body, so everyone was in some way ill, and illness was cured by repentance in a Chamber of Silence, by herbs and by ritual music. Adepts with harmonised spirits would feign death and be reborn perfected, while others went to earth-prisons. They also expected an apocalypse that only 18,000 seed people would survive.

The Hanzhong state was divided into 24 districts, each linked with one of the Five Phases, a period of the year and a constellation. Families were entered in civil registers, updated at the three Sanyuan feasts, when the five pecks of rice were also given. A person's rank rose with the number of divine generals they commanded against demons. Offenders confessed, were pardoned three times, and were then set to community service such as road repair.

The only significant text surviving from Hanzhong is the Xiang'er commentary to the Dao De Jing, which reads that book as addressed to all humanity rather than to a sage alone. The movement took Daoism beyond the literate and wealthy to every class, including the illiterate and non-Chinese, and formed the first organised Daoist priesthood. The Northern and Southern Celestial Masters emerged from it in the 4th and 5th centuries, and later movements such as the Shangqing and Lingbao traditions descend from it.
we-shall-overcome: Tindley's hymn "I'll Overcome Some Day" carried the epigraph "Ye shall overcome if ye faint not", drawn from Galatians 6:9. Tindley wrote about fifty gospel hymns, among them "We'll Understand It By and By" and "Stand by Me". His songs used pentatonic intervals, blue thirds and sevenths, and short refrains in which a congregation could join, and many of his hearers had been freed from slavery only 36 years before he first published.

A letter on the front page of the United Mine Workers Journal of February 1909 mentions a strike where every meeting opened with a prayer and the song "We Will Overcome", the first sign of such a song being sung in a secular and mixed-race setting. The tune has been altered until it echoes "No More Auction Block for Me", and music scholars have also noted a resemblance between its first half and the Catholic hymn "O sanctissima" and between its second half and the hymn "I'll Be All Right".

In October 1945 the members of the Food, Tobacco, Agricultural, and Allied Workers union, mostly African American women, began a five-month strike against the American Tobacco Company in Charleston, South Carolina. One of the strikers, Lucille Simmons, led a slow version of "We'll Overcome" to end each day's picketing. Zilphia Horton, the music director of the Highlander Folk School, learned it from her, and "We Will Overcome" was printed in the People's Songs Bulletin with her introduction. Pete Seeger learned the song from Horton, changed "will" to "shall" because the vowel sings more openly, and added verses.

Guy Carawan, who became Highlander's music director in 1959, brought it back to the school, where student activists sang it in jail after police raids on Highlander in 1959 and 1960. Julian Bond credits Carawan with teaching it at the founding meeting of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee in 1960.

In August 1963 Joan Baez led a crowd of 3,000 in the song at the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington. President Lyndon Johnson used the phrase when he addressed Congress on 15 March 1965, after the attacks of Bloody Sunday at Selma. Martin Luther King Jr. recited its words in his last sermon at Memphis on 31 March 1968, and more than 50,000 people sang it at his funeral.

The Richmond Organization had registered a copyright on the lyrics in 1960, but in 2017 a judge ruled that the registered work was not sufficiently different from the public-domain "We Will Overcome", and in January 2018 the company agreed to stop asserting copyright claims. The song and songs based on it have been used in protests worldwide.
webster-ashburton-treaty: The border disputes went back to the vague wording of the Treaty of Paris of 1783 and to the faulty Mitchell Map used in negotiating it. An arbitration before King William I of the Netherlands in 1831 had produced no binding decision, and clashes between Americans and New Brunswickers in the Aroostook War of 1838–1839 made a settlement pressing. The treaty was negotiated in Washington over ten months, largely at Ashburton House on Lafayette Square, under the new administration of President John Tyler. Daniel Webster negotiated for the United States and Alexander Baring, 1st Baron Ashburton, for Britain.

In the east the treaty divided the disputed land along the Maine border, giving Britain the Halifax–Quebec road, which its military wanted as Lower Canada's only winter link to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. It kept the old, inaccurate survey of the 45th parallel, so that a half-built American fort known as Fort Blunder stayed on United States soil, assigned the Indian Stream area to the United States and settled the questions left by the Caroline Affair. In the west it fixed the line from Lake Superior to the Lake of the Woods along the traders' route by Grand Portage and the Pigeon River, gave Sugar Island to the United States and reaffirmed the 49th parallel to the Rocky Mountains.

Article 10 listed seven crimes subject to extradition, from murder and piracy to forgery, but not slave revolt or mutiny. The two navies were to keep minimum anti-slaving squadrons off West Africa, though without a mutual right to search, so the effect on the trans-Atlantic slave trade was small. The negotiators passed over the Creole case of 1841, in which 128 enslaved people were freed at Nassau after a revolt on an American brig.

The United States ceded 5,000 square miles of the disputed territory in Maine, kept 7,000, and received 6,500 square miles further west, including the Mesabi Range. To win over the Senate, Webster showed senators a map of doubtful origin by which Benjamin Franklin had supposedly conceded most of the disputed land to Britain. When Whigs in Parliament criticised the treaty, Macaulay contrasted the humble, caressing, wheedling tone of Ashburton's letters with Webster's firm, resolute manner. The treaty left the Oregon question and the ownership of Machias Seal Island unresolved.
wehrmacht: The word Wehrmacht, from wehren, to defend, and Macht, power, had long been used for any nation's armed forces. After the First World War the Treaty of Versailles limited the army to one hundred thousand men and the navy to fifteen thousand, with at most six battleships, six cruisers and twelve destroyers, and it forbade submarines, tanks, heavy artillery and an air force. A new force, the Reichswehr, was established on 23 March 1921.

After Paul von Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, Adolf Hitler became commander in chief. In that month the entire military took the Hitler oath, a pledge of personal obedience, on the initiative of Defence Minister Werner von Blomberg and General Walther von Reichenau. Hitler was surprised at the offer, and the view that he imposed the oath is false. In 1935 the Reichswehr was replaced by the Wehrmacht, made up of the Heer, the Kriegsmarine and the Luftwaffe, and conscription returned.

Hitler made himself Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. After the Blomberg-Fritsch Affair he abolished the Ministry of War and put the Wehrmacht High Command, the Oberkommando der Wehrmacht, under Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel in its place. Early campaigns in Poland, France and elsewhere relied on combined arms tactics of aircraft, tanks and infantry, which foreign journalists called Blitzkrieg. The advance into the Soviet Union brought its first major defeat at the Battle of Moscow in 1941, and by late 1942 Germany was losing the initiative in all theatres.

Resistance within the forces began with the Oster conspiracy of 1938. After the defeat at Stalingrad trust in Hitler's leadership waned, and on 20 July 1944 a group of officers led by Claus von Stauffenberg attempted to assassinate him. The attempt failed, 4,980 people were executed, and the military salute was replaced by the Hitler salute. The Wehrmacht's unconditional surrender took effect on 8 May 1945.

German forces, including the Waffen-SS and collaborator units, lost about 5,318,000 men killed, dead in custody or missing. The Wehrmacht cooperated closely with the SS and its Einsatzgruppen and committed war crimes, chiefly in the Soviet Union, Poland, Yugoslavia, Greece and Italy. Of 3.2 million Soviet prisoners taken between the start of Operation Barbarossa and the following spring, 2.8 million died in German hands.

After the war former officers and veterans' groups promoted the myth of a clean Wehrmacht, an apolitical force innocent of the regime's crimes. German historians began to challenge this view in the late 1970s and the 1980s. Historians have also reassessed the Wehrmacht's fighting power, noting that it often inflicted heavier losses than it took while outnumbered.
wei-qing: Wei Qing was born Zheng Qing, the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji, a low-ranking official serving at the estate of Princess Pingyang, Emperor Wu's elder sister, and of a servant woman known as Wei Ao. Mistreated in his father's household and made to herd sheep, he ran back to his mother in his early teens, served as a stableboy on the estate and took her family's surname.

When Princess Pingyang gave his half-sister, the singer Wei Zifu, to Emperor Wu around 139 BCE, he went with her and became a horseman of the royal guard. Grand Princess Guantao, mother of Empress Chen Jiao, had him kidnapped to be killed, but palace guards led by Gongsun Ao rescued him, and the emperor gave him high posts in response.

In 129 BCE, as General of Chariots and Cavalry, he led one of four columns of 10,000 cavalry against the Xiongnu; while the others failed, he raided their holy site Longcheng, the first proper Han victory over them. In 127 BCE he outflanked the princes of Loufan and Baiyang, took over a million cattle and drove them from the Hetao region, where the city of Shuofang was built; he was made Marquess Changping. In 124 BCE a night assault from Gaoque surprised the Right Worthy Prince's camp and took about 15,000 captives, and Wei Qing became Grand General.

In the Mobei campaign of 119 BCE he and Huo Qubing each led 50,000 cavalry and 100,000 infantry and charioteers across the Gobi. Meeting the main army of Chanyu Yizhixie, Wei Qing held its charges with chariots arranged in rings and archers until a sandstorm at dusk let him attack both flanks, routing the Xiongnu and pursuing them to the region of present-day Ulaanbaatar. The flanking force of Li Guang and Zhao Yiji lost its way, and Li Guang killed himself rather than face a court martial; the historian Sima Qian, among others, blamed Wei Qing.

After 119 BCE Wei Qing saw little fighting and stayed at Chang'an as Grand Master of the Horse and Grand General, advising on military matters. He kept a low profile and refused to hire scholars to praise him. He died in 106 BCE and was buried in a tomb modelled on Mount Lu, joined to Huo Qubing's and to the emperor's own. He did not see the destruction of his clan in the turmoil of 91 BCE, in which his sister Empress Wei and Liu Ju died and his son Wei Kang was executed.
wei-river: The Wei River is 818 km long and drains an area of 135,000 square kilometres. It is the largest tributary of the Yellow River. It rises in the mountains of southern Weiyuan County in Gansu, less than 110 km from the Yellow River at Lanzhou. Because the Yellow River turns sharply north there to form the Ordos Loop, the two rivers do not meet for more than 2,000 km further along the Yellow River's course.

The Wei runs east past Tianshui, enters Mount Long and emerges as the principal river of the Guanzhong Basin. It passes Baoji, Xianyang, Xi'an and Weinan and joins the Yellow River at Tongguan County, near where Shaanxi, Shanxi and Henan meet. Its tributaries include the Luo, Jing, Niutou, Feng and Chishui. The valley has a continental climate, with hot summers and cool, dry winters. Its natural steppe-forest vegetation has been transformed by human activity, and it is mostly agricultural.

In Chinese myth the giant Kua Fu drained the Yellow and Wei rivers to quench his thirst as he pursued the Sun. The valley was one of the early cradles of Chinese civilisation. The capitals of the Zhou, Qin, Han and Tang dynasties were situated along it, and the area of Dingxi near its headwaters has numerous Stone Age sites. The valley is likely the earliest centre of Chinese civilisation and the site of China's first major irrigation works. Some Chinese historians believe the Wei is the ancient Jiang River that gave its name to the families of Shennong and the Yan emperor, credited with early agriculture there.

The headwaters served as China's natural gateway to the west. The Northern Silk Road ran from Chang'an through Baoji and Tianshui, then to Lanzhou and Dunhuang, and looped north of the Taklamakan on its way to Kashgar. The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake had its epicentre in the valley.

The Sanmenxia Dam, built in 1960, caused extensive sedimentation in the lower reaches. The Baojixia diversion works of 1972 created an irrigation district of 128,000 hectares, which reduced flows. Heavy rain in September 2003 caused flooding that killed over 30 people and displaced over 300,000. A train bridge over the Wei appeared on the 5000-yuan note of the first series of the renminbi, dated 1953.
wei-zheng: Wei Zheng, courtesy name Xuancheng and posthumous name Wenzhen, was born in 580, shortly before the founding of the Sui dynasty. His family was from Julu Commandery, roughly modern Xingtai in Hebei. His father, Wei Changxian, was a county magistrate under Northern Qi. Wei lost his father early and was poor, but had great expectations and did not care about making wealth. At one point he became a Taoist monk. He liked study and paid particular attention to works on strategy.

At the end of that reign he joined the rebellions. In 617 Yuan Baozang of Wuyang Commandery rebelled and submitted to Li Mi, and invited Wei to his staff as secretary. Li Mi was impressed by Wei's submissions and made him his own secretary.

In 618 Wei advised Li Mi to take a defensive stance against the Sui general Wang Shichong, but the proposal apparently never reached him. Wang defeated Li Mi, who fled to the Tang and surrendered to Emperor Gaozu, and Wei followed him. Wei later persuaded Xu Shiji, and then Yuan Baozang, to submit to the Tang. Captured by Dou Jiande in 619, he served Dou as secretary until Dou fell to Li Shimin in 621. Wei then went to Chang'an, where the Crown Prince Li Jiancheng made him his librarian.

As Li Jiancheng's rivalry with his brother Li Shimin sharpened, Wei repeatedly urged him to act first and kill Li Shimin. In 626 Li Shimin killed Li Jiancheng and forced Gaozu to yield the throne. Impressed by Wei's faithfulness, he did not punish him. As Emperor Taizong he made Wei the Baron of Julu, allowed him to attend Li Jiancheng's funeral procession, and often invited him to his bedroom to talk. In 627 Wei advised against attacking Feng Ang, whom rumour called a rebel, and Taizong instead sent an envoy, which pacified the Lingnan region.

Wei became a chancellor for about 13 years and led the editing of the Book of Sui, composed in 636. He emphasised propriety and opposed overextending the state. His advice was not always accepted, but the emperor conceded to it with some regularity. After he died on 11 February 643 Taizong called him a mirror that showed the mistakes of the court and built him an elaborate tomb. Later false accusations led to the destruction of the stone monument. After the failed campaign against Goguryeo in 646, Taizong, believing Wei would have stopped him, restored the monument. Wei is venerated as a door god in some Chinese and Taoist temples, usually with Li Shiji.
wei-zhongxian: Little is known of Wei's life before the court. He is presumed to have been born in Suning County, about 100 miles south-east of Beijing, and to have castrated himself at the age of 21; Ming records claim he did so to escape gambling debts. Through a relative of his mother he entered service in the Forbidden City and took the name Li Jinzhong. In 1605 he was given the task of serving meals to Lady Wang and her infant son, and when the prince's mother died in 1619 the boy treated Wei and Madame Ke as his parents in all but name.

The deaths of the Wanli Emperor and the Taichang Emperor in 1620 brought a succession crisis. The Donglin activist Yang Lian, who did not want the Taichang Emperor's consort Lady Li to rule as regent, had the 15-year-old prince proclaimed emperor in his own right, and with Lady Li set aside Wei and Madame Ke could sway the court more easily.

The Tianqi Emperor cared more for carpentry and building than for government, and Wei was made Brush-Holding Eunuch of the Directorate of Ceremonial. Orders from the palace were issued in the names of both the emperor and the Depot Minister. Fourteen of his relatives were ennobled or given hereditary military posts, and many local officials built temples in his honour.

Opposition grew: the censor Zhou Zongjian impeached him in July 1622, and in 1624 Yang Lian accused him of 24 crimes, some of them fabricated. Both attempts failed and turned Wei against the Donglin party. How far he directed the arrests, torture and killings that followed is not known, though his control of the emperor's edicts made him party to them in some degree.

When the Tianqi Emperor died in 1627, no coup followed, though a Donglin sympathiser claimed Wei had tried to have Empress Zhang adopt his nephew. The Chongzhen Emperor, enthroned on 2 October 1627, at first kept him, but after more than a hundred officials denounced him he listed Wei's crimes on 8 December and exiled him to Fengyang. Warned of a possible rebellion, he ordered Wei's arrest, and Wei and his secretary hanged themselves at an inn 150 miles south of Beijing.

His corpse was dismembered and displayed in his home village in 1628, 161 associates were punished and 24 sentenced to death, and Madame Ke was beaten to death. Plays and stories about him appeared within months, and a television series dramatised his power in 2009.
wei-zhuang: Traditional sources give no date for Wei Zhuang's birth; the modern literary historian Xia Chengtao placed it in 836 from clues in his poems. His style name was Duanyi. His family came from Duling, a town near Chang'an, and traced its descent to Wei Jiansu, a chancellor under Emperor Xuánzong; of his direct forebears only his great-grandfather Wei Shaowei, a mid-level official, is known. He was said to be easy-going and careless of detail, and became known in his youth for his beautiful poetry.

The rebellion of Huang Chao, who took Chang'an around the new year of 881 and drove Emperor Xizong to flee, struck just as Wei was due to sit the examinations. His long poem on the catastrophe speaks through a woman of the Qin region whose husband is killed and children starve, and who curses Huang Chao and longs for the true emperor's return.

After passing the jinshi examination in 894, Wei served as secretary to a regional governor and then as Zuo Bujue, a junior adviser at court. Emperor Zhaozong sent him with Li Xun to Xichuan to commission the warlord Wang Jian, who kept both on his staff; Wei's documents for Wang were praised as plain yet expressive. In 903 he carried tribute to the court and won the goodwill of Zhu Quanzhong. After Zhu had Zhaozong assassinated in 904, Wei advised Wang to refuse the imperial messenger and break openly with Zhu.

When Zhu ended the Tang in 907 and founded the Later Liang, Wei strongly favoured Wang taking the imperial title himself. At his suggestion Wang declared three days of mourning for the Tang and then proclaimed the state of Shu, known as Former Shu. Wang put Wei in charge of the Office of Chancellors, in effect a chancellor, and in 908 made him Menxia Shilang with the chancellor's designation. The new state's government structure, penal code and ceremonies were all said to have been drafted by Wei.

Wei died in 910 and received the posthumous name Wenjing, civil and comforting. He left 20 volumes of works, one volume of the declarations he drafted for Wang Jian and one of writings on his travels in Shu. His poems, in the shi and ci forms, were collected in five volumes edited by his younger brother Wei Ai.
wei-zifu: Wei Zifu was the fourth child and youngest daughter of a housemaid in the household of Princess Pingyang, Emperor Wu's elder sister; her father presumably died around the time of her birth. Her younger half-brother Wei Qing was born of her mother's affair with a minor official of the household. She was trained at the estate in dancing and the four arts and was skilled at singing and composing. In the spring of 139 BCE the emperor, visiting his sister after a ritual at Bashang, noticed her among the dancers and took her back to Chang'an, with Wei Qing as a stableboy.

Empress Chen, the emperor's childless first wife, made him set her aside, and for more than a year she was a neglected palace maid. The emperor saw her again when she joined a line of maids waiting to be sent home, and she soon became pregnant, which silenced talk that he could not father children. After Empress Chen's mother, Princess Guantao, had Wei Qing kidnapped, the emperor made her a consort and raised her brother to high office. Empress Chen was deposed in 130 BCE for using witchcraft, and soon after Wei Zifu bore the emperor's first son, Liu Ju.

As empress she was recorded as modest and careful, keeping her clan out of trouble, and the historian Sima Qian called her fine in virtues. By 123 BCE her family held five marquessates, and a folk song said that Wei Zifu dominated the world. Even after the emperor came to favour other consorts, he left the palaces and the Shaofu in her charge when he was away from the capital.

In 91 BCE the witchcraft trials removed most of her son's allies, among them her brother-in-law the prime minister and his son, two of her daughters and Wei Qing's eldest son Wei Kang. After Liu Ju's rising failed in five days of street fighting in Chang'an, the emperor sent officials to seize her seal, and she killed herself on 9 September 91 BCE. She was buried in a small coffin outside the Fu'ang Gate. Her great-grandson Liu Bingyi, who survived as an infant in prison, became Emperor Xuan in 74 BCE, cleared her name, built her a larger mausoleum and gave her the title Thoughtful Empress Wei.
weikersheim: Weikersheim is a town in the Main-Tauber district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The township covers 80.92 square kilometres of the Tauberland, a landscape of muschelkalk crossed by many river valleys, above all those of the Tauber and the Vorbach. The lowest point of the municipal area, 213 metres above sea level, lies on the Tauber near Elpersheim, and the highest, 444 metres, to the south-east near the border with Oberndorf. Part of the federally protected Steinriegel landscape between Weikersheim and Elpersheim nature reserve lies within its bounds.

Town rights were granted to Weikersheim in 1313. As one of the seats of the House of Hohenlohe, the town centre was dominated until 1756 by Weikersheim Castle, the residence of the Hohenlohe-Weikersheim line. During the German mediatization of 1806 to 1809 Weikersheim was awarded to the Kingdom of Württemberg, whose government assigned it to Oberamt Mergentheim. In 1938 the Oberamt was reorganized as Landkreis Mergentheim. Between 1 January 1972 and 1 January 1975 Weikersheim incorporated eight municipalities, and in the administrative reorganization of Baden-Württemberg it was assigned to the newly created Main-Tauber district.

In 2000 the old town and palace were placed under protection as cultural monuments. The coat of arms shows a large silver W below a golden crown on a red field. The first seal associated with the town, dated 1435, contained the W; from 1593 it was supported by two lions and set above images of the Sun, Moon and the planet Mercury. Baden-Württemberg awarded the present arms, based on the original pattern, on 7 November 1949. Notable people connected with the town include Raphael Levi Hannover (1685–1779), a German Jewish mathematician and astronomer, and Joseph von Maier (1797–1873), a rabbi and Landesrabbiner.
weil-der-stadt: Weil der Stadt lies in the valley of the River Würm, about 30 km west of the centre of Stuttgart, in the Stuttgart Region of Baden-Württemberg, and is often called the Gate to the Black Forest. It has about 19,000 inhabitants.

The name Weil derives from the Latin word villa, an estate or manor, and the suffix der Stadt, the town, was added to distinguish it from nearby villages of the same name, such as Weil im Dorf and Weil im Schönbuch. The modern name is unusual because it contains the dative article der rather than the nominative die. The town's coat of arms bears the motto SPQR, recalling its supposed Roman origins.

The village of Wile was first mentioned in 1075, when it was described as the property of the abbey of Hirsau. It had existed for centuries before as an important trading place, and in 1272 it became a free imperial city. In 1294 Augustinian monks became established in the town. It was completely destroyed during the Thirty Years' War in 1648 and subsequently rebuilt, and it is still dominated by buildings from that period. Its fortifications, with city walls, gates and several towers, have survived largely intact.

Weil der Stadt is best known as the birthplace of the astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571 to 1630), and it bears the unofficial title Keplerstadt. Another native was the Protestant reformer Johannes Brenz (1499 to 1570). The cityscape is dominated by the church steeple of St. Peter and Paul. The town keeps a traditional carnival, called Fasnet, which is based on Alemannic traditions shared by towns in south-western Germany and Switzerland. According to the account kept there, the town escaped destruction in World War II when a French artillery barrage was called off in honour of its being Kepler's birthplace.
weilburg: Weilburg lies in the Lahn valley between the Westerwald and the Taunus, just upstream from where the Weil flows into the Lahn, 80 km southeast of Koblenz. The Old Town stands on and around a rocky hill that the Lahn almost encircles. The earliest traces of settlement nearby are thought to be La Tène finds from the Scheuernberger Kopf near Kirschhofen. The site gave control of the Lahn and of two long-distance routes, the Hohe Straße from Frankfurt to Cologne and the Via Publica from Flanders to Bohemia.

Weilburg was first mentioned in 906 in a chronicle by Abbot Regino of Prüm as a fortification called Wilineburch. King Conrad I founded a church and abbey there, and the St. Walpurgis monastery was founded in 912. In 918, on his deathbed at the castle, Conrad recommended that his brother Eberhard deliver the imperial insignia to his bitterest rival, the Saxon duke Heinrich, an episode known as the Weilburger Testament. From 993 to 1062 the town was gradually given to the Bishopric of Worms, which about 1225 pledged overlordship to the House of Nassau.

Count Johann I of Nassau made his residence there in 1355, turning the castle into a palace and building the town fortifications, and in 1359 a stone bridge over the Lahn. Count Johann Ernst, who lived from 1664 to 1719, expanded the Renaissance high palace and laid out a park, so that Weilburg became one of the best preserved small German residence towns of the age of absolutism. From 1806 it was the seat of government of the new Duchy of Nassau, until Duke William moved his residence to Biebrich in 1816. Prussia annexed the duchy in 1866, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire.

Weilburg has just under 13,000 inhabitants and is the third largest town of the Limburg-Weilburg district in Hesse. Schloss Weilburg, dating to the 14th century with Renaissance and Baroque parts, takes in almost half the Old Town and has been a museum since 1935, when Charlotte of Nassau-Weilburg, Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, sold it to Prussia. The Luxembourg ruling house kept the burial chapel of its ancestors. The town is also known for loam buildings in the Pisee style and for its Gymnasium Philippinum, which grew out of a school founded in 1540.
weimar: The oldest records of Weimar date to 899, and its name derives from Old High German words for holy and for standing water. It was the seat of the County of Weimar, first mentioned in 949, one of the most powerful jurisdictions in early medieval Thuringia, and fell to the Wettins after 1346. The Reformation was introduced in 1525, and Martin Luther stayed in the city several times. After the Ernestines lost the Schmalkaldic War in 1547 and Wittenberg passed to the Albertines, the ruler made Weimar his residence in 1552, and it remained one until the end of the monarchy in 1918.

The period from the regency of Anna Amalia, which began in 1758, through her son Carl August to Goethe's death in 1832 is called the golden or classical age. Goethe, Schiller, Herder, Wieland and Bertuch lived there. Goethe moved to Weimar in 1775 and served the Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach as Privy Councilor. A liberal Saxe-Weimar constitution came into effect in 1816. In 1842 Franz Liszt became the Grand Ducal court conductor and organised the premiere of Richard Wagner's Lohengrin in 1850. Friedrich Nietzsche moved to the city in 1897 and died there three years later.
