The Weimar Republic's constitution was drafted in the city rather than in Berlin because the capital was considered too dangerous for the National Assembly after street rioting during the Spartacist uprising. Reich President Friedrich Ebert hoped the choice would remind the Allies of Weimar Classicism while they deliberated the Treaty of Versailles. Artists and architects including Walter Gropius, Wassily Kandinsky and Paul Klee founded the Bauhaus there. The Nazis held a party convention in Weimar in 1926, and the first concentration camps were set up near the city in 1933.

Weimar is a city in Thuringia, in central Germany between Erfurt and Jena, with a population of about 65,000. It was the capital of Thuringia until 1948. Two World Heritage Sites include buildings in the city: Classical Weimar, with 11 sites linked to the 18th and early 19th centuries, and the Bauhaus sites. The Bauhaus University, the Liszt School of Music and the Duchess Anna Amalia Library are among its institutions.
weimar-constitution: After the First World War the imperial government collapsed in the German revolution of 1918–1919. The moderate left, led by Friedrich Ebert of the Social Democrats, defeated the far left parties that wanted a soviet republic and called an election on 19 January 1919, in which women had equal voting rights with men for the first time, for a National Assembly to draft a constitution. Because Berlin was unsettled, it met at Weimar, a name Ebert wished to recall to the Allies as the city of Goethe and Schiller while they deliberated the terms of the Versailles Treaty.

The first draft was written by the liberal lawyer Hugo Preuss, who headed the Ministry of the Interior, largely on the Frankfurt Constitution of 1849. In July 1919 the Assembly moved quickly through it, mostly without public discussion, and adopted it on 31 July by 262 votes to 75 with one abstention. Ebert, the first president, signed it on 11 August, and it took effect on the 14th.

The constitution had 181 articles in two parts, one on the organisation of the Reich and one on the fundamental rights and duties of Germans. It made the Reich a republic whose power derived from the people, with a Reichstag elected by equal, secret ballot of all Germans over 20, and a Reichsrat representing the states. The president commanded the armed forces, appointed and dismissed the chancellor and, under Article 48, could suspend civil liberties in an emergency. Individual rights included equality before the law, the abolition of privileges of birth and rank, protection of the home and of correspondence, a guarantee of arrest being notified within a day, freedom of expression, and freedom of religion with no state church.

William L. Shirer called it on paper the most liberal and democratic document of its kind the twentieth century had seen, yet its legitimacy was weak in German eyes. Preuss intended a strong president as a replacement monarch above the parties. Article 48 was meant for rare use but was invoked 205 times before Adolf Hitler became chancellor, and the Reichstag Fire Decree of 1933 used it to suspend civil rights. The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933, passed by 441 votes to 94 after the 81 Communist members were forcibly excluded, made the other provisions a dead letter, though the constitution was never formally repealed.

Hitler still used it to give his dictatorship the look of legality. The Allied Control Council repealed the Enabling Act on 20 September 1945, and the constitution was replaced in 1949 by the Basic Law of West Germany and the constitution of East Germany, which copied many passages from the 1919 text.
weimar-republic: The Weimar Republic is dated from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933. Its official name remained the German Reich, but it was more commonly called the German Republic, and the name Weimar comes from the city where its National Assembly met from 6 February to 11 August 1919 and adopted the constitution. A rebellion among sailors at Wilhelmshaven on 29 October 1918 spread into the Kiel mutiny on 3 November, and sailors, soldiers and workers began electing councils modelled on the soviets of the Russian Revolution. The power takeovers were achieved with little or no violence.

Early years were marked by hyperinflation, political murders and two attempted coups by contending paramilitaries. From 1924 to 1929 the republic was relatively stable, a period known in Germany as the Goldene Zwanziger, with a growing economy and a cultural flourishing. Under the Locarno Treaties of 1925 Germany recognised most territorial changes made by the Treaty of Versailles, and in 1926 it joined the League of Nations. The stability rested partly on American loans, and when American banks withdrew credit after the Great Depression began in 1929, unemployment rose to 4 million in 1930.

In the Reichstag election of September 1930 the Nazi Party won 19% of the vote. From March 1930 President Paul von Hindenburg backed chancellors who governed by presidential decree: Heinrich Brüning, Franz von Papen and Kurt von Schleicher. On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor. The Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act of 1933 gave him broad power to act outside parliamentary control, and he used it to suspend civil liberties and set up a one-party dictatorship.

The constitution of 1919 created a federal semi-presidential republic. The Reichstag was elected by universal suffrage using proportional representation, and the Reichsrat represented the states. The president commanded the military, held extensive emergency powers and appointed and removed the chancellor, who answered to the Reichstag. Under the Treaty of Versailles the army, the Reichswehr, was limited to 100,000 men. Historians still debate why the republic failed and group the causes as economic, institutional and the roles of individuals. Nazi propaganda called the period the time of the System.
weingarten-wurttemberg: Weingarten lies in the valley of the Schussen River in the District of Ravensburg, with Ravensburg to the south and Friedrichshafen on Lake Constance. Before 1865 the town was called Altdorf, from the Frankish alach for church, so that the name means a village with the parish church; Weingarten was then the name of the abbey alone, which stood on the Martinsberg above the town.

An Alemannic burial place of the 5th century was excavated near the old town in 1954 to 1957. In the 8th century the region became part of the Frankish empire, and around the 9th century the Elder Welfs became counts of the Schussengau and made Altdorf their seat. In 1056 Welf IV moved the ancestral seat to the new castle of Ravensburg and founded a Benedictine abbey on the Martinsberg, which was named Weingarten Abbey. In 1191 Frederick Barbarossa acquired the Schussengau from Welf VI by a contract of inheritance. After the Hohenstaufen line ended with Conradin's death in Naples in 1268, the abbey won the status of an Imperial Abbey, while Altdorf was ruled by the imperial bailiff of Swabia.

The abbey became one of the wealthiest monasteries in southern Germany, with about 306 km2 of estates, until it was confiscated in the secularisation of 1803. Weingarten went first to the House of Nassau and in 1806 was incorporated into Württemberg, while Altdorf had passed to the dukedom of Württemberg. Barracks made it a military site in the 19th century, and an engineering industry developed in the second half of the century. In 1922 monks from Beuron founded a new Benedictine abbey. Since 1949 most of the abbey buildings have housed a teachers' college.

The Abbey Church of St. Martin and Oswald is the largest Baroque church north of the Alps, about half as long as St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Its organ by Joseph Gabler has four manuals and nearly 7,000 pipes. The relic of the holy blood of Jesus Christ is carried in the Blutritt, a large equestrian procession of about 3,000 riders held on the Friday after Ascension. The Alemans Museum displays finds from the burial place, and the Schlössle, built around 1550 for the imperial bailiff, houses the municipal museum.
weissenburg-in-bayern: The history of the town is generally traced back to the Roman fort built in the area towards the end of the first century. The settlement, which included baths, lay on the border of the Roman Empire and appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana from the 4th century under the name Biriciana. Germanic tribes destroyed the fort and settled in what is still the town centre. The name Weißenburg is first mentioned in a deed of 867. The town became the seat of a royal residence under the Franks, and according to legend Charlemagne stayed there to supervise the construction of the Fossa Carolina.

Weißenburg became a free imperial city in 1296 and continued to grow until the Reformation. Following the example of Nuremberg it joined the Protestant side, but it suffered heavily in the wars that followed. Its rights as a free imperial city and imperial estate were restored in the final peace treaty.

Despite its small size and economic weight it was, like the other fifty or so free imperial cities, virtually independent. It lost its independence in 1802 and became part of the Bavarian kingdom in 1806. A railway between Nuremberg and Augsburg through the town supported industrialisation, and after World War II over 6,000 refugees and expelled people settled there.

Weißenburg in Bayern is the capital of the district of Weißenburg-Gunzenhausen in Middle Franconia, with 18,345 inhabitants. Many Roman ruins survive, among them a Roman bath excavated in 1977 and made into a museum. The medieval town wall stands almost intact with its towers, and the Gothic Town Hall has hosted the town's elected members since 1476.

The Wülzburg, a fortress about 2 kilometres east of the centre on a hill 200 metres above the town, began as a Benedictine monastery of the 11th century and was converted into a fortress from 1588 to 1605. It is one of the best-preserved Renaissance fortresses in Germany. Charles de Gaulle was imprisoned there in the First World War, and the Czech composer Erwin Schulhoff was held there by the Nazis before he died of tuberculosis.
weissenfels: Weißenfels is the largest city of the Burgenlandkreis district in southern Saxony-Anhalt, central Germany, on the river Saale about 30 kilometres south of Halle. The area is perhaps first mentioned in 806, when Charles the Younger, King of the Franks, fought and killed two West Slavic princes nearby, Miliduch of the Sorbs and Nessyta. The settlement arose around a castle at a ford over the Saale and received municipal rights in 1185. It belonged to the Electorate of Saxony from 1485.

The Thirty Years' War badly damaged the town, and its population fell from 2,200 to 960. On 7 November 1632 the body of King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden was first laid out there, the day after he was killed at the Battle of Lützen. Duke Augustus, of the Saxon House of Wettin, established the Duchy of Saxe-Weissenfels in 1656 and made the town its capital and residence. From 1660 he built the Baroque Neu-Augustusburg Castle on a hill, completed in 1680, which was the duchy's administrative and cultural centre until the duchy ended in 1746.

Composers such as Johann Philipp Krieger and Georg Philipp Telemann worked there, and in 1713 Johann Sebastian Bach dedicated his hunting cantata BWV 208 to Duke Christian. According to John Mainwaring, Duke Johann Adolf I discovered the musical talent of the young George Frideric Handel. With the extinction of the Wettin line in 1746 the town fell back to Saxony, and after 1815 it went to the Prussian Province of Saxony.

By 1900 Weißenfels was one of the largest shoe-making centres in Germany, with 64 factories employing about 3,200 people. In 1950 it was designated the centre of shoe manufacture in East Germany, with a workforce that eventually reached 5,000, and the last factory closed in 1991. Food processing has since grown. The castle's chapel keeps a pipe organ completed in 1673, for which Bach wrote the Toccata and Fugue in F major.
welf-i-duke-of-bavaria: Welf was the son of Albert Azzo II, Margrave of Milan, and Kunigunde of Altdorf. When his maternal uncle Welf, Duke of Carinthia, died childless in 1055, he inherited the uncle's property. In 1062 he married Ethelinde of Northeim, daughter of Otto, Duke of Bavaria. His father remained firm in the interests of Pope Gregory VII, but Welf's marriage and his German inheritance made him more concerned with German affairs, and he supported Emperor Henry IV. He was the first member of the House of Welf branch of the House of Este.

When Duke Otto became an enemy of Henry IV and lost his duchy, Welf stayed loyal to the emperor, repudiated and divorced Ethelinde at Henry's command and in 1070 was appointed Duke of Bavaria at Goslar in Otto's place. The Bavarians accepted him quietly. During the Investiture Controversy he changed sides, supporting Pope Gregory VII and the election of Rudolf of Rheinfelden in March 1077. Henry declared him deposed, but with the support of his Bavarians and his father in Italy he kept his place and openly defied the ban in May 1077.

After Gregory died in 1085 Welf, though still on the side of the church, relaxed his efforts for Rudolf. After his divorce he had married Judith of Flanders, daughter of Baldwin IV, Count of Flanders, and widow of Tostig Godwinson. In 1089 his son Welf married Matilda of Tuscany, which strengthened ties with the pope, but when the younger Welf divorced her in 1095 the father made amends with Henry IV and was reconfirmed as duke.

In 1099 Welf joined the expedition later known as the Crusade of 1101, with William IX of Aquitaine, Hugh of Vermandois and Ida of Austria. He prevented a clash between crusaders who had been pillaging Byzantine territory and the Pecheneg mercenaries of the Byzantine emperor. After passing Heraclea in September his Bavarians were ambushed and massacred by the Turkish troops of Kilij Arslan I, the Seljuq Sultan of Rûm. Welf himself escaped and died on the way back at Paphos in Cyprus on 6 November 1101. He was buried at Weingarten Abbey and succeeded as duke by his son Welf II.
welf-vi: Welf VI was the third son of Henry IX, Duke of Bavaria. He inherited the family's possessions in Swabia, including the counties of Altdorf and Ravensburg, while his eldest brother Henry the Proud received the duchies of Bavaria and Saxony and his brother Conrad entered the church. Henry married him to Uta, daughter of Godfrey of Calw, count palatine of the Rhine, and on Godfrey's death in 1131 Welf disputed the inheritance of Calw with Godfrey's nephew Adalbert. His sister Judith was the mother of Frederick Barbarossa, who was at most a decade younger than his uncle.

When King Conrad III of Germany confiscated Bavaria in 1142, Welf rebelled. Although he and Conrad went on the Second Crusade together, Welf and his son Welf VII were defeated by Conrad's son Henry Berengar at the Battle of Flochberg. Peace came in 1152, when Barbarossa was elected king, and in October that year at Würzburg the new king gave Welf, as head of his house, the duchy of Spoleto, the margraviate of Tuscany and the principality of Sardinia among other Italian lands.

From the 1150s father and son also fought a feud with Hugh of Tübingen, count palatine of Swabia, which peaked between 1164 and 1166 and was settled by the emperor, largely in favour of Welf and his son. In 1167 Welf VII died of malaria at Rome while campaigning with Barbarossa against Pope Alexander III. Henry the Lion claimed all the Welf estates; Welf asked a large sum for them, which Henry did not raise, and the Italian states went to the emperor, though Welf stayed in charge of the Italian duchies until 1173.

After Henry the Lion was stripped of his estates in 1179, the Welf lands Henry had acquired returned to Welf, and at his death on 15 December 1191 they passed to Barbarossa's heir, the duke of Swabia. So the Swabian Welf lands went to the Hohenstaufen, while the male line descended from Henry the Lion kept its lands in northern Germany. Welf was a patron of churches and was buried in Steingaden Abbey, the Premonstratensian house he founded, beside his son. He was also the patron of the Historia Welforum, the first medieval chronicle of his dynasty.
well-meet-again: The song was first recorded by Vera Lynn with Arthur Young, who accompanied her on the Hammond Novachord, an early electronic keyboard. It was written in D major at a tempo of 92 beats a minute. It became one of the best-known songs of World War II, speaking to servicemen leaving to fight and to the families they left behind, and it gave its name to the 1943 musical film We'll Meet Again, in which Lynn starred in a loose version of her own life as a forces' sweetheart.

Lynn recorded it again in 1953 with fuller instrumentation and a chorus of British Armed Forces personnel, and that version reached number 29 on the American charts in 1954. The song has been credited as one of the first to use the Novachord, the first polyphonic synthesizer.

During the Cold War Lynn's recording was among the music kept in 20 underground radio stations of the BBC's Wartime Broadcasting Service, meant to provide information and raise morale for 100 days after a nuclear attack. Stanley Kubrick used her 1953 recording, with bitter irony, over the nuclear destruction that ends his 1964 film Dr. Strangelove. The Byrds closed their debut album Mr. Tambourine Man with it, and Pink Floyd's song Vera on The Wall of 1979 refers to its words and to Lynn.

It is traditionally played on 5 May to close the Liberation Day Concert in Amsterdam, marking the end of World War II in the Netherlands. Lynn sang it in London in 2005 on the 60th anniversary of VE Day. On 5 April 2020 Queen Elizabeth II referred to it in a televised address during the COVID-19 pandemic; that year a duet of Lynn and Katherine Jenkins, first released in 2014, reached number 72 on the UK Singles Chart for NHS charities, and after the 75th anniversary of VE Day Lynn's solo version reached number 55.
well-of-moses: The work was made for Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, at the Carthusian monastery of the Chartreuse de Champmol, which he founded as a burial place just outside Dijon, the Burgundian capital. It is regarded as the masterpiece of the Dutch sculptor Claus Sluter, who was assisted by his nephew Claus de Werve. Because the ducal accounts survive, the commission and the progress of the work are unusually well documented. The stone came from Asnières, near Dijon, and the style joins the elegance of International Gothic to a northern realism, with a monumental quality unusual in either.

The structure had four parts: the well itself, about four metres deep and fed by water brought from the nearby river Ouche; a hexagonal pier sunk in its centre; a terrace 2.8 metres across on top of the pier; and the cross rising from the middle. Around the pier stand the six prophets who foretold the death of Christ on the Cross, Moses, David, Jeremiah, Zechariah, Daniel and Isaiah, with six weeping angels on slender colonnettes at the corners between them. All the figures were painted and gilded by Jean Malouel, and some of the paint remains.

Jeremiah, the favoured prophet of the Carthusian order, is a hidden portrait of Philip the Bold: his face resembles the duke's statue in the church portal, and he alone wears purple and green, the colours of Burgundy, instead of blue or gold. The lost Calvary was long assumed to include the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalen and St John, but recent research suggests a single figure, the Magdalen, embracing the foot of the Cross.

The work stood in the central courtyard of the main cloister. A building was put over it in the 17th century, when the upper parts were already suffering from the weather, and it was damaged again in 1791, during the French Revolution. The name Well of Moses appears only in the 19th century. The surviving fragments of the Crucifixion, among them the head and torso of Christ, are in the Musée Archéologique in Dijon, while the base with its sculptures remains in what is now the Hospital de la Chartreuse.
wellerman: In 1831 the Weller brothers founded a whaling station at Otago Heads, near modern Dunedin, seventeen years before Dunedin itself was established. From 1833 they sold provisions to whalers from their base at Otakou, and their employees became known as wellermen. New Zealand whalers worked from the shore, processing carcasses on land. At its peak in 1834 the Otakou station produced 310 tons of whale oil a year and led a network of seven stations, employing as many as 85 people at Otago alone. Joseph Weller died of tuberculosis in 1835, the brothers were declared bankrupt in 1840, and the station closed in 1841.

The origin of the song itself is unknown. Neil Colquhoun recorded it in 1966 from a man then in his 80s, who said his uncle had taught it to him, and included it in his book New Zealand Folksongs: Songs of a Young Country in 1973.

The lyrics follow a whaling ship, the Billy o' Tea, in its hunt for a right whale, while the crew hope for a wellerman to bring them sugar, tea and rum. The chorus looks to the end of the tonguing, the cutting of strips of blubber to render into oil. Later verses tell of the captain's determination to land the whale as time passes and the four whaling boats are lost, and in the last verse the ship is still locked in its struggle, with the wellerman making his regular call.

More than ten recordings were made between 1971 and 2005, among them one by Gordon Bok, Ann Mayo Muir and Ed Trickett in 1990. The Wellington Sea Shanty Society recorded it in 2013, and the Longest Johns included it on Between Wind and Water in 2018. In early 2021 a version by the Scottish singer Nathan Evans spread on TikTok and set off a wider interest in sea songs; a remix by 220 Kid and Billen Ted reached number one on the UK Singles Chart. Though often called a shanty, it is more accurately a ballad, or forebitter.
wellington: Wellington stands at the south-western tip of the North Island, between Cook Strait and the Remutaka Range. Steep hills shape and constrain much of the city. The Kāpiti Coast lies to the north, and the Remutaka Range divides the city from the plains of the Wairarapa. It lies at 41° 17' South and has a temperate maritime climate, generally windy all year with high rainfall.

In Māori oral history the explorer Kupe stayed in the harbour from about 925, and a later explorer, Whatonga, named it Te Whanganui-a-Tara after his son Tara. Iwi such as Rangitāne and Muaūpoko settled the area first; the disruptions of the Musket Wars in the early 19th century left them overwhelmed by northern iwi such as Te Āti Awa, who centred themselves at Pipitea.

European settlement began in 1839, when Colonel William Wakefield arrived to buy land for the New Zealand Company to sell to British settlers. In 1840 Captain William Mein Smith, the company's first Surveyor General, designed the town as interconnected grids that in practice spread along valleys and lower hill slopes. The settlers named it in November 1840, on the directors' suggestion, after Arthur Wellesley, the first Duke of Wellington, in recognition of his support for the company's principles of colonisation.

Earthquakes in 1848 destroyed most brick buildings, which led to the widespread use of timber. The Wairarapa earthquake of 1855, of an estimated magnitude of at least 8.2, raised land out of the harbour; much of it was later reclaimed and is now part of the central business district. The capital moved to Wellington in 1865, a status established by convention rather than in legislation.

Wellington is the capital of New Zealand and its third-largest city, with 210,800 people in the city and a metropolitan area including Lower Hutt, Porirua and Upper Hutt. The government, Parliament and Supreme Court are based there. Its architecture includes the Old Government Buildings, one of the largest wooden buildings in the world, and the Beehive, the executive wing of Parliament Buildings. It is the home of the National Archives, the National Library and the national museum, Te Papa, and is one of the country's chief seaports.
welser-family: The family, which claimed descent from the Byzantine general Belisarius, can be traced to the 13th century, when its members held official posts in Augsburg. In the 15th century the brothers Bartholomew and Lucas Welser traded widely with the Levant and elsewhere, with branches in the main trading centres of southern Germany and Italy and in Antwerp, London and Lisbon, and branches of the family settled at Nuremberg and in Austria. Lucas's son Antony, who died in 1518, was one of the first Germans to use the sea route to the East opened by Vasco da Gama.

By the Contract of Madrid of 1528, Charles V rewarded the Welsers for financing his election in 1519 with privileges in the African slave trade and the conquest of the Americas, and Bartholomeus Welser V received Venezuela as security for a large loan. From 1528 to 1556 seven expeditions plundered and exploited local societies, and the first governors, Ambrosius Alfinger, Nicolas Federmann and Georg von Speyer, captured and enslaved indigenous people after failing to find gold. Bartholomeus's son Bartholomeus VI and Philipp von Hutten were executed at El Tocuyo by the Spanish governor Juan de Carvajal in 1546, the year the family lost its rule.

The Welsers had begun sugar production in Santo Domingo by 1523, and in the following years thousands of enslaved Africans were transported to the Americas. They also found copper in Cuba. Bartholomeus Welser V was ennobled in 1532.

Philippine Welser, daughter of Franz Welser, secretly married Archduke Ferdinand, second son of Emperor Ferdinand I, and their children were barred from the rank of archduke; Markus Welser, a humanist and historian, became mayor of Augsburg in 1611. Like the Fuggers, the family stayed Catholic after the Reformation. The Augsburg main line died out in 1797 and the Nuremberg branch in 1878, while the Ulm branch, imperial barons from 1713, survives and administers the Welser Family Foundation, founded on 1 April 1539.
welsh-people: The English words Wales and Welsh descend from the Anglo-Saxon wealh, itself from a Proto-Germanic word derived from the name of the Gaulish people the Romans called Volcae. It first meant inhabitants of the Roman Empire in general, then the Britons in particular, and as their territories shrank it came to name the area that best kept continuity with pre-Anglo-Saxon Britain. The Romans met tribes in what is now Wales that they called the Ordovices, the Demetae, the Silures and the Deceangli. All the peoples of southern Britain were Britons who spoke Common Brittonic, a Celtic language that seems to have arrived in the Iron Age, though some archaeologists see no evidence of large-scale migration and favour cultural diffusion.

When the Roman legions left Britain around 400, a Romano-British culture remained where the Romans had settled. The people of what is now Wales kept speaking Common Brittonic with much Latin influence, and it evolved into Old Welsh. Offa's Dyke, raised in the mid-8th century, formed a barrier between Wales and Mercia. How the native population came to think of itself as Welsh is not clear. The Welsh word Cymry, from a Brythonic word meaning fellow-countrymen, drew on the relationship with the Brittonic peoples of the Old North in England and Scotland. Probably in use before the 7th century, it is attested in a praise poem to Cadwallon ap Cadfan around 633, and after about 1100 it prevailed over the older Brythoniaid.

Immigration followed the Norman Conquest, and the Landsker Line dividing the Pembrokeshire Englishry from the Welshry can still be traced. The population of Wales more than doubled from 587,000 in 1801 to 1,163,000 in 1851 and reached 2,421,000 by 1911, mostly in the coal-mining districts. English, Irish and Italian migrants came during the Industrial Revolution.

Before the 20th century many Welsh people spoke only Welsh. Parts of the culture are closely tied to the language, notably the Eisteddfod tradition, poetry and aspects of folk music and dance. Forms of Christianity have dominated religious life for more than 1,400 years, and Wales has a long tradition of nonconformism and Methodism. The Sunday Closing (Wales) Act of 1881 was the first legislation issued specifically for Wales since the Middle Ages. The flag shows the red dragon, which Henry VII carried at Bosworth in 1485 and which is recorded as a Welsh symbol in the Historia Brittonum around 820. Welsh emigrants settled in England, Pennsylvania, Canada, Brazil and Patagonia, where the settlement is called Y Wladfa.
welshpool: Welshpool, in Welsh Y Trallwng, is a market town and community in Powys, Wales, historically in Montgomeryshire. It lies low on the River Severn, four miles from the border with England, and the Welsh name means the marshy or sinking land. In English it was at first called Pool, and the name was changed to Welshpool in 1835 to distinguish it from Poole in Dorset. The Long Mountain forms a backdrop to the town and once served as the last ground of defence for fortresses, when the site was a swampy marsh. Powis Castle stands to the south-west.

St Cynfelin is reputed to have founded two churches in the town, St Mary's and St Cynfelin's, in the 5th and 6th centuries. The parish roughly coincides with the medieval commote of Ystrad Marchell in the cantref of Ystlyg, in the Kingdom of Powys. After its prince was forced to flee Mathrafal in 1212 by the prince of Gwynedd, Welshpool served briefly as capital of Powys Wenwynwyn, or South Powys; help from the English crown restored the dynasty. In 1284 the family converted the principality into a marcher lordship, the Lordship of Powys, and the heir Owain called himself Owen de la Pole, after the town.

Forces of Owain Glyndŵr devastated the town in 1400 at the start of his rebellion against Henry IV. Adam of Usk was priest of St Mary's in 1411. The waymarked National Trail called Glyndŵr's Way, 135 miles long, ends in Pont Howell Park beside the Montgomery Canal.

The 2011 census counted 5,948 people in the town and 6,664 in the community, which also includes Cloddiau and Pool Quay. St Mary's Church is a Grade I listed building. Its tower keeps lower courses of a church of about 1250, the nave was rebuilt in the 16th century, and Bishop William Morgan, translator of the Bible into Welsh, was vicar there from 1575 to 1579. The town also has an octagonal brick cockpit built in the early 18th century and a town hall completed in 1874. It is the starting point of the Welshpool and Llanfair Light Railway, and its livestock market is the largest one-day sheep market in Europe.
wen-xuan: Xiao Tong, the eldest son and heir of Emperor Wu of Liang, compiled the anthology at the Liang capital Jiankang, modern Nanjing, with the help of his closest associates. His official biographies say that by the age of four he had memorised the Five Classics, and by his early teens the library of the Eastern Palace held over 30,000 volumes. In his preface he explains that four kinds of writing were left out: the Classics, the works of the philosophical masters such as the Zhuangzi and the Mencius, collections of speeches such as the Intrigues of the Warring States, and histories such as the Zuo Tradition.

The pieces are arranged in 37 categories, from Rhapsodies (fu) and Lyric Poetry (shi), Chu-style Elegies and Sevens to Edicts, Memorials, Letters, Proclamations of War, Treatises, Inscriptions, Epitaphs and Offerings. The fu and shi are the largest and most important groups. Its 55 fu include most of the major works of the form, such as Sima Xiangru's Fu on the Excursion Hunt of the Emperor, Yang Xiong's Fu on the Sweet Springs Palace, Ban Gu's Fu on the Two Capitals and Zhang Heng's Fu on the Two Metropolises. After Xiao Tong died in 531 he received the posthumous name Zhaoming, and the collection became known as the Zhaoming Wen xuan.

The first annotations, by Xiao Tong's cousin Xiao Gai, appeared sixty to seventy years later, and the students of Cao Xian made it a branch of study. Li Shan's commentary, submitted to Emperor Gaozong of Tang in 658, is still the most important tool for reading the text; the commentary of the Five Officials, of 718, is longer but full of far-fetched glosses. The poet Du Fu advised his son to master its principles. In Japan, as the Mon-zen, it was required reading for the aristocracy by the Heian period. Hu Kejia's Kao Yi of the early 19th century underlies most modern printings.
wenceslaus-i-duke-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was the son of Vratislaus I, Duke of Bohemia of the Přemyslid dynasty, and Drahomíra, the daughter of a chief of the Havelli, who was baptized at her marriage. His grandmother Ludmila, converted to Christianity with his grandfather Bořivoj I by Cyril and Methodius, saw that he was educated in Old Church Slavonic, and he was sent to the college at Budeč. In 921, when he was about 13, his father died and Ludmila became regent. Jealous of her influence, Drahomíra arranged for her to be killed, and assassins murdered Ludmila at Tetín Castle on 15 September 921. Drahomíra then became regent and began measures against Christians. When Wenceslaus was 18, the Christian nobles who remained rebelled, and she was exiled to Budeč.

With the nobles' support Wenceslaus took control of the government. He reined in the dependent dukes who had become restive under the regency and used Christianity to strengthen his state. After the fall of Great Moravia, Bohemia faced raids by the Magyars and the eastern campaigns of the Saxon and East Frankish king Henry the Fowler. Early in 929 the joint forces of Duke Arnulf of Bavaria and Henry reached Prague in a sudden attack that forced Wenceslaus to resume payment of a tribute first imposed by Arnulf of Carinthia in 895.

Wenceslaus introduced German priests and favoured the Latin rite over the old Slavic rite, which had gone out of use in many places for want of priests. He also founded a rotunda consecrated to St Vitus at Prague Castle, the basis of the present St Vitus Cathedral.

In September 935 nobles allied with his younger brother Boleslav plotted to kill him. After Boleslav invited him to a feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian at Stará Boleslav, three of Boleslav's companions stabbed him to death, and Boleslav ran him through with a lance. The killing has been seen as a turning point, since Boleslav I renounced the Franks, centralised power and expanded the territory of Bohemia.

A cult of Wenceslaus arose at once, and within a few decades four biographies were in circulation, influencing the medieval idea of the rex justus, the righteous king. Otto I posthumously conferred the royal title on him, which is why legend and song call him king. His feast day, 28 September, has been a public holiday in the Czech Republic since 2000, and John Mason Neale published the carol Good King Wenceslas in 1853.
wenceslaus-i-duke-of-luxembourg: Wenceslaus was born in Prague on 25 February 1337, the only child of John the Blind, King of Bohemia, and Beatrice of Bourbon; chroniclers often called him Wenceslaus of Bohemia. His parents' marriage contract laid down that a son of the marriage would inherit the County of Luxembourg, King John's paternal heritage, with the lands belonging to it. In 1352 he married Joanna, daughter of John III, Duke of Brabant and Limburg, and Marie d'Évreux.

In 1353 his half-brother Charles IV, King of Bohemia and elected Holy Roman King, entrusted their father's county to him, and in 1354 Charles raised Luxembourg to the status of a duchy. When Joanna inherited Brabant and Limburg, Wenceslaus had to fight his brother-in-law Louis II of Flanders, who claimed a share of the duchy. He could not prevent the Flemings from seizing Brussels, but Everard 't Serclaes drove them out of the city in an audacious coup.

Internal disorders then occupied much of his rule. In 1371 he overestimated his military strength and went to war with William II, Duke of Jülich. The defeat at Baesweiler cost him part of his army and several noblemen, and he spent 11 months in captivity.

Wenceslaus died in Luxembourg on 7 December 1383, leaving Joanna as sole ruler of Brabant, and Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia succeeded him in Luxembourg as Wenceslaus II. It has been speculated that he died of leprosy. At his last wish his heart was taken from his body and sent to his wife in Brussels, and he is buried in a crypt at Orval Abbey in Belgium.
He was also a poet. The lyric verse interpolated in Jean Froissart's Méliador is his work, identified by Auguste Longnon in the 1890s: 79 poems, of them 11 ballades, 16 virelais and 52 rondeaux.
wenceslaus-ii-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was the only surviving son of Ottokar II of Bohemia and Kunigunda, daughter of Rostislav Mikhailovich, lord of Slavonia, and Anna of Hungary. In November 1276 Rudolf I, King of the Romans, compelled Ottokar to give up his claims to Austria and keep only Bohemia and Moravia, and Wenceslaus was betrothed to Rudolf's daughter Judith. Ottokar died on 26 August 1278 in the Battle on the Marchfeld, shortly before his son's seventh birthday.

Otto V, Margrave of Brandenburg, governed until Wenceslaus returned to Bohemia in 1283, aged twelve. He then ruled without a regent but under the influence of his mother and her partner Záviš of Falkenstein. He married Judith on 24 January 1285, and in 1290 he had Záviš beheaded for alleged treason and began ruling independently.

In 1291 High Duke Przemysł II of Poland ceded the Duchy of Kraków to Wenceslaus. After Przemysł's death in 1296 Wenceslaus became overlord of Poland, and in 1300 he had himself crowned its king. In 1298 silver was discovered at Kutná Hora. He made its production a royal monopoly and issued the Prague groschen, which became the most popular of the early Groschen-type coins. Between 1300 and 1340 the mine may have produced as much as 20 tons of silver a year. In 1300 he issued the mining code Ius regale montanorum, and he founded cities such as Plzeň in 1295.

In 1301 Andrew III of Hungary died and the Árpád dynasty became extinct in the male line. Wenceslaus accepted the crown from a party of Hungarians on behalf of his young son, who was betrothed to Andrew's only child, Elizabeth, and was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1301. In 1303 some of the son's supporters switched to Charles Robert of Anjou. Wenceslaus invaded Buda with a large army in 1304 but, having considered the situation, took his son and the Hungarian crown back to Bohemia.

Wenceslaus died on 21 June 1305, aged 33, probably of tuberculosis, and was succeeded by his son Wenceslaus III, the last of the Přemyslid kings. His realm stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Danube, and he is considered one of the most important Czech kings. His son could not maintain it, and soon after the early death of Wenceslaus II it began to crumble.
wenceslaus-iii-adam-duke-of-cieszyn: Wenceslaus III Adam was the second and only surviving son of Wenceslaus II, co-Duke of Cieszyn, and of Anna, a daughter of Frederick I, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and he was born after his father's death. His grandfather, Duke Casimir II, raised him as his only heir and on his death in 1528 left the duchy to him under the regency of his mother and the Bohemian magnate Jan of Pernštejn, called the Rich. The young duke was educated at the imperial court in Vienna but adopted the Evangelical faith. Although he counted as an adult from his mother's death in 1539, Jan of Pernštejn kept the government until 9 May 1545, giving up the regency only in return for Místek and Friedland as a pledge.

Under Wenceslaus the economy of the duchy stabilised and grew, though the lands in Upper Silesia won by Casimir II and the Duchy of Opava had been lost during the regency. The Reformation took real effect from about 1540: the Franciscan and Dominican convents of Cieszyn and later the Benedictine house at Orlová were closed, and part of their property went to the town hospital, where the duke, trained in medicine, cared for the poor, notably during the epidemic of 1570. On 24 June 1573 he issued the Land Ordinance of the Duchy of Cieszyn, a body of rules for all its inhabitants.

Despite his Lutheranism he served the House of Habsburg faithfully, attending the coronation of Maximilian II as King of Hungary at Bratislava in 1563 and the funeral of Ferdinand I in Vienna in 1565. In 1573 he built fortifications near Mosty u Jablunkova against a possible Turkish attack and stood without success for the Polish throne. The debts of his eldest son, Frederick Casimir, forced him to sell Fryštát, Skoczów and Bielsko to other Piast dukes after the son's death in 1571.

He died of apoplexy after a long illness on 4 November 1579 and was buried in the former Dominican church in Cieszyn. He married first Maria of Pernštejn, his guardian's daughter, in 1540, and secondly Sidonia Catharina of Saxe-Lauenburg in 1567; both wives supported Protestantism in the duchy. Of the nine children of the two marriages, the only son to outlive him was Adam Wenceslaus, born in 1574.
wenceslaus-iii-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was born in Prague on 6 October 1289, the son of Wenceslaus II of Bohemia and Judith of Habsburg, and was the only one of their sons to survive infancy. His mother died on 18 June 1297, and on 12 February 1298 he was betrothed to Elizabeth, the only child of Andrew III of Hungary. Andrew was the last male of the House of Árpád, though the legitimacy of his rule had not been universally accepted. In 1300 his father, who had occupied parts of Poland, was crowned King of Poland at Gniezno.

When Andrew III died on 14 January 1301, Charles I of the House of Anjou was crowned king by an archbishop-elect, backed by Pope Boniface VIII. Bribed by Wenceslaus II's agents, most Hungarian lords and prelates offered the crown to the boy. He was crowned with the Holy Crown at Székesfehérvár on 27 August 1301 and signed his charters as Ladislaus, but the Croatian lords stayed loyal to Charles, and Hungary had split into provinces held by about a dozen powerful lords, so his rule was nominal. The pope declared Charles the lawful king on 31 May 1303.

In August 1304 his father took him back to Bohemia with the Holy Crown. He succeeded in Bohemia and Poland on 21 June 1305, and on 9 October handed his Hungarian claim and the crown to Otto III of Bavaria at Brno. He broke his engagement and married Viola of Teschen. In Bohemia he gave large land grants to young friends, and in Poland Władysław I Łokietek took Kraków in early 1306.

Wenceslaus planned to invade Poland, dismissed his favourites and made his brother-in-law Henry governor, but on 4 August 1306 he was stabbed at Olomouc, aged sixteen. His assassin was never identified. He was the last male Přemyslid ruler of Bohemia.
wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia: Wenceslaus was born in Nuremberg on 26 February 1361, the eldest son of Charles IV by his third wife, Anna of Svídnická, a descendant of the Silesian Piasts. He was raised by the Prague archbishops Arnošt of Pardubice and Jan Očko of Vlašim. His father had him crowned King of Bohemia at the age of two, in 1363, and obtained the Electoral Margraviate of Brandenburg for him in 1373. When the electors chose him King of the Romans on 10 June 1376, two of the seven votes, those of Brandenburg and Bohemia, were held by Charles and his son themselves. He was crowned at Aachen on 6 July.

To secure his son's election Charles had revoked the privileges of many imperial cities and mortgaged them to nobles. In response fourteen Swabian cities formed the Swabian League of Cities. The league was defeated at Döffingen on 24 August 1388, and in 1389 Wenceslaus proclaimed an arrangement at Cheb that prohibited leagues between cities while confirming their autonomy.

In Bohemia he held a tenuous grip on power and clashed repeatedly with the nobility led by the House of Rosenberg; twice he was imprisoned for long spells by rebellious nobles. After officials of the king tortured and murdered the archbishop's vicar-general, Saint John of Nepomuk, in 1393, a noble rebellion followed, and in 1394 he was arrested while his cousin Jobst of Moravia became regent. His family weakened him further, because Charles had divided his holdings among his sons and relatives. In religious matters he sought to protect Jan Hus and his followers, and under the Decree of Kutná Hora in 1409 Hus's party drove German academics from the University of Prague.

The four Rhenish electors accused him of failing to keep the public peace or end the Schism. At Lahneck Castle on 20 August 1400 they declared him deposed for futility, idleness, negligence and ignobility and chose Rupert, Count Palatine, as King of the Romans. Wenceslaus never acknowledged this. In 1402 his half-brother Sigismund of Hungary captured him and held him in Vienna; he escaped on 11 November 1403 and returned to Prague.

After 1411 Wenceslaus agreed to give up his claim to the crown of the Romans provided he kept Bohemia, and Sigismund reigned as king. Wenceslaus was twice married and had no children. He was a patron of the arts, and the Wenceslas Bible, an illuminated manuscript, was drawn up between 1390 and 1400. He died in 1419 of a heart attack during a hunt near his castle Nový Hrad at Kunratice, leaving Bohemia in political crisis; fifteen years of Hussite Wars followed.
wenceslaus-of-plock: Wenceslaus, also called Wańko, was the third son of Bolesław II of Płock and the only one by his second wife Kunigunde, daughter of King Ottakar II of Bohemia; he was probably named after his uncle, King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia. Unlike his older half-brothers Siemowit II and Trojden I, he received no district of his own until their father died in 1313. The division pleased no one and led to a brief war between the three brothers in 1316. That year he married Elisabeth, a daughter of Gediminas, Grand Duke of Lithuania.

He first tried to stay neutral between the Teutonic Order and Poland. He refused to testify at the Teutonic-Polish trial in Inowrocław, and on 14 April 1321 at Golub he agreed with the Knights that the Masovian rulers would refuse passage to Lithuanian troops fighting the Order, yet in 1323 he let Lithuanian troops cross his land to invade the district of Dobrzyń. A surprise attack on Płock by Władysław I the Elbow-high in 1325 ended this policy, and on 2 January 1326 at Brodnica the dukes of Masovia allied against him.

In the Polish-Teutonic War that broke out in 1326 Wenceslaus strongly supported the Order. Władysław besieged and burned Płock, but Gostynin held out, and with the Order's help the Masovian dukes drove the Polish army from their lands. In 1329 an army led by King John of Bohemia, with the help of the Teutonic Knights, invaded Płock and forced Wenceslaus to surrender, and on 29 March he paid homage to John, who was also a claimant to the Polish throne.

Little is known of his last years; probably discouraged by both Poland and the Order, he withdrew from politics. He died at Wyszogród on 23 May 1336 and, according to Jan Długosz, was buried in Płock Cathedral. His wife Elisabeth outlived him until 1364. They had two children: a son, Bolesław III, who died in 1351, and a daughter, Anna, who married Henry V the Iron, Duke of Żagań.
wendish-crusade: The Wends were the Polabian Slavs, made up of the Abrotrites, Rani, Liutizians, Wagarians and Pomeranians, who lived east of the Elbe. German expansion under Henry the Fowler and Otto the Great had brought bishoprics at Meissen, Brandenburg, Havelberg and Oldenburg, but in 983 a great Slavic rebellion reversed the gains, and the Elbe became the eastern limit of German-Roman control. In the early 12th century the archbishoprics of Bremen, Magdeburg and Gniezno sought conversion by peaceful means, through missionaries such as Vicelin, Norbert of Xanten and Otto of Bamberg.

The Magdeburg Letter, sent around 1107 to 1110, first urged a crusade against the Wends, calling their land our Jerusalem and praising its richness in meat, honey and corn. The fall of Edessa in 1144 led Pope Eugenius III and Bernard of Clairvaux to preach the Second Crusade. North German Saxons were reluctant to go east and told Bernard at Frankfurt on 13 March 1147 that they wished to campaign against the Slavs instead. Eugenius III issued the bull Divina dispensatione on 11 April 1147, granting the same indulgences as for the Middle East.

Adolf II of Holstein had already settled Wagria, and in June 1147 Niklot, chief of the Obodrites, invaded it first and destroyed newly settled Fleming and Frisian villages. Adolf then signed a peace treaty with him. The remaining crusaders, mostly Danes, Saxons and Poles with some Bohemians, under the papal legate Anselm of Havelberg, targeted the Obodrite fort Dobin and the Liutizian fort Demmin.

At Dobin, Henry the Lion, Archbishop Adalbert II of Bremen and the Danes Canute V and Sweyn III faced Niklot, who avoided pitched battles and defended the marshland. One Danish army was defeated by the garrison. Henry withdrew after Niklot agreed that the garrison be baptised. At Demmin the bishops and the margraves Conrad I and Albert the Bear failed, though Albert recovered Havelberg. A contingent diverted to Pomerania reached Szczecin, already Christian, and dispersed there.

The crusade failed to convert or destroy the Wends but weakened them. The Saxons affirmed their hold on Wagria and Polabia, received tribute from Niklot, who kept the Obodrite land east of Lübeck, and enabled colonisation of the Bishopric of Havelberg. Helmold blamed the armies' attention to plunder. Bernard had forbidden truces and tribute, so the tribute contributed to his view that the crusade had failed. The conversions at Dobin were largely token, and the Slavs returned to their beliefs once the armies left.

Only the Danes made lasting conversions: they retook Rügen in 1168 and kept Prince Jaromit in power after he accepted Christianity. The crusade encouraged German settlers and began a long campaign against the Wends that lasted through the rest of the 12th century.
wends: The name Wends refers not to one people but to various peoples, tribes or groups, depending on where and when it was used. According to one theory, Germanic peoples first applied it to the ancient Veneti, who are mentioned by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy as inhabiting the Baltic coast. For medieval Scandinavians, Wends meant the Slavs living near the southern shore of the Baltic, such as the Obotrites, the Rugian Slavs, the Veleti or Lutici and the Pomeranian tribes. In the south, Germans used the form Winde for the Slavs of Bavaria Slavica or the Slovenes, a usage preserved in names such as Windischgraz.

In the first millennium CE some West Slavs moved into the lands between the Elbe and the Oder and assimilated the remaining Germanic population. They split into many small tribes, separated by woodland and sheltered in round wooden and clay strongholds. Some joined into larger units. The Obotrites were led by dukes, while the Lutici remained independent and met in the temple of Rethra. In 983 many Wend tribes took part in a great uprising against the Holy Roman Empire, which delayed Germanisation by about two centuries.

After 983 the Wends came under pressure from Germans, Danes and Poles. A German expedition destroyed Rethra in 1068/69, and the Wend crusade took place in 1147. In 1168 a Danish crusade under Bishop Absalon and King Valdemar the Great captured and destroyed Arkona and tore down the statue of the god Svantevit. With the surrender of the Rugian Wends the last independent pagan Wends were defeated. From the 12th to the 14th centuries German settlers moved into their lands in large numbers in the Ostsiedlung, and new towns were founded under German law.

The Wends were gradually assimilated into German-speaking culture, and the Polabian language was spoken in parts of Lower Saxony and Brandenburg until the 17th or 18th century. Many place names in central and northern Germany are of Slavic origin, among them Delitzsch and Rochlitz, and the names of Leipzig and Berlin are most likely Wendish. The Dukes of Mecklenburg, Rügen and Pomerania had Wendish ancestors. The Danish kings used the title King of the Wends from 1362, and the Swedish kings were styled kings of the Swedes, the Goths and the Wends from 1540. Both usages were dropped in 1972 and 1973. In 1854 Wends from Lusatia emigrated to Texas.
wenzel-anton-von-kaunitz-rietberg: Wenzel Anton was born in Vienna on 2 February 1711, one of 19 children of Maximilian Ulrich, Count of Kaunitz, and Maria Ernestine von Rietberg, an heiress of the House of Cirksena. The Kaunitz family belonged to the ancient Bohemian nobility, and through his mother's marriage portion the family inherited the immediate County of Rietberg in Westphalia. As the second son he was first meant for the church and held a canonry at Münster at thirteen, but after his elder brother died he studied law and diplomacy at Vienna, Leipzig and Leiden.

He became a member of the Imperial Aulic Council in 1735, served as ambassador at Turin from 1742 and from 1744 as minister plenipotentiary in the Austrian Netherlands, and he signed the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle on 23 October 1748 reluctantly, since it confirmed Prussia in Silesia and Glatz.

Kaunitz had long opposed the alliance with Britain that had existed since 1731. He argued to Empress Maria Theresa that Frederick II of Prussia was the most wicked and dangerous enemy of Austria and that Silesia could be regained only by an alliance with Russia and France. She entrusted him with the execution of this plan, and as ambassador at Versailles from 1750 to 1752 he laid the groundwork for it. As State Chancellor from 1753 to 1792 he reorganised the foreign office on the Ballhausplatz.

The Treaty of Versailles of 1756, the Diplomatic Revolution, moved Austria from an ally of Britain to an ally of France and Russia, while Prussia allied with Britain and Hanover, and this lineup framed the Seven Years' War, which did not bring Silesia back. In 1761 he founded the Austrian Council of State, and after the war he became a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire.

Under Joseph II, whose reforms Kaunitz found too fast, the two quarrelled and Kaunitz several times offered his resignation. He backed the First Partition of Poland in 1772 and won the Innviertel for Austria in the Treaty of Teschen of 1779. He worked to subject the Catholic Church to the state, and he patronised Christoph Willibald Gluck and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. He pressed for the Austro-Turkish War of 1788–1791, which proved costly and gained no anti-Prussian aim.

After Joseph II died, Leopold II blamed Kaunitz for the war's failure and sharply restricted his powers. Kaunitz resigned on the accession of Francis II in July 1792 and died in Vienna in 1794. He was buried in the family vault at Slavkov. His granddaughter Eleonora married Klemens von Metternich, who later held the same office.
wenzhou: Wenzhou, formerly called Yongjia, lies at the lower reaches and estuary of the Ou River on the south-eastern coast of China, between the Zhejiang-Fujian Hills to the west and the East China Sea. The Ou, Feiyun and Ao rivers drain the area, and the terrain falls from mountains in the west to plains, tidal flats and offshore islands in the east. The Caowan Mountain site, excavated in 2002, shows human activity here some 5,000 years ago, in the Neolithic period. A Neolithic cultural complex represented by the Haochuan culture gave rise to the Ou people, also called the Ouyue, part of the wider Yue people, whose capital was at Dong'ou.

The Ou had established the polity of Dong'ou by at least the fourth century BCE, and it surrendered to the Han dynasty in 138 BCE. That year Yongning County was created, the first county-level administration in Wenzhou. Later names were Yongjia Commandery from 323 and Wenzhou Prefecture from 675. The walled city first established in the 4th century remained the seat of the prefecture and county until 1958. After the Tang takeover in the early 7th century Yongjia became a major trading port, with marine trade with Japan beginning in 659. It was authorised as a foreign trade port in the Song and Yuan periods and is regarded as one of the places of origin of Chinese celadon.

In 1367 the Ming dynasty took Wenzhou from an anti-Yuan revolt. Pirates called wokou were active off its coast, and the Ming court set up a tightly organised garrison system for coastal defence. Wenzhou became a treaty port under the Chefoo Convention of 1876, and a customs office opened the next year. Steamship travel allowed local scholars to return with hospitals, schools and libraries. Britain set up a consulate on Jiangxin Islet in 1894, and in 1984 Wenzhou was named among China's first 14 open coastal cities.

After 1978 Wenzhou was among the first places in China to try market-oriented reforms, the Wenzhou Model, building on households with savings of over 10,000 yuan that had appeared in the 1970s. Since the 1990s large numbers of its people have migrated within China and abroad, forming communities such as Belleville in Paris and Prato in Italy. The city has the highest proportion of religious believers among Chinese cities, with Buddhism the predominant religion, and has more Christians than any other Chinese city, which has earned it the name China's Jerusalem.
werner-munzinger: Werner Munzinger was born at Olten on 4 April 1832, a son of Josef Munzinger, a member of the Swiss Federal Council. He studied science and history at the University of Bern and Oriental studies at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and the Sorbonne. In 1852 he went to Cairo to improve his Arabic, and for a French trading house he led a commercial expedition to parts of the Red Sea.

After serving as French consul at Massawa until 1855, Munzinger moved to Keren and spent six years exploring the lands of the Bogos, whose customs and law he described in 1859. In 1861 he joined Theodor von Heuglin's attempt to explore Central Africa, then led the expedition himself from Khartoum, reaching Kordofan in 1862 but failing to reach Darfur and Wadai. He managed the British consulate on the Ethiopian border from 1865 and became French consul at Massawa after the British invasion of Ethiopia in 1868. According to Augustus B. Wylde, he married a woman of Hamasien and persuaded the local warlord Wolde Mikael to cede that province to France, but the Franco-Prussian War stopped the French expedition he had prepared at Toulon in 1870.

In July 1870 he went with Captain S. B. Miles into the interior of southern Arabia. He then entered the service of Khedive Ismail as governor of Keren and Massawa, placed the Bogos under Egyptian rule again and developed the port of Massawa. His published works include Ostafrikanische Studien of 1864 and a vocabulary of the Tigré language of 1865.

During the Egyptian-Ethiopian War he was chosen to open contact with Menelik II, king of Shewa, a potential ally of Egypt. In late 1875 he set out from Tadjoura with 350 men towards Ankober, planning to cross the Danakil Desert and climb into the highlands by the Awash Valley. On the night of 14 November, Afar and Issa warriors attacked the force near Aussa and killed Munzinger, his wife, their child and most of the soldiers; only a few escaped to Tadjoura. The defeat ended Egypt's hopes of expanding at Ethiopia's expense.
wernigerode: Wernigerode lies at about 250 metres above sea level on the Holtemme river, on the north-eastern flank of the Harz Mountains and at the foot of their highest peak, the Brocken. The Northern Harz Boundary Fault crosses its borough, and along it runs the watershed between the Weser and the Elbe. The town lies in the rain shadow of the Harz, so less rain falls there than in comparable places without the mountains. It stands on the German Timber-Frame Road.

No written source gives the date of the town's founding. The name suggests a protected clearance settlement, the suffix rode meaning clearing, and the first area settled was the Klint, where a lowland castle called the Schnakenburg stood. The town is first mentioned in 1121, in connection with Count Adalbert of Haimar, who moved there from the region near Hildesheim and was henceforth titled Count of Wernigerode. On 17 April 1229 it received town rights on the model of Goslar's. A new settlement, later called the Neustadt, grew up outside the old town's walls as people arrived from the surrounding villages.

The counts were vassals of the margraves of Brandenburg from 1268 and of the archbishops of Magdeburg from 1381. When the family died out in 1429 the county fell to the counts of Stolberg, who founded the Stolberg-Wernigerode branch in 1645. It surrendered its military and fiscal independence to Prussia in 1714 but kept some sovereign rights until 1876, and its counts were raised to princely rank in 1890. After the Napoleonic Wars the town became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony in 1815. After 1945 it lay close to the inner German border and was part of East Germany.

Wernigerode has a Gothic town hall with a timber facade from 1498. Some of the old houses that escaped the town's many fires are adorned with wood-carving. The castle of the princes of Stolberg-Wernigerode rises above the town. The original dates from the 12th century, and the present castle was built between 1862 and 1893 by Karl Frühling and includes parts of the medieval building. The Harzer Schmalspurbahn, a narrow-gauge railway, leads from the town to the Brocken. The Hasseröder brewery was founded there in 1872, and the town is a site of the Harz University of Applied Studies.
wesel: Wesel stands at the confluence of the Lippe and the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, and it is the capital of the Wesel district. The city grew from a Franconian manor first recorded in the 8th century. In the 12th century the Duke of Clèves took possession of it, and in the 15th century it became a member of the Hanseatic League. It was second only to Cologne in the lower Rhine region as an entrepôt, a clearing station for the transshipment and trading of goods.

A Walloon community with French-language church services was noted in Wesel in 1545, and a French Huguenot commune was founded there in 1688. In 1590 the Spanish captured the city after a four-year siege, and it changed hands between the Dutch and the Spanish several times during the Eighty Years War. A French force under Louis II de Bourbon, Prince de Condé, captured it in 1672. The Hohenzollerns of the Margraviate of Brandenburg inherited Wesel in 1609 but could not take control of it until the Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678.

In 1805 the city was ceded to the French Empire under the Treaty of Schönbrunn. It became part of the Grand Duchy of Berg under Joachim Murat in 1806 and was annexed to France itself in January 1808. The French fortified it heavily, building the Citadelle Napoleon at Büderich, which was renamed Fort Blücher after the Napoleonic Wars, when the city passed to Prussia in 1815.

As a strategic depot Wesel was bombed by the Allies, and air raids on 16 to 19 February 1945 destroyed 97 per cent of the town. The Wehrmacht blew up the bridges over the Rhine and Lippe, and on 23 March a bombardment by over 3,000 guns and a raid by RAF bombers prepared Operation Plunder, the Allied crossing of the Rhine. Operation Varsity dropped 18,000 troops behind the town. The population fell from almost 25,000 in 1939 to 1,900 in May 1945. In 1946 Wesel became part of North Rhine-Westphalia. A restored 15th-century city hall, the Willibrordi-Dom and the citadel remain among its sights.
weser: The Weser is the longest river wholly in Germany. Together with the Werra, which rises in Thuringia, it is 744 km long, while the Weser itself measures 452 km. Weser and Werra are the same word in different dialects, the difference reflecting the old linguistic border between Central and Low German that passes through Hannoversch Münden. The name probably derives from an Old Germanic word meaning flow or ooze, and is cognate with the Wear in England and the Vistula in Poland. After Hannoversch Münden the river runs between the Wiehengebirge and the Weserbergland to the Porta Westfalica, then on to Bremen. Its largest tributary, the Aller, joins south of Bremen.

Between Minden and the North Sea the river has been largely canalised for ships of up to 1,200 tons, and eight hydroelectric dams stand at the ends of adjacent weir streams. A large reservoir, the Edersee on the Eder, the main tributary of the Fulda, keeps enough water in the river for shipping all year. Its dam, built in 1914, was bombed and severely damaged by British aircraft in May 1943, causing great destruction and about 70 deaths downstream, and was rebuilt within four months.

The Weser enters the North Sea in the southernmost part of the German Bight, where it splits into two arms, the Alte Weser and the Neue Weser, which are the waterways for ships bound for Bremerhaven, Nordenham and Bremen. The Alte Weser Lighthouse replaced the Roter Sand Lighthouse in 1964. Since the 19th century the river has been deepened twelve times, which altered the tides and caused severe ecological damage and a greater risk of flooding along its banks.
weser-renaissance: Between the start of the Reformation and the Thirty Years War the Weser region saw a building boom. The river carried trade and ideas and marked the north–south extent of a cultural region that reached west to Osnabrück and east as far as Wolfsburg. Castles, manor houses, town halls, houses and churches of the period survive in unusually high density, because the region's economy recovered only slowly from the Thirty Years War and there was no money for the baroque rebuilding seen in parts of southern Germany.

In the 16th century the nobility turned medieval castles into residences. Early ones often had two wings; later the favoured plan was an enclosed courtyard whose wings met at corner towers holding staircases, a form the lesser nobility soon copied. The Zwerchhaus, a cross-gable with so-called welsch or Italian gables, served as a sign of power on castles such as Detmold, Celle and Bückeburg, where it could be seen from far beyond the ramparts.

Burghers copied these forms to show their growing influence. Town halls such as those of Celle and Lemgo received gables along their sides, and Bremen's a whole Renaissance facade. Large townhouses with a great gateway into an inner hall rose from Nienburg to Minden, Hamelin, Höxter, Hannoversch Münden and Einbeck. Other marks of the style are bossage stone, projecting bays called Utluchten and double windows. In churches the pulpit was raised and set facing the pews, as in the castle chapels of Celle and Bückeburg.

The term was coined around 1912 by Richard Klapheck, and Max Sonnen used it in 1918 in his book Die Weserrenaissance, classing buildings on purely formal grounds. The idea of an independent regional style grew out of the nationalistic thinking of the late 19th century. In 1964 Jürgen Soenke and the photographer Herbert Kreft published an inventory under the same title that called the style folk art; it ran to six editions by 1986 and made the term widely known.

Hitchcock gave the term international standing in his German Renaissance Architecture of 1981, while stressing its links with Renaissance architecture as a whole. Research by the Weser Renaissance Museum at Brake Castle, founded in 1986, has since criticised the notion of a regional identity, pointing instead to architectural drawings, architects from elsewhere, builders working across regions and the Europe-wide demands of court fashion.
wesley-merritt: Merritt was born in New York City and graduated from the United States Military Academy in 1860. He was commissioned a second lieutenant in the 2nd Dragoons and served at first in Utah under John Buford, becoming adjutant of the unit when it was renamed the 2nd Cavalry Regiment. In 1862 he was made captain and served as aide-de-camp to Brigadier General Philip St. George Cooke, then in 1863 as adjutant to Major General George Stoneman during Stoneman's Raid in the Battle of Chancellorsville.

Slightly wounded at the Battle of Brandy Station, he was appointed brigadier general of volunteers on 29 June 1863, a direct step from captain that he shared that day with Elon J. Farnsworth and George Armstrong Custer. At Gettysburg he led the Reserve Brigade in the assault on the Confederate right flank after Pickett's Charge. He took command of the 1st Division of the Cavalry Corps after Buford's death in December 1863 and fought at the Battle of Yellow Tavern.

In Major General Philip Sheridan's Valley Campaigns of 1864 his division routed the Confederate forces at the Third Battle of Winchester, then burned barns, mills and crops across the Shenandoah Valley. He was Sheridan's second-in-command in the Appomattox Campaign and one of the commissioners for the surrender at Appomattox Court House. After the war he served on the frontier, commanding Fort Davis, Texas, and later the 5th Cavalry at the Battle of Slim Buttes, and he sat on the court of inquiry into Major Marcus A. Reno's conduct at the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

From 1882 to 1887 he was superintendent of West Point, and as commander of the Department of the Missouri he sent troops into the Oklahoma District before the Land Rush of 1889. In the Philippines in 1898 he led the Eighth Army Corps; he and Commodore George Dewey kept Emilio Aguinaldo unaware of their plans and arranged with Governor General Fermín Jáudenes for the Spanish garrison to surrender after token resistance. Major General Elwell Stephen Otis relieved him on 30 August.

Merritt retired from the army in 1900. His first wife, Caroline Warren Merritt, died in 1893; on 24 October 1898 he married Laura Williams Caton in London. He died of complications of arteriosclerosis at Natural Bridge, Virginia, on 3 December 1910 and is buried at West Point Cemetery. He was portrayed in the Filipino film Heneral Luna (2015).
wessex: The Anglo-Saxons believed that Wessex was founded by Cerdic and Cynric of the Gewisse, though some consider this a legend. The two main sources for its early history are the West Saxon Genealogical Regnal List and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, which sometimes conflict. The first event that can be dated with reasonable certainty is the baptism of King Cynegils by Birinus at the end of the 630s, perhaps in 640. Birinus became bishop of the West Saxons with his seat at Dorchester-on-Thames. Cynegils's successor Cenwealh was a pagan at his accession but was baptised a few years later, after an exile in East Anglia, and Wessex became firmly Christian. He established a second bishopric at Winchester.

Wessex's fortunes were transformed in 802 by the accession of Egbert. In 825 or 826 he defeated King Beornwulf of Mercia at Ellendun and seized Surrey, Sussex, Kent and Essex. In 829 he conquered Mercia and secured the overlordship of the king of Northumbria, though Mercian independence was restored in 830. In 851 his son Æthelwulf crushed a Danish army at the Battle of Aclea.

The Great Heathen Army, which landed in 865, overwhelmed Northumbria and East Anglia, and in 871 invaded Wessex. At the beginning of 878 the Danes overran much of the kingdom and Alfred took refuge in the Somerset Levels, but he gathered an army and defeated them at the Battle of Edington. He issued a law code, built ships and organised an army and a system of burhs. His son Edward the Elder annexed London and Oxford, and by 918 took direct control of Mercia after the death of his sister Æthelflæd. In 927 Æthelstan conquered Northumbria, bringing all England under one ruler for the first time.

The Kingdom of Wessex was thus transformed into the Kingdom of England. After Cnut the Great conquered England in 1016 he created the earldom of Wessex, and in 1066 Harold Godwinson reunited the earldom with the crown, after which Wessex ceased to exist. The wyvern or dragon often used to symbolise it was popularised only in the 19th century, largely through the writings of E. A. Freeman. Thomas Hardy took the name for a fictionalised setting of his novels in Dorset and neighbouring counties, and Wessex remains a common term for the area.
west-africa: West Africa is the westernmost region of Africa. Its climate is shaped by the dry Sahara to the north and east, which produces the Harmattan winds, and by the Atlantic Ocean to the south and west, which brings seasonal monsoons, so that biomes range from tropical forest to dry land. The Sahel, a transition zone between the Sudanian savannas and the Sahara, crosses several of its countries. The United Nations defines the region as 16 countries, from Mauritania and Senegal to Nigeria, with an area of about 6.1 million square kilometres.

West African hunter-gatherers occupied the coast by 12,000 years ago and moved north as far as Mali, Burkina Faso and Mauritania between 12,000 and 8000 years ago. Centralised states followed, beginning with Dhar Tichitt from 1600 BCE and Djenné-Djenno from 300 BCE. The Ghana Empire flourished roughly between the 2nd and 12th centuries CE and gave way to the Mali Empire. Positioned at a crossroads of trade between North Africa and the Sahel, the region supplied gold, ivory and advanced ironworking.

Portuguese traders began establishing settlements along the coast in 1445, followed by the French, English, Spanish, Danish and Dutch, and the African slave trade began not long after. It encouraged the formation of states such as the Bono state, the Bambara Empire and Dahomey, which exchanged slaves for European firearms. In the early 19th century Fulani reformist jihads swept across the region, among them Usman dan Fodio's Fulani Empire, which replaced the Hausa city-states. Britain and France then controlled nearly the whole region. Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah became the first West African colony to gain independence, in 1957, and by 1974 the region's nations were entirely autonomous.

The region is culturally and demographically diverse, home to the Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Akan, Mandé, Wolof, Songhai, Kanuri, Zarma, Tuareg and many other peoples. Islam, Christianity and traditional African religions are the most common religions. Its traditional building styles include the Sudano-Sahelian style in the inland areas and coastal forest styles, and typical formal dress includes the boubou robe and the Akan kente cloth.
west-africa-squadron: The Slave Trade Act 1807, passed on 25 March 1807, barred British subjects from the Atlantic slave trade and allowed the seizure of ships equipped for it. Enforcing it against foreign vessels proved hard. During the Napoleonic Wars the small force could stop any ship of an enemy nation, but Portugal, a major slave-trading power and Britain's ally, evaded the Act until a convention of February 1810 let British ships police Portuguese traffic. Two privateers, Dart and Kitty, briefly hunted slavers for government bounties.

After 1815 Viscount Castlereagh secured a declaration against the trade at the Congress of Vienna, but the early treaties were weak: until 1835 the Squadron seized foreign ships only if captives were found aboard, and some captains threw captives overboard to escape the fine of £100 a head. Courts were set up at Freetown, from 1817 as Mixed Commission Courts with British and foreign officials. Commodore Sir George Ralph Collier, the first commodore, had six ships for more than 5,000 kilometres of coast.

From 1819 the Squadron worked from a naval station at Freetown, and most of the Africans it freed settled in Sierra Leone. Slavers turned to fast Baltimore clippers, and the Navy answered with captured clippers of its own, such as HMS Black Joke, taken from Brazil in 1827, and from the 1840s with paddle steamers. In the middle of the century about 25 vessels and 2,000 men were engaged, with 1,000 local sailors. The United States Navy sent ships from 1820, and more after the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842.

The Squadron took about 6% of transatlantic slave ships. Between 1830 and 1865 almost 1,600 of its sailors died on duty, mostly of disease. Freed captives from inland were often left to find their way home, and up to a quarter of those who could not stay in Freetown are estimated to have died; others joined the Royal Navy or the West India Regiments, and about 35,850 went to the West Indies as apprentices.

Robert Pape and Chaim Kaufmann have called it the most expensive international humanitarian intervention in modern history. Others hold it was poorly resourced and not chiefly responsible for the end of the trade. Howard W. French argues its impact has been overstated, and John Rankin has noted that African and diaspora sailors, notably the Kru, made up one-fifth of its crews.
west-african-vodun: Vodún, also called vodúnsínsen, meaning spirit worship, has no central authority and shows much diversity among its practitioners, known as vodúnsɛntó or vodúnisants. Its followers believe in a single divine creator, below whom an uncountable number of spirits, the vodún, govern different aspects of nature and society. Some are tied to particular cities and others to families.

The word comes from the Gbé languages and means spirit, God, divinity or presence. Belief is centred on efficacy rather than on faith. Followers hold that the vodún physically manifest in shrines, which are not mere images but their incarnations, and that an object's power comes from its acɛ, divine power. New spirits are readily admitted, and some practitioners call Jesus Christ the vodún of the Christians.

Initiation gives a person the power of a vodún and brings long-term obligations to honour, feed and pay the spirit, which in turn promises protection, abundance, long life and a large family. It may last from a few months to a few years, though Fá initiation in Benin usually takes less than a week. Spirits are given offerings, and animal sacrifice, called vɔ in Fon, nourishes the spirit's acɛ and the meat is eaten by the attendees.

Many cults include possession, when a person receives the spirit and speaks as it, giving advice. Divination, above all Fá, is performed by diviners called bokónó. The all-male secret societies Oró and Egúngún command respect, and Egúngún is held to have spread west from the Yoruba of Oyo. Charms called bǒ are used for healing and protection.

Before European colonialism, Vodún was not a single religion but, in the words of the anthropologist Timothy R. Landry, a social system of countless spirit and ancestor cults, some of them bound up with political structures. In the 18th century the Fon-dominated kingdom of Dahomey became a vassal of the Oyo Empire, and many Yoruba traditions passed to the Fon and Ewe, so that Vodún overlaps with Yoruba religion.

Enslaved vodúnsɛntó were carried to the Americas during the Atlantic slave trade, and their religions influenced Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo and Brazilian Candomblé Jejé. Christian missions worked in the region from the 18th century. After Mathieu Kérékou seized power in Dahomey in 1972, he made it a Marxist-Leninist state, banned Vodún ceremonies during the rainy season in 1973 and pressed further measures against the religion, so that initiations were done in secret and shortened.
