He travelled slowly and observed with care; his main aims were to study the peoples he met and to collect plants and animals. He investigated the watershed between the Nile and the Congo, argued successfully against the hydrographical theories of Georg Schweinfurth, and established that the Welle and the Ubangi were one river. His ethnographic observations of the Azande, then called the Niam-Niam, are counted especially valuable, though parts of them are unsubstantiated.

In 1884 the Mahdist rising stopped him from going home through the Sudan as he had planned, and an expedition his brother fitted out in St Petersburg in 1885 failed to reach him. Junker turned south instead. He left Wadelai on 2 January 1886, travelled by way of Uganda and Tabora, and reached Zanzibar in November 1886.

In 1887 the Royal Geographical Society awarded him its gold medal. His findings appeared as Reisen in Afrika, published in three volumes in Vienna between 1889 and 1891, and an English translation by A. H. Keane followed in three volumes in 1890 to 1892. He died at St Petersburg on 13 February 1892.
wilhelm-karl-duke-of-urach: Wilhelm Karl Florestan Gero Crescentius, Count of Württemberg, was born on 3 March 1864, the elder son of Wilhelm, 1st Duke of Urach, head of a morganatic branch of the royal house of Württemberg, and his second wife Princess Florestine of Monaco. At the age of four he succeeded his father as Duke of Urach. He grew up largely in Monaco, where his mother often managed the government. Through his mother he was a legitimate heir to the throne of Monaco, but under French pressure Monaco recognised Louis, the only son of Albert I, and later Louis's illegitimate daughter Charlotte as heirs ahead of him, so that he stood third in line. He renounced his rights in 1924.

Wilhelm entered the army in 1883 as a professional officer. At the outbreak of the First World War he was a Generalleutnant commanding the 26th Infantry Division. The division was largely destroyed at the Somme in 1916 while holding the Schwaben Redoubt. From 1917 he commanded the 64th Corps on the Western Front until it was deactivated on 10 December 1918. Erwin Rommel was among his aides.

He was also considered for other thrones. In 1913 he was among the princes thought of for Albania, supported by Catholic groups in the north, but Prince William of Wied was chosen in 1914. In 1917 he sounded out the possibility of becoming Grand Duke of Alsace-Lorraine after the war.

On 4 June 1918 the Council of Lithuania voted to invite him to become king of an independent Lithuania, and he was elected on 11 July 1918 as Mindaugas II. He was a Roman Catholic and not a Hohenzollern, whereas Emperor William II wanted Lithuania in personal union with Prussia. Four socialist members of the council left in protest, and the German government did not recognise the choice. He never visited Lithuania, staying at Lichtenstein Castle, and on 2 November 1918, as Germany's defeat became clear, the council reversed its decision. Wilhelm died on 24 March 1928.
wilhelm-maybach: Wilhelm Maybach was born on 9 February 1846 in Heilbronn, in the Kingdom of Württemberg, the son of a carpenter. His mother died in 1854 and his father in 1856, and a philanthropic institution at Reutlingen took him in. Its founder, Gustav Werner, noticed his technical inclination and sent him to its engineering workshop. By the age of 19 he was a qualified designer working on stationary engines. His workshop manager, Gottlieb Daimler, then 29, took him on as his main assistant, a post he held until Daimler's death in 1900.

Maybach followed Daimler to Karlsruhe in 1869 and to the Deutz gas engine works in Cologne in 1872, where he became chief designer. When Daimler left Deutz after disagreements with Nicolaus Otto in 1880, Maybach followed him to Cannstatt. In their workshop in a garden summer house they developed small engines that ran fast. In 1883 they patented one, running at 750 rpm, and a smaller version of their engine of 1885, nicknamed the grandfather clock, was installed on a wooden bicycle, creating the first motorcycle. Maybach also helped to fit engines to a boat in 1887 and to an airship in 1888, and in 1889 they built their first automobile designed from scratch.

Daimler and Maybach founded the Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft in 1890, but new financiers doubted that automobiles would pay, and Maybach left the board in 1891. His engine for the Phoenix, designed in 1894, used four cylinders and a spray-nozzle carburettor and won him the title King of Designers in France. In 1900 he designed a low, powerful car for the dealer Emil Jellinek, whose daughter Mercedes gave the engine its name. He left the company in 1907 after being moved to an inventors' office.

In 1909 Maybach and his son Karl founded an engine company for Count Zeppelin's airships, later called Maybach-Motorenbau, at Friedrichshafen. The Treaty of Versailles banned airship production in Germany, so after 1919 the firm made diesel engines and then, from 1921, complete luxury cars, beginning with the Maybach W3. Its V12 car was the first German 12-cylinder automobile, but only a few dozen were sold in the postwar economic crisis. Maybach died in Stuttgart on 29 December 1929 and was succeeded by Karl. From about 1935 the firm built almost all the engines for German tanks and half-tracks in the Second World War. Maybach himself never owned a car and walked or took the tram.
wilhelm-murr: Murr was born in Esslingen am Neckar and grew up there in poverty, losing both parents at the age of 14. After commercial training and military service from 1908 to 1910 he worked as a salesman at the Maschinenfabrik Esslingen. In the First World War he rose to Vize-Feldwebel, was wounded and received the Iron Cross, 2nd class. He was active in the antisemitic employees' union known as the DHV, read Theodor Fritsch, joined the Deutschvölkischer Schutz- und Trutzbund and entered the Nazi Party in 1923, rejoining in August 1925.

After fierce intra-party fighting he ousted the Gauleiter Eugen Munder, and Adolf Hitler appointed him Gauleiter on 1 February 1928. He founded the NS-Kurier in 1931, sat in the Reichstag from 1930 and led the Nazi faction in the Landtag of Württemberg from 1932. In 1933 the Landtag, under Nazi pressure, chose him as State President in succession to Eugen Bolz; on 6 May he became Reichsstatthalter, with his rival Christian Mergenthaler as Prime Minister. In 1938 he organised a press campaign and demonstrations that drove Bishop Johannes Baptista Sproll of Rottenburg out of the province.

As Reich Defense Commissioner of Military District V from 1939 he held power over much of military and civil administration, and he became SS-Obergruppenführer on 30 January 1942. The Holocaust against Jews and the mentally ill went ahead in Württemberg with Murr carrying out the orders of Hitler and the Party unconditionally. His only son Winfried shot himself in January 1944 to forestall a court-martial for rape; Murr assured Hitler of his loyalty that March.

On 10 April 1945 Murr ordered Stuttgart defended to the utmost, threatening with execution and Sippenhaft anyone who raised white flags, then fled the city on 19 April under a false name. French troops arrested him near Schröcken in Vorarlberg on 13 May, when he called himself Walter Müller. At Egg he and his wife took poison. The Americans had listed him as a potential war criminal; on 16 April 1946 the grave at Egg was opened, and his former dentist identified him by his teeth.
wilhelm-solf: Wilhelm Heinrich Solf was born on 5 October 1862 into a wealthy and liberal family in Berlin. He studied Oriental languages, Sanskrit above all, at Berlin, Göttingen and Halle, took a doctorate in philology in 1885 and wrote an elementary Sanskrit grammar under the Indologist Richard Pischel. After a post at the library of the University of Kiel he joined the consular service in 1888 and was sent to Calcutta, but left after three years to study law at Jena, where he took a second doctorate in 1896.

In the Colonial Department of the Foreign Office he served briefly as a district judge in Dar es Salaam in 1898, and in 1899 he chaired the council of the provisional municipal government of Apia in Samoa.

The Tripartite Convention of 1899 gave the western Samoan islands to Germany, and Solf became governor on 1 March 1900, at the age of 38. He was known as a careful administrator who drew Samoan traditions into his government but used banishment when his authority as the Kaiser's deputy was challenged. He encouraged plantation agriculture, and the higher tax revenue paid for a public school system, a hospital and better roads and harbours; the colony had become self-sufficient by the time Erich Schultz succeeded him.

As secretary of the Colonial Office from 1911 he toured the German colonies in West and East Africa in 1912 and 1913 and designed coats of arms for them, never used because of the war. He opposed unrestricted submarine warfare and lobbied for a negotiated peace. Appointed the last imperial foreign minister in October 1918, he negotiated the armistice of 11 November and resigned on 13 December 1918.

From 1920 to 1928 he represented Germany in Japan, first as chargé d'affaires and then as ambassador, and helped restore relations with its wartime enemy, which led to the German-Japanese Treaty of 1927. A member of the German Democratic Party, he backed Paul von Hindenburg's re-election in 1932. He died on 6 February 1936. His widow Johanna and their daughter Lagi, born in Samoa in 1909, later hosted the anti-Nazi gatherings known as the Frau Solf Tea Party.
wilhelm-von-humboldt: Humboldt was born in Potsdam and died in Tegel. His father, Alexander Georg von Humboldt, belonged to a prominent noble family from Pomerania and was a major in the Prussian Army; he was rewarded for his service in the Seven Years' War with the post of royal chamberlain. Wilhelm and his younger brother Alexander were the two sons of his marriage to Maria Elisabeth Colomb. Wilhelm was educated at home and never finished his comparatively short university studies at Frankfurt (Oder) and Göttingen. In June 1791 he married Caroline von Dacheröden; they had eight children, of whom five survived to adulthood.

Between 1802 and 1819 Humboldt was a diplomat: Prussian minister at Rome from 1802, then ambassador at Vienna from 1812. At the congress of Prague in 1813 he was instrumental in drawing Austria into an alliance with Prussia and Russia against Napoleon. He signed the peace treaty at Paris and the treaty between Prussia and defeated Saxony in 1815, and attended the congress at Aachen in 1818. The increasingly reactionary policy of the Prussian government made him give up political life in 1819.

In 1809 the Prussian king asked him to leave Rome and lead the directorate of education. He had hoped to become minister of education but never did, and he would have preferred to stay in Rome. He installed a standardised system of public instruction from basic schools to secondary education, standardised state examinations and inspections, created a department to oversee curricula and textbooks, and founded Berlin University. His model went beyond vocational training: he wrote to the king that people cannot be good craftworkers, merchants or soldiers unless they are good and well-informed human beings and citizens.

In 1791 and 1792 he wrote The Limits of State Action, one of the boldest defences of the liberties of the Enlightenment, though it was not published until 1850. It influenced John Stuart Mill's On Liberty of 1859, and Humboldt outlined an early version of what Mill called the harm principle. A section on education appeared in the Berlinische Monatsschrift in December 1792 as "On public state education".

As a linguist he studied Basque and translated Pindar and Aeschylus into German. His two visits to the Basque country produced Researches into the Early Inhabitants of Spain by the help of the Basque language (1821), which has since been superseded in its details. He died while preparing a major study of the ancient Kawi language of Java, whose introduction appeared in 1836 as The Heterogeneity of Language and its Influence on the Intellectual Development of Mankind. It introduced the idea of the inner form of language, holding that a language's structure expresses the inner life and knowledge of its speakers.
wilhelmina-of-the-netherlands: Wilhelmina Helena Pauline Maria of Orange-Nassau was born on 31 August 1880 at Noordeinde Palace in The Hague, the only child of King William III and his second wife, Emma of Waldeck and Pyrmont. Her father was 63 at her birth. His three sons by his first marriage had died or were dying, and in 1887 the king settled the throne on his only surviving child. He died on 23 November 1890, and the ten-year-old Wilhelmina became queen. She turned 18 on 31 August 1898 and was sworn in at the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam on 6 September.

She married Duke Henry of Mecklenburg-Schwerin on 7 February 1901. The marriage was unhappy, and she suffered several miscarriages and a stillbirth before Princess Juliana was born on 30 April 1909. The birth was met with relief, since a childless queen would have been succeeded by a German prince.

The Netherlands stayed neutral in the First World War, partly through her political influence, though the Allies included it in their blockade of Germany. After the war she gave asylum to the fleeing Kaiser Wilhelm II. When the socialist leader Pieter Jelles Troelstra sought to abolish the monarchy in the unrest after the war, her popularity helped restore confidence, notably when she rode through crowds in an open carriage with her daughter. Her investments in the United States made her the world's richest woman.

On the voyage to Britain in 1940 she arrived on 13 May. There she took charge of the government in exile, and relations with her ministers were tense. With the help of the minister Pieter Gerbrandy she removed the prime minister Dirk Jan de Geer, who believed the Allies would not win and wished to negotiate a separate peace. Her broadcasts on Radio Oranje were awaited by listeners who had to hide to hear them. On 5 August 1942 she became the first queen to address the United States Congress, and in 1944 she was admitted to the Order of the Garter.

She was disappointed that the old political factions returned to power in 1945. Ill health forced her to hand her duties to Juliana temporarily in 1947 and again on 12 May 1948, and she abdicated on 4 September 1948 after a reign of 57 years and 286 days. She retired to Het Loo Palace, where she wrote the memoir Lonely but Not Alone, and died there on 28 November 1962. At her request her funeral, in the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft, was entirely in white.
wilhelmine-of-bayreuth: Wilhelmine was born in Berlin on 3 July 1709, the eldest daughter of Frederick William I of Prussia and Sophia Dorothea of Hanover, and a granddaughter of George I of Great Britain. She shared the unhappy childhood of her brother Frederick the Great, whose friend and confidante she remained all her life except for one short interval. Her governess beat and abused her until the governess was replaced. As the eldest daughter she was the subject of marriage plans. Her mother wished her to marry her nephew Frederick, Prince of Wales, but the British would offer marriage only in exchange for concessions her father would not accept, while her father preferred a Habsburg match.

In 1731 Wilhelmine married her kinsman Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, who had been engaged to her younger sister Sophie until her father changed the plan. She accepted only under threats from her father and to lighten her brother's disgrace. The marriage was at first happy but was clouded by limited funds and by the margrave's affair with Dorothea von Marwitz, which her brother resented and which estranged them for about three years. Her only child, Elisabeth Fredericka Sophie, was born on 30 August 1732.

When her husband inherited in 1735 the pair set about making Bayreuth a miniature Versailles. They rebuilt the summer residence, now part of the Hermitage, rebuilt the great Bayreuth opera house, built a second opera house and a theatre, and reconstructed the palace. They developed what is called the Bayreuth Rococo style. They also founded the University of Erlangen. These projects brought the court to the verge of bankruptcy. She surrounded herself with wits and artists and the court was visited by Voltaire and Frederick the Great. She also acted as her brother's eyes and ears in southern Germany.

Wilhelmine was a lutenist, a student of Sylvius Leopold Weiss, and employed Bernhard Joachim Hagen. Her compositions include a concerto in G minor for harpsichord, strings and continuo, an opera, Argenore, performed in 1740 for her husband's birthday, short songs called Cavatinen, and a flute sonata of about 1730. Her memoirs, Memoires de ma vie, were written or revised in French between 1748 and her death and were first printed in 1810. They are regarded as entertaining but not very trustworthy.

She died at Bayreuth on 14 October 1758, the day of Frederick's defeat at the Battle of Hochkirch. He suffered a week of severe illness and a depression from which he never fully recovered. On the tenth anniversary of her death he had the Temple of Friendship built at Sanssouci in her memory.
wilhelmshaven: The Siebethsburg castle, built before 1383, was a pirate stronghold until the Hanseatic League destroyed it in 1433. Four centuries later the Kingdom of Prussia planned a fleet and a harbour on the North Sea. In 1853 Prince Adalbert of Prussia arranged the Jade Treaty with the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, by which Oldenburg ceded 3.13 km2 (1.21 sq mi) of its territory at the Jade Bight to Prussia. In 1869 King William I of Prussia founded the town as an exclave of the Province of Hanover and as a naval base for Prussia's developing fleet, while all its hinterland remained part of Oldenburg. A shipyard, the Kaiserliche Werft Wilhelmshaven, developed there, and trams ran from 1913.

The pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee was launched at Wilhelmshaven on 30 June 1934, and the battleship Tirpitz, the largest European warship of the Second World War, was built at the same yard between 1936 and 1941. In 1937 Wilhelmshaven merged with the adjacent town of Rüstringen, and the united city became part of the Free State of Oldenburg. In World War II it was the main base of the Kriegsmarine. Allied bombing destroyed two thirds of the town's buildings, although the shipyard, the main target, remained operational. On 28 April 1945 the Polish First Armored Division captured the city and took the surrender of the whole garrison, including over 200 ships.

After 1945 the shipyard was totally disarmed under the British commander in chief and military businesses were prohibited. The city used the opportunity to provide a site for the Olympia Werke, a typewriter factory, which employed 7,000 workers in 1953. In 1947 the council chose the figure of a Frisian warrior as the city's emblem. A British boarding school for the children of service personnel stayed in the city from 1947 to 1972.

Wilhelmshaven is on the western side of the Jade Bight, has 76,089 inhabitants and is Germany's only deep-water port and its largest naval base. The deep channel led to the building of the first oil tanker jetty at the end of the 1950s, and the city has since been the most important German import terminal for crude oil, with pipelines supplying refineries in the Rhine-Ruhr region and Hamburg. The container terminal JadeWeserPort has been operational since 2012. The nearby Lower Saxony Wadden Sea National Park, part of a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site, supports a large tourism industry.
wilhelmus: The melody of the Wilhelmus is a contrafactum of a Catholic French song, Autre chanson de la ville de Chartres assiégée par le prince de Condé, which mocked the failed siege of Chartres in 1568 by the Huguenot prince the Prince of Condé. The Dutch text replaced the ridicule of one Protestant prince with a tribute to another, William of Orange. The earliest known notation of the tune dates from 1574, when it was still sung at a rapid, military pace.

The authorship of the words is uncertain. Soon after the song appeared it was ascribed either to Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, or to the politician Dirck Coornhert, but neither ever claimed it, and some odd rhymes are taken as a sign that an experienced poet did not write it. The oldest surviving complete Dutch text is in a Geuzenliedboek printed in 1577–1578.

The Wilhelmus is a monologue in the first person, spoken by William of Nassau, who describes how he tries to stay faithful to Philip II of Spain while serving God and his conscience. Its first stanza presents his quarrel as one with the king's emissaries in the Low Countries, such as the Duke of Alba, rather than with the king himself. The text has 15 stanzas, and their first letters form the acrostic Willem van Nassov, a contemporary spelling of Nassau.

The stanzas are arranged symmetrically, so that the first and fifteenth resemble one another in meaning, as do the second and fourteenth, and so on towards the eighth. That stanza compares William to David fleeing the tyranny of King Saul, and the Spanish crown to Saul.

During the Dutch Revolt the song served as a political and military signal. It was sung by a soldier during the siege of Haarlem in 1573 and played mockingly by Spanish musicians at the siege of Alkmaar the same year. In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company used it at sea and in colonial wars, and in 1626 Adriaen Valerius published a slower, solemn version for singing at home to the lute. In the 18th century it became a quick Orangist march, the Prinsenmars, and the young Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote seven variations on it at The Hague in 1766.

Wilhelmina asked for the Wilhelmus at her inauguration in 1898, and on 10 May 1932 it replaced the older song. During the German occupation of the Second World War it was taken up by all factions of the Dutch resistance.
wiligelmo: Wiligelmo, also called Wiligelmus or Guglielmo da Modena, was among the earliest sculptors in Italy to make large architectural sculpture. He must have worked at Modena Cathedral from about 1099 to about 1110. There he made the four Genesis reliefs, the dedication plaque, two torch-bearing putti and the decoration of the central portal of the west facade, many figured capitals of the exterior, and probably the large single figures of the metopes, now in the Museo Lapidario Estense.

Other works by his hand are four large prophets from the portal jambs of the old cathedral at Cremona, made before the earthquake of 1117, and fragments of three Labours of the Months from a lost portal of the Cluniac abbey church of San Benedetto Po. All are carved in marble.

The Genesis reliefs, about one metre tall, once formed a continuous frieze on each side of the central portal; some scholars think they were meant for the entrance of the crypt, and the Campionesi reassembled parts of his work later in the 12th century. One panel shows the Creation and Temptation of Adam and Eve; another combines Lamech blinding Cain with an arrow and Noah's family leaving the Ark.

His figures are large and stocky, shown in profile with big heads and feet, solemn faces and angular, dramatic movement, usually set under decorative arches. Scholars once linked him with the early Romanesque schools of Aquitaine and Aragon, but now tend to see these as independent developments. His sources were provincial Roman sculpture, including that of the Constantinian era, Carolingian and Ottonian ivories, metalwork and local manuscript painting. Most of his sculptures carry inscriptions naming the figures or giving biblical, secular or liturgical texts.

Masters of his workshop carved the side portals of Modena: the Master of San Geminiano the Porta dei Principi and the Master of the Artù the Porta della Pescheria, with smaller, livelier figures. The Porta dei Principi is the first known two-storey porch-portal on column-bearing lions or atlantids, a north Italian form associated with Wiligelmo. A pupil, the Master of Astolfo, carved the main portal jambs at Nonantola, and the young Nicholaus also belonged to the workshop.
willamette-valley: The valley is closed by mountains on three sides: the Cascade Range to the east, the Oregon Coast Range to the west and the Calapooya Mountains to the south, which divide it from the Umpqua River valley; the Columbia River is generally taken as its northern edge. Much of its fertility comes from the Missoula Floods, which broke from Glacial Lake Missoula about 40 times between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago, filled the valley as far south as Eugene and left volcanic and glacial soil across its floor. Its climate mixes Mediterranean and oceanic features, with wet, mild winters and dry, sunny summers.

Human habitation began an estimated 16,000 years before the present. The Kalapuya, with Molala and Chinook peoples, lived on salmon, deer, camas bulbs and acorns and used fire to keep the oak savanna open; some 16,000 Kalapuyans are estimated to have lived there in the early 19th century. As many as 90 per cent may have died in an epidemic of fever and ague between 1830 and 1833. In the early 1850s the US government coerced the valley's Indigenous peoples into giving up their lands and moving to the Grand Ronde Reservation, and children were taken from their parents to boarding schools such as the Chemawa Indian School; the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community call this removal a Trail of Tears.

The Hudson's Bay Company controlled the fur trade from Fort Vancouver in the 1820s and 1830s. The first European settlements were at Oregon City and Champoeg, and the missionary Jason Lee founded today's Willamette University at Salem, the first institution of higher learning on the West Coast. After the Oregon Trail opened in 1841, settlers poured in, and the Oregon Treaty of 1846 ended joint US–British occupancy. The valley led the way to statehood less than 16 years later.

The valley holds about 70 per cent of Oregon's people, including its five largest cities, Portland, Eugene, Salem, Gresham and Hillsboro. Its farms produce more than 170 crops and livestock items, among them most of North America's hazelnuts and Christmas trees, and it has more than 500 wineries. Less than one-tenth of one per cent of the original savanna survives.
willehad: Willehad was born in Northumbria and probably received his education at York under Ecgbert. He was a friend of Alcuin. After his ordination he went to Frisia about the year 766, preaching at Dokkum and in Overijssel, to continue the work of Boniface, whom the Frisians had killed in 754. He barely escaped with his life when Frisians wanted to kill him and withdrew to the area around Utrecht, and he and his companions were threatened again after they destroyed some pagan temples.

At an assembly in Paderborn in 777 Saxony was divided into missionary zones, and the zone between the Weser and the Elbe, called Wigmodia, was given to Willehad. From 780 he preached to the Saxons on commission from Charlemagne. In 782 the Saxons under Widukind rebelled against Charlemagne; Willehad was forced to flee to Frisia, and a number of his assistants and friends were killed. He used the time to travel to Rome, where he reported on his work to Pope Adrian I.

On his return he retired for a time to the monastery of Echternach, in present-day Luxembourg, where he spent two years working in the scriptorium and gathering his missionary team again. After Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons he preached around the lower Elbe and the lower Weser. As bishop his diocese was the part of Saxony and Friesland near the mouth of the Weser, and he chose as his see Bremen, a place first mentioned in documents of 782.

The cathedral he built at Bremen was dedicated in 789, and Anschar later praised it for its beauty. Willehad also built a small church at Blexen, and he died there, at a place that is today part of Nordenham, on 8 November 789. He was buried in the cathedral of Bremen.

Anschar compiled a life of Willehad, and the preface he wrote for it was considered a masterpiece for its age. In 860 a sick girl from Wege (Weyhe) travelled to his grave and was reportedly cured there by a miracle; the account is the first mention of that village in any historical document.
willem-drees: Willem Drees was born in Amsterdam on 5 July 1886 into an orthodox reformed middle-class family. His father, a banker, died when Drees was five, and he could continue his studies thanks to the support of his uncle Frits. He rejected the Christian creed at the age of eighteen. After hearing a speech by Pieter Jelles Troelstra in December 1902 he became a democratic socialist, and he joined the Social Democratic Workers' Party (SDAP) on his eighteenth birthday.

Drees chaired the party's branch in The Hague until 1931 and sat on the municipal council from 1913 to 1941. As alderman from 1919 he was responsible for social affairs, and after 1931 for finance and public works. He favoured a pragmatic, reformist course. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1933, he opposed the National Socialist Movement in the Netherlands, saying in 1935 that fascists are not opponents but enemies.

Drees succeeded Willem Albarda as party leader on 14 May 1940. During the German occupation he was taken hostage to Buchenwald concentration camp on 7 October 1940, was moved to Sint-Michielsgestel in 1941 and was released on 11 May 1942 because of poor health. He then took a prominent part in the illegal executive committee of the SDAP. After the war he became Minister of Social Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister on 25 June 1945, and in February 1946 he was a co-founder of the Labour Party (PvdA) and its first leader.

After the 1948 general election Drees formed a cabinet with the Catholic People's Party and became Prime Minister on 7 August 1948. He held the office until 22 December 1958 in four successive cabinets. His years in office saw decolonisation, economic reconstruction, the establishment of the Dutch welfare state, and international integration, including Benelux, NATO and the European Economic Community. His cabinets also faced the North Sea flood of 1953. He advocated austerity and was known for thrift and simplicity: he went to work on foot or by bicycle.
Drees received the honorary title of Minister of State on 22 December 1958. He remained active as a historian and author. He died in The Hague on 14 May 1988, at the age of 101.
willem-piso: Willem Piso was born Willem Pies in Leiden, in the Dutch Republic, the son of Cornelia van Liesvelt and the church organist Hermann Pies. He appears under several names: Willem Pies in Dutch sources, Gulielmus Piso in Latin, Guilherme Piso in Portuguese writing on Brazil, and Piso as the standard author abbreviation for the plant names he gave. He began studying medicine at the University of Leiden at about the age of twelve and took his medical degree at the University of Caen in France on 4 July 1633, some ten years after he first enrolled.

Piso settled in Amsterdam as a physician and then entered the service of the Dutch West India Company under Johan Maurits van Nassau-Siegen, governor of Dutch Brazil. He sailed with a scientific and artistic team that included the naturalist Georg Marcgrave. In Brazil he studied tropical diseases and the medicinal properties of local plants, and noted the importance of fresh food in keeping European soldiers and seamen from illness. He returned with Nassau-Siegen to the Dutch Republic in 1644.

At home he helped organise the expedition's scientific results. The Historia Naturalis Brasiliae, written with Marcgrave and first published by Joannes de Laet, was one of the earliest European descriptions of the natural history of Brazil. Piso's four parts, De medicina Brasiliense, examined tropical diseases and Indigenous remedies, among them ipecacuanha root and the leaves of jaborandi. In 1655 he became inspector of the Amsterdam Medical College and later its dean.

In 1658 Piso published a second edition of the Historia under his name alone, titled De Indiae Utriusque re naturali et medica. He is said to have tried to undermine Marcgrave's work in it, and its many careless errors drew criticism from Marcgrave's brother and later from Linnaeus. Piso died in Amsterdam on 28 November 1678, at about 67. The plant genera Pisonia and Pisoniella, of the family Nyctaginaceae, are named after him, as are the mangrove tree crab Aratus pisonii and the minor planet 11240 Piso.
willemstad: Punda was established in 1634, when the Dutch West India Company captured the island from Spain. It was originally called de punt, "the point", and was built as a walled city. It soon became one of the major centres of the Atlantic slave trade, which triggered rapid population growth. In 1674 Sephardic Portuguese Jews from Amsterdam and Recife, Brazil, who had settled as traders, built the Curaçao synagogue. In the late 17th century there were over 200 houses inside the walls.

In 1675 it was decided to build Pietermaai outside the walls, separated from the city by about 500 metres in which no building was allowed, so as not to obstruct the cannons of Fort Amsterdam. The name Willemstad, "William Town", honours William II or William III, Prince of Orange, and is first recorded in 1680. Otrobanda, its name from the Papiamentu otro banda, "the opposite side", was founded in 1707, and Scharloo followed. By 1818 the population was 9,536. On 13 May 1861 it was decided to demolish the walls and build houses in the gap.

Around 1925 the oil and phosphate industries stimulated growth. Royal Dutch Shell, which had built the refinery in 1915, created Julianadorp and Emmastad between 1945 and 1955 for its workers. On 30 May 1969 a strike at a subcontractor of the refinery turned into the Curaçao uprising, a riot in which two people died, 300 were arrested and part of the historic centre was burnt down. In 1985 Shell closed the refinery, which then employed 12,000 people, and the government bought it for one guilder.

Willemstad is the capital and largest city of Curaçao, a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and was capital of the Netherlands Antilles until its dissolution in 2010. Its historic centre has four quarters: Punda and Otrobanda, either side of the Sint Anna Bay, an inlet leading into the natural harbour of the Schottegat, and Scharloo and Pietermaai Smal on the smaller Waaigat harbour. The Curaçao synagogue is the oldest surviving synagogue in the Americas. The centre and the harbour entrance were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. Punda and Otrobanda are linked by the Queen Emma Bridge, a long pontoon bridge.
william-adelin: William Ætheling, commonly called Adelin, was born in Winchester on 5 August 1103. His father, King Henry I of England, had married his mother, Matilda of Scotland, to conciliate his English subjects. Matilda was descended from Edmund Ironside and was a great-niece of Edward the Confessor, so the marriage joined the new Norman rulers of England with the old Anglo-Saxon dynasty. Henry's hopes for the succession rested on William, whom the chronicler Henry of Huntingdon described as a prince so pampered that he seemed destined to be food for the fire.

William was invested as Duke of Normandy during his father's lifetime, a title he held more in name than in practice. Henry made the investiture when pressed by Louis VI of France to do homage for Normandy; as a king, he was loath to comply, and in 1115 offered to have William do it instead. The offer was accepted in 1120, after a period of war, and William did homage to Louis in the middle of that year. He received the homage of the Norman barons in 1115 and of the English barons in March 1116.

In February 1113 Henry betrothed William to Matilda of Anjou, eldest daughter of Count Fulk V of Anjou, to secure Anjou's loyalty. They married in June 1119 at Lisieux. After his mother's death in 1118, William served as regent in England in her place, advised by royal administrators such as Roger of Salisbury, and was sometimes called rex designatus, king designate.

William died in the White Ship disaster of 25 November 1120. He and his companions were crossing the Channel from Barfleur in the Blanche-Nef, the swiftest and most modern ship in the royal fleet. They had stayed drinking on shore until after dark, and in the middle of the night the drunken helmsman drove the ship onto a rock. William got into a dinghy but went back to rescue his illegitimate half-sister Matilda FitzRoy, Countess of Perche; the dinghy was overloaded and capsized. His wife was on another ship.
His death left the succession uncertain. After Henry died in 1135, William's sister Empress Matilda and her cousin Stephen of Blois fought a long war for the English throne, known as the Anarchy.
william-blake: William Blake was born on 28 November 1757 in Soho, London, the third of seven children of James Blake, a hosier, and Catherine Blake. He attended school only long enough to learn to read and write and was otherwise educated at home by his mother. The family were Moravians and English Dissenters. The Bible was a profound influence on him throughout his life,.

On 4 August 1772 he was apprenticed to the engraver James Basire for seven years and then became a professional engraver. In 1779 he entered the Royal Academy, where he came to detest the ideas of its first president, Joshua Reynolds, who prized general truth and general beauty. Blake wrote in the margin of Reynolds's Discourses that to generalise is to be an idiot. In 1782 he married Catherine Boucher, who became his partner in work as printer and colourist.

About 1783 patronage allowed him to publish his first poems, Poetical Sketches. In 1784 he opened a print shop with James Parker and began to work with the radical publisher Joseph Johnson, whose circle included Joseph Priestley, Mary Wollstonecraft and Thomas Paine. Blake had great hopes for the French and American revolutions but despaired at the Reign of Terror.

In 1788 he invented relief etching, or illuminated printing, with which he produced most of his later books. He drew words and images backwards in acid-resistant varnish on copper plates and let acid bite away the rest, so that the design stood in relief. His commercial work consisted largely of intaglio engraving. In 1800 he moved to Felpham in Sussex to illustrate the works of William Hayley, and began Milton there. He returned to London in 1804 and began Jerusalem.

Blake lived in London all his life except for three years at Felpham, and was considered mad by contemporaries for his idiosyncratic views. He was hostile to the Church of England and to almost all organised religion, and was influenced by Emanuel Swedenborg. His early work, such as The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, is rebellious and protests against dogmatic religion. In the later Milton and Jerusalem he presents a humanity redeemed by self-sacrifice and forgiveness. The preface to Milton includes the poem beginning And did those feet in ancient time, which became the words of the anthem Jerusalem.
Blake died on 12 August 1827 at Fountain Court, off the Strand, having worked on his Dante series that day. Largely unrecognised during his life, he became a seminal figure of the Romantic age,.
william-bligh: Bligh was born on 9 September 1754, though it is not clear where. He was baptised on 4 October 1754 at St Andrew's Church in Plymouth, where his father, Francis, served as a customs officer, and his ancestral home of Tinten Manor in Cornwall is also a possibility. His mother, Jane Pearce, née Balsam, was a widow. He was signed for the Royal Navy at the age of seven, a common way of recording sea experience for a commission, and in September 1771 he was transferred to HMS Crescent, where he stayed three years.

Bligh first came to notice as Master of Resolution under Captain James Cook, who praised him on the voyage that proved Cook's last. In 1787 he took command of HMAV Bounty to carry breadfruit trees from Tahiti to the Caribbean, where the plant was wanted as food for enslaved Africans on British plantations. On 28 April 1789 Fletcher Christian, a master's mate who had been Bligh's friend, led a mutiny. Bligh and eighteen loyalists were set adrift in the open launch, and after a voyage of more than 3,500 nautical miles they reached Kupang in Timor.

The causes are debated: some sources describe Bligh as a tyrant, others argue he was no worse than the average captain and that the crew were drawn back to life in Tahiti. He was honourably acquitted at the court-martial in October 1790 and published a narrative of the mutiny. From 1791 to 1793 he commanded HMS Providence on a second breadfruit voyage, which succeeded as a transport but not as a food, since most of the enslaved people refused it.

The ackee, Blighia sapida, is named for him. At the Battle of Camperdown on 11 October 1797 his ship Director captured the Batavian flagship Vrijheid, and he received the Naval Gold Medal. He was a captain whose crews took part in the mutinies at Spithead and the Nore.

Bligh became governor of New South Wales in 1806 and moved against the rum trade of the New South Wales Corps. His confrontational style angered settlers and officials, among them John Macarthur, and on 26 January 1808 the Corps arrested him in the Rum Rebellion, an act the Foreign Office later declared illegal. Major Johnston was cashiered after a court martial, and Bligh was promoted to rear admiral and in 1814 to vice-admiral, though he never again held an important command. He surveyed Dublin Bay and died in London on 7 December 1817.

His logbooks of the mutiny were inscribed on the UNESCO Australian Memory of the World register in 2021, and the films of 1935 and 1962 largely perpetuate the image of him as a tyrant, while that of 1984 attempts a more neutral portrayal.
william-bradford-governor: William Bradford was born in Austerfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and baptised on 19 March 1590, into a family that owned a large farm. His father died when he was just over a year old, and his mother died in 1597, leaving him an orphan at seven in the care of two uncles. At twelve he began to hear the preaching of the Rev. Richard Clyfton, who wanted the Church of England to drop every vestige of Roman Catholic practice, and he met William Brewster at Scrooby manor.

After King James I took the throne in 1603, secret meetings were held at Scrooby, and the congregation, led by Clyfton and the Rev. John Robinson, decided to sever its ties with the church. Many were arrested in 1607. They left England unlawfully, and Bradford, then eighteen, reached the Dutch Republic by 1608. In Leiden he claimed his inheritance in 1611, bought a house, worked as a fustian weaver, and in 1613 married Dorothy May.

The congregation wished to found its own colony because its children were taking up Dutch customs and language. After three years of negotiation, about fifty Separatists left Delftshaven on the Speedwell in July 1620. Some passengers joined the Mayflower, which sailed from Plymouth, England, on 6/16 September 1620 with 102 passengers. Bradford was among the first to sign the Mayflower Compact at Cape Cod on 11/21 November. He joined the exploring parties, and while he was away his wife Dorothy fell overboard and drowned. The settlers began building at Plymouth on 25 December 1620. By the end of that winter half of the 100 settlers had died.

After the death of Governor John Carver in April 1621, Bradford was chosen governor, a post he held off and on for the rest of his life. He relied on the soldier Myles Standish for military advice and kept the alliance made in March 1621 with Massasoit, sachem of the Pokanokets, which also led to tensions with the Narragansetts. In 1624 the colony's government became a governor and five assistants. Bradford later served as a commissioner of the United Colonies of New England and twice as its president.

His best-known work, Of Plymouth Plantation, is a detailed history in journal form of the colony and its settlers. He wrote its first part in 1630 and later brought it up to 1646. He drew parallels between daily life and the Bible, intending to show divine providence at work. It disappeared by 1780, reappeared in the Bishop of London's library at Fulham Palace, and was returned to Massachusetts on 26 May 1897. He died on 9 May 1657 and was buried on Burial Hill in Plymouth.
william-c-gorgas: William Crawford Gorgas was born on 3 October 1854 in Toulminville, Alabama, the first of six children of Josiah Gorgas and Amelia Gayle Gorgas; his maternal grandparents were Governor John Gayle and the diarist Sarah Ann Haynsworth Gayle. He studied at the University of the South and at Bellevue Hospital Medical College and joined the US Army Medical Corps in June 1880, serving at Fort Clark, Fort Duncan and Fort Brown in Texas.

At Fort Brown in 1882–84 he was sent to control an epidemic of yellow fever. He caught the disease while caring for Marie Cook Doughty, who nearly died of it; they recovered together and married, and their immunity meant they were sent to later outbreaks. After the Spanish–American War he became Chief Sanitary Officer in Havana in 1898, where with Robert Ernest Noble he drew on the work of Major Walter Reed and the Cuban doctor Carlos Finlay on mosquito transmission. By draining the breeding ponds of the Aedes aegypti mosquito and isolating patients in screened rooms, he brought yellow fever cases down from 784 to zero within a year.

On the canal he drained ponds and swamps, fumigated, used mosquito netting and built public water systems. Finlay's approach was at first met with scepticism and opposition, but the measures saved thousands of lives among the workers. Gorgas was president of the American Medical Association in 1909–10, and in 1914 he and George Washington Goethals received the first Public Welfare Medal of the National Academy of Sciences. During the First World War he asked for the founding of the Boston School of Occupational Therapy in 1918. He was also a Georgist, who held that Henry George's Single Tax would bring sanitary living conditions to the poor.

Gorgas retired in 1918 at the age of 64. King George V made him an honorary KCMG at the Queen Alexandra Military Hospital in the United Kingdom, where he died on 3 July 1920; he was given a funeral in St Paul's Cathedral and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The Gorgas Memorial Institute of Tropical and Preventive Medicine was founded in 1921, Panama's Ancon Hospital was renamed after him in 1928, and his name stands on the frieze of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
william-caxton: Caxton's parentage and date of birth are not certain. Records place his birth between 1415 and 1424, based on the payment of his apprenticeship fees in 1438. In the preface to his first printed work, the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, he says he was born and educated in the Weald of Kent, and Tenterden, Tonbridge and Hadlow have each been proposed as his birthplace. By 1438 he was in London, where the registers of the Mercers' Company record his apprenticeship to Robert Large, a wealthy dealer in luxury goods who served as Lord Mayor of London in 1439. Large died in 1441 and left Caxton £20, less than some other apprentices received.

Caxton was making trips to Bruges by 1450 and had settled there by 1453. He prospered in trade and became governor of the Company of Merchant Adventurers of London. His business brought him into the household of Margaret, Duchess of Burgundy, sister of Edward IV, and his travels, including to Cologne, let him observe the new printing industry. With a Fleming, Colard Mansion, he set up a press in Bruges. The first book printed in English, in 1473, was his own translation, the Recuyell. In its epilogue he writes that his pen was worn and his eye dimmed with copying it by hand, so he practised and learnt to print it.

In 1476 he set up the first press in England, in the Almonry at Westminster. The first book known to have been produced there was an edition of Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales. He printed chivalric romances, classical works and English and Roman histories, among them Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in 1485 and the first English translation of Aesop's Fables in 1484. He is credited with as many as 108 books, 87 of them different titles, and translated 26 of the titles himself.

Caxton worked under pressure to publish quickly, and his limited skill as a translator often led him to carry French words straight into English. Because his books sold widely, he is credited with helping to establish the London dialect, later called Chancery Standard, as the standard form across England, although Richard Pynson, who began printing in London in 1491 or 1492, pushed standardisation further. After Caxton's death, Wynkyn de Worde, a Fleming, became owner of the printing house and carried it on for forty-three years.
william-clito: William Clito was born on 25 October 1102, the son of Duke Robert Curthose of Normandy and Sibylla of Conversano. His nickname Clito was a Medieval Latin term equivalent to the Anglo-Saxon Aetheling, meaning a man of royal blood, or prince. His father was defeated and captured by his brother, King Henry I of England, at the Battle of Tinchebrai in 1106, and Henry placed the boy in the custody of Helias of Saint Saens, count of Arques, who had married a natural daughter of Duke Robert. In August 1110 the king suddenly demanded that William be handed over. Helias's household hid him and smuggled him to his master, who fled the duchy and found safety among Henry's enemies.

William's first refuge was with Robert de Bellême, and after Robert's capture in 1112 he and Helias went to the court of his cousin Count Baldwin VII of Flanders. Baldwin allied with Louis VI of France and Fulk of Anjou, and fighting began in earnest by 1118. Baldwin was mortally wounded in September 1118 and died in June 1119. Louis VI then took up William's cause, and in the Battle of Brémule, which began by accident, the French were decisively defeated and Louis escaped with Clito.

The drowning of Henry's only legitimate son, William Adelin, in the wreck of the White Ship on 25 November 1120 made Clito the most plausible heir to the English throne. Fulk of Anjou betrothed his daughter to him with the county of Maine as dowry, but Henry had the marriage annulled in August 1124 for kinship, and an aristocratic revolt in Normandy in William's favour was beaten at Bourgthéroulde in March 1124.

Charles the Good, count of Flanders, was murdered on 2 March 1127 by the Erembalds, and with Louis's support William was elected count. He faced four other claimants, and Henry rallied the count of Hainault, the duke of Lower Lorraine and Flemish claimants against him. Henry's wool sanction against Flanders, his financial support of rival claimants and William's exactions on the Flemish towns brought a general revolt that left William without most of his county.

By April 1128 Thierry of Alsace had appeared as a further claimant. William won a victory at Axspoele, and on 12 July he and Godfrey I of Louvain began the siege of Aalst. There he was wounded in the arm in a scuffle with a foot soldier, the wound turned gangrenous, and he died on 28 July 1128, aged twenty-five. He was buried at the abbey of Saint Bertin in St. Omer and left no children. Henry I pardoned the followers for whom William had asked.
william-count-of-schaumburg-lippe: Born Friedrich Wilhelm Ernst in London on 9 January 1724, William was the son of Albrecht Wolfgang, Count of Schaumburg-Lippe, and his first wife, Countess Margarete Gertrud of Oeynhausen, who was said to be an illegitimate daughter of George I of Great Britain and his mistress Ehrengard Melusine von der Schulenburg. He went with his father on campaign in Dutch service in the War of the Austrian Succession, was present at the Battle of Dettingen in 1743 and then fought in Austrian service in their Italian campaign. He succeeded his father as count on 25 October 1748.

As count and Generalfeldzeugmeister of the Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg he sided with Prussia in the Seven Years' War, led the allied artillery at the Battle of Minden and was rewarded with command of all the allied artillery. He also held the rank of British field marshal. In 1762, at the request of the Marquis of Pombal, he commanded the allied troops in Portugal against the Spanish invasion as generalissimo. Through marches and counter-marches he ensured that an enemy with a three-to-one superiority always met defenders in a good position and never risked an all-out attack. At Pombal's request he stayed for a year after the peace of 1763; two children of his, Joseph and Olimpia, were born at Elvas.

On 12 November 1765 he married Countess Marie Barbara Eleonore of Lippe-Biesterfeld; their daughter Emilie lived from 1771 to 1774, and a son born in 1772 died unnamed. He died at Wölpinghausen on 10 September 1777 and was succeeded by his cousin Philipp II Ernst of Lippe-Alverdissen. William was the first to work out a theory of purely defensive war, which he held to be the only kind justified on ethical grounds: "Only defensive warfare is justified!"

Its core was the fortified landscape, combining strongholds, an armed rural population and soldiers who worked the land in peacetime. His ideas, his support for universal conscription and his opposition to corporal punishment form a bridge to the people's war planned against Napoleon by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau and to Scharnhorst's military reforms. A bust of him stands in the Walhalla.
william-duke-of-julich-cleves-berg: William was born on 28 July 1516 in Düsseldorf, the only son of John III, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, and Maria, Duchess of Jülich-Berg. When his father died in 1539 he took over the Duchy of Cleves and the County of Mark, and although his mother lived until 1543 he also became Duke of Berg and Jülich and Count of Ravensberg. His humanistic education was directed by Konrad Heresbach, and in 1545 William founded a humanistic gymnasium in Düsseldorf.

William held the neighbouring Duchy of Guelders as heir of his distant relatives, the Egmond dukes. Emperor Charles V claimed it for himself, since the Egmond dukes had sold their right of inheritance. William allied with the King of France and married Jeanne d'Albret, heiress of Navarre, on 14 June 1541, when she was 12 years old. The French gave him no help, and he was overwhelmed and had to surrender. Under the Treaty of Venlo, Guelders and the County of Zutphen joined the Habsburg Netherlands, and the marriage was annulled by papal dispensation on 12 October 1545.

William then set out to strengthen his own lands, since the old medieval walls had proved no match for the imperial artillery. Jülich, Düsseldorf and Orsoy became the main fortresses of Jülich, Berg and Cleves, and Jülich and Düsseldorf were made into residences. The Italian architect Alessandro Pasqualini of Bologna drew the plans; at Jülich the citadel, built from 1548 to 1580, still stands with parts of the Renaissance palace. In religion William tried to uphold the Erasmian church but did little to stop the spread of Lutheranism, and after 1554 he had a Lutheran preacher teach his sons.

On 18 July 1546 William married Maria of Austria, daughter of Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor. Their daughters married Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia, Philipp Ludwig, Count Palatine of Neuburg, and John I, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, among others. The elder son, Karl Friedrich, died in 1575 aged 20, so the duchies passed to the younger, Johann Wilhelm, Bishop of Münster. William died in Düsseldorf on 5 January 1592.
william-duke-of-nassau: Wilhelm, whose full given names were Georg Wilhelm August Heinrich Belgicus, was born on 14 June 1792 at Kirchheimbolanden. He was the eldest son of Frederick William, Duke of Nassau, and Burgravine Louise Isabelle of Kirchberg. With the Nassau troops he took part on the side of the Seventh Coalition in the Battle of Waterloo against Napoleon.

On 24 June 1813 at Weilburg he married Princess Louise of Saxe-Altenburg, daughter of Frederick, Duke of Saxe-Altenburg, who until 1826 had been the last Duke of Saxe-Hildburghausen. She died on 6 April 1825. They had eight children, of whom four died in childhood. After her death he married her niece, Princess Pauline of Württemberg, at Stuttgart on 23 April 1829.

On 9 January 1816 Wilhelm succeeded his father as Prince of Nassau-Weilburg and joint Duke of Nassau with his father's cousin Frederick Augustus of the Nassau-Usingen branch. When Frederick Augustus died on 24 March 1816, Wilhelm inherited the Usingen territories and became sole ruler of the Duchy of Nassau, keeping the title of Duke for the rest of his reign. He was sovereign Prince of Nassau-Weilburg until its incorporation into the duchy. He died at Bad Kissingen in August 1839, on 20 or 30 August, the day being given both ways.

His descendants reached many thrones. His son Adolphe became Grand Duke of Luxembourg, and the crown of Luxembourg passed to Nassau through the male line when William III of the Netherlands left only a daughter to rule his main realm. His daughter Sophia married King Oscar II of Sweden, and the present Belgian, Danish, Norwegian and Swedish royal families, as well as the Grand Ducal Family of Luxembourg, descend from this marriage. His daughter Helene married George Victor, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont, and the Dutch and Swedish royal families descend from this marriage. His son Nikolaus Wilhelm married, morganatically, Natalia Alexandrovna Pushkina, daughter of Alexander Pushkin and Natalya Goncharova.
william-duke-of-saxe-weimar: William was born on 11 April 1598, the third surviving son of Johann II, Duke of Saxe-Weimar, and Dorothea Maria of Anhalt. His brothers included Bernard of Saxe-Weimar, the Protestant general, and Ernest I, Duke of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg, later called the Pious. Like his brothers John Ernest I and Frederick he studied at the University of Jena, and in 1613 and 1614 he travelled with them through France, Great Britain and the Netherlands. On 24 August 1617, at his mother's funeral, he took part in founding the Fruitbearing Society.

In 1620 he took charge of the lands of his elder brother Johann Ernst, who had been placed under the ban of the Empire for refusing to submit to the emperor. In 1622 and 1623 he formed the German Friedbund, a patriotic federation for the German states and religious liberty, endowed by his maternal uncle Louis I of Anhalt-Köthen. In the Thirty Years' War he fought alongside his brothers under Ernst von Mansfeld and Georg Friedrich, Margrave of Baden-Durlach, and later under Christian the Younger of Brunswick. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden advanced him quickly, but after the king's death Axel Oxenstierna kept him from a command as lieutenant general, and William accepted the Peace of Prague in 1635.

When the family lands were divided in 1640 he kept Weimar and Jena, while his younger brother Albrecht received Eisenach; on Albrecht's childless death in 1644 William took the whole inheritance. He married Eleonore Dorothea of Anhalt-Dessau in Weimar on 23 May 1625, and their sons included John Ernest II of Saxe-Weimar, Adolf Wilhelm of Saxe-Eisenach and Bernhard II of Saxe-Jena.

After Louis I of Anhalt-Köthen died in 1650, the members of the Fruitbearing Society chose William as his successor, and he led it from 8 May 1651, though in a mainly representative role. In 1648 he wrote the words of the hymn Herr Jesu Christ, dich zu uns wend, sung in Thüringen before the Sunday sermon; Johann Sebastian Bach and Johann Gottfried Walther both set it for organ, Bach in BWV 632 of the Orgelbüchlein. William died on 17 May 1662.
william-dunbar: Dunbar first appears in 1474 as a new student in the Faculty of Arts at the University of St Andrews, where he took his bachelor's degree in 1477 and his master's in 1479; as students then usually entered at fourteen, his birth is put in 1459 or 1460. A satirical line in The Flyting of Dumbar and Kennedie suggests he came from East Lothian. He was ordained a priest at an unknown date. He travelled with an embassy to Denmark and France in 1491 and 1492, and in 1501 and 1502 went to England on the staff of Andrew Forman, Bishop of Moray.

From 1500 he held a pension at the court of James IV, recorded only as a servitour, and most of his poetry dates from these years. Several poems appeared in the Chepman and Myllar prints of 1508, the first books printed in Scotland. In 1510 his pension was set at eighty pounds Scots, three times the salary of Hector Boece as Principal of King's College, Aberdeen. The last reliable record is a payment in May 1513; after the king's death at Flodden that September the accounts lapse, and when they resume in 1515 he is no longer listed. Sir David Lyndsay spoke of him as dead in 1530.

Many poems ask the king for advancement, above all a church benefice, as in Quone Mony Benefices Vakit, and in The Petition of The Gray Horse, Auld Dunbar he asked for a new suit of clothes for Christmas. Meditatioun In Wyntir reflects on age and disappointed hopes, and the Lament for the Makaris, each verse ending Timor mortis conturbat me, remembers the Scots poets who had died.

About a hundred and one poems are ascribed to him, at least ninety generally accepted. Beside courtly allegory such as The Goldyn Targe, in which the dreamer fails to ward off Dame Beauty's arrows with Reason's shield, he wrote religious poems on the Nativity, Passion and Resurrection, satires on Edinburgh's merchants, the Court of Session and the would-be aviator John Damian, and comic pieces such as The Ballad of Kynd Kittok. In the Flyting he and Walter Kennedy traded insults that also reflect the divide between the Scots of the Lothians and Gaelic Carrick.

Walter Scott called him unrivalled among Scotland's poets, and the Scottish Literary Renaissance of the mid-20th century, led by Hugh MacDiarmid and Sydney Goodsir Smith, took him as its model with the call to go back to Dunbar. He is commemorated in Makars' Court in Edinburgh.
william-ernest-grand-duke-of-saxe-weimar: William Ernest was born in Weimar on 10 June 1876, the eldest son of Karl August of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, heir to the grand duke, and his wife Princess Pauline of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach. His father died before him, so on 5 January 1901 he succeeded his grandfather, Grand Duke Karl Alexander. Until 1909 his heir was a distant cousin, Prince Hermann of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, who was then disinherited; Hermann's younger brother stood as heir presumptive until William Ernest's eldest son was born.

William Ernest created a new town centre in Weimar under the direction of Hans Olde, Henry van de Velde and Adolf Brütt, had the University of Jena rebuilt by Theodor Fischer and reconstructed Weimar's theatres. A marble statue of Karl Alexander, completed in 1911, stood in a setting by Brütt that marked off the old town from the new quarter, and a preservation law kept the Art Nouveau style of the new area out of the old town.

As a grandson of Princess Sophie of the Netherlands he was in line for the Dutch throne after Queen Wilhelmina. Fearing German influence or even annexation, some Dutch lawyers sought to change the constitution to exclude him, while another proposal would have made him or his heirs choose between the Dutch and Weimar thrones. The birth of Wilhelmina's daughter Juliana in 1909 made his succession unlikely, and the constitutional amendment of 1922 ended it.

His first wife, Princess Caroline Reuss of Greiz, whom he married in Bückeburg on 30 April 1903, died in 1905; the official cause was pneumonia after influenza, though other sources have suggested suicide. In 1910 he married Princess Feodora of Saxe-Meiningen. After his abdication he fled with his family to their estate in Silesia. His private life, in which he was known as a sadist, made him hated, and on the day he abdicated he was called the most unpopular prince in all Germany. He died at Heinrichau in Silesia on 24 April 1923.
william-ewart-gladstone: Gladstone was born on 29 December 1809 at 62 Rodney Street in Liverpool, the fourth son of Sir John Gladstone, a wealthy Scottish merchant, slave owner, planter and Tory politician. He was named after his father's friend William Ewart, another Liverpool merchant. The family name was changed from Gladstones to Gladstone by royal licence in 1835. He studied at Eton and Oxford and entered the House of Commons in 1832 as a High Tory, winning a seat at Newark with 887 votes; the Duke of Newcastle controlled about a quarter of its small electorate.

Gladstone served in both of Sir Robert Peel's governments and was President of the Board of Trade from 1843 to 1845. When Peel's government fell in 1846 he followed Peel into the Peelite faction, which merged into the new Liberal Party in 1859. He was Chancellor of the Exchequer under Lord Aberdeen from 1852 to 1855, and again from 1859 to 1866 under Lord Palmerston and Lord Russell. In October 1862 he said in a speech at Newcastle that Jefferson Davis and the Confederate leaders had "made a nation", which caused consternation on both sides of the Atlantic. He became leader of the Liberal Party in 1867. He had earlier been a fierce critic of the Opium Wars, calling the trade "infamous and atrocious".

Gladstone's first ministry, from 1868 to 1874, passed the disestablishment of the Church of Ireland and the introduction of secret voting. Told that he was about to become prime minister while he was felling a tree at Hawarden, he declared: "My mission is to pacify Ireland." After electoral defeat in 1874 he resigned the party leadership. From 1876 he made a comeback on moral opposition to the Ottoman massacres of Bulgarians, publishing Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East on 6 September 1876. His Midlothian campaign of 1879 to 1880 is considered the first modern political campaign in Britain.

His second ministry, from 1880 to 1885, saw the Third Reform Act, an Irish Coercion Act in 1881 and a Second Land Act that gave Irish tenants fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale. Public outrage at the death of General Gordon at Khartoum forced him to resign. His brief 1886 ministry was dominated by a home rule proposal for Ireland that was defeated in the Commons and split the Liberals. In 1893 a second Government of Ireland Bill passed the Commons but was defeated in the House of Lords. He resigned in March 1894, aged 84, the oldest prime minister, and left Parliament in 1895.
william-fitzosbern: William FitzOsbern was the son of Osbern the Steward, a nephew of Duchess Gunnor, wife of Duke Richard I of Normandy. Osbern served as steward to his cousin Duke Robert I and became one of the guardians of the young Duke William. Through his marriage to Emma, daughter of Count Rodulf of Ivry, Osbern acquired a large property in central Normandy, including the honours of Pacy and Breteuil. William was probably raised at the ducal court and, like his father, became one of the duke's stewards. With his wife Adeliza de Tosny he founded Lyre Abbey and later Cormeilles Abbey.

He was among the earliest advocates of the invasion of England, and tradition holds that at the Council of Lillebonne he convinced the doubters among the Norman barons. His younger brother Osbern FitzOsbern, a chaplain of Edward the Confessor who held the church of Bosham in Sussex, was well placed to pass on news from England. FitzOsbern is one of the few proven companions of the Conqueror known to have fought at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Created Earl of Hereford in 1067, he held major lands in Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, Oxfordshire and the Isle of Wight, and in the summer of 1067 governed England with Bishop Odo of Bayeux while the king was in Normandy. In 1069 he kept the peace at York and probably played a major part in crushing the revolt of Eadric the Wild, before pushing west to begin the Norman conquest of the Welsh kingdom of Gwent. Castles attributed to him include Carisbrooke, his chief residence, Wigmore, Clifford, Berkeley and Monmouth.

In 1070 Count Baldwin VI of Flanders died, leaving his county and young sons to his widow Richilde, Countess of Mons and Hainaut, whose rule was challenged by her brother-in-law Robert the Frisian. She offered herself in marriage to FitzOsbern, who hurried to Flanders with his army in the hope of becoming count, and he was killed at Cassel on 22 February 1071. His son William of Breteuil succeeded him in Normandy, and Roger de Breteuil became 2nd Earl of Hereford in England and Wales.
william-gopallawa: William Gopallawa was born on 17 September 1896 at the Dullewe Maha Walauwa in Dullewe, a suburb of Matale. Through his mother, Tikiri Kumarihamy Dullewe, he was related to Dullewe Dissava, a signatory of the Kandiyan Convention of 1815 on behalf of the Sinhalese. His father, Tikiri Bandara Gopallawa, died when he was three. He was educated at the Dullewe village school, St. John's College, Dharmaraja College and St. Anthony's College in Kandy. After sitting the Cambridge Senior Certificate Examination in 1917 he joined the staff of the Buddhist English School in Matale, where he helped to set up a library and a scout troop.

In 1920 he joined Ceylon Law College in Colombo and in 1924 was enrolled as a proctor and notary public, practising in Matale, Dumbara and Kandy. In 1926 he won a seat on the Matale Urban Council, on which he served until 1939, five of those years as chairman, the youngest urban council chairman in Ceylon at the time. He stood unsuccessfully for the State Council in 1936.

In 1939 he became the first municipal commissioner of Kandy, and he was named municipal commissioner of Colombo in 1951, serving until 1957. He was made a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 1953. In 1960 he became the second Ceylonese ambassador to China, and in September 1961 he was recalled and sent as ambassador to the United States.

In 1962 Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike named him Governor-General after Sir Oliver Goonetilleke was implicated in a failed military coup attempt. He was the second native Ceylonese governor-general and the first Buddhist to hold the post for Queen Elizabeth II. After the 1965 general election, which the United National Party won, he invited that party to form a government rather than delay as the outgoing government wished, a decision said to have averted a leadership crisis.

When Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka on 22 May 1972, he became its first president, a largely ceremonial post like the one it replaced. He stepped down in February 1978, when Prime Minister J. R. Jayewardene drafted a new constitution that created the executive presidency.
william-harvey: Harvey was born on 1 April 1578, the eldest of nine children of Thomas Harvey, a jurat of Folkestone who served as its mayor in 1600, and Joan Halke. He was educated at Folkestone and the King's School in Canterbury, and entered Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, in 1593, taking his Bachelor of Arts in 1597. He then travelled through France and Germany to Italy and entered the University of Padua in 1599, where he came to know Fabricius and read his work on the valves of the veins. He graduated Doctor of Medicine at Padua on 25 April 1602.

Returning to England, Harvey took a Cambridge doctorate in the same year and became a fellow of his college. He joined the Royal College of Physicians on 5 October 1604, married Elizabeth Browne a few weeks later, and was elected a Fellow of the College in 1607. As Lumleian lecturer from 4 August 1615 he began lectures on anatomy in April 1616, intending to cut up as much as possible before the audience and to illustrate man by the structure of animals. In 1618 he became Physician Extraordinary to James I.

After the De Motu Cordis appeared in 1628 he is said to have fallen mightily in his practice because of the criticism of other physicians, but he was re-elected Censor of the College in 1629 and later became its treasurer. From 1632 he served Charles I as Physician in Ordinary, and the king's hunts gave him many deer to examine. He was also a sceptic about witchcraft. Sent to examine a woman accused in 1632, he dissected her toad and found it ordinary, and his report on four Lancashire women in 1634 led to their acquittal.

The De Motu Cordis, a quarto of 72 pages in 17 chapters, was printed at Frankfurt, where an annual book fair would spread it quickly. Harvey wrote that the heart's movement was so rapid that he was almost tempted to think it could be understood only by God. With only a small lens he had to rely on reasoning in places. Before him Galen held that blood passed between the ventricles through invisible pores, and Ibn al-Nafis had described blood moving from the heart to the lungs and back. Some doctors said they would rather err with Galen than proclaim the truth with Harvey.

His On Animal Generation (1651) began with the development of the hen's egg. It stated that all life comes from the egg, which was the first definite statement against spontaneous generation. Harvey retired from public life after the surrender of Oxford in 1646 and died at Roehampton on 3 June 1657, probably of a cerebral haemorrhage.
william-henry-harrison: William Henry Harrison was born on 9 February 1773 at Berkeley Plantation on the James River in Virginia, the youngest of seven children of Benjamin Harrison V, who signed the Declaration of Independence and served as governor of Virginia. He was the last United States president born a British subject. On 16 August 1791, aged 18, he was commissioned an ensign in the United States Army and assigned to Fort Washington at Cincinnati during the Northwest Indian War. He married Anna Tuthill Symmes on 25 November 1795, after eloping when her father refused permission.

Harrison was appointed secretary of the Northwest Territory in 1798 and elected its delegate to Congress in 1799, where he championed settlers who wanted lower land prices. As governor of Indiana Territory from 10 January 1801 he made his home at Vincennes, built Grouseland there in 1805 and founded a university that was incorporated as Vincennes University in 1806. His treaties with American Indian leaders ceded large tracts of land to the nation. Resistance to expansion grew under Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa. After the War of 1812 he sat in the House of Representatives from 1816 to 1819 and was elected to the Senate in 1824. He lost the presidential race of 1836 as one of four Whig candidates and won in 1840.

Harrison took the oath of office on 4 March 1841, a cold, wet day, without a hat or overcoat, and delivered the longest inaugural address in American history, at 8,445 words. His brief term was marked by a struggle with Henry Clay over patronage. After a walk in the rain on 24 March he fell ill, and his doctors diagnosed pneumonia. John Tyler was sworn in on 6 April. His death exposed an ambiguity in Article II of the Constitution about whether the vice president became president or only assumed the duties of the office. Congress voted his widow Anna a pension of $25,000.
william-henry-prince-of-nassau-saarbruck: William Henry was born in Usingen on 6 March 1718, the fifth son of William Henry of Nassau-Usingen, who died weeks before his birth, and Princess Charlotte Amalia of Nassau-Dillenburg. His mother ruled as guardian and regent until her death in 1738 and raised her sons in the Calvinist faith. He studied at the University of Strasbourg in 1730 and 1731, probably also at the University of Geneva, and his Grand Tour took him to the court of Louis XV.

His brother Charles acted as regent until William Henry came of age in 1741, when the brothers divided their inheritance: Charles took Nassau-Usingen on the right bank of the Rhine and William Henry Nassau-Saarbrücken on the left bank, with about 22,000 inhabitants one of the smallest principalities of the Holy Roman Empire.

He served with his Royal-Allemand regiment in the War of the Austrian Succession, sold it in 1742 to the Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt, and later fought with his own troops in the Seven Years' War. Close to France, he travelled often to Paris and was promoted to field marshal. On 28 February 1742 he married Sophie, daughter of Count George William of Erbach, at Erbach.

At home he separated administration from justice, standardised taxes, introduced a cadastre on the Austrian model and promoted potato cultivation and pest control. He nationalised the mines and leased the ironworks to entrepreneurs such as Cerf Beer. His building in Saarbrücken, which had suffered in the Thirty Years' War and the War of the Reunions, included Saarbrücken Castle, the Louis Church and the Basilica of St. John, besides hunting lodges such as Schloss Jägersberg.

William Henry died in Saarbrücken on 24 July 1768. His spending on building left an immense debt to his son and successor Louis, though his buildings still dominate the city. He is seen as an example of both the possibilities and the limits of enlightened absolutism: he upheld legal reform, economic stimulus and religious tolerance, yet allowed his subjects no part in government, regulated every area of life by decree and harshly suppressed social protest.
william-hobson: William Hobson was born on 26 September 1792 in Waterford, in the Kingdom of Ireland, the son of Samuel Hobson, a barrister, and Martha Jones, and grew up in an Anglo-Irish Anglican family. He entered the Royal Navy as a Volunteer 2nd Class on 25 August 1803, served in the Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812, became a midshipman in 1806 and was commissioned first lieutenant on 11 November 1813.

Much of his early service was against piracy in the Caribbean. On 29 September 1822 his sloop Whim was captured off Cuba by the pirate leader Pepe Diablito; he and his men were mistreated, then set adrift without provisions and rescued days later by Lieutenant Hugh Nurse of the Eliza. In 1823, commanding the schooner HMS Lion, he took a series of pirate vessels, which brought him promotion to commander on 18 March 1824 and the nickname Lion Hobson.

In command of HMS Ferret he captured the Spanish schooner Fingal on 3 February 1826 with 58 enslaved people from Africa aboard; the Mixed Commission Court condemned the vessel and ordered their emancipation. He married Eliza Ann Elliott at Nassau in December 1827 and was made post captain from 9 July 1828. In 1837 he sailed in HMS Rattlesnake to New Zealand after news of an inter-tribal Maori war, and his report proposed British enclaves there on the model of the Hudson's Bay Company.

In 1839 London appointed him consul and lieutenant-governor under George Gipps, governor in Sydney, with instructions to treat with the Maori for the cession of the islands. He reached the Bay of Islands aboard HMS Herald on 29 January 1840, helped draft the Treaty of Waitangi and headed its British signatories, saying to each chief who signed, He iwi tahi tātou, we are now one people. After New Zealand became a Crown colony he was sworn in as governor on 3 May 1841.

Hobson suffered a second stroke and died on 10 September 1842. He was buried in the Symonds Street cemetery in Auckland on 13 September with military honours.
