Many Māori attended, performing uhunga, expressions of grief, as for one of their own great chiefs. Hobsonville, Hobson Bay, Mount Hobson and streets in Auckland and Wellington are named after him.
william-howard-taft: William Howard Taft was born on 15 September 1857 in Cincinnati, Ohio, to Alphonso Taft and Louise Torrey. His father served as a judge and an ambassador, and was United States Secretary of War and Attorney General under President Ulysses S. Grant. Taft attended Yale University and the Cincinnati Law School. After admission to the Ohio bar he was appointed assistant prosecutor for Hamilton County in October 1880 and Collector of Internal Revenue for Ohio's First District by President Chester A. Arthur in 1882. His professional goal was always a seat on the Supreme Court.

In 1890 Harrison appointed Taft Solicitor General, and from 1892 to 1900 he served as a federal judge of the Sixth Circuit. In 1900 President William McKinley asked him to join the commission to organise a civilian government in the Philippines, with the assurance of the next Supreme Court vacancy. Taft accepted on condition that he head the commission, and sailed in April 1900. In 1902 he refused a Supreme Court seat from Theodore Roosevelt because his work in the islands was not done. He became Secretary of War in 1904, and Roosevelt made him his chosen successor.

Taft defeated William Jennings Bryan in 1908 and was sworn in on 4 March 1909. As president he focused on East Asia more than Europe and repeatedly intervened to prop up or remove Latin American governments. He restructured the State Department, which was for the first time organised into geographical divisions. He brought 70 antitrust suits in four years, against Roosevelt's 40 in seven, and made six appointments to the Supreme Court. Disputes over the tariff, conservation and antitrust cases separated him from Roosevelt, who challenged him for the Republican nomination in 1912. Taft kept a bare majority of delegates and Roosevelt left the party. In the three-way election Taft carried only Utah and Vermont, and Woodrow Wilson won.

He returned to Yale as a professor and worked against war through the League to Enforce Peace. In 1921 President Warren G. Harding appointed him chief justice. On the court he was conservative on business issues, individual rights advanced under him, and his work on administrative reform culminated in the Judiciary Act of 1925.

In poor health, Taft resigned in February 1930 and died on 8 March 1930. He was the first president and the first Supreme Court justice buried at Arlington National Cemetery. He is the only person to have been both president and chief justice.
william-i-count-of-nassau-siegen: William was born at Dillenburg on 10 April 1487, the fourth and youngest son of Count John V of Nassau-Siegen and Landgravine Elisabeth of Hesse-Marburg. He spent most of his youth in Siegen, learnt French and German during stays in the County of Vianden, and at ten was sent to the court at Heidelberg, where he learnt Latin. He also visited the court of Elector Frederick III the Wise of Saxony. When his eldest brother Henry inherited their uncle Engelbert II's lands in the Netherlands in 1504, and his brother John died the same year, William became the sole heir of their father.

He succeeded in 1516 to a county of about 1,600 square kilometres and some 37,500 people in 15 towns and 550 villages. It was mainly agricultural, but its chief income came from the iron ore of the Sieg and Dill regions, and the counts discussed prices, wages and working hours with the iron workers.

In 1518, under the influence of Martin Luther's theses, he had Archbishop Albert of Mainz stop the sale of indulgences in Nassau, and in 1521 he witnessed Luther's appearance at the Diet of Worms, though he did not openly adopt Luther's teaching while his brother Henry, a firm supporter of the emperor and the Catholic Church, held sway over him. He later promoted the Lutheran faith and took part in the Schmalkaldic League and in the negotiations leading to the Peace of Passau.

His reign was dominated by the long dispute with Landgrave Philip I of Hesse over the rich County of Katzenelnbogen, with its Rhine tolls. The legal battles and the rebuilding of Dillenburg Castle as a fortress left Nassau in debt of 512,576 guilders, with interest taking half its income.

After the settlement of Frankfurt brought payments from Hesse, he held a triple wedding at the rebuilt castle on 6 June 1559. He died on 6 October 1559, and his son John VI succeeded him. His eldest son by his second wife, Juliane of Stolberg-Wernigerode, became William the Silent, Prince of Orange, and through his two sons William is counted the progenitor of the Dutch royal house. Why he was called the Rich is unknown: historians have suggested his many children or his income.
william-i-duke-of-aquitaine: William, called the Pious, was born on 22 March 875, the son of Bernard Plantapilosa and Ermengard. He inherited rule of Auvergne, where he was count from 886, and of the Limousin. Sometime before 898 he married a daughter of Boso of Provence and Ermengard of Italy, a member of the Bosonid family. In 893 he conquered Poitou and Aquitaine on behalf of Ebalus Manser. He kept Aquitaine for himself and was proclaimed duke, succeeding Ebalus. His possessions extended from Austrasia to Toulouse and included the Autunois and the Mâconnais.

As duke William made numerous monastic foundations, and the most important was Cluny Abbey, a Benedictine house. In its charter he stipulated that there would be no outside control over the abbey, which would answer directly only to the pope. This was especially striking because most monasteries were privately owned, and the family or individual who owned one appointed its abbots and officials, which led to the appointment of untrained and unordained men. William also nominated Cluny's first abbot, Berno of Baume. The arrangement led to the reforms known as the Clunian reforms, and Cluny became an important political and religious centre.

A sign of William's independence in Aquitaine is that he had deniers minted in his own name at Brioude. He died on 6 July 918 and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Julien. He had no sons and was succeeded by a nephew, William the Younger, the son of his sister Adelinda and Acfred I of Carcassonne. He had a daughter, Engelberga, and possibly another.
william-i-duke-of-julich: William was the eldest son of Gerhard V of Jülich and Elisabeth of Brabant-Aarschot, a daughter of Godfrey of Brabant. Some authors number him William V, as the fifth count; others call him William VI, because they count the son and co-ruler of Count William IV as William V. On 26 February 1324, in Cologne, he married Joanna of Hainaut. He was brother-in-law to both Edward III of England and Emperor Ludwig IV.

William spent enormous sums to have his brother Walram of Jülich made Archbishop of Cologne over Adolph II of the Marck, and gained important positions through him. In 1337 he played a central part in the German-English alliance that marked the start of the Hundred Years' War, and for a time he served Flanders as a field captain in that war. He supported the Habsburgs against the House of Luxembourg in the Carinthian war of succession, but after the alliance collapsed and his brother-in-law died he went over to Emperor Charles IV. In 1352 he imposed an inheritance tax on Heinsberg-Valkenburg and Monschau.

Part of the Jülich knighthood rose against inclusion in his growing territorial state, and his own sons joined them. They imprisoned him in 1349 and released him in 1351 under public pressure. He seems to have held the title of Earl of Cambridge from 1340 until his death.

His marriage policy enlarged the lands of his house, above all the marriage of his son Gerhard to Margaret of Ravensberg, heiress of Berg and Ravensberg. William died in February 1361, and as Gerhard had died before him, Jülich passed to his second son, also named William. William and Joanna are buried at Nideggen. Their daughters married into the houses of the Marck, Heinsberg and Isenburg-Wied, and Elizabeth married John Plantagenet, 3rd Earl of Kent.
william-i-elector-of-hesse: William was born on 3 June 1743 in Kassel, the eldest surviving son of Frederick II, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, and Princess Mary of Great Britain, a daughter of George II. His father abandoned the family in 1747 and converted to Catholicism in 1749, and the marriage was annulled in 1755.

William's grandfather granted the newly acquired county of Hanau to his daughter-in-law and grandsons, so that William was technically its reigning prince under his mother's regency. From 1747 the boys lived in Denmark, supported by Protestant relatives. On 1 September 1764 William married his first cousin Wilhelmina Caroline of Denmark and Norway at Christiansborg Palace, and they lived for two decades mostly in Denmark.

The family moved to Kassel in 1785, when William succeeded to the landgraviate as William IX on his father's death on 31 October. He was said to have inherited one of the largest fortunes in Europe. The banker Mayer Amschel Rothschild supervised his properties and tax collection, and during the Napoleonic Wars William used the Frankfurt Rothschilds to hide his fortune from Napoleon. The money reached Nathan Mayer Rothschild in London and helped fund British operations in Portugal and Spain.

In 1803 he was created Prince-Elector of Hesse. His electorate was annexed by the Kingdom of Westphalia under Jérôme Bonaparte, and William lived in exile in Denmark until the French were expelled from Germany. He was restored in 1813, after the Battle of Leipzig, and began building a monumental palace in Kassel, the Chattenburg, which stopped after his death.

He declared himself King of the Chatti, a title the European powers refused to recognize at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818; they granted him instead the grand ducal style of Royal Highness, but he judged the title of Prince-Elector superior and chose to remain an Elector.

William died in Kassel in 1821 and was succeeded by his son William. With his wife he had four children, of whom the heir William (1777 to 1847) and two daughters reached adulthood. He also had several mistresses and fathered over twenty recognized illegitimate children, providing some financial means for each of them. Hesse-Kassel remained an electorate until Prussia annexed it in 1866.
william-i-of-provence: William and his elder brother Rotbold I were sons of Boson II of Arles and his wife Constance, who has been thought, from her name, to be a daughter of Charles Constantine of Vienne. Both brothers bore the title of count at the same time, and it is not known whether they ruled the whole of Provence jointly or divided it. Rotbold held no other title while William lived, which suggests that William had gained a certain supremacy.

In 975 or 979 William took the title of marchio, or margrave, and in 980 he was installed as Count of Arles. At the Battle of Tourtour in 973, helped by the counts of the High Alps and the viscounts of Marseille and Fos, he routed the Saracens of Fraxinet for good. He then reorganised the lands east of the Rhône, which King Conrad of Burgundy had granted him, and with royal consent he and his heirs controlled the fisc in Provence. With Isarn, Bishop of Grenoble, he repopulated the Dauphiné, and in 970 he settled an Italian count, Ugo Blavia, near Fréjus to bring the land back into cultivation.

His first marriage, to Arsinde, daughter of Arnaud I of Carcassonne, was childless. In 984, against papal advice, he married Adelaide-Blanche of Anjou, daughter of Fulk II of Anjou. Their children included Constance of Arles, who married Robert II of France, and William II of Provence.

Ralph Glaber's chronicle calls him dux, and a charter of 992 names him pater patriae. He gave land to Cluny and retired to become a monk, dying at Avignon some time after 29 August 993; he was buried in the church of Saint-Croix at Sarrians. His brother succeeded him as margrave. The principality soon began to shrink, as the castles of his vassals, which he had kept under close control, became the allods of those who held them.
william-i-of-sicily: William was the fourth son of King Roger II of Sicily and Elvira of Castile, grandson of Count Roger I of Sicily and great-grandson of Tancred of Hauteville. He grew up with little expectation of ruling. The deaths of his three older brothers, Roger, Tancred and Alfonso, between 1138 and 1148 changed matters, though he was still poorly prepared when his father died. His epithet, the Bad, seems little merited and expresses the bias of the historian Hugo Falcandus and of the baronial class against the king and the official class who guided him.

William kept his father's administration and promoted the chancellor Maio of Bari, a man of low birth with the title ammiratus ammiratorum, who held real power at first. Maio continued Roger's policy of excluding much of the nobility from central administration.

On the mainland, however, royal authority still depended on the cooperation of counts and barons in Apulia and the Terra di Lavoro. They were encouraged to revolt by Pope Adrian IV, the Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Comnenus and the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I. At the end of 1155 Byzantine troops took Bari and other towns. William landed and destroyed the Byzantine fleet and army at Brindisi on 28 May 1156, and by the Treaty of Benevento of 18 June 1156 Adrian abandoned the rebels and confirmed him as king.

The African dominions were lost to the Almohads. A revolt began in Sfax in 1156 and nothing was done to put it down, and Mahdia surrendered on 11 January 1160, ending the African empire. In November 1160 Maio was murdered in Palermo by Matthew Bonello. The royal palace was then stormed, and the king and his family were captured, but the people and the army rallied round him. He recovered power, had Bonello blinded and reduced the rest of the kingdom. His son Roger was killed by a wayward arrow, though Falcandus has the king kicking him dead.

Afterwards William entrusted the government to a triumvirate of Matthew of Ajello, Count Sylvester of Marsico and Bishop Palmer of Syracuse. His last years were peaceful, and he supported the true pope against the Holy Roman Emperor, so that Alexander III was installed in the Lateran Palace in November 1165 by a guard of Normans. He died on 7 May 1166 and was buried in Palermo Cathedral, later moved to Monreale Cathedral by his son and heir, William II of Sicily. By his wife Margaret of Navarre he had four sons.
william-i-of-the-netherlands: William was born on 24 August 1772, the son of the last stadtholder, William V, Prince of Orange, and Wilhelmina of Prussia. In 1791 he married his cousin Wilhelmina of Prussia, daughter of King Frederick William II. As commander of the Dutch field army he fought in the Flanders campaign of 1793–95 against the French, but the Batavian Revolution forced the family into exile in 1795. In 1803 he received the Principality of Nassau-Orange-Fulda as compensation, and he lost it in 1806 after fighting on the Prussian side at Jena–Auerstedt. In 1809 he served with the Austrian army and was wounded at Wagram.

After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, a provisional government invited William back. He landed at Scheveningen on 30 November 1813, refused the title of king and proclaimed himself Sovereign Prince of the Netherlands. The Allies also gave him the former Austrian Netherlands, and on 16 March 1815 he proclaimed the kingdom, urged by the powers at the Congress of Vienna. He later gained Luxembourg in exchange for ceding his German lands to Prussia. The constitution gave him near-absolute powers, with ministers responsible only to him. He was nicknamed the King-Merchant for his trade policies. In 1817 he founded the universities of Leuven, Ghent and Liège, and in 1822 the Algemeene Nederlandsche Maatschappij.

The constitution divided the 110 seats of the Second Chamber equally between north and south, though the south had 3.5 million people against 2 million in the north. William, a strong supporter of the Reformed Church, imposed Dutch as the official language in Flanders and required schools to teach the Reformed faith and the Dutch language. Many in the Catholic south resented this, and also felt economically disadvantaged. After riots in Brussels in August 1830 the Belgian Revolution followed. He sent his sons to invade in the Ten Days' Campaign the next year, but French intervention was threatened, and he fought on until 1839, when the Treaty of London dissolved the united kingdom.

William disapproved of the constitutional changes of 1840, which introduced ministerial responsibility, and he grieved the loss of Belgium. He also intended to marry Henrietta d'Oultremont, a Roman Catholic. He abdicated on 7 October 1840 in favour of his eldest son, William II. He spent his last years in Berlin, where he died on 12 December 1843 at the age of 71. A new national anthem, Wien Neêrlands Bloed, replaced the Wilhelmus during his reign and remained in place until 1932.
william-i-of-wurttemberg: Born Frederick William Karl at Lüben on 27 September 1781, he was the son of Duke Frederick William Charles of Württemberg and Augusta of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. His parents' marriage was one of strife, and his mother, who sought sanctuary from it, died in 1788. In 1790 his father and his two sons moved to Ludwigsburg Palace, where the boys received a strict education. In 1805 he returned to Stuttgart as Württemberg was forced to ally with Napoleon. When Talleyrand suggested a coup in which the son would replace his father, Frederick William opposed it, an act regarded as the main reason for his later aversion to Napoleon.

King Frederick died on 30 October 1816, in the Year Without a Summer, when Württemberg suffered crop failures and famine. His son chose his second name as regnal name, simplified the royal title and the coat of arms, reduced the state flag to black and red, announced an amnesty and replaced most of the ministers. His reforms led the Estates to approve a constitution on 25 September 1819. In his reign of 47 years Württemberg moved from a kingdom of different denominational principalities and a heterogeneous agricultural country to a constitutional state with a common identity. On 28 September 1818 an agricultural festival with horse races and prizes for cattle-breeding was held on the Cannstatter Wasen, the origin of the Cannstatter Volksfest.

In foreign policy he imagined a third major German power beside Prussia and Austria, formed of Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover and Württemberg. The plan never succeeded. After poor harvests in 1846 and 1847 liberal demands grew, and in March 1848 he reinstated the liberal press law of 1817 and agreed to a liberal government under Friedrich Römer. He was the only German monarch forced to recognise the Frankfurt Constitution of 1848. After the revolution failed he followed reactionary policies. In the Crimean War he pushed for the neutrality of the German Confederation, and on 27 September 1857 he organised a meeting in Stuttgart between Napoléon III and Tsar Alexander II.

He died on 25 June 1864 at Rosenstein Castle in Bad Cannstatt and was buried in the Württemberg Mausoleum. In old age European princes often sought his advice, and his biographer Paul Sauer called him the Nestor among the princes of Europe. He married three times. By his second wife, Grand Duchess Catherine Pavlovna of Russia, he had two daughters, one of whom, Sophie, married King William III of the Netherlands. By his third wife, Pauline, he had a son, Charles, who succeeded him as king.
william-ii-duke-of-bavaria: William was born on 5 April 1365, a son of Albert I of Bavaria and Margaret of Brieg. Allied with the Hooks, one of the two factions that divided Holland, he was in conflict with his father until 1394. In 1385 he married Margaret, a daughter of Philip the Bold of Burgundy, at the Burgundian double wedding in Cambrai, at which his sister, also named Margaret, married John the Fearless. In 1404 he succeeded his father as count of Holland, Hainaut and Zeeland and duke of Bavaria-Straubing; in Hainaut he is counted as William IV.

In 1408, at the Battle of Othée, William joined John the Fearless of Burgundy and Louis VII of Bavaria in defeating the citizens of Liège, who had risen against William's brother John, the bishop of Liège. As a result William, as count of Hainaut, no longer had to pay homage to the bishop.

His rule in Holland was troubled by internal strife. Lord John V of Arkel backed William's enemies there until William conquered Arkel in 1412; John accepted defeat and Arkel was annexed to Holland. As count of Holland William also claimed Friesland, which earlier counts had failed to conquer. Only Stavoren had been taken, in 1398, and William sent expeditions of his own, but the Frisians regained Stavoren in 1414.

William died on 31 May 1417 of an infection caused by a dog bite. Before his death he had made his nobles swear allegiance to Jacqueline, his only child by Margaret of Burgundy. The war of succession that followed between Jacqueline and her uncle John, the bishop of Liège, was the last episode of the Hook and Cod wars, and in the end it brought Holland and Hainaut into Burgundian hands. The duchy of Bavaria-Straubing was divided among the dukes of Bavaria, and the largest part went to Bavaria-Munich in 1429.
william-ii-elector-of-hesse: William was born on 28 July 1777, the eldest surviving son of William I, Elector of Hesse, and Wilhelmina Caroline of Denmark and Norway. In 1813 he took part with the Hessian troops in the War of the Sixth Coalition against Napoleon. On 13 February 1797, in Berlin, he married Princess Augusta of Prussia, the fourth daughter of King Frederick William II of Prussia. They had six children, three of whom died in infancy; among the others were Friedrich, the future elector, and Marie Fredericka, who married Bernhard II, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen.

He succeeded his father in 1821 as Elector of Hesse, a title that had lost its meaning with the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. On his accession he halted the building of the Chattenburg palace and turned instead to enlarging the Residenzpalais in Kassel.

His private life was entangled. With his mistress Emilie Ortlöpp, daughter of Johann Christian Ortlöpp, he had eight children; she was created Countess of Reichenbach-Lessonitz in 1821, and the children bore the title of count or countess of Reichenbach-Lessonitz. Several months after Augusta died on 19 February 1841, William married Emilie morganatically and their children were legitimated. She died less than two years later, in 1843.

Months after Emilie's death William made a third morganatic marriage, to Caroline, Baroness of Berlepsch, whom he created Countess of Bergen in 1846; the marriage was childless, and she later married Karl Adolf Graf von Hohenthal. William died on 20 November 1847 and was succeeded by his eldest surviving son, Frederick William, the last Elector of Hesse, so that William was the penultimate holder of the title. Through the Reichenbach-Lessonitz line his descendants include Princess Tatiana of Greece and Denmark.
william-ii-of-england: William's date of birth is not known, but according to the historian Frank Barlow it fell by 1060. He was the third of four sons of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders: Robert Curthose was the eldest, Richard the second and Henry the youngest. William became king of England on his father's death in 1087, when Robert inherited Normandy. Relations among the brothers were strained, and the chronicler Orderic Vitalis tells of an incident at L'Aigle in 1077 or 1078 when William and Henry emptied a chamber pot on Robert, causing a brawl that their father had to end.

The division of the Conqueror's lands left nobles with estates on both sides of the Channel unsure which brother to please, and many wanted England and Normandy united again. They revolted in favour of Robert in the Rebellion of 1088, led by Bishop Odo of Bayeux. Robert failed to appear, and William won the English with silver and promises of better government. In 1091 he invaded Normandy and forced Robert to cede part of his lands. Malcolm was killed at the Battle of Alnwick on 13 November 1093.

In the Church, William kept Canterbury vacant for years after Lanfranc died in 1089 and took its revenues. When he fell ill in 1093 he named Anselm archbishop, but they disagreed over many issues, and Anselm went into exile in October 1097. Robert pledged Normandy to William for 10,000 marks in 1096 before leaving on the First Crusade, and William raised the sum by a heavy tax on all England. In 1097 he began the original Westminster Hall.

William went hunting in the New Forest on 2 August 1100 and was killed by an arrow through the lung. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he was shot by one of his own men, and later writers name Walter Tirel, who fled. Henry, who was in the hunting party, rode to Winchester, seized the treasury and was crowned within days. Modern historians disagree: Barlow holds that accidents were common and there is no hard evidence of murder, while others find the suspicion of a plot credible.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle said William was hated by almost all his people. Chroniclers were mostly churchmen and were hostile after his struggles with the Church. William never married and had no children, and some writers have speculated about his sexuality. His remains lie in Winchester Cathedral, and a memorial stone at Beaulieu Abbey and the Rufus Stone near Minstead recall his death.
william-ii-of-holland: William was the eldest son and heir of Count Floris IV of Holland and Matilda of Brabant. His father was killed at a tournament at Corbie when William was only seven years old. His paternal uncles William and Otto, bishop of Utrecht, were his guardians until 1239. He was Count of Holland and Zeeland from 1234 until his death.

With the help of his maternal uncle Duke Henry II of Brabant and Konrad von Hochstaden, Archbishop of Cologne, William was elected king of Germany after Pope Innocent IV excommunicated Emperor Frederick II. He succeeded Landgrave Henry Raspe of Thuringia, who had died within a year of his own election as anti-king. William extended his father's hunting residence into a palace worthy of his new status, later called the Binnenhof, which began the city of The Hague. He then besieged Aachen for six months before capturing it from Frederick's followers, and only then could Archbishop Konrad crown him king.

On 25 January 1252 he married Elizabeth, daughter of the Welf duke Otto of Brunswick-Lüneburg, which brought him a degree of theoretical support from some German princes, and on 25 March 1252 he was elected King of the Romans a second time, at Brunswick. His power, however, never extended beyond the Rhineland. In Holland he fought Countess Margaret II of Flanders for control of Zeeland, and defeated the Flemish army at Westkapelle in July 1253. He granted city rights to Haarlem, Delft, 's-Gravenzande and Alkmaar, and from 1254 fought several wars against the West Frisians, for which he built castles at Heemskerk and Haarlem.

On 28 January 1256, in a battle near Hoogwoud, William was lost and tried to cross a frozen lake alone. His horse fell through the ice, and the Frisians killed him and buried him in secret under the floor of a house. His son Floris V recovered the body 26 years later, took terrible vengeance on the West Frisians, and had his father buried in Middelburg. Contemporary sources, including the chronicle of Melis Stoke, portray William as an Arthurian hero. A golden statue of him stands on the Binnenhof in The Hague, the inner court of the parliamentary complex of the Netherlands.
william-ii-of-sicily: William was born in Palermo to King William I and Margaret of Navarre. His father died when he was twelve, and the government came under his mother's regency, run first by the chancellor Stephen du Perche until a coup in 1168, then by Walter Ophamil, archbishop of Palermo, and Matthew of Ajello. William was declared adult in 1171. The sources leave his character indistinct: he is described as secluded and pleasure-loving, seldom leaving his palace, yet his reign had an ambitious foreign policy. He championed the papacy and was in secret league with the Lombard cities against Frederick Barbarossa.

His marriage in February 1177 to Joan, daughter of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, marked his high position in European politics. He had refused Barbarossa's offer of his daughter Beatrice in 1173, so as not to offend the pope, and in July 1177 he sent a delegation to sign the Treaty of Venice with the emperor.

William first attacked Ayyubid Egypt, where Saladin threatened the Latin kingdom of Jerusalem. In July 1174 a force of 30,000 men landed before Alexandria, but Saladin's arrival made the Sicilians re-embark in disorder. After the death of the Byzantine Emperor Manuel Comnenus in 1180 he turned against the Byzantine Empire. Dyrrhachium was captured on 11 June 1185, and the fleet took Corfu, Cephalonia, Ithaca and Zakynthos on its way to Thessalonica, which fell in August 1185 and was sacked.

Troops marching on the capital were defeated on the Strymon on 7 November 1185 by the army of Emperor Isaac Angelus under Alexios Branas. In 1189 William made peace with Isaac, giving up all the conquests. His admiral Margarito kept the eastern Mediterranean open for the Franks and forced Saladin to retire from Tripoli in the spring of 1188.

In 1184 William released his aunt Constance from her convent and in January 1186 married her to Henry, son of Frederick Barbarossa, causing an oath to be taken to her as heir presumptive. William died at Palermo in November 1189, leaving no surviving children. Norman officials led by Matthew of Ajello then supported his cousin Tancred of Lecce, rather than Constance, to avoid German rule. The nickname the Good arose only decades after his death, from the end of the troubles of his father's reign and the wars under his successor. Dante places him in Paradise.
william-ii-of-villehardouin: William was born around 1211 in the castle of Kalamata, the second son of Geoffrey I of Villehardouin, who had begun the Frankish conquest of the Morea after the Fourth Crusade, and his wife Elisabeth. Growing up in the Morea, he spoke Greek like a native and felt at home among both Franks and Greeks. He held the Barony of Kalamata in fief and ruled Achaea as regent while his elder brother, Geoffrey II, campaigned in defence of Constantinople. He succeeded his childless brother in the summer of 1246.

After the conquest of Monemvasia and the building of his castles, William joined the crusade of Louis IX of France against Egypt in 1249 with 400 knights and 24 ships, and Louis rewarded him with the right to mint coins in the style of the French denier tournois. In the early 1250s most Frankish rulers of Greece acknowledged him as overlord. His claim to part of Negroponte on Euboea in 1255 set off the War of the Euboeote Succession against Venice and Guy I de la Roche, Lord of Athens, which ended with William's victory in Attica in May 1258.

He then allied with Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus, marrying his daughter Anna, and marched against the Nicaeans. After his release from captivity the Byzantines used their new forts in the Morea to seize further lands, and William turned to Charles I of Anjou. By the Treaty of Viterbo of 24 May 1267 he swore fealty to Charles and accepted Charles's descendants as his heirs, and his daughter Isabella was to marry Charles's son Philip. In 1268 he led 400 knights for Charles at the Battle of Tagliacozzo.

William died on 1 May 1278. Historian Kenneth M. Setton called him the most lordly of the princes of Achaea, and Marino Sanudo the Elder wrote that merchants could travel his lands safely without cash. Achaea never regained its power after Pelagonia and passed into the orbit of Neapolitan politics. William was also a trouvère: two of his compositions survive in the Manuscrit du Roi.
william-ii-of-wurttemberg: William II, born Wilhelm Karl Paul Heinrich Friedrich on 25 February 1848, was the only child of Prince Frederick of Württemberg and Princess Catherine Frederica of Württemberg, who were first cousins. His growing years coincided with a progressive diminution of Württemberg's sovereignty during German unification. In 1870 the kingdom took Prussia's side in the Franco-German War, and in 1871 it became a state of the German Empire.

William succeeded his childless maternal uncle Charles I on 6 October 1891. This did not depart from the Salic law that governed succession in the German states: he was the nearest agnatic heir, as the senior male-line descendant of Frederick I of Württemberg through his younger son Prince Paul. William held the rank of Generalfeldmarschall in the First World War.

He was considered a popular monarch and used to walk his two dogs in the public parks of Stuttgart without bodyguards, greeted by his subjects with a simple Herr König. Although his kingdom was landlocked, he was a yachting enthusiast and was instrumental in founding the Royal Yacht Club of Württemberg on Lake Constance in 1911.

His first wife, Princess Marie of Waldeck and Pyrmont, whom he married in 1877, died in 1882 after the birth of their third child, a stillborn daughter; their son Ulrich had died in infancy in 1880. William, already depressed, is said never to have recovered. In 1886 he married Princess Charlotte of Schaumburg-Lippe, and the marriage was childless.

In 1918 William was deposed along with the other German rulers, and he abdicated on 30 November 1918, ending more than 800 years of rule by the House of Württemberg. He was the last German ruler to abdicate in the wake of the November Revolution. He died at Bebenhausen in 1921 without a male heir, and the royal branch of the house became extinct. Headship of the house passed to Albrecht, Duke of Württemberg, of the Catholic cadet branch at Altshausen.
william-iii-count-of-nevers: William was born about 1107 at Auxerre, a son of William II of Nevers and his wife Adelaide. His brother Renaud of Nevers was Count of Tonnerre until he died in 1148 while taking part in the Second Crusade, and another brother, Robert, is mentioned only in a charter of 1134. Their sister Anne married William VIII, Count of Auvergne, known as William the Old, and was the mother of Robert IV, Count of Auvergne. William is recorded as co-signing legal decisions of his father in charters of 1121 and 1134.

On 21 September 1137 the chronicler Orderic Vitalis records him in the company of Geoffrey V of Anjou when Geoffrey entered the Duchy of Normandy. This was part of the struggle between Matilda, Countess of Anjou, and her cousin Stephen of England, which lasted from 1135 to 1154 and is known as The Anarchy.

William joined Louis VII of France on the Second Crusade. His father died on 21 August 1148, and William succeeded him as Count of Nevers and of Auxerre. At about the same time he is thought to have succeeded his brother in Tonnerre, and so held the three counties together.

William died on 21 November 1161. He had married Ida of Sponheim, a daughter of Engelbert, Duke of Carinthia, and of Uta of Passau. Their sons were William IV, Count of Nevers, who died on 24 October 1168, and Guy, Count of Nevers, who died on 19 October 1175. A third son, Renaud of Nevers, Lord of Decize, died on the Third Crusade at the Siege of Acre. Of their daughters, Adelaide married Renaud IV, Count of Joigny, and a second, Ermengarde, is also recorded.
william-iii-duke-of-aquitaine: William was born in Poitiers, the son of Ebalus Manzer and Emilienne, when his father was already in middle age. His byname, Tête d'étoupe in French and Caput Stupe in Latin, came from the colour of his hair. The chief sources for his rule are Ademar of Chabannes, Dudo of Saint-Quentin and William of Jumièges. According to Ademar, his wife was Gerloc, also called Adèle, a daughter of Rollo of Normandy; the less reliable Dudo has William marrying her perhaps about 936, in a match that William I of Normandy may have arranged.

William claimed the duchy of Aquitaine from his father's death, but the royal chancery recognised his ducal title only in the year before his own death. He also became count of Auvergne in 950. Soon after the death of King Rudolph in 936, Louis IV made him cede some land to Hugh the Great; he did so with grace, but relations with Hugh then worsened. In 950 Hugh, reconciled with Louis, was granted the duchies of Burgundy and Aquitaine and tried to conquer Aquitaine with the king's help, but William defeated them.

Louis's successor Lothair feared William's power and in August 955 joined Hugh in besieging Poitiers. The city held out, but William gave battle and was routed. After Hugh's death his son Hugh Capet was named duke of Aquitaine, yet he never tried to take up the fief, because William had made peace with Lothair.

William was given the abbey of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand, which stayed in his family after his death, and he built a library in the palace of Poitiers. He died on 3 April 963. His son William succeeded him in Aquitaine, and a daughter, Adelaide, married Hugh Capet.
william-iii-of-england: William was born on 4 November 1650 at The Hague, the only child of the stadtholder William II, Prince of Orange, who died before his birth, and Mary, Princess Royal, daughter of Charles I of England. His mother took little personal interest in him, and from April 1656 the Calvinist preacher Cornelis Trigland gave him daily instruction in the Reformed religion. After his father's death most provinces left the office of stadtholder vacant.

In 1672, the Rampjaar or disaster year, France and its allies England, Münster and Cologne invaded the Dutch Republic, and the French army overran Gelderland and Utrecht. William withdrew into Holland, where the dikes were flooded, and the people turned against de Witt and his allies. William became Louis XIV's chief opponent and reorganised the Dutch army. In 1677 he married his first cousin Mary, elder daughter of the Duke of York, later James II.

James's reign was unpopular with British Protestants. In June 1688 the birth of a son, James Francis Edward Stuart, displaced Mary from first place in the succession. William, invited by leading English Protestants, landed at Brixham in November 1688 with a Dutch force, and James was deposed. A Convention Parliament met on 22 January 1689. William insisted on reigning as king in his own right, and he and Mary were offered the crown jointly. Parliament passed the Toleration Act 1689 and, in December 1689, the Bill of Rights, which limited the royal prerogative. William disliked such limits but agreed to abide by the statute.

A minority, the Jacobites, refused to recognise William, and over 400 clergy, the nonjurors, would not take oaths of allegiance. He spent each campaigning season abroad in the Nine Years' War against France, while Mary governed. She died of smallpox on 28 December 1694. The Treaty of Rijswijk of 20 September 1697 ended the war, and Louis XIV recognised William as king. After the death in 1700 of Anne's last surviving child, the Act of Settlement 1701 named Sophia, Electress of Hanover, and her Protestant heirs as heirs to the throne.

William died at Kensington Palace on 8 March 1702, aged 51, of pneumonia after a fall from his horse broke his collarbone. Some Jacobites toasted the mole whose burrow had tripped the horse as the little gentleman in the black velvet waistcoat. He was buried in Westminster Abbey beside Mary, and Anne succeeded him. Contemporaries, even his enemies, praised him as a field commander. In Ulster he is called King Billy, and his victory at the Boyne in 1690 is commemorated each year in the Twelfth of July parades of the Orange Order.
william-iii-of-the-netherlands: William was born on 19 February 1817 in the Palace of the Nation in Brussels, the eldest son of the future King William II and Anna Pavlovna of Russia. He and his brothers were raised by military men and expected to join the army, and he studied for a time at Leiden University without taking a degree. On 18 June 1839 he married his cousin Sophie of Württemberg in Stuttgart. The marriage was unhappy, and she bore him three sons, William, Maurice and Alexander.

William disliked the constitutional changes of 1848 introduced by his father and Johan Rudolf Thorbecke, seeing them as useless limits on royal power, and he would have preferred to govern as an enlightened despot like his grandfather William I. His father died on 17 March 1849, when William was a guest at Raby Castle, and he was reluctant to return to take the throne.

His first act as king was to install the cabinet of Thorbecke, designer of the liberal constitution of 1848, which had stripped the crown of most of its political powers. When the Catholic hierarchy of bishops was restored in 1853, he found growing conservative support and a reason to dismiss Thorbecke. In the first two decades of his reign he dismissed several cabinets and dissolved parliament several times. In the Luxembourg Coup of 1856 he unilaterally imposed a reactionary constitution on Luxembourg. In 1867 France offered to buy Luxembourg, which almost brought war between Prussia and France until the Second Treaty of London confirmed Luxembourg as independent.

He grew unpopular with his bourgeois-liberal subjects but stayed popular with the common man. Queen Sophie died in 1877, and in 1879 William married Emma of Waldeck and Pyrmont, who was 41 years younger. Their daughter Wilhelmina was born in 1880 and became heir presumptive in 1884, after the last of William's sons from his first marriage died.

William fell seriously ill with a kidney ailment in 1887 and was increasingly demented in 1889 and 1890, when the Council of State and then Queen Emma became regents. He died at Het Loo Palace in 1890, and Emma served as regent for Wilhelmina until 1898. Having reigned for 41 years, he is the second-longest reigning Dutch monarch, surpassed only by Wilhelmina.
william-iron-arm: William of Hauteville was a son of Tancred of Hauteville by his first wife Muriella. Tancred had many sons and his possessions were not enough for all of them, so William and many of his brothers had to seek their fortunes elsewhere. The brother Serlo stayed in Normandy to inherit their father's possessions, while William went to southern Italy.

Around 1035 or later he travelled there with his brothers Drogo and Humphrey to strengthen the ranks of Rainulf Drengot, Count of Aversa, the first Norman mercenary lord to be granted a fief. Together they took part in a military operation led by Guaimar IV of Salerno against Pandulf IV, Prince of Capua. In time William and his brothers entered the direct service of Guaimar.

Guaimar sent them, with other Norman and Lombard forces, to help a Byzantine attempt to conquer Sicily. Between 1038 and 1040 William fought there and distinguished himself at Messina and Troina. At the siege of Syracuse, led by the general Georgios Maniakes, he is said to have charged and single-handedly killed the emir of the city, which gave him the nickname Iron Arm. Dissatisfied by unpaid wages and an unfair division of loot, the Normans sent their leader Arduin to protest, and Maniakes humiliated him. Normans and Lombards then left the expedition and returned to Guaimar.

In 1040 a Lombard rebellion began in Apulia under the nobleman Argyrus. Arduin asked his former Norman soldiers for help, offering them control of Melfi, and the Normans won victories at Montemaggiore on 4 May 1041 and Montepeloso on 3 September 1041. During the rebellion the Lombard and Norman forces struggled to keep a leader, since the successive figureheads were refused or bribed by the Byzantines. William kept the Normans under his control.

In September 1042 William was named Count of all the Normans in Apulia, with his capital at Melfi. Guaimar IV recognised the title, gave him his niece Guida in marriage and granted him Ascoli as a personal fief. William declared himself Guaimar's vassal, and Guaimar took the title of Duke of Apulia and Calabria. William marched against Byzantine Bari without success, then turned to Lucania and Calabria, where in 1044 he built the castle of Scribla. He died between May and September 1046 and was succeeded by his brother Drogo. His rise began the fortunes of the House of Hauteville.
william-iv-duke-of-bavaria: William was born in Munich on 13 November 1493, the son of Albert IV and Kunigunde of Austria, a daughter of Emperor Frederick III. His father had fixed the succession of the firstborn prince in 1506, which made William the sole heir. His younger brother Louis refused a spiritual career, arguing that he had been born before the edict took effect. With the support of his mother and the States-General, Louis forced William in 1516 to accept him as co-regent. Louis then ruled the districts of Landshut and Straubing, and in general the brothers governed in concord.

William at first sympathised with the Reformation but changed his mind as it grew more popular in Bavaria. In 1522 he issued the first Bavarian religion mandate, which banned the spread of Martin Luther's works. After an agreement with Pope Clement VII in 1524 he became a political leader of the German Counter-Reformation, though he stayed in opposition to the Habsburgs because Louis X claimed the Bohemian crown. In 1525 both dukes, allied with the Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg, helped to put down the peasant uprising in South Germany.

The conflict with the Habsburgs ended in 1534, when the dukes reached an agreement with Ferdinand I at Linz. In 1546 William supported Emperor Charles V in his war against the Schmalkaldic League, but he did not succeed in preserving the Palatine electoral dignity. His chancellor for 35 years was Leonhard von Eck. Louis shared the rule until 1545.

On 23 April 1516, before a committee of gentry and knights at Ingolstadt, William issued the purity regulation for brewing Bavarian beer, which allowed only barley, hops and water. It remained binding until 1986, when European Union rules ended it as an obligation. In 1523 the appointment of Ludwig Senfl began the rise of the Bavarian State Orchestra, and the Eckbibel, a biblical translation of 1537 that Johann Eck wrote at William's order, answered Luther theologically and is written in Bavarian Upper German.

William was a major collector and patron of art. He commissioned a series of paintings that included Albrecht Altdorfer's Battle of Issus; most of the collection is now in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. His expansion of the Neuveste and its first court garden began the history of the Munich Residenz as a representative palace. In 1546 he and his son Albert V had Dachau Palace rebuilt as a Renaissance palace. William died in Munich in 1550 and was buried in the Frauenkirche; Albert succeeded him.
william-iv-grand-duke-of-luxembourg: William was born on 22 April 1852, with the French name Guillaume Alexandre, and succeeded his father, Adolphe. Although the duchy of Nassau was annexed by Prussia after the Austro-Prussian war of 1866, he and his heirs kept the title of Duke of Nassau. William was a Protestant, the religion of the House of Nassau. On 21 June 1893, at Fischhorn Castle in Zell am See, he married Infanta Marie Anne of Portugal, a daughter of the former King Miguel I of Portugal. He believed that Luxembourg, a Catholic country, should be headed by a Catholic monarch, and the marriage made his successors Catholic.

William became Grand Duke on 17 November 1905. Like his father, he did not take part in politics, although the Constitution vested considerable power in him. When his uncle, Prince Nikolaus-Wilhelm, died in 1905, the only other legitimate heir of the House of Nassau-Weilburg was a cousin, Georg Nikolaus, Count of Merenberg, the child of a morganatic marriage. In 1907 William declared the Counts of Merenberg non-dynastic and named his eldest daughter, Marie-Adélaïde, heiress presumptive to the throne.

William died on 25 February 1912, and he is the last monarch of Luxembourg to have died on the throne. He and Marie Anne had six daughters. Marie-Adélaïde became grand duchess in her own right on his death and abdicated in 1919, when her younger sister Charlotte succeeded her. Charlotte married her first cousin, Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma, a son of Marie Anne's younger sister. Another daughter, Princess Antonia, married Rupprecht, Crown Prince of Bavaria, as his second wife, and Princess Sophie married Prince Ernst Heinrich of Saxony. William held foreign honours including the Knight of the Elephant of Denmark in 1876, the Seraphim of Sweden-Norway in 1889 and the Black Eagle of Prussia in 1890.
william-iv-landgrave-of-hesse-kassel: William was born in Kassel on 24 June 1532, the eldest son of Philip the Magnanimous and Christine of Saxony. When his father died in 1567 the Landgraviate of Hesse was shared among the four sons of Philip's first marriage, and William became the first Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, founding the oldest of the Hessian lines, which survives today.

He worked to protect the Lutheran Reformation and to unite the different branches of Protestantism against Catholicism, though he was unwilling to use force for it. At home he issued many ordinances, appointed expert officials and put his limited finances in order. A law of primogeniture protected his lands from the kind of division that had reduced his father's inheritance. He married Sabine of Württemberg, daughter of Christoph, Duke of Württemberg; their son Maurice succeeded him on his death on 25 August 1592.

His interest in astronomy may have been stirred by Petrus Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum. About 1584 his observatory at Kassel adopted most of the mechanical improvements that made Tycho Brahe's instruments superior, and from then on its observations were nearly as accurate as Tycho's, although an assumed solar parallax of 3' made its longitudes 6' too large. Unlike Tycho, the Kassel astronomers used clocks to measure the difference in right ascension between Venus and the sun before sunset.

The main result was the Hessian star catalogue of about a thousand stars, published by Albert Curtz in Historia coelestis at Augsburg in 1666; other observations were edited by Willebrord Snell at Leiden in 1618. William was also a keen botanist. Carolus Clusius and Joachim Camerarius the Younger gathered exotic plants for him, often from Italy, and Sabine used his garden to make medicines. He also collected botanical books, among them works by Lobelius and Clusius.
william-iv-of-the-united-kingdom: William was born on 21 August 1765 at Buckingham House, the third child and son of George III and Queen Charlotte. With two elder brothers, George, Prince of Wales, and Prince Frederick, he was not expected to inherit the Crown. He was educated by private tutors at Richmond and Kew Palace, and at thirteen joined the Royal Navy as a midshipman. He was present at the Battle of Cape St Vincent in 1780, and was arrested with his shipmates after a drunken brawl in Gibraltar before being hastily released. He was later nicknamed the "Sailor King".

He ceased active service in 1790 and was never given a command during the Napoleonic Wars; his rank as admiral from 1798 was purely nominal. From 1791 to 1811 he lived with the Irish actress Dorothea Bland, known as Mrs Jordan, and they had ten children. In 1818 he married Princess Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen. As Lord High Admiral from 1827 he clashed repeatedly with his Council, and the king asked for his resignation in 1828 after he put to sea with a squadron for ten days without saying where.

George IV died on 26 June 1830 and William succeeded him at the age of 64. He discouraged pomp, and walked unaccompanied through London and Brighton. The Duke of Wellington said he did more business with William in ten minutes than with George IV in as many days. The general election of 1830 brought the Whigs under Lord Grey to power, and Grey pledged to reform an electoral system that had seen few changes since the fifteenth century, in which small boroughs such as Old Sarum, with seven voters, elected two members while Manchester and Birmingham elected none. The Reform Act 1832 refashioned it. His popularity was eroded by the Reform Crisis.

In Hanover, William signed a new constitution in 1833 that empowered the middle class and expanded the role of the parliament; his brother Ernest Augustus later revoked it. He supported Belgian independence and favoured Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha for its throne. In 1834 he became the last British sovereign to choose a prime minister against the will of Parliament, when he disliked the policies of Lord Melbourne's government.

William died on 20 June 1837 with no surviving legitimate children. The British throne passed to his niece Victoria, but under Salic Law a woman could not rule Hanover, so that throne went to his brother Ernest Augustus. His death ended the personal union of Britain and Hanover that had lasted since 1714. The main beneficiaries of his will were his eight surviving children by Mrs Jordan.
william-iv-prince-of-orange: William was born in Leeuwarden on 1 September 1711, six weeks after the death of his father, John William Friso, head of the Frisian branch of the House of Orange-Nassau. His mother was Landgravine Marie Louise of Hesse-Kassel. He succeeded his father as Stadtholder of Friesland and, under his mother's regency until 1731, of Groningen. In 1722 he was elected Stadtholder of Guelders. The four other provinces, Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and Overijssel, had decided in 1702, after the death of William III, to appoint no stadtholder, which began the Second Stadtholderless Period.

In 1733 William was made a Knight of the Order of the Garter. On 25 March 1734 he married, at St James's Palace, Anne, Princess Royal, eldest daughter of King George II of Great Britain. They had three children, of whom Carolina and William V survived infancy. In 1739 William inherited the estates of the Nassau-Dillenburg branch of his family, and in 1743 those of the Nassau-Siegen branch.

The War of the Austrian Succession broke out in 1740. The Dutch Republic sided with Austria in 1747, to keep a buffer zone between itself and France, and French troops invaded the Austrian Netherlands. In a few weeks they took most of the towns where the Dutch kept troops under the Barrier Treaty, as well as the main towns of Zeelandic Flanders. The Republic was divided internally, and the Dutch decided that they needed a single strong executive and turned to the House of Orange. William moved with his family from Leeuwarden to The Hague, and on 4 May 1747 the States General named him General Stadtholder of all seven provinces and made the office hereditary for the first time.

William was at first popular, despite little experience of state affairs. He stopped the practice of indirect taxation by which independent contractors made large sums for themselves. He was also a Director-General of the Dutch East India Company, and his alliance with the business class deepened while the gap between rich and poor grew. He appointed Duke Louis Ernest of Brunswick-Lüneburg field marshal of the Dutch States Army two years later. William died of a stroke at The Hague on 22 October 1751.
william-ix-duke-of-aquitaine: William was born on 22 October 1071, the son of William VIII of Aquitaine and his third wife, Hildegarde of Burgundy. Because of his father's earlier divorces and his parents' consanguinity, the Church at first regarded him as illegitimate, and his father made a pilgrimage to Rome to seek papal approval of the marriage and of the boy's legitimacy. William inherited the duchy at fifteen, in 1086. In 1094 he married Philippa, daughter and heiress of William IV of Toulouse. In 1098 he and Philippa captured Toulouse, for which they were threatened with excommunication. At Philippa's urging he gave land in northern Poitou to Robert of Arbrissel, which became Fontevraud Abbey.

William joined the Crusade of 1101, mortgaging Toulouse to finance it. He fought mostly skirmishes in Anatolia and was often defeated. In September 1101 his army was destroyed by the Seljuk Turks under Kilij Arslan I at Heraclea, and according to Orderic Vitalis he reached Antioch with only six companions. Orderic also reports that he later told of the miseries of his captivity in rhythmic verses.

His relations with the Church were rocky. He was excommunicated in 1114 and again for taking Dangereuse, the wife of his vassal Aimery I de Rochefoucauld, whom he installed in the Maubergeonne tower at Poitiers. Philippa retired to Fontevraud and died there on 28 November 1118. William was readmitted to the Church around 1120 after concessions that may have included taking part in the Reconquista. Between 1120 and 1123 Aquitanian troops fought beside the Castilians in an attempt to take Cordoba. He died on 10 February 1126.

Eleven of his songs survive, in Occitan, composed under his title as Count of Poitou. They treat sex, love, women, his own prowess and feudal politics. One, traditionally numbered eighth, is of doubtful attribution because of its different style and language, and another exists in two quite different versions. In several poems he honours a woman he calls midons. Pos de chantar m'es pres talenz, possibly written around his first excommunication, muses on mortality and renounces chivalry and pride.

An anonymous 13th-century vida calls him one of the most courtly men in the world and a great deceiver of women, but it may rest on a literal reading of songs written in the first person. The nickname the Troubadour was applied only in the nineteenth century. His children included William X, his successor, and Raymond, later Prince of Antioch.
william-johnson: Johnson was born around 1715 in County Meath, the eldest son of Christopher Johnson and Anne Warren, of a family that lived comfortably if modestly. His uncle, the naval officer Sir Peter Warren, had bought land on the south side of the Mohawk River, and about 1738 Johnson arrived with twelve Irish Protestant families to settle it, buying enslaved Africans to clear the land, the first of many slaves he owned. In 1739 he set up on his own on the north bank at a place he called Mount Johnson, trading directly with New York merchants and cutting into Albany's Indian trade.

In 1746, during King George's War, he became New York's sole agent to the Iroquois and, with the Mohawk chief Hendrick Theyanoguin, recruited warriors against the French, paying bounties for scalps under the Scalp Act of 1747. He resigned in 1751 after quarrels over his expenses, but at the Albany Congress of 1754 the Mohawk made his return the condition for restoring the Covenant Chain. At Lake George on 8 September 1755 he was wounded, Hendrick was killed and the French commander Baron Dieskau was captured; Parliament voted Johnson £5,000. The historian Julian Gwyn wrote, "Never was such an insignificant encounter so generously rewarded." At Niagara in 1759 he led nearly 1,000 Iroquois warriors and took command when General John Prideaux was killed.

After the war he used his office to acquire Native land, about 170,000 acres by his death, which made him one of the largest landowners in British America; Gwyn calls him one of the principal exploiters of the Indians. He founded Johnstown in 1762, opened a free school there for white and Mohawk children, and negotiated with Pontiac the treaty of 1766 that ended Pontiac's War.

Johnson died of a stroke at Johnson Hall on 11 July 1774 during an Indian conference, and the Six Nations recognised his nephew and son-in-law Guy Johnson as his successor. In his will he acknowledged children by Catherine Weisenberg and Molly Brant. During the American Revolution the rebel New York legislature seized his lands, as his heirs were Loyalists. Johnson Hall became a National Historic Landmark in 1960, and much of his papers was lost in the New York State Library fire of 1911.
william-knox-darcy: William Knox D'Arcy was born on 11 October 1849 in Newton Abbot, Devon, the son of the solicitor William Francis D'Arcy. He attended Westminster School until 1866, when his father's bankruptcy led the family to emigrate to Australia, where they settled in Rockhampton, Queensland. He studied law, joined his father's practice and began to speculate in land. In 1872 he married Elena Birkbeck, the daughter of a mining engineer from Illinois who had managed a silver mine in Mexico.

In 1882 D'Arcy joined a syndicate with Walter Russell Hall, Thomas Skarratt Hall and the Morgan brothers that opened a mine on Ironstone Mountain, later renamed Mount Morgan, south of Rockhampton. The deposit was rich, and in October 1886 the syndicate became the Mount Morgan Gold Mining Company, with D'Arcy a director and its largest shareholder. With his fortune he moved to England in 1889, bought the Stanmore Hall mansion and a house on Grosvenor Square, and kept a private box at Epsom racecourse.

In 1900 he agreed to fund a search for oil and minerals in Persia, a country he never visited. The concession he obtained in 1901 for £20,000 covered 480,000 square miles, all of Persia except five northern provinces, and gave the Iranian government 16% of the company's annual profits. Drilling began under George B. Reynolds at Chiah Surkh at the end of 1902, but by 1904 D'Arcy had spent £160,000 and was overdrawn at Lloyds Bank. In 1905 the Burmah Oil Company became a major investor in a new Concession Syndicate.

Operations moved to Shardin in 1906, and in 1907 the search shifted to Masjed Soleyman, where drilling began in January 1908. By April, with no success and D'Arcy almost bankrupt, the venture was close to collapse, and in early May D'Arcy and Burmah telegraphed Reynolds to cease work and come home. Reynolds delayed, and on 26 May 1908 he struck oil at 1,180 feet.

D'Arcy became a director of the new Anglo-Persian Oil Company in April 1909, though the backing of Burmah Oil and the British Admiralty left him a shareholder rather than its leading figure. By 1911 the company had a pipeline from the field to a refinery at Abadan. The agreement on the Iranian government's share of the profits remained in effect until Iran nationalised the industry in March 1952. He died on 1 May 1917, aged 67.
william-lloyd-garrison: Garrison was the youngest son of immigrants from the British colony of New Brunswick. His father, Abijah Garrison, a merchant-sailing pilot and master, moved the family to Newburyport in 1806 but lost work after the Embargo Act of 1807 and deserted the family in 1808. His mother, Frances Maria Lloyd, began calling the boy by his middle name to keep her family name; she died in 1823. He worked as a typesetter, which helped him later run his newspaper, and he often composed his editorials directly in type.

At twenty-five he joined the anti-slavery movement, later crediting John Rankin's Letters on Slavery of 1826. For a short time he was associated with the American Colonization Society, which promoted resettling free Black Americans in West Africa. By late 1829 or 1830 he rejected colonization and publicly apologised for his error. In 1829 he became co-editor with Benjamin Lundy of the Quaker newspaper Genius of Universal Emancipation in Baltimore. There he moved from Lundy's gradualism to a demand for immediate and complete emancipation, and he ran a column, The Black List, reporting the cruelties of slavery.

In 1831 he returned to New England and co-founded the weekly The Liberator with Isaac Knapp. In January 1832 he organised the New-England Anti-Slavery Society, and in December 1833 abolitionists from ten states founded the American Anti-Slavery Society. His appeals for women to take part sparked controversy over women's right to a political voice. In December 1837 he announced that The Liberator would support the rights of woman to their utmost extent. In 1834 he married Helen Eliza Benson; they had two daughters and five sons, of whom two died as children.

He promoted what he called no-governmentism, rejecting the validity of a government engaged in war, imperialism and slavery. He began as an advocate of Christian pacifism, but at the outbreak of the American Civil War he accepted armed struggle as a means of abolition and supported President Abraham Lincoln. In May 1865 he proposed dissolving the American Anti-Slavery Society, but Wendell Phillips argued that its task was not complete until Black Southerners had full political and civil equality, and the resolution was defeated 118 to 48. Garrison resigned and ended The Liberator at the end of 1865. He died on 24 May 1879. Leo Tolstoy was influenced by his writings and published a short biography of him in 1904.
william-longsword: William was born overseas to Rollo, while he was still a pagan, and his wife more danico, Poppa of Bayeux, whose parentage is uncertain. Poppa was a Christian and seems to have passed her beliefs to her son, who according to his planctus was baptised probably at the same time as his father. He is sometimes called duke of Normandy, but the title dux did not come into common use until the eleventh century. At the time he was known as count of Rouen, and the chronicler Flodoard called both Rollo and William principes of the Normans. The byname Longsword first appears in later eleventh-century sources.

William succeeded Rollo in 927. Early in his reign, in 933 or 934, Normans who thought him too Gallicised rebelled under Riulf, who besieged him in Rouen, according to Dudo of Saint-Quentin; William sallied out and won a decisive battle. In 933 he recognised King Rudolph of Western Francia, who gave him lordship over much of the Breton lands, including Avranches, the Cotentin Peninsula and the Channel Islands, though these lay outside Carolingian power. The Bretons resisted under Alan II, Duke of Brittany, but they were defeated with great slaughter. In 935 he married Luitgarde, daughter of Count Herbert II of Vermandois, and arranged his sister Adela's marriage to William, Count of Poitou.

After Rudolph died in January 936, William's promise of loyalty helped persuade the exiled Louis IV to return as king. In 939 he went to help his brother-in-law Herluin II of Montreuil against Arnulf I of Flanders, who retaliated by attacking Normandy. William was excommunicated for destroying several of Arnulf's estates, but he pledged loyalty to Louis IV in 940 and was confirmed in the lands given to his father. He also began the Norman monastic revival, rebuilding Jumièges Abbey on a grander scale.

A peace treaty brokered by Louis IV in 941 limited Norman expansion into Breton lands. On 17 December 942 William was ambushed and killed by followers of Arnulf on an island on the Somme at Picquigny, while attending a peace conference. He had no children with Luitgarde but fathered a son, Richard, with Sprota, his wife more danico. Richard, then aged ten, succeeded him as ruler of Normandy.
william-louis-count-of-nassau-dillenburg: William Louis was born on 13 March 1560 at Dillenburg in Hesse, the eldest son of John VI, Count of Nassau-Dillenburg, and his first wife, Elisabeth of Leuchtenberg. He served as a cavalry officer under William the Silent. On 25 November 1587 he married his cousin Anna of Nassau, daughter of William the Silent and Anna of Saxony and elder sister of Maurice of Nassau. She died less than six months later, on 13 June 1588, and he never remarried. He succeeded as Count of Nassau-Dillenburg in 1606 and also held the stadtholdership of Groningen and Drenthe.

With Maurice, his cousin and brother-in-law, he commanded the Dutch States Army and helped plan the Republic's strategy against Spain from 1588 to 1609. His place in the Military Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries rests on a letter he wrote to Maurice on 8 December 1594. Reading the Tactica of Aelianus Tacticus, who discussed how Roman soldiers armed with sword and spear used the countermarch, he realised that the same movement could serve men with firearms.

In the letter he described drill by which musketeers kept up fire in good battle order: as soon as the first rank had fired it would march to the back, the second rank would fire in turn, then the third and the following ranks, so that by the time the last rank had fired the first had reloaded. He added a diagram to show the movement.

He was nicknamed Us Heit, West Frisian for our father. He died on 13 July 1620 at his home, the Stadhouderlijk hof in Leeuwarden, and was buried in the Grote or Jacobijnerkerk. Leeuwarden honoured him with a statue on its government square.
william-lovett: Lovett's father drowned before he was born. A self-educated man, he moved to London as a young man to find work as a cabinet maker, joined the Cabinetmakers Society and later became its president. He first came to national notice as founder of the Anti-Militia Association, whose slogan was no vote, no musket, and he was active in wider trade unionism through the Metropolitan Trades Union and in Owenite socialism. In 1826 he married Mary Solly of Pegwell in Kent, who supported him in his work; they had two daughters.

After the Reform Act 1832 he joined Henry Hetherington in the War of the Unstamped, the campaign against taxes on newspapers. The London Working Men's Association limited its membership to 100 working men, with 35 honorary members including Feargus O'Connor, and it remained strictly a working-class body, unlike the Birmingham Political Union. Its first aim was education, but the bill of 1838 drew it into Chartism; the bill was signed by Lovett, five other members and six Radical MPs, among them Daniel O'Connell.

When the Chartist Convention moved to Birmingham on 13 May 1839, the authorities broke up gatherings in the Bull Ring, and the Convention's placards called the police a bloodthirsty and unconstitutional force. As secretary Lovett took responsibility and was arrested with John Collins, who had taken the placards to the printer; both were sentenced to twelve months. In prison they wrote Chartism, a New Organisation of the People.

In 1841 he founded the National Association for Promoting the Political and Social Improvement of the People, which was to carry out his New Move of education for poor workers and their children, paid for by a penny a week from signers of the national petition. O'Connor attacked it in the Northern Star, its membership never passed 500, and its hall, opened in 1842, closed in 1857. A believer in temperance and in teaching through kindness, Lovett later kept a bookshop and finished his autobiography, The Life and Struggles of William Lovett. He died poor on 8 August 1877 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.
william-lyon-mackenzie: Mackenzie was born in Dundee on 12 March 1795; both his grandfathers had fought for Charles Edward Stuart at Culloden, and his father, a weaver, died a few weeks after his birth. He emigrated with his friend John Lesslie in 1820 and worked in Montreal, then for the Lesslie family's bookselling and drugstore business in York and Dundas. In 1824 at Queenston he bought a press and founded the Colonial Advocate, refusing government subsidies. On 8 June 1826 rioters wrecked its office and threw its type into the bay; he sued eight of them, and the settlement funded his campaign.

Elected for York County in 1827, he refused to treat or bribe voters and listed his opponents' alleged wrongdoing in The Parliament Black Book for Upper Canada. The assembly expelled him for libel after he called it a sycophantic office; he won the by-election of 2 January 1832 by 119 votes to 1 and was expelled again. In 1834 he won St. David's Ward with the largest vote of any alderman, and the council chose him as Toronto's first mayor by 10 votes to 8. He designed the city's first coat of arms and sat as judge of its Police Court.

After Britain rejected reform in March 1837, he organised vigilance committees across the province and met the Patriote leaders of Lower Canada. When the rebels gathered at Montgomery's Tavern in December, they chose him as leader, and government troops defeated them. In Buffalo, on 11 December 1837, he called for Upper Canadian independence and rallied American support for an invasion, which breached the Neutrality Act. Tried in June 1839, he argued that the Caroline affair meant Britain and the United States were at war, was sentenced to eighteen months and served more than ten before Martin Van Buren pardoned him.

His newspapers in New York failed, and he published two books of documents on corruption among New York officials. Granted amnesty in 1849, he won Haldimand County in 1851, defeating George Brown, and sat until 1858; his motion to abolish the Court of Chancery led Robert Baldwin to resign from the cabinet. He died on 28 August 1861. Historians have found his writing disordered and his politics impulsive. His last home in Toronto became the Mackenzie House museum, and Walter Seymour Allward's monument to him has stood in Queen's Park since 1940.
william-macgregor: MacGregor was born on 20 October 1846 at Hillockhead, in the parish of Towie in Aberdeenshire, the eldest son of John MacGregor, a crofter, and his wife Agnes. He taught at Tillyduke and worked as a farm labourer before his schoolmaster and the local doctor encouraged him to study. He entered Aberdeen Grammar School in 1866 and the University of Aberdeen in 1867, graduating in medicine in 1872 and taking his MD in 1874, and became a medical assistant at the Royal Lunatic Asylum in Aberdeen.

Contemporaries described him as sincere, discriminating and courageous, and he spoke Italian, French and German. As Governor of Newfoundland from 1904 to 1909 he faced a general election that returned two parties in equal number. He refused the premier, Sir Robert Bond, a dissolution before the House had sat; after Bond's defeat in the House he suggested Bond resign, and a second election returned Sir Edward Morris with a good majority. Many authorities approved MacGregor's conduct.

He was appointed Governor of Queensland on 2 December 1909. On 28 June 1913, himself a pioneer of tropical medicine, he opened the new building of the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Townsville, and in August 1913 he chaired the first meeting of the Historical Society of Queensland and became its patron. He retired in July 1914 and was made a privy councillor that year.

In 1883 he had married Mary Jane Cocks, daughter of the harbourmaster of Levuka in Fiji. In retirement he lived at Chapel-on-Leader in Berwickshire. The deaths in 1918 of his son-in-law, Admiral Sir Alfred Paget, and of his daughter Alpina made his last year a sorrowful one. He died after an operation on 3 July 1919 and was buried beside his parents at Towie.

He left his ethnological and ornithological collections to the University of Aberdeen. Specimens gathered in his Papuan years went to the Queensland Museum, a museum in Sydney and the botanical department in Melbourne. The suburbs of MacGregor in Brisbane and Macgregor in Canberra are named after him.
william-marshal-1st-earl-of-pembroke: William was the second son of the Anglo-Norman nobleman John Marshal and Sybilla of Salisbury, born in Wiltshire or Berkshire. When King Stephen besieged Newbury Castle in 1152, he held the boy William hostage to secure John's surrender of the castle. John used the time to reinforce it, and when Stephen threatened to hang the boy, John replied that he still had the hammer and the anvil with which to forge better sons.

As a younger son with no lands to inherit, William was sent at about twelve to the household of William de Tancarville in Normandy, where his training as a knight began. He was knighted in 1166 on campaign in Upper Normandy, and in 1167 he first took part in a tournament, where, in the words of his later biography, he found his calling.

In 1170 Henry II made him tutor-in-arms to his son Henry the Young King, and from 1176 to 1182 William and the prince gained wealth and prestige in tournaments. In late 1182 he was accused of an affair with the Young King's wife, Margaret of France. Thomas Asbridge thinks the charge was probably invented by his enemies. William left the prince's service by early 1183. On returning from the Holy Land he rejoined Henry II and in 1189, covering the king's flight from Le Mans, unhorsed Richard, killing his horse rather than the prince. Richard nonetheless welcomed him at court.

He supported John's claim to the throne in 1199 and helped defend Normandy until 1203. A quarrel followed when he did homage to Philip II in 1204 to keep his Norman lands, and in 1207 he went to Leinster against John's wishes. On the death of John, on 11 November 1216 at Gloucester, the royal council named him protector of the nine-year-old Henry III, with the new title rector regis et regni. At about seventy he led the charge at the Battle of Lincoln in 1217, and after the French withdrawal he reissued Magna Carta.

In early 1219 William fell ill, left the Tower of London for Caversham and entrusted the regency to the papal legate Pandulf Verraccio. He took vows as a Knight Templar on his deathbed, fulfilling a promise made on crusade, and died on 14 May 1219. He was buried in the Temple Church in London, where his stone effigy survives.

His family commissioned The History of William the Marshal, completed by 1226 and rediscovered by Paul Meyer in 1861, which allowed a detailed reconstruction of a man previously a shadowy figure. David Carpenter has called the Battle of Lincoln second only to Hastings as the most decisive in English history.
william-massey: Massey was born on 26 March 1856 into a Protestant farming family at Limavady in County Londonderry. His parents settled in New Zealand in 1862, but he stayed in Ireland for eight more years to finish his schooling, at Limavady National School and in Derry. Arriving on 10 December 1870, he worked as a farmhand before buying his own farm at Māngere in 1876, which earned him the nickname Farmer Bill. In 1882 he married Christina Allan Paul; they had seven children. He was a member of the Orange Order, the Oddfellows and the Freemasons, and held British Israelite ideas.

After losing Franklin to Benjamin Harris in 1893, Massey won a by-election for Waitemata in 1894 and from 1896 held Franklin until his death. As chief whip he held the leaderless conservative opposition together and formally became Leader of the Opposition in September 1903. Against Joseph Ward's Liberals he made gains with charges of corruption and cronyism in the civil service, and in February 1909 he founded the Reform Party from his New Zealand Political Reform League.

Mounted units of the Legion of Frontiersmen, among them the young Bernard Freyberg, rode to Wellington as special constables against the strikers of 1912 and 1913, which made Massey hated on the left and admired by many conservatives. One of his government's first acts enabled some 13,000 Crown tenants to buy their farms. After the 1914 election left Parliament deadlocked he formed a war coalition with Ward in 1915, dissolving it in 1919 and winning a majority alone.
