The root points to divine possession or inspiration and ecstatic divination. In the 11th century Adam of Bremen explicitly linked Wodan with the Latin furor, writing Wodan id est furor.

The Roman historian Tacitus, in his late 1st-century work Germania, recorded that among the gods the Suebi chiefly worshipped Mercury, to whom they offered human as well as other sacrificial victims. Through the interpretatio romana this is generally taken to refer to Odin, with Thor as "Hercules" and Týr as "Mars".

Old English royal genealogies record Woden as an ancestor of the kings of Lindsey, Mercia, Deira and Bernicia, and of Wessex and East Anglia, in seven of the eight genealogies. Only Essex traced its ancestry instead to Saxnot. Some genealogies give his father as Frealaf from the 8th century onward. The Welsh Historia Brittonum of the 9th century also places Woden in the pedigree of Hengist, with the ancestry "filii Frealaf, filii Fredulf, filii Finn, filii Fodepald, filii Geta", Geta being said to be the son of a god other than Yahweh. Other pedigrees reach further back through Geat, Beaw and Sceldi to Sceaf, who is the son of Noah from the Bible.

In such Old English texts the god is treated as a human ancestor of royalty, an approach scholars call euhemerism. Elsewhere in the Germanic world Odin was held to rule war and the dead, and he is depicted wielding a spear.

The modern English weekday Wednesday derives from Old English Wōdnesdæg, "day of Wōden". Cognates occur in Middle Low German and Middle Dutch Wōdensdach, modern Dutch woensdag, Old Frisian Wērnisdei and Old Norse Óðinsdagr, from which come Danish, Norwegian and Swedish onsdag. All derive from Late Proto-Germanic Wodanesdag, a calque of the Latin Mercurii dies, "day of Mercury", seen in Italian mercoledì and French mercredi.

Richard Wagner, in his opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen, called the god Wotan, a spelling of his own invention that combines the Old High German Wuotan with the Low German Wodan. Most forms of the modern religious movement Heathenry venerate him.
wolaita-zone: Wolaita lies about 300 kilometres south of Addis Ababa, bordered by the Omo River on the west, the Bilate River on the east and Lake Abaya on the south-east, with Gamo, Kembata, Hadiya and the Oromia Region as other neighbours. Most of the land lies between 1,500 and 1,800 metres, with Mount Damota rising at its centre. The deep red soils allow two crops a year when the rains are steady, and rain falls in two seasons between March and October. Besides Wolaita Sodo, the main towns include Areka, Boditi, Tebela, Bale Hawassa, Gesuba and Gununo.

The Wolaita count more than 50 kings in four dynasties, who bore the title Kawo. The last Kawo, Tona Gaga, led a resistance that was among the bloodiest campaigns of Menelik II's expansion, and the kingdom was incorporated into the Ethiopian Empire after a battle led by Menelik himself.

Under the Transitional Government of 1991-94 the Wolaita had a region of their own, Kilil 9, which was merged into the Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples' Region in 1995. A plan in 1997 to merge them with neighbouring peoples as WOGAGODA, with a composite language, met fierce opposition and was abandoned; thousands were detained and hundreds killed. Wolaita became a zone of its own in 2000, when North Omo was divided. Its council asked for a referendum on statehood in December 2018. After a first vote in February 2023 was marred by irregularities, the referendum was rerun in the zone on 19 June 2023, and the results placed it in the new South Ethiopia Regional State.

Wolaita Sodo is the capital. The 2007 census counted 1,501,112 people, 96.31% of them Wolayta and most speaking Wolayttattuwa; just over half were Protestants and 43.04% Ethiopian Orthodox. Agriculture supports more than 90% of rural people, with maize, haricot beans, taro, sweet potato, enset and coffee among the main crops. The new year festival Gifaataa is held each September, and the Mochena Borago rock shelter on Mount Damota has late Pleistocene deposits excavated by the University of Florida from 2006 to 2008.
wolf-dietrich-von-raitenau: Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau was born on 26 March 1559 at Hofen Castle in Lochau, near Bregenz in Further Austria. His father was the Habsburg colonel Hans Werner von Raitenau; his mother, Helene von Hohenems, was a niece of Pope Pius IV, a sister of Mark Sittich von Hohenems Altemps, Bishop of Constance, and a sister-in-law of Cardinal Charles Borromeo. He received an ecclesiastical education at the Collegium Germanicum in Rome and joined the Salzburg cathedral chapter in 1578.

On the death of Archbishop George of Kuenburg in 1587, who had been in constant conflict with the chapter, Raitenau was elected as a compromise candidate and ordained by Urban of Trennbach, Bishop of Passau. He continued the harsh Counter-Reformation measures of his predecessors, invited Franciscan and Augustinian friars and in 1589 expelled all Protestants from the city. Later he grew milder and reformed the liturgy and the administration of the archbishopric's lands, which alienated the Roman Curia.

Well read and a follower of Niccolò Machiavelli, he saw himself as a Renaissance prince of an absolutist state, and as a collector and builder he did much to spread Baroque architecture north of the Alps. After fire devastated Salzburg Cathedral on the night of 11 December 1598, the Venetian architect Vincenzo Scamozzi drew plans for its rebuilding, a master plan for the Residenzplatz and the Salzburg Residenz. In 1606 Raitenau built a castle for his mistress Salome Alt, with whom he had fifteen children.

His fall came from a dispute with Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria. In 1609 he refused to join Maximilian's Catholic League, and in October 1611 his forces invaded the Berchtesgaden Provostry, which the House of Wittelsbach also claimed; Bavarian troops then campaigned in Salzburg. Deserted by his chapter and abandoned by Emperor Rudolf II, he was captured fleeing to Carinthia, deposed and imprisoned for life by his nephew and successor, Mark Sittich von Hohenems, first at Hohenwerfen Castle and then in Hohensalzburg, where he died on 16 January 1617. The new cathedral was raised under Mark Sittich, with Santino Solari as architect, and Mark Sittich turned the castle of Salome Alt into Mirabell Palace.
wolfenbuttel: Wolfenbüttel stands on the Oker river near its confluence with the Altenau, about 13 kilometres south of Brunswick and 60 kilometres south-east of Hannover. It lies roughly half-way between the Harz mountains in the south and the Lüneburg Heath in the north. It is the southernmost of 172 towns in northern Germany whose names end in büttel, meaning residence or settlement.

A first settlement, probably on a small islet in the Oker, was founded in the tenth century. It was mentioned in 1118 as Wulferisbuttle, when the Saxon count Widekind of Wolfenbüttel built a water castle on the trade route from Brunswick to Halberstadt and Leipzig. Henry the Lion destroyed it in 1191 and Duke Albert I of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1255, and Albert took it from the House of Asseburg in 1258. The Welf duke Henry I of Brunswick rebuilt the castle from 1283. By 1432 the town was the permanent residence of the princes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.

The Schmalkaldic War devastated it in 1542, and Duke Julius rebuilt it in Renaissance style, with waterways laid out by Hans Vredeman de Vries. He granted the citizens market rights in 1570 and founded the Ducal Library two years later. Danish troops occupied the town in 1626 in the Thirty Years' War, and in June 1641 Swedish forces defeated the Austrians in the Battle of Wolfenbüttel but failed to occupy it. The composer Michael Praetorius was Kapellmeister there in 1604, and Leibniz and Lessing directed the library. The ducal court returned to Brunswick in 1753, and Wolfenbüttel declined in importance.

Wolfenbüttel has about 52,000 inhabitants and is the administrative capital of Wolfenbüttel District. It has the largest concentration of timber-framed buildings in Germany, around 1,000, largely undamaged by the war. The Herzog August Library, founded in 1572, holds about 10,000 manuscripts and is rich in Bibles, incunabula and books of the Reformation. It houses the Codex Carolinus and the Bible of Henry the Lion from 1170. The baroque Schloss Wolfenbüttel is now partly a museum, and the Jägermeister distillery has its headquarters in the town.
wolfgang-amadeus-mozart: Mozart was born on 27 January 1756 at Getreidegasse 9 in Salzburg, the capital of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, an ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire. He was the youngest of seven children, five of whom died in infancy. His father, Leopold Mozart, a native of Augsburg, was a minor composer and an experienced teacher who became deputy Kapellmeister of the Salzburg orchestra in 1763. Mozart was trained on the harpsichord and also became skilled at violin, singing and dancing.

At five he was competent on keyboard and violin, had begun to compose and had performed before European royalty. His father took him on a grand tour of Europe and then three trips to Italy. A fruitless search for employment in 1777 to 1779 led through Paris, Mannheim and Munich and back to Salzburg. While visiting Vienna in 1781 his quarrels with his Salzburg employers came to a head and he was dismissed.

Mozart stayed in Vienna for the rest of his life, achieving fame and some financial success but no long-term security. His early Vienna years produced the opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail, the Great Mass in C minor and the Haydn Quartets. He composed more than a dozen piano concertos there. In 1783 he bought a fortepiano by Anton Walter, which he played often in the city's concerts, and which survives in Salzburg. He lived at the centre of the Viennese musical world and knew Joseph Haydn and some of the court of Emperor Joseph II.

In his final years he wrote the last three symphonies, ending with the Jupiter, the serenade Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the Clarinet Concerto, and the operas Le nozze di Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte and Die Zauberflöte. Biographers rely on about 1500 pages of family letters, early biographies and surviving manuscripts, and they judge the publisher Friedrich Rochlitz untrustworthy, since he published false stories to increase sales.

Mozart died on 5 December 1791 at the age of 35, leaving the Requiem largely unfinished. Publishers soon sought a complete edition of his works. Breitkopf & Härtel and Johann Anton André negotiated with his widow Constanze, and the publication helped rescue her and her two children from poverty. Ludwig Ritter von Köchel completed the first catalogue in 1862, and his numbers, marked K or KV, remain the standard way to identify a work.

His music with Haydn's stands as an archetype of the Classical style, with clarity, balance and transparency as its hallmarks. He almost single-handedly developed the Classical piano concerto. Ludwig van Beethoven, fifteen years his junior, was deeply influenced by his work. Salzburg, which he left in frustration in 1781, has two museums in his former homes, the Salzburg Festival and the International Mozarteum Foundation.
wolfgang-count-palatine-of-zweibrucken: Wolfgang was born on 26 September 1526, the only son of Louis II, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, and of Elisabeth of Hesse, daughter of Landgrave William I of Hesse. When his father died in 1532 he became duke of Zweibrücken as a child, and his uncle Rupert ruled for him as regent until 1543. With Rupert's support the Reformation was introduced in Zweibrücken in 1537. In 1545 Wolfgang married Anna of Hesse, daughter of Landgrave Philip I of Hesse, and they had thirteen children.

In 1548 the Emperor Charles V occupied Wolfgang's Protestant lands and brought back Catholic practice, and Wolfgang regained them only in 1552. Despite the Peace of Augsburg of 1555, several ecclesiastical states in Germany were secularised in 1557, and he obtained a few of them; in the same year the Contract of Heidelberg gave him Palatinate-Neuburg. In 1566 he served as a cavalry officer in the Turkish Wars.

In 1569, during the third of the French Wars of Religion, he came to the aid of the Huguenots with 14,000 mercenaries, an intervention financed in part by Queen Elizabeth I of England. He invaded Burgundy but was killed in the campaign, on 11 June 1569, and was buried at Meisenheim.

His lands were divided among his five sons, from whom three branches descended: Philip Louis founded the House of Palatinate-Neuburg, John that of Palatinate-Zweibrücken and Charles that of Palatinate-Birkenfeld, while Otto Henry and Frederick left no surviving sons. Palatinate-Neuburg inherited the Electorate of the Palatinate in 1685, and its cadet branch Palatinate-Sulzbach Bavaria in 1777. Palatinate-Birkenfeld then inherited both in 1799 and gave rise to the later kings of Bavaria, while a cadet branch of Palatinate-Zweibrücken provided kings of Sweden from 1654, among them Charles X Gustav, a grandson of John.
wolfgang-of-regensburg: Wolfgang came of the family of the Swabian Counts of Pfullingen. After schooling at Reichenau Abbey he followed his friend Henry of Babenberg to Würzburg to hear the Italian grammarian Stephen of Novara. When Henry became Archbishop of Trier in 956 he called Wolfgang there to teach in the cathedral school, and at Trier Wolfgang came to know the reforming St. Maximin's Abbey and the monk Ramuold. After Henry's death in 964 he entered the Benedictine abbey of Einsiedeln and was ordained priest by Ulrich of Augsburg in 968.
At Ulrich's request and the wish of Emperor Otto the Great, he was sent to preach to the Hungarians, who had settled in Pannonia after the Battle of the Lechfeld in 955.

After Bishop Michael of Regensburg died on 23 September 972, Piligrim, Bishop of Passau, obtained Wolfgang's appointment, and he became bishop at Christmas 972. He gave St. Emmeram's Abbey abbots of its own again, ending the bishops' long hold on it as abbots in commendam, and made Ramuold its abbot; many German bishops later followed his example. A supporter of the Gorze reform, he reformed the convents of Obermünster and Niedermünster, founded the convent of St. Paul, Mittelmünster, in 983 and helped renew Niederaltaich Abbey. He accepted Emperor Otto II's plan to reduce his diocese for the new Diocese of Prague, whose first bishop was Dětmar, went with Otto II on the campaign to Paris in 978 and attended the Diet of Verona in 983.
During a dispute between Duke Henry II of Bavaria and Otto II he spent a year at Mondsee in 976 and then lived as a hermit by the lake now called the Wolfgangsee, until a hunter found him.

He fell ill on a journey down the Danube and died in the chapel of Saint Othmar at Pupping on 31 October 994. He was buried in the crypt of Saint Emmeram and canonised in 1052. He is the patron saint of woodcutters, and art shows him with an axe, after the story that he threw it into the forest to find the site of his cell. Michael Pacher's altar at St. Wolfgang honours him, and Otloh of St. Emmeram wrote his life about 1050.
wolfgang-prince-of-anhalt-kothen: Wolfgang was born on 1 August 1492 in Köthen, a prince of the House of Ascania and the second but eldest surviving son of Waldemar VI, Prince of Anhalt-Köthen, and Margarete, daughter of Günther XX, Count of Schwarzburg. In 1500, at the age of eight, he was admitted to the University of Leipzig. When his father died in 1508 he took over the government of the principality, with his residence at Köthen.

Wolfgang met Martin Luther in 1521 and later said that Luther had won his heart. With Luther's help he introduced the Reformation in Anhalt-Köthen in 1525 and in Anhalt-Bernburg in 1526, after the Electorate of Saxony. In 1526 he joined a defensive alliance of Evangelical states against Emperor Charles V, a prelude to the Schmalkaldic League. On 19 April 1529 he was one of the six princes who drew up the Protestation at Speyer, asking the Diet to lift the ban on Luther and his teachings. In 1534 he ordered the first church visitations in Anhalt-Köthen and gave confiscated Catholic church property to the towns.

In 1538 he enlarged the castle at Bernburg with the Wolfgang wing, making it the largest Renaissance castle in northern Germany, and when fire destroyed the old castle of Köthen in 1547 he made Bernburg his permanent seat. Outlawed after the Battle of Mühlberg, he took refuge in Saxony, where Elector Maurice appointed him Governor of Magdeburg in 1551. The Peace of Passau of 1552 released him from the ban.

In 1544 Wolfgang gave up his rights over Anhalt-Dessau in favour of his cousins while keeping Anhalt-Bernburg. In 1562 he signed all his territories over to his cousins, keeping only Coswig, and by 1564 he had moved to Zerbst. He died there on 23 March 1566, unmarried and childless.
wolfgang-william-count-palatine-of-neubu: Wolfgang William was born on 4 November 1578 at Neuburg an der Donau, the son of Philip Louis, Count Palatine of Neuburg, and Anna of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, a daughter of William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. His uncle John William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, had no heirs, and Wolfgang William hurried to secure the duchies for himself. Neuburg was small and weak, surrounded by stronger powers such as Bavaria and the Electoral Palatinate, and the Jülich succession would bring both more land and a richer economy. Though a Lutheran, he travelled to Prague in person to seek the Emperor's support, and he also tried to win France and England, without success.

Wolfgang William negotiated with his main rival for the succession, Johann Sigismund of Brandenburg, and the two agreed to the Treaty of Dortmund in 1609. The treaty broke down when he converted to Catholicism before his marriage to Magdalene of Bavaria in 1613. He later agreed to settle the War of the Jülich Succession with his rival and became the first ruler of Palatinate-Neuburg who was also Duke of Jülich and Berg.

In 1615 he was made a Knight of the Order of the Golden Fleece. Because he kept a strict policy of neutrality in the Thirty Years' War, his territories escaped widespread destruction. In 1636 he moved his residence to Düsseldorf and tried to stabilise and spread Catholicism in his lands. Disputes over church property led in 1651 to the short Düsseldorf Cow War.

Wolfgang William died at Düsseldorf on 14 September 1653, and his son Philip William inherited his lands. He married three times: in 1613 Magdalene of Bavaria, the mother of Philip William; in 1631 Catharina Elisabeth Charlotte of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, daughter of John II, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, whose two children, Ferdinand Philip and Eleonore Franziska, died young; and in 1651 Countess Maria Franziska of Fürstenberg-Heiligenberg, with whom he had no children.
wolfram-von-eschenbach: Little is known of Wolfram's life. No historical documents mention him, and his works are the sole evidence. In Parzival he speaks of wir Beier, meaning we Bavarians, and the dialect of his works is East Franconian. On this and on geographical references the present-day Wolframs-Eschenbach near Ansbach has been officially designated his birthplace, but the evidence is circumstantial, and at least four other places in Bavaria are named Eschenbach. His works point to several possible patrons, most reliably Hermann I of Thuringia, which suggests he served at a number of courts. He often alludes to his own poverty, and in Parzival he states that he is illiterate, a claim that some scholars treat with scepticism and many have credited.

He is best known for Parzival, sometimes regarded as the best of the German Arthurian romances. It is based on Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished Perceval, le Conte du Graal, and is the first surviving German work to treat the Holy Grail, which Wolfram presents as a gemstone. His narrator expresses disdain for Chrétien's version and names as his source a poet from Provence called Kyot.

He also wrote the fragmentary Titurel and the unfinished Willehalm, both after Parzival. Titurel mentions the death of Hermann I, which dates it after 1217, and tells of the lovers Schionatulander and Sigune. Willehalm, based on the Old French chanson de geste Aliscans, is set against wars between Christians and Saracens and survives in 78 manuscripts. His nine surviving songs, five of them dawn-songs, are regarded as masterpieces of Minnesang; no melodies survive.

The 84 surviving manuscripts of Parzival show its popularity over the next two centuries. Many manuscripts of Willehalm include a continuation written in the 1240s by Ulrich von Türheim, and around 1272 a poet named Albrecht, generally presumed to be Albrecht von Scharfenberg, expanded Titurel as the Jüngere Titurel. The modern rediscovery of Wolfram begins with Johann Jakob Bodmer's translation of Parzival in 1753. Richard Wagner drew on it for the libretto of Parsifal, and Wolfram appears as a character in Wagner's Tannhäuser.
wolgast: Wolgast lies in the district of Vorpommern-Greifswald, on the Peenestrom, facing the island of Usedom. A movable bascule bridge known as the Blaues Wunder gives access to the Baltic Sea by road and railway. The town was founded by the Wends on an island in the sound. On the mainland opposite the island with the castle a new planned town was built in the course of the Ostsiedlung, the German settlement eastwards.

The occupation of the region by Wartislaw I, Duke of Pomerania, led to the conversion of Pomerania by Otto of Bamberg in 1128, and thousands of Low German settlers came from Groningen and Drenthe. Wolgast became the seat of a Pomeranian castellany and played an important role in the 12th-century warfare between Pomeranians, Rani and Danes. A Danish-Rani fleet attacked it in 1162, and the Danes attacked again in 1167 and 1168. After a failed assault in 1177 and a campaign in 1179 in which the fleet accepted money instead of a surrender, it came under Danish control in 1185, when the Pomeranian duke accepted Danish suzerainty. It remained a Danish bridgehead after the Danes lost most of Pomerania in 1227.

The date of the German town law is not known, but a letter written in or before 1259 confirms the town, and Duke Bogislaw IV confirmed the Lübeck law in 1282. Wolgast was the capital of Pomerania-Wolgast, an inner partition of the duchy, and its castle was built as a Renaissance residential palace on what is called Castle Island. The ducal line of Pomerania-Wolgast became extinct when Philipp Julius died without issue.

Between the 1670s and the 1720s hundreds of men of the town enlisted in the VOC and emigrated to South Africa. Russian forces burned the town in 1713 during the Great Northern War, in retaliation for Swedish arson in Altona; only the church, four chapels and four other buildings were spared. After the Swedish withdrawal from Pomerania in 1815 the town passed to the Prussian Province of Pomerania, and the last remnants of the palace were removed in 1849. In the 19th century Wolgast prospered as a port for the grain trade.

Most houses of the Old Town date from the 18th and 19th centuries because of the fire of 1713. St Peter's Church, in brick Gothic, was inaugurated around 1415, and St Gertruden Chapel is a 15th-century Gothic building. The painter Philipp Otto Runge was born in the town, and his house is now a museum.
wolin: The town stands on the island of Wolin in the Baltic Sea, off the Polish coast. The Strait of Świna separates the island from Usedom, and the Strait of Dziwna from mainland Pomerania. It has an area of 265 square kilometres, its highest point is Mount Grzywacz at 116 metres, and its forests and postglacial hills surround the Wolin National Park. Its towns are Dziwnów, Międzyzdroje, Świnoujście and Wolin. The ford across the Dziwna on which Wolin lies has been used since the Stone Age.

Excavations show a settlement at the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries, which was then abandoned for about a century. At the end of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century the ground was levelled and a new settlement built, with fortifications from the first half of the 9th century. The Bavarian Geographer, a mid-9th-century document, mentions the Slavic Wolinians with seventy strongholds, and Ibrahim ibn Jakub named the town Weltaba in 965. Around 896 a new port was built and the town received a palisade, a rampart and a retaining wall. Archaeologists believe it was a great trade emporium, stretching four kilometres along the shore and rivalling Birka and Hedeby.

In 967 the island came under Duke Mieszko I of Poland, whose influence ended around 1007. Wolin became known for pirates, and in 1043 the Norwegian king Magnus the Good attacked it. Boleslaw III Wrymouth captured it in the early 12th century, the inhabitants accepted Christianity, and in 1140 Pope Innocent II created a diocese there. In 1185 the dukes of Pomerania became vassals of Denmark, and in 1227 of the Holy Roman Empire. The island accepted Lutheranism in 1535, was captured by Sweden in 1630, passed to Prussia in 1720 and belonged to the German Empire from 1871. In 1945 it became part of Poland and its German-speaking population was expelled.

Some scholars have thought Wolin the basis for the semi-mythical Jomsborg and Vineta, while others, such as Gerard Labuda, reject the identification. Adam of Bremen called the town the largest in Europe, but excavations have found no harbour for the 360 warships he claimed. Its 20 hectares of finds make it the second largest Baltic marketplace of the Viking Age after Hedeby, and Slavs and Scandinavians lived there.

Wolin is the main tourist attraction of north-western Poland. Its sights include the Wolin National Park, the Gothic church of St Nicholas in Wolin, the Regional Museum, the Świnoujście Lighthouse, and the resort of Międzyzdroje. Each year the island hosts a large Germanic-Slavic Viking festival, and its protected traditional drink is the mead Trójniak woliński leśny.
wolter-von-plettenberg: Plettenberg was born at Meyerich Castle in Welver, Westphalia, the first child of Berthold von Plettenberg and Gosteke Lappe. He went to the fort of Narva at ten and joined the Teutonic Order in Riga at about fourteen. He was the Order's trade counsellor in 1481 and commander of Rositten Castle from 1482 to 1488, and in 1489 Grand Master Johann Freytag von Loringhoven made him marshal, the military leader of Livonia. On 30 March 1491 he defeated the Archbishopric of Riga and the city of Riga at Neuermühlen, establishing the Order as the protector of Livonia. He was elected master on 7 July 1494.

When Moscow closed the Hanseatic office in Novgorod in 1494, Livonia drifted towards war. Plettenberg allied with Alexander Jagiellon of Lithuania in the Treaty of Wenden of 1500 and won at the Siritsa River in August 1501 against a Russian army about twice the size of his own, but dysentery, a defeat at Helmet and a failed siege of Pskov followed. At Lake Smolina on 13 September 1502 his 5,000 men beat about 12,000 Russians. The peace of 1503 with Ivan III was renewed in 1509, 1521 and 1531, and he kept Livonia neutral between Poland-Lithuania and Muscovy.

In 1525 he took northern Estonia, including Tallinn, under his direct rule from the Prussian branch of the Order. When the Reformation reached Livonia, he allowed Lutheran services from 1522, so that it was introduced without bloodshed, but he himself remained Catholic and in 1525-1526 refused to secularise the Order, despite pressure from Riga, Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach and the Hanseatic League. He was made a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire in 1526, confirmed by Emperor Charles V in 1530, and named Hermann von Brüggenei his successor in 1532.

He died at Wenden Castle on 28 February 1535, aged about 85; legend says he died in full armour in an armchair by the fire. He is buried in Cēsis at St. John's church. Baltic German and Estonian historians have traditionally considered him one of the most capable and successful leaders in Livonian history. His bust stands in the Walhalla memorial near Regensburg, and reliefs of about 1515 show him with the Madonna at the gateway of Riga Castle.
womens-march-on-versailles: Fear of famine was ever present among the urban poor at the end of the Ancien Régime, and rumours of a Pacte de Famine to starve them were readily believed. After the storming of the Bastille, price inflation and severe shortages were common in Paris, and most workers spent nearly half their income on bread. Calls for a mass demonstration at Versailles had been made before, notably by the Marquis of Saint-Huruge in August. A banquet held on 1 October by the officers at Versailles for the newly arrived Flanders Regiment was reported in firebrand newspapers as a gluttonous orgy.

On the morning of 5 October a young woman struck a marching drum among market women in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine who were infuriated by the shortage and price of bread. More women joined from other markets, many with kitchen blades and makeshift weapons. At the Hôtel de Ville the crowd, perhaps as many as ten thousand, demanded bread and arms. Their aims widened to bringing the king, the court and the Assembly to Paris. They travelled to Versailles in about six hours, dragging cannons from the city hall.

At Versailles Maillard addressed the Assembly, and Maximilien Robespierre spoke in support of the women. A delegation of six women met Louis XVI, who promised food. At about six the next morning protesters found a small palace gate unguarded and entered. A guard was killed and beheaded, a second was struck down wounded, and at least one more was killed. Lafayette reconciled the former French Guards with the royal guards, and appeared with the king on a balcony, where the cry of Vive le Roi went up. He then brought out Marie Antoinette and kissed her hand.

At about one o'clock on 6 October the crowd, grown to over sixty thousand, escorted the royal family and a hundred deputies back to Paris, a journey of about nine hours, some marchers bearing pikes with the heads of the guards.

The royal family settled in the Tuileries Palace, where the king reportedly asked for a history of Charles I of England. The National Constituent Assembly followed within two weeks. Some fifty-six monarchien deputies stayed away, and many, like Jean Joseph Mounier, left the country. Suspicion fell on Louis Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, as an instigator, but an investigation proved nothing. Historians describe the march as a defining moment of the Revolution, which ended the king's independence and made no further open resistance by him possible.
womens-social-and-political-union: The Women's Social and Political Union was founded on 10 October 1903 at the Pankhurst family home, 62 Nelson Street, Manchester. Emmeline Pankhurst, her daughters Christabel and Sylvia and her late husband Richard had been active in the Independent Labour Party. Emmeline felt that it did not serve women, and told a group of its women: Women, we must do the work ourselves. Membership was open to women only and had no party affiliation. In 1905 the group persuaded the Liberal MP Bamford Slack to introduce a suffrage bill, which was talked out; the publicity spurred rapid growth. The journalist Charles E. Hands coined the term suffragette in the Daily Mail in 1906 in derision, and the women embraced it.

In 1906 the WSPU began demonstrations and lobbies of Parliament. Prime Minister Campbell-Bannerman told a delegation to go on pestering, and militancy was established. In 1907 a group of prominent members left to form the Women's Freedom League. In 1908 the WSPU adopted purple, white and green as its colours, and held a Women's Sunday rally in Hyde Park of some 300,000 people. Its newspaper Votes for Women was founded in 1907 by Frederick and Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence.

After Prime Minister Asquith shelved the Conciliation Bill in 1910, the WSPU turned to direct action. A window-smashing on 21 November 1911 led to 160 arrests, and the bill was defeated in March 1912 by 14 votes. Members set fire to postboxes and committed arsons that killed at least five people and injured at least 24. Emmeline Pankhurst claimed responsibility for the bomb at David Lloyd George's house in February 1913 and was sentenced to three years' penal servitude. Imprisoned members hunger-struck and were force-fed, which led to the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913. Emily Davison died at the Epsom Derby in June 1913. Emmeline Pethick-Lawrence was expelled in 1912, and Sylvia Pankhurst's East London Federation in 1914.

On the outbreak of war in 1914 the government released all suffragette prisoners, and Christabel Pankhurst, then in Paris, declared that the WSPU would give patriotic support to the war. It took part in the white feather campaign, and Emmeline Pankhurst led 30,000 women through London in 1915 in a Women's Right to Serve procession. Dissenters included Kitty Marion and Dorothy Evans. In November 1917 Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst dissolved the WSPU in favour of the Women's Party. After the Parliament (Qualification of Women) Act 1918, Christabel lost a Staffordshire seat in the general election by 778 votes, and the party wound itself up in 1919.
wonhyo: Wonhyo was born in Amnyang, modern Gyeongsan, and spent the early part of his career studying under various Korean Buddhist teachers and living at Hwangnyongsa Temple. The hagiographies date his attempted journey to Tang China, made with his friend Uisang to study the Yogācāra teachings of Xuanzang's school, to 661. Sheltering from a storm in the region of Baekje, Wonhyo drank in the night from what he took for a gourd, and in the morning found that the shelter was an old tomb and the vessel a human skull. The experience showed him, the story says, that the world is a creation of the mind.

Wonhyo later left the priesthood after an affair with a princess named Yoseok and spread Buddhism among the common people as a layman, calling himself a Layman of Minor Lineage. He went from town to town teaching through songs and dances, is said to have visited bars and brothels, and slept in the homes of common people; his followers saw this as skilful means. At other times he lived alone in the mountains or along rivers. He became a popular folk hero, and his son Seol Chong became a Confucian scholar of Silla. He died at Hyeolsa in 686, and his son interred his remains at Bunhwangsa.

Wonhyo wrote more than 80 works, of which only a part survives. His most influential commentaries, on the Vajrasamādhisūtra, the Awakening of Faith and the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, were respected throughout Korea, China and Japan, and influenced the Huayan masters Fazang, Li Tongxuan and Chengguan. His central project was the harmonisation of disputes (hwajaeng): instead of ranking Buddhist teachings in a hierarchy, as Chinese commentators such as Zhiyi did, he sought to show that seemingly conflicting doctrines rest on a single deeper truth, and that disputes arise from grasping the literal meaning of words.

At the centre of his thought is the One Mind of the Awakening of Faith, the non-dual source of both samsara and nirvana, on which he wrote nine commentaries. His collaboration with Uisang led to the establishment of the Hwaeom school in Korea.
woodblock-printing: Woodblock printing is a technique used widely throughout East Asia and originating in China in antiquity, first as a method of printing on textiles and later on paper. Each page or image is made by carving a wooden block so that only some areas and lines remain at the original level; these are inked and show in the print. Carving the blocks is skilled and laborious work, but a large number of impressions can then be printed. The earliest surviving examples on cloth from China date to before 220 CE, and printing existed in Tang China by the 7th century.

Inscribed seals of metal or stone, especially jade, and inscribed stone tablets probably inspired the invention. Copies of classical texts on tablets were set up in Luoyang in the Han dynasty for scholars to copy, and ink-squeeze rubbings recorded in the Sui bibliography are believed to have led to early duplication of texts.

Under the Song dynasty, the Directorate of education and other agencies used block prints to disseminate standard versions of the Classics, histories, philosophical works, encyclopaedias and books on medicine and war. From 932 to 955 the Twelve Classics were printed. In 971 work began at Chengdu on the complete Buddhist canon, which needed 130,000 blocks, took ten years to carve and was printed in 983. Block printing made books cheaper, and by the eleventh century their price had fallen to about a tenth. Even so, the historian Endymion Wilkinson notes that it never supplanted manuscripts, which remained dominant in imperial China, and elite scholars often preferred them.

Printing spread early. The Great Dharani Sutra, found at Bulguksa in South Korea in 1966, dates between 704 and 751. In Japan Empress Shōtoku ordered a million copies of a dhāraṇī sutra around 770. In Korea the Goryeo Daejanggyeong, carved again from 1237 after the first blocks burned in the Mongol invasion of 1232, was finished in 1248 with 81,258 blocks. In Japan in the Edo period, woodblock printing produced illustrated books and ukiyo-e prints.

Woodblock printing spread across Eurasia by 1000 CE. The Islamic world used a block technique called ṭarsh from 900 to 1444, mostly for protective amulets, and it reached Muslim Spain in the 10th century. In India it became chiefly a method of printing textiles. In Europe the technique was used for textile patterns by the mid-14th century and for images on sheets by the end of that century, and block books appeared in the mid-15th century. In East Asia it remained the most common way of printing books until the 19th century.
woodes-rogers: Woodes Rogers was the eldest son of Woods Rogers, a successful merchant captain who held shares in many ships. He spent part of his childhood in Poole before the family moved to Bristol, and in November 1697 he was apprenticed to the Bristol mariner John Yeamans. He completed his apprenticeship in November 1704 and the following January married Sarah Whetstone, daughter of Rear Admiral Sir William Whetstone, and in 1706 his father died at sea, leaving him the family's ships and business. He also took part in the Atlantic slave trade, and continued to do so for the rest of his life.

During the War of the Spanish Succession, William Dampier proposed a privateering voyage against Spain, and Rogers led it in the frigates Duke and Duchess, leaving Bristol on 1 August 1708. He put down a mutiny, kept his crews from scurvy with limes, captured Guayaquil for a modest ransom and took the Spanish ship Nuestra Señora de la Encarnación y Desengaño off Mexico, being wounded in the face. His brother was killed in the Pacific. The investors roughly doubled their money, but Rogers was sued by over 200 of his crew and forced into bankruptcy. His book A Cruising Voyage Round the World sold well, partly because of Selkirk's story.

As governor of the Bahamas, Rogers arrived on 24 July 1718; the pirate Charles Vane escaped his trap, but Nassau and New Providence were secured. On 9 December 1718 he tried ten captured men, and eight were hanged. A Spanish attack in February 1720 withdrew in the face of two frigates and 500 militia. Unpaid for his outlay on defences, he sailed for Britain in March 1721, found a new governor appointed and was imprisoned for debt.

Rogers helped the author of A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates, which made him a national hero again. George I granted him a pension, and George II reappointed him governor. In his second term he dissolved the colonial assembly when it objected to a local tax. He died in Nassau on 15 July 1732. Piracy expelled, commerce restored remained the motto of the Bahamas until independence in 1973.
woodlark-island: Woodlark Island is the main island of the Woodlark Islands archipelago in the Solomon Sea. The wider group also takes in Madau, Boagis, Nusam and Nanon to the west, Nubara to the east and the Marshall Bennett group to the south-west. Inhabitants of some other islands in the province call it Murua. The island has a volcanic core of Tertiary age and a wide belt of limestone formed mainly by corals, and coral reefs are still active around its shores.

A quarry at Tubukuia mountain was an important source of stone for Suloga axes, which were traded as far west as the Gulf of Papua. An extinct marine gharial, Gavialis papuensis, lived on the island in the Pleistocene or Holocene and was presumably hunted to extinction by the first human settlers.

The island takes its English name from the Australian whaling ship Woodlark under Captain George Grimes, which called in the 1830s. Other whalers came for water and wood, and islanders sometimes served in their crews. In 1841 all but one of the surviving crew of the wrecked whaler Mary were killed there. The Pontifical Institute for Foreign Missions sent five priests and two brothers in 1852, and Giovanni Battista Mazzucconi was killed in 1855 by an islander named Avicoar who opposed the mission.

Richard Ede and Charles Lobb, traders from the nearby Laughlan Islands, found gold in 1895. In 1896–97 some 400 white miners and 1,600 Papuan labourers produced 20,000 ounces of gold. The anthropologist Fred Damon estimated that the population fell from about 2,200 at first European contact to between 700 and 900 by about 1915. On 30 June 1943, in Operation Chronicle, the United States 112th Cavalry Regiment landed on Woodlark, and Seabees of the 60th Naval Construction Battalion built an airbase at Guasopa Bay.

The people speak Muyuw, an Austronesian language of the Kilivila–Louisiades group. An unofficial count in 2010 put the population at around 6,000, with the largest settlements at Kulumadau and Guasopa and the largest village at Kaulay. Ebony logging has been an important source of income since the 1970s, and a plan to turn 70% of the island over to palm oil was dropped after islanders opposed it.
woodrow-wilson: Thomas Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia, the son of Joseph Ruggles Wilson, a Presbyterian pastor, and Jessie Janet Woodrow. Before he was two the family moved to Augusta, Georgia. After a PhD in history and political science at Johns Hopkins University he taught at Bryn Mawr College from 1885 to 1888, where his 1887 article The Study of Administration argued that public administration should be a field of study of its own. In June 1902 the trustees of Princeton University made him its president. He raised admission standards, introduced academic departments and groups of students guided by preceptors, and worked to keep African Americans out of the school. He served as governor of New Jersey from 1911 to 1913.

In the 1912 election Wilson defeated President William Howard Taft and the former president Theodore Roosevelt, and became the first Southerner elected president since Zachary Taylor. In April 1913 he addressed Congress in person to set out his New Freedom programme. Its early measures included the Revenue Act of 1913, which began the modern income tax, and the Federal Reserve Act. His administration intervened often in Latin America, sending troops to occupy the Dominican Republic and intervene in Haiti, and in his first year he authorised the widespread imposition of racial segregation in the federal bureaucracy.

The United States declared neutrality when the First World War began in 1914, and Wilson was narrowly re-elected in 1916 on the slogan He Kept Us Out of War. After Germany began unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917 and the Zimmermann Telegram became public, he asked Congress in April 1917 for a declaration of war. He issued the Fourteen Points, which the Allies and Germany accepted as a basis for peace. He led the American delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, the first incumbent president to travel to Europe, and secured the League of Nations as part of the Treaty of Versailles. At home he rejected a Republican compromise that would have let the Senate ratify the treaty and join the League.

Wilson had a stroke in October 1919 that left him incapacitated, and his wife and his physician controlled access to him. Republicans won the 1920 election in a landslide. He died in February 1924 at the age of 67. Historians have criticised him for supporting racial segregation, while crediting his administration with the Federal Reserve, the Federal Trade Commission and the graduated income tax, and regarding him as a key figure in the making of modern American liberalism.
woody-guthrie: Woodrow Wilson Guthrie was born on 14 July 1912 in Okemah, a small town in Okfuskee County, Oklahoma. His parents, Nora Belle Sherman and Charles Edward Guthrie, named him after Woodrow Wilson, then Governor of New Jersey and the Democratic candidate who won the presidency that autumn. His father was a businessman who owned up to thirty plots of land in the county and stood as a Democratic candidate for local office. Guthrie left Okemah in 1929, after his mother, who suffered from Huntington's disease, was institutionalised, and followed his father to Pampa, Texas. He married Mary Jennings in 1933 and they had three children.

During the Dust Bowl, Guthrie left his wife and children in Texas and joined the thousands of migrants who went to California in search of work. In Los Angeles he became known on the radio station KFVD as a performer of hillbilly music and traditional folk music with his partner Maxine Crissman, known as Lefty Lou, and he began to write the protest songs of his later album. He befriended Will Geer and John Steinbeck and wrote a column for the communist newspaper People's World from May 1939 to January 1940. The station's owners were uncomfortable with his politics after he wrote a song praising the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, and he left for New York.

There the folk music community embraced him. He made several hours of recordings of conversation and song for the folklorist Alan Lomax at the Library of Congress, and recorded Dust Bowl Ballads for Victor Records. In February 1940 he wrote This Land Is Your Land in response to the overplaying of Irving Berlin's God Bless America. He took its melody from an old gospel song, and did not record it until April 1944. Throughout his life he was associated with communist groups, although there is no evidence that he was a member.

By the late 1940s Guthrie's health was declining and his behaviour was erratic. He received various diagnoses before it was determined in 1952 that he had Huntington's disease, inherited from his mother. He died of its complications at Creedmoor Psychiatric Center on 3 October 1967, and his remains were cremated and scattered at sea. In the folk revival of the late 1950s and 1960s a new generation took up his songs, among them Bob Dylan, who visited him in hospital. His son Arlo Guthrie became a musician. The Woody Guthrie Archives, the largest collection of his material, are held at the Woody Guthrie Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
worcestershire: Worcestershire is a largely rural ceremonial county of 1,741 km2 in the West Midlands of England. The River Severn flows through its centre from north to south across a wide plain, and the River Avon passes through Evesham. The Malvern Hills in the south-west hold Worcestershire Beacon, the county's highest point at 425 m, a small part of the Cotswolds lies in the south-east, and part of the Wyre Forest in the north-west. Besides Worcester, the main settlements are Kidderminster, Redditch, Bromsgrove, Evesham and the spa town of Malvern.

The area was first populated at least 700,000 years ago, became largely agricultural in the Bronze Age, and was dominated by hill forts in the Iron Age. In Roman times Droitwich, called Salinae, was probably the most important settlement because of its salt. The area became the heartland of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the Hwicce, was absorbed by Mercia during the 7th century, and was made a shire in the early tenth century to defend the estates of the See of Worcester and of abbeys such as Pershore, Westminster and Evesham. It became part of the unified Kingdom of England in 927.

The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded that in seven of the twelve hundreds the Crown had no authority, which was held by the bishop and abbots. In 1263 Worcester's Jewish residents were attacked by a baronial force and most were killed. Simon de Montfort was killed at the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265. In 1642 the Battle of Powick Bridge was the first major skirmish of the English Civil War, and the county, on the Royalist front line, suffered heavy taxation and the pressing of men. Clubmen bands formed to keep the war from their localities. The Battle of Worcester in 1651 was the last major engagement of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.

In the 19th century Worcester made gloves and porcelain, Kidderminster carpets, and Redditch needles, springs and hooks, while Droitwich Spa produced salt, as it had since Roman times. Malvern became a spa town because its water was believed to be very pure. The county holds Berrow's Journal, founded in 1690 and said to be the world's oldest continually published newspaper. The composer Edward Elgar was born at Broadheath, and Tolkien wrote that any corner of the county was home to him. Its boundaries changed several times: in 1974 it was merged with Herefordshire, and it was re-created as a county on 1 April 1998.
workers-party-of-ethiopia: The Derg, a committee of low-ranking officers and enlisted men, overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974, abolished the monarchy and declared itself socialist. Its Soviet backers pressed it to create a civilian vanguard party. Mengistu Haile Mariam, chairman from 1977, at first argued that none was needed, but growing armed opposition changed his view, and in December 1979 he formed the Commission for Organizing the Party of the Working People of Ethiopia, COPWE, as a temporary vanguard party, alongside mass organisations such as the Revolutionary Ethiopia Youth Association. By 1983 COPWE had about 50,000 members and some 6,500 cells, and 79 of the 123 members of its Central Committee were soldiers.

The party was founded on 12 September 1984, the tenth anniversary of the revolution, and replaced COPWE. Its Politburo of eleven, seven surviving Derg members including Mengistu and four civilian ideologues and technocrats, became the chief decision-making body, and the Central Committee grew to 183 members, with congresses every five years. Mengistu's wishes generally prevailed, and the Politburo served more as his mouthpiece than as a real governing body. Loyalty to the Derg counted for more than Marxist–Leninist conviction in admitting members. Nationally the membership leaned towards soldiers and towards peoples such as the Tigray and Amhara that had favoured a unified Greater Ethiopia, though civilians and other groups held many regional and local posts.

The constitution of 1987 dissolved the Derg and made the party the formulator of the country's development and the leading force of state and society, giving it more power than the government itself and local leaders almost free rein.

By the late 1980s Ethiopia had been ravaged by droughts and by the Derg's mismanagement, and world communism was in decline. Soviet support ended in 1990, multi-party politics spread across Africa and armed insurrection grew in the Ethiopian Civil War. Mengistu fled the country a week before the rebels took power in 1991. The Transitional Government of Ethiopia dissolved the party in May 1991, and most of its leaders were imprisoned for crimes alleged against them. An attempt to register a party of the same name was rejected in August 2022.
world-health-organization: International cooperation on disease began with the International Sanitary Conferences, the first of which met in Paris on 23 June 1851 and which continued until 1938. The first was almost solely concerned with cholera. With the causes of epidemic diseases still disputed, agreement was hard to reach: seven conferences over 41 years were convened before any produced a multi-state agreement. The seventh, at Venice in 1892, finally resulted in a convention on the sanitary control of shipping through the Suez Canal, and in 1897 a convention on bubonic plague was signed by sixteen of the nineteen states attending.

The conferences led to the founding of the Pan-American Sanitary Bureau in 1902 and the Office International d'Hygiène Publique in 1907, and the League of Nations created its own Health Organization in 1920. After World War II, the United Nations assembled the health organizations to form the WHO. The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 and began its work on 1 September 1948, taking over the assets and duties of the League's Health Organization and the Paris office, including the International Classification of Diseases.

The organisation is governed by the World Health Assembly, made up of its member states, which elects an executive board of 34 health specialists, selects the director-general and approves the budget. Its funds come mainly from member states, and then from private donors. The headquarters in Geneva was designed by the Swiss architect Jean Tschumi and inaugurated in 1966. Its regional divisions were created between 1949 and 1952, following the model of the Pan American Health Organization, and it has six regional offices and 150 country offices.

The organisation played a leading role in the eradication of smallpox, the near-eradication of polio and the development of an Ebola vaccine. It launched its Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988, working with Rotary International, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and UNICEF, and helped to reduce cases by 99%. In the 1970s it dropped its commitment to a global malaria eradication campaign as too ambitious. Since the late 20th century, new actors in global health such as the World Bank and the Gates Foundation have weakened its role as coordinator, and it also coordinated the international response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
world-trade-organization: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was set up by a multilateral treaty of 23 countries after World War II, alongside other new institutions for economic cooperation such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. A proposed International Trade Organization never started, because the United States and other signatories did not ratify its treaty, so the GATT slowly became a de facto international organisation, operating for almost half a century as a provisional, semi-institutionalised treaty regime. Seven rounds of negotiation between 1949 and 1979 first cut tariffs. The Kennedy Round of the mid-sixties produced an anti-dumping agreement, and the Tokyo Round of the seventies made the first major attempt to tackle barriers that were not tariffs.

The eighth round, the Uruguay Round, was launched at Punta del Este in September 1986. It extended the system to services and intellectual property and reformed trade in agriculture and textiles. Its Final Act, the Marrakesh Agreement, was signed on 15 April 1994, and the WTO was established on 1 January 1995, with its headquarters in Geneva.

The WTO provides a framework for negotiating trade agreements and for settling disputes among its members. Its agreements cover goods, services and intellectual property, and rest on non-discrimination, expressed in the most-favoured-nation and national treatment provisions, with exceptions for purposes such as environmental protection and national security. Its highest body, the Ministerial Conference, usually meets every two years and decides by consensus. The General Council, made up of representatives of all members, handles day-to-day business, and a Secretariat led by a Director-General administers the organisation.

Unlike the GATT, whose rules were ambiguous and which let members block dispute settlement, the WTO has more numerous and more precise obligations, and members that do not comply may face punishment. Its consensus rule has also contributed to deadlock. Ministerial conferences have sometimes been contentious: the Seattle conference of 1999 provoked large demonstrations, and Doha in 2001 approved China's entry.

The Doha Development Round, launched in November 2001, aimed to make globalisation more inclusive and to cut barriers and subsidies in farming. Talks stalled over differences between developed nations and major low-income and lower-middle-income countries, and over agricultural subsidies in the European Union and the United States. The Hong Kong conference agreed to phase out agricultural export subsidies, and the Bali Ministerial Declaration of 2013 addressed bureaucratic barriers to commerce. Economic studies generally find that the WTO has boosted trade and reduced trade barriers. Critics argue that the benefits of free trade are not shared equally, that its agreements may disadvantage developing countries and that commercial interests have been put before environmental and labour concerns.
world-wide-web: Tim Berners-Lee was motivated by the problem of storing, updating and finding documents and data files in CERN, a large and constantly changing organisation, and of distributing them to collaborators outside it. In his design he rejected the tree structure used in the existing CERNDOC documentation system and in the Unix filesystem, as well as approaches that tagged files with keywords, as in the VAX/NOTES system. He adopted instead concepts he had put into practice in his private ENQUIRE system of 1980. Learning of Ted Nelson's hypertext model of 1965, in which documents are linked in unconstrained ways through hot spots embedded in the text, helped confirm that his concept was sound.

A competing system, Gopher, was created in 1991 around a hierarchical model of menus that held pointers to documents and to other menus, whereas a document on the Web holds both its content and its links. Gopher grew at first, with nearly seven thousand servers known by April 1994, but then declined while the Web accelerated. Its more rigid structure, bad early publicity and the decision not to follow open collaboration principles were among the reasons.

The Internet and the Web are not the same thing. The Internet is a global system of interconnected computer networks, while the Web is a collection of documents and other resources linked by hyperlinks and URLs and fetched with the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The usual document is a web page written in Hypertext Markup Language, which supports text, images, audio, video and scripts as well as links. A browser requests a page from a web server, and in the 1990s following links from page to page came to be called browsing or web surfing.

The prefix www in many web addresses follows the old practice of naming a host after the service it provides, as ftp or news were. No standard requires it. According to Paolo Palazzi, who worked at CERN with Berners-Lee, its popular use was accidental: the project page was meant to sit at www.cern.ch, with info.cern.ch as CERN's home page, but the records were never switched, and others copied the practice. The first web server was nxoc01.cern.ch.

Links break as pages are moved or replaced, a phenomenon called link rot, and the Internet Archive, active since 1996, is the best known of many efforts to archive websites. Archie, an index of FTP files released in 1990, was the first search engine. In December 2007 Unicode passed ASCII and Western European encodings as the most used character map on the Web.
worlds-parliament-of-religions: In 1893 Chicago hosted the World Columbian Exposition, and so many people were coming from all over the world that smaller conferences, called Congresses and Parliaments, were scheduled alongside it. The World's Parliament of Religions was an initiative of the Swedenborgian layman and judge Charles Carroll Bonney. Another principal organiser was the Unitarian minister Jenkin Lloyd Jones, and the clergyman John Henry Barrows was appointed first chairman of the General Committee. It was by far the largest of the congresses held with the Exposition.

The Parliament opened on 11 September 1893 at the World's Congress Auxiliary Building, now the Art Institute of Chicago, and ran to 27 September. It was the first organised interfaith gathering. Swami Vivekananda introduced Hinduism at the opening session. Initially nervous, he began with the words Sisters and brothers of America, and the crowd of thousands gave him a standing ovation that lasted two minutes. Anagarika Dharmapala of Sri Lanka represented what was then called Southern Buddhism, and Soyen Shaku attended from Japan. The Jain scholar Virchand Gandhi spoke so coherently that the Buffalo Courier reported his lectures were heard with close attention.

Other speakers included the Reform rabbi Kaufmann Kohler and Gaston Bonet-Maury, a Protestant historian. Islam was represented by Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb, a convert, and Theosophy by William Quan Judge and Annie Besant. Henry Jessup was the first to discuss the Baháʼí Faith publicly in the United States. Absent were the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who were not invited, Native American religious figures, Sikhs and other Indigenous and Earth centered religionists, who were not represented until the 1993 Parliament.

The 1893 Parliament had a lasting effect, and it is recognised as the birth of the worldwide interfaith movement. It inspired Sarah Farmer to dedicate her camp at Greenacre in Eliot, Maine, to peace. In 1894 representatives of at least seventeen faiths gathered there and raised what is believed to be the world's first peace flag, and Vivekananda and Dharmapala visited to teach.

The Parliament of the World's Religions was incorporated in 1989 to organise a centennial conference, held in 1993 at the Palmer House hotel in Chicago. More than 8,000 people attended, and a document, Towards a Global Ethic, mainly drafted by Hans Küng, set its tone. The 14th Dalai Lama gave the keynote address on the closing day. Later Parliaments met in Cape Town in 1999, Barcelona in 2004 and Melbourne in 2009, and the Parliament has been headquartered in Chicago.
woyzeck: The play is loosely based on the true story of Johann Christian Woyzeck, a Leipzig wigmaker who later became a soldier. In 1821, in a fit of jealousy, he murdered Christiane Woost, a 46-year-old widow with whom he had been living, and he was later publicly beheaded. Georg Büchner left his play in a fragmentary state when he died in February 1837, and it was first made public only through a heavily edited and augmented version by Karl Emil Franzos, who published it in periodicals and then in his edition of Büchner's collected works.

Franz Woyzeck is a lonely soldier stationed in a provincial German town, living with Marie, the mother of his child, who was born out of wedlock. He earns extra money by doing menial jobs for the Captain and by taking part in medical experiments conducted by the Doctor, who tells him that he must eat nothing but peas. His mental health breaks down, and he begins to experience apocalyptic visions. Marie turns her attention to a handsome drum major.

Woyzeck confronts the drum major, who beats and humiliates him, and then stabs Marie to death by a pond. The fragment as Büchner left it ends with Woyzeck disposing of the knife in the pond while trying to clean himself of the blood. Some scholars, notably A. H. J. Knight and Fritz Bergemann, hold that a trial scene was part of the original conception, and what may be the start of a courtroom scene survives. Franzos inserted the stage direction "ertrinkt" (he drowns), an emendation that Knight said almost amounts to a forgery, though most versions still use drowning as the ending.

Franzos struggled with Büchner's microscopically small handwriting, and the pages had faded so badly that they had to be chemically treated to make the text readable. He misread the title character's name in the manuscripts as Wozzeck, and the play bore that title in its first productions. It was first performed at the Residenztheater in Munich on 8 November 1913, produced by Max Reinhardt. A new edition by Georg Witkowski in 1921 introduced the corrected title Woyzeck.

Woyzeck has become one of the most influential and most often performed German plays. Because it is unfinished, productions have taken liberties with the order of scenes, and each arrangement makes a different statement. Alban Berg made an opera from it in 1925. Ingmar Bergman directed a stage version at the Royal Dramatic Theatre in Stockholm in 1969, and Werner Herzog directed a film in 1979. Later productions reset the story in a psychiatric hospital, in an army of 1951 and in a distribution centre.
wroclaw: Wrocław lies on the banks of the Oder in the Silesian Lowlands, at an elevation of around 105 to 156 metres, and is supplied within the city limits by four tributaries: the Bystrzyca, Oława, Ślęza and Widawa. It is the capital of the Lower Silesian Voivodeship, created in 1999, and a major transport hub on routes between Western and Central Europe and the rest of Poland.

A place called Budorigum, at or near the site, appears on Claudius Ptolemy's map of 142 to 147 CE. The Ślężans, a West Slavic tribe, built a fortified gord on Ostrów Tumski. The city became part of the Piast-ruled Polish state in the late 10th century, and the Diocese of Wrocław was founded in 1000 under the Archbishopric of Gniezno. From the 13th century migration from German-speaking regions contributed to its growth, and German gradually became its predominant language. In the 14th century it passed to the Bohemian Crown.

The Reformation reached the city in 1518, but from 1526 Silesia was ruled by the Catholic House of Habsburg. During the Thirty Years' War the city lost thousands of inhabitants to plague. In 1811 the Viadrina university of Frankfurt an der Oder was moved to Breslau and united with the Jesuit university, forming what is now the University of Wrocław. It became part of the German Empire in 1871. In November 1939 the Germans imprisoned 173 Polish professors from Kraków's universities in the city before deporting them to Sachsenhausen. After 1945 it became part of Poland, and its German inhabitants who had not fled were expelled between 1945 and 1949.

Wrocław is the third-largest city of Poland and the historical capital of Silesia, with over 130,000 students. Its Market Square is one of the largest in Europe, and its Town Hall is the oldest preserved in Poland. The Centennial Hall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Old Town, with Brick Gothic and Baroque buildings, is on Poland's list of national monuments. The Wrocław Zoo is the oldest in Poland, and the city has been the seat of a Catholic archdiocese since the diocese of 1000.
wu-ding: Wu Ding, whose personal name was Zi Zhao, is the earliest figure in Chinese history mentioned in contemporary records. Later historians had thought the annals of the Shang dynasty little more than legend until oracle bone inscriptions from his reign were unearthed at his capital Yin, near modern Anyang, in 1899. They have been radiocarbon dated to 1254 to 1197 BCE, give or take ten years. The Shang practised succession by agnatic seniority, and before him succession had been split between two lines. His predecessors were three of his uncles, among them Pan Geng, who moved the capital to Huanbei, and then his father Xiao Yi. A tradition says he was sent away from the capital in his father's reign.

Sima Qian's Shiji lists him as the twenty-second Shang king, while the inscriptions record him as the twenty-first. Chapter XXI of the Book of Documents describes him staying silent at the start of his reign, even after three years of mourning, in order to cultivate his virtue. He first appointed his former tutor Gan Pan chief minister. After Gan Pan died, the chancellor was Fu Yue, whom he found, according to the Shiji and the Shangshu, after Heaven told him in a dream to expect such a man. His realm grew far larger than his ancestors', but control of distant lands was nominal, and he delegated power to regional lords who paid tribute, harvest portions and military support.

Oracle bones record wars with the fang peoples. According to the Bamboo Annals, in his thirty-second year he sent troops against the Guifang and after three years annexed them. A Shang force of up to thirteen thousand fought Ba under the command of Fu Hao, but Ba stayed independent. Women held greater official power than in later periods: his consort Fu Hao was a military commander, and Fu Jing seems to have overseen agriculture.

He died in the fifty-ninth year of his reign according to all sources, none of them contemporary. His year of death is unknown, with opinions ranging from 1197 to 1180 BCE and 1192 BCE commonly accepted. Tomb 1400 at Xibeigang is very likely his grave. Later tradition regarded him as one of the most esteemed Shang kings. Subsequent kings honoured him on the ding day, and he received the temple name Gaozong. His descendants addressed him as Grandfather Ding and Ancestor Ding. More than half of all Shang inscriptions date from his reign, and the earliest oracle bone script on tortoise plastrons and ox scapulae, with divination about war, human sacrifice and the economy, was unearthed at Yinxu.
wu-guang: Wu Guang was born in Yangxia, in present-day Taikang County in Henan, and his courtesy name was Shu. In the reign of the Second Qin Emperor, in August or September 209 BCE, he and Chen Sheng were military captains ordered to lead 900 soldiers to Yuyang, south-west of present-day Miyun County near Beijing, to help defend the northern border against the Xiongnu. Storms made it clear that they could not reach Yuyang by the deadline, and under the law soldiers who failed to reach their posts on time were executed.

Believing themselves doomed, the two captains led their men into rebellion. They announced that Fusu, the crown prince of Qin who had been wrongly forced to commit suicide, and Xiang Yan, a general of Chu, were alive and joining their cause, and they proclaimed the restoration of Chu. People who felt deeply oppressed by the Qin regime joined them quickly. Against the advice of Zhang Er and Chen Yu, Chen Sheng declared himself King of Rising Chu and set up his capital at Chen County, in present-day Huaiyang, Henan.

Chen Sheng made Wu Guang acting King of Chu and sent him west toward Qin proper. His forces became bogged down besieging Xingyang, in Henan. His generals feared that Qin reinforcements under Zhang Han would soon arrive and attack them from two sides, and they wanted to end the siege and face Zhang Han directly. Doubting that Wu Guang would change his plans, they assassinated him and took over the army. In later Chinese and Taoist temples he sometimes appears as a door god, usually paired with Chen Sheng.
wu-peifu: Wu Peifu was born on 22 April 1874 in Shandong and received a traditional Chinese education. He later joined the Baoding Military Academy and became a professional soldier who rose quickly, joining the New Army, renamed the Beiyang Army in 1902, which the modernising Qing general Yuan Shikai had created. After the fall of the Qing in 1911 and Yuan's failed attempt to proclaim himself emperor, power in China passed to regional military leaders. In 1915 Wu became commander of the 6th Brigade.

After Yuan's death in 1916 the Beiyang Army split into hostile factions, including Duan Qirui's Anhui clique, Zhang Zuolin's Fengtian clique and the Zhili clique of Feng Guozhang. When Feng died in 1919, Cao Kun took the Zhili leadership with Wu's support. Wu then helped build an alliance against the Anhui clique, signing a draft treaty in November 1919 with representatives of Tang Jiyao and Lu Rongting at Hengyang. When fighting broke out in July 1920, as commander-in-chief he outflanked the enemy and attacked its headquarters. The Anhui army crumbled within a week and Duan Qirui fled to the Japanese settlement at Tianjin.

The Zhili and Fengtian cliques then shared power until they quarrelled over the premiership and over Wu's anti-Japanese stance. In the first Zhili–Fengtian War, from April to June 1922, Wu feigned a retreat, trapped the western wing of the Fengtian army and forced Zhang Zuolin to retreat towards Shanhaiguan, giving Zhili control of Beijing. In 1923 Wu used troops to break a strike on the Hankou–Beijing railway, killing 35 workers, which badly damaged his standing with the Chinese public.

In the second war with Fengtian, called the Jade Marshal and widely expected to win, Wu saw his ally Feng Yuxiang desert the front and seize Beijing in a coup, and he was defeated near Tianjin. He kept a base in Hubei and Henan until the Kuomintang's Northern Expedition of 1927 forced him to withdraw to Zhengzhou.

Wu never held political office during his years as a warlord. After the Second Sino-Japanese War began he refused to cooperate with the Japanese. In 1939, invited to lead a puppet government in North China, he said he would do so only if every Japanese soldier left China, and then returned to retirement. He went to a dentist in December 1939 with a toothache, had a tooth extracted, and died two weeks later, ostensibly of sepsis.
wu-qi: Wu Qi first sought military office in the state of Lu. Accounts of his early career say that, to calm the doubts of the ruler he served, he killed his own wife, and that when officials slandered him he had them killed or forced them to flee. In the service of Wei he was appointed Protector of the West River, a post he later left.

In 384 BCE King Dao of Chu made him prime minister of the State of Chu. There he reorganised and modernised the administration of the state, work that earned him many enemies at court, and his career and life ended in 381 BCE.

The Wei Liaozi, a military treatise of the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE, preserves stories that show his view of command. On the eve of a battle his subordinates offered him a sword, and he refused it, saying that banners and drums, the means of leading and directing troops, were all a general required: to command the troops and direct their blades was the commander's role, and to wield a single sword was not.

In another story a soldier broke ranks before a battle, charged the enemy line, killed two men and came back with their heads. Wu Qi had him put to death at once, and when his officers protested that the man was a fine warrior he answered that he was, but that he had disobeyed orders. Like Sun Tzu in The Art of War, Wu Qi placed discipline and obedience above individual bravery, treating the general as the brain of the army and the soldiers as its limbs.

He and Sun Zi are often named together, as Sun-Wu, as military strategists of similar standing. Two books on war were said to be by Wu Qi, but one was lost, leaving the Wuzi, one of the Seven Military Classics, as the only surviving record of his military thought.
wu-sangui: Wu Sangui was born on 8 June 1612 in Suizhong, in northeastern China, to Wu Xiang and Lady Zu; his ancestral home was Gaoyou, Jiangsu. His father and uncle had fought in many battles, and the young Wu took an early interest in war and politics. In 1627 he became a first-degree military scholar at fifteen, and he and his brothers joined the army of the general Zu Dashou. In 1630 he rode with about twenty men into a Manchu encirclement to rescue his father, killing the Manchu general, and became a guerrilla general before the age of twenty.

Wu rose to full general of Ningyuan in 1639 and built a force of 20,000 troops, with an elite battalion of 1,000 as his bodyguard. In the Ming defeat at Songshan in August 1641 52,000 members of the Ming elite army died; Wu escaped by a main road the Manchus had left lightly held, and was demoted three ranks in May 1642 rather than executed. In early 1644 the Chongzhen Emperor called him to defend Beijing against Li Zicheng, but Beijing fell on 25 April and the emperor killed himself, so Wu held Shanhai Pass instead.

Li Zicheng seized Wu's family, including his father Wu Xiang and his concubine Chen Yuanyuan. Wu killed Li's envoy and asked the Manchu regent Dorgon for help. Li defeated Wu on 21 May, and the next day Wu accepted Dorgon's terms. On 22 May 1644 he opened the pass to the Qing, and their combined forces defeated Li on 27 May. Li executed thirty-eight members of Wu's household, and the Manchus entered Beijing. Wu was made Prince Who Pacifies the West, suppressed rebels in Shaanxi and Sichuan, and in 1662 sent an army into Burma that captured and killed the Yongli Emperor of the Southern Ming.

Wu ruled Yunnan, and later Guizhou, with little interference and with large subsidies from the Qing court, which he spent on his army. When the Kangxi Emperor decided in 1673 to dissolve the three vassal states of Wu, Shang Kexi and Geng Jingzhong, Wu rebelled on 28 December 1673. By April 1676 his side held eleven provinces, but he halted south of the Yangzi for three months, and his allies surrendered one by one.

In 1678 he declared himself emperor of the Great Zhou and died in October. His grandson Wu Shifan continued the struggle until the revolt was defeated in December 1681. In Chinese folklore Wu Sangui is regarded as a traitor, his name a byword for betrayal, while his story with Chen Yuanyuan is a classic love story.
wu-state: Wu was a state of the Western Zhou and the Spring and Autumn period that lay outside the Zhou cultural sphere. It was also known as Gouwu or Gongwu, from the pronunciation of the local language. It stood at the mouth of the Yangtze, east of Chu and south of Qi, and its territory reached north to Xuzhou and Lianyungang, west to the Dabie Mountains and south to Lake Tai. Its first capital was Meili, in modern Wuxi, then Helü's City, and later Gusu, probably modern Suzhou. Sima Qian recorded a founding myth: Taibo, eldest son of Gugong Danfu, and his brother Zhongyong left Zhou so that their youngest brother Jili, father of King Wen, could inherit, and settled in Wu.

Wu rose in the 6th century BCE with the help of Jin, which found it a useful ally against Chu. In 584 BCE it rebelled against Chu on the advice of Wuchen, a Jin minister who had defected from Chu. Wu Zixu, whose father and brother King Ping of Chu had murdered, fled to Wu and helped Prince Guang assassinate King Liao and take the throne as King Helü. In 506 BCE Helü led the army against Chu with his brother Fugai, Wu Zixu and Sun Tzu, and defeated a strong Chu army at the Battle of Boju. King Zhao of Chu fled to Sui and the Wu army captured the Chu capital, Ying. Wu defeated Qi in 484 BCE.

Chu then aided the rise of Yue, Wu's southern neighbour. Wu captured the Yue king Goujian, but King Fuchai of Wu let him live as his servant and then return home. While Wu campaigned in the north, Goujian attacked in 482 BCE and took the capital. Wu could not recover, and Yue absorbed the state in 473 BCE. Fuchai's sons were exiled, and their descendants took Wu as their clan name.

Wu is generally regarded as having developed the first Chinese navy, with classes of ships described in a dialogue between Helü and Wu Zixu preserved in the Yuejueshu. Wu and Yue were masters of metallurgy, and their swords, with a high proportion of tin, bore inscriptions and inlay.
