Sima Qian wrote that the people of Wu wore their hair short and tattooed their bodies, and its language differed from the Old Chinese of the central states. Wu is still a name for the region around Suzhou and Shanghai and for Wu Chinese, and was used by Eastern Wu of the Three Kingdoms and by Wu and Wuyue of the Ten Kingdoms.
wu-taibo: Taibo is a posthumous name, meaning literally Great Senior (Amongst Brothers), a reference to his yielding of the throne. His personal name is unknown, though as a son of King Tai of Zhou his surname was almost certainly Ji, and because he founded Wu he is sometimes called Wu Taibo. His birth and death dates are unknown; he is placed around 1150 BCE. According to Sima Qian he was born into the Ji clan of predynastic Zhou and had two younger brothers, Zhongyong and Jili.

King Tai wished his youngest son Jili to inherit power, so Taibo and Zhongyong travelled south-east and settled at Meili, in present-day Jiangsu Province. There Taibo and his followers set up the State of Wu, with Meili as its capital. Wang Chong's Lunheng records that he joined local society by cutting his hair and tattooing his body, and that the people of Wu then wore hats and belts after his appearance.

Dong Zhongshu records in the Chunqiu Fanlu that Taibo ruled with a moral and charismatic authority comparable to that of Shangdi. During his rule he is said to have developed irrigation, encouraged farming and dug the Taibo River, known today as the Bodu River.

On the death of King Tai, Taibo returned to Mount Qi, where the Zhou had moved. King Ji tried to abdicate in his favour, and when Taibo declined he tried twice more. At the third refusal Taibo declared that, having cut his hair and tattooed his body like the people of Wu, he was a mutilated person who could not enter a ritual hall, and King Ji desisted.

Taibo died without an heir and passed the throne to his brother Zhongyong. His shrine was set up at what is now Meicun; the original wooden building was destroyed in later wars and has been renovated several times, and most of the present structure dates from the Qing dynasty. A stone carved with Confucius's comment on him still stands there. The Analects has a chapter named after him, and he is customarily held to be the ancestor of all people with the surname Wu.

His grand-nephew, King Wu of Zhou, overthrew the Shang dynasty at the Battle of Muye and afterwards made Zhouzhang, a great-grandson of Zhongyong, King of Wu. Envoys of the Cao Wei and Jin dynasties to Japan recorded that the Wajin people claimed descent from Taibo, and several scholars have suggested that the Yamato people and the imperial dynasty descend from the Wu ruling clan.
wu-zetian: Wu Zetian was born in 624, and her personal name was Wu Zhao. Her birthplace is not documented, and scholars place it variously at Wenshui, at Lizhou in modern Sichuan, or at the capital Chang'an. She was first a concubine of Emperor Taizong, who gave her the art name Wu Mei, meaning glamorous. By early 650 she was a concubine of Emperor Gaozong, with the title Zhaoyi, the highest ranking of the nine concubines of the second rank. Gaozong was inexperienced and often incapacitated by dizzy spells, and he was named heir only because of the disgrace of his two older brothers.

In 655 Wu became Gaozong's empress consort, and in 656 the heir apparent Li Zhong was deposed in favour of her son Li Hong. In 657 she and her allies took reprisals against officials who had opposed her elevation: several chancellors were sent to remote prefectures, and in 659 Zhangsun Wuji was exiled and forced to commit suicide. After Gaozong suffered a debilitating stroke in 660 she effectively administered the empire for him until his death in 683, and she then became empress dowager and regent. Her third son, Li Zhe, took the throne in 684 as Zhongzong for about six weeks.

In 690 she had Emperor Ruizong yield the throne to her, proclaimed the Zhou dynasty and became emperor, and she is remembered as the only undisputed female sovereign in Chinese history. Her de facto rule lasted 45 years. She institutionalised the use of informants and enforced stringent legal measures, purged members of the Tang royal house and veteran officials of earlier administrations, and reformed the civil service to promote merit. She patronised Buddhism, literature and the arts and campaigned against Turkic and Tibetan incursions. Her rule formed part of the High Tang period, a peak in China's political power and cultural influence, though her later governance became increasingly autocratic and extravagant.

Wu was removed in the Shenlong Coup, which abolished the Zhou dynasty and restored the Tang, and she died on 16 December 705, a few months later. Traditional historians believed that she had killed her own children, but these rumours seem to have surfaced 400 years after her death and probably owed much to the belief that a woman was unfit to hold imperial power. Chinese writers call her Wu Hou as empress, and Wu Zetian, her posthumous title, is the name by which she is generally known.
wu-zhou: Before taking the throne Wu Zhao had long held power. From 655 she presided over court meetings in the name of her husband, Emperor Gaozong, and after his death she ruled through her sons, who reigned as puppet emperors while power lay in her hands. In 690 she deposed Emperor Ruizong of Tang and proclaimed herself huangdi of the new dynasty, naming it after the ancient Zhou dynasty, from whom she believed herself descended.

The capital was Luoyang, renamed Shendu, the Divine Capital. Buddhism and Daoism were the state religions, and both served the empress's propaganda: she claimed to be an incarnation of Maitreya, Buddhist clergy produced texts foretelling a female universal ruler, and she had 100,000 copies of The Great Spell of Unsullied Pure Light, which also predicted a female monarch, printed and distributed. In Daoist temples she placed statues of Laozi's mother as Sage Mother, a title she took herself.

Her reign began and continued with extensive violence, secret police and a network of informers; historians debate how far accounts of it are exaggerated and how much was needed for her survival against the old noble clans of the northern China plain. She expanded the civil service examinations, opening them to men of all classes, and reduced the power of the old official class. Late in her reign her lovers, the two Zhang brothers, brought corruption into government. Court officials killed them, she abdicated the next day, and her son Emperor Zhongzong of Tang was restored in the Shenlong Coup of 705.

Traditional Chinese historiography treats the dynasty as part of the Tang, since Wu had been a Tang empress consort, was buried in the Qianling Mausoleum and was its only ruler. Its lasting marks include the emphasis on merit-based examinations, large parts of the Longmen Grottoes and a body of literature: sixty-one essays under her name are in the Quan Tangwen and forty-six poems in the Complete Tang Poems, and the Zhuying ji anthology published in this period influenced later Tang poetry.
wu-zixu: Wu Zixu, whose given name was Wu Yun, was the second son of Wu She, Grand Tutor to Crown Prince Jian of Chu. When King Ping of Chu kept for himself a Qin princess chosen as his son's bride, the corrupt official Fei Wuji persuaded him that Wu She and the prince would rebel, and the king had Wu She executed. Forced to write summoning his sons to the capital, Wu She drew the elder, Wu Shang, to die with him, while Wu Zixu fled. The accounts of his life in the Records of the Grand Historian and other classics differ, showing the influence of folklore.

Pursued with Prince Jian's son, Prince Sheng, he was sheltered near Zhaoguan, the last pass before Wu, by the physician Donggao Gong; legend says his hair turned white from the strain, and the change helped him escape. In Wu he became adviser to Prince Guang and helped him assassinate King Liao of Wu, after which the prince ruled as King Helü. In 506 BCE he joined the invasion of Chu with Helü, his brother Fugai and Sun Tzu. After the victory at the Battle of Boju he exhumed King Ping's corpse and gave it 300 lashes, and he was made Duke of Shen.

Under King Fuchai he was distrusted, while the minister Bo Pi, bribed by Yue, was heeded. Ordered to kill himself, he asked that his eyes be hung on the city gate so that he could watch Yue take the capital; ten years later King Goujian of Yue conquered Wu.

Wu Zixu became a model of loyalty in Chinese culture and is worshipped in eastern China as Taoshen, God of the Waves, long held to be the god of the tidal bore of the Qiantang River. Some believe the Dragon Boat Festival first commemorated him rather than Qu Yuan, though his cult as a water deity can be traced only to the Han dynasty. In 2006 a memorial to him was completed in Suzhou.
wuchang: Wuchang is the oldest of the three cities that merged into modern Wuhan, the capital of Hubei Province. It stood on the right (southeastern) bank of the Yangtze River, opposite the mouth of the Han River. The other two cities, Hanyang and Hankou, were on the opposite bank, separated from each other by the Han. The name Wuchang remains in common use for the part of urban Wuhan south of the Yangtze, although administratively that area is split between several districts. The historic centre lies in the modern Wuchang District, which has an area of 82.4 square kilometres.

In 221 the warlord Sun Quan moved the capital of Eastern Wu to È county and renamed it Wuchang, literally prospering from military, for its role in supplying the military bases set up before the Battle of Red Cliffs. He proclaimed himself emperor of Eastern Wu in 229 and moved the capital to Jianye. Sun Hao, emperor from 264 to 280, moved it back to Wuchang in 265.

The name of the town switched between Wuchang and Jiangxia several times over the following centuries. After 1301 the Wuchang prefecture, headquartered in the town, became the capital of Hubei province. The Wuying Pagoda, the oldest standing building in Hubei, was built around the time of the fall of the Southern Song dynasty. During the Taiping Rebellion the area changed hands several times after the Taiping captured the city in the Battle of Wuchang in 1852.

At the end of the Qing Empire, Wuchang was the seat of the Huguang Viceroyalty, which combined Hubei and Hunan and was among the most important in the empire alongside Nanjing and Guangzhou. It had an arsenal, a mint and ironworks for rails. Though closed to foreign trade and residence, it held a considerable number of Catholic and Protestant missionaries within its walls. The population of the cities on both banks was estimated at 800,000 around 1911.

On 10 October 1911 the New Army stationed in the city started the Wuchang Uprising, a revolt against the Qing dynasty. Now called Double Ten Day, it was the catalyst of the Xinhai Revolution, which led to the Republic of China. In 1912 the Wuchang prefecture was abolished and a new Wuchang county was created. In 1926 the town was promoted to a city and merged with Hankou and Hanyang to form Wuhan. After 1949 the urban part was divided into the Wuchang, Qingshan and Hongshan districts, and in 1995 the rural remainder, still called Wuchang County, became Jiangxia District of Wuhan.
wuchang-uprising: China's defeat by Japan in 1895 divided intellectuals. Reformers initiated the Hundred Days' Reform, which failed after the Wuxu Coup by Empress Dowager Cixi. Revolutionary groups emerged, and in 1905 leaders such as Sun Yat-sen and Song Jiaoren met in Tokyo and formed the Tongmenghui.

Unrest was heightened by a railway crisis. In 1910 the Qing court, short of money partly because of indemnity payments after the Boxer Protocol, adopted the policy of Sheng Xuanhuai to secure foreign loans by nationalising railway lines. Resistance, strongest in Sichuan, grew into the Sichuan Railway Protection Movement. In September 1911 the Viceroy of Sichuan arrested its leaders and ordered troops to fire on protesters, and troops were diverted to Sichuan from central China, which later helped the uprising to succeed.

In the Wuhan area two groups, the Wenxueshe led by Jiang Yiwu and the Gongjinhui led by Sun Wu, negotiated with the Tongmenghui from September 1911. The uprising planned for 6 October was postponed. On 9 October a bomb Sun Wu was preparing in the Russian concession at Hankou exploded and injured him. Hospital staff identified him and alerted the Qing authorities. The revolutionaries in the New Army at Wuchang faced arrest, and Jiang Yiwu decided to rise at once. The plot leaked to the Viceroy of Huguang, Ruicheng, who arrested and executed several members.

On the evening of 10 October Wu Zhaolin, as provisional commander, led the revolutionary soldiers in a mutiny against the Qing garrison. They captured the viceroy's residence and strategic points after intense fighting, and Ruicheng fled. On 11 October the mutineers set up a Hubei military government and persuaded the officer Li Yuanhong to head it. On 12 October they took Hankou and Hanyang. The Qing court called on Yuan Shikai and the Beiyang Army, who retook Hankou on 1 November and Hanyang on 27 November before Yuan began to negotiate secretly with the revolutionaries.

The uprising surprised many revolutionary leaders. Sun Yat-sen was in the United States seeking funds and learned of it from a newspaper. By the end of December 1911 eighteen provinces had agreed to secede from the Qing. Sun returned and was elected provisional president. On 1 January 1912 representatives declared the Republic of China, and he was sworn in. After negotiations with Yuan Shikai, Empress Dowager Longyu announced the abdication of the child emperor Puyi on 12 February 1912, which ended the Qing dynasty after almost three centuries. Taiwan commemorates 10 October as the National Day of the Republic of China.
wuffa: The East Anglian dynastic tally in the Anglian collection names Wuffa as the son of Wehha and the father of Tytila. His name is a diminutive of the Old English word for wolf, and the dynasty's name, Wuffingas, means literally the kin of Wuffa; the family ruled the East Angles until 749. The kingdom had grown from migrants who arrived in south-east Suffolk from the area now known as Jutland, and it was bounded by the North Sea, by forests to the south and by the Fens to the west.

Bede regarded Wuffa as the first king of the East Angles and called him the grandfather of Rædwald. The Historia Brittonum, written a century later, instead names a Guillem Guercha as the first king and Uffa as his son. The 19th-century historian Sir Francis Palgrave held that Guercha was a distortion of Wuffa's own name, but D. P. Kirby concluded that the Historia meant Wehha. The 13th-century chronicler Roger of Wendover has Wuffa ruling from 571 to 578, though the origin of this information is unknown; the historian Michael Wood places his rule around 575.

It has been suggested that Wuffa's dynasty may have come from a Germanic people known as the Warni, and he has been identified with the King of the Angli whose sister, according to the Byzantine scholar Procopius, was betrothed to a 6th-century Warni prince called Radigis.

For lack of documentary evidence scholars cannot say whether Wuffa really lived, and the identity of the first East Anglian king cannot be known with certainty. The historian Martin Carver has argued that he is best regarded as an emblematic figure drawn from a royal origin myth. Later East Anglian kings claimed their right to rule through descent from him, as the kings of Kent claimed descent from Oisc. He is believed to have founded the Suffolk village of Ufford, a name commonly read as Uffa's ford.
wuffingas: The Kingdom of East Anglia, whose land today forms the English counties of Norfolk and Suffolk, was founded by peoples migrating from northern Europe during the 5th and 6th centuries. The main sources for its royal genealogy, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Bede's Ecclesiastical History, were compiled long after the kingdom was formed, and a 9th-century pedigree of Ælfwald in the Anglian collection traces his descent from the god Wōden. The Historia Brittonum names Wehha, father of Wuffa, as the first of the line, which perhaps places the dynasty's origins in the middle of the 6th century.

Bede gave Rædwald's father as Tytil and his grandfather as Wuffa, and the 13th-century chronicler Roger of Wendover gave dates of 571 and 578 for their accessions. Wuffa is thought to mean little wolf, which would make the dynastic name mean kin of the wolf, the same in origin as the Wulfings of Beowulf and Widsith. Parallels between the Sutton Hoo burials and the Swedish burials at Vendel led some historians, among them Rupert Bruce-Mitford, to propose a Scandinavian origin for the dynasty; others regard this as unproven.

Nothing is known of the dynasty's members before Rædwald, who ruled from about 599 and is the first East Anglian king known to have ruled. Ecgric also belonged to the house, though his descent is not settled: he may have been Sigeberht's brother or step-brother. The last Wuffing king was Ælfwald, who died in 749. The Viking invasions of the 9th century and the Dissolution of the monasteries in the 16th destroyed many documents of the dynasty's rule.

The land between the Orwell and the watersheds of the Alde and Deben may have been an early centre of royal power, based at Rendlesham or Sutton Hoo, two early medieval cemeteries on the tidal estuary of the River Deben, 11 km from the North Sea. In the early 7th century Gipeswic, modern Ipswich, began to grow as a centre of foreign trade, Botolph's monastery at Iken was founded by royal grant in 654, and Bede named Rendlesham as the site of Æthelwold's royal dwelling.

By the end of Ælfwald's reign East Anglia held a group of church centres closely tied to the dynasty: the sees at Dommoc and Helmham, the foundations at Ely and Dereham made by daughters of Anna, the minster at Blythburgh and the monastery Sigeberht founded before he abdicated and died in battle. After 749 the kingdom was ruled either by the kings of Mercia or by kings whose genealogy is not known. The author Sam Newton has argued that Beowulf may have been composed in Ælfwald's reign, and in 1997 the Eastern Angles Theatre Company performed The Wuffings, a play by Kevin Crossley-Holland and Ivan Cutting, on a beach near Sutton Hoo.
wuhan: Wuhan lies in east-central Hubei, on the eastern Jianghan Plain, where the Han River flows into the Yangtze. The two rivers divide the urban area into three districts, Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang, known together as the Three Towns of Wuhan. The name joins Wu, for Wuchang, and Han, for Hankou, whose name means Mouth of the Han. The city has long been called the Nine Provinces' Thoroughfare, and its position has also exposed it to flooding.

The Wuhan area has been settled for about 3,500 years. Panlongcheng, an archaeological site associated mainly with the Erligang culture, lies in Huangpi District. In the Han dynasty Hanyang became a fairly busy port, and walls were built to protect Hanyang in 206 and Wuchang in 223, the latter marking the foundation of Wuhan. In 223 Sun Quan, leader of the Eastern Wu, ordered the Yellow Crane Tower built on the Wuchang side, one of the Four Great Towers of China.

On 10 October 1911 the Wuchang Uprising, launched by followers of Sun Yat-sen, led to the collapse of the Qing state, ending 2,000 years of dynastic rule. In 1927 the Kuomintang government moved its capital from Guangzhou to Wuhan and combined Wuchang, Hankou and Hanyang into Wuhan City. Wuhan was briefly a capital again in 1937, as a provisional wartime capital, and in 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, it was the site of the Battle of Wuhan. After 1949 the Communists rebuilt its war-damaged industry, and Wuhan Iron and Steel opened in 1958.

Wuhan is the capital of Hubei and the largest city in the province. It is a major transport hub and the centre of Central China, with institutions such as Wuhan University and the Huazhong University of Science and Technology.
wujing-zongyao: Emperor Renzong of Song sponsored the compendium because he was concerned that many officials were unfamiliar with the military classics, and partly in response to the Song dynasty's war with the Tanguts of Western Xia. He also wrote its preface. The chief editor, Zeng Gongliang, was a government official rather than a general, and the historian Lorge takes this to mean the book was likely written for other officials. Much was copied from older works whose authors go unnamed; Ralph D. Sawyer calls it "essentially a cut-and-paste job".

The book divides Chinese warships into six categories, among them tower ships, covered swoopers and sea hawk ships, a typology that reappeared in naval texts for centuries. Its illustrations of ships were copied into the Wubei Zhi of about 1628 and into Japanese works as late as Kanazawa Kanemitsu's Wakan Senyōshū of 1766.

Its three gunpowder formulas are for a bomb launched from a trebuchet, a similar bomb with hooks to catch on wooden structures, and a poison-smoke bomb. The low-nitrate powder of the time burned rather than exploded, and the book also describes fire arrows shot from bows or crossbows and the swallow-tail incendiary lowered onto besiegers from city walls. It gives the oldest illustration of a Chinese flamethrower, a brass tank with a double-acting piston pump that shot a continuous blast of flame, with instructions for its use and repair. For the compass, a thin leaf of iron cut like a fish was heated red-hot, quenched with its tail pointing north and floated on water, so that its head pointed south.

It is one of 347 military treatises the History of Song lists for the Song period, and one of very few to survive. The original copy in the Imperial Library was lost when the Jurchens sacked Kaifeng in 1126, and only a few manuscripts remained, since the government allowed few people to read it. A new edition was made in 1231, and the whole work was reprinted in 1510, the oldest copy extant, which Joseph Needham judged the most faithful to the original. Late in the Ming dynasty Fan Jingwen wrote a continuation, the Xu Wujing Zongyao, because he felt the reprints in circulation were out of date.
wulfhere-of-mercia: Wulfhere was the son of Penda of Mercia, who was killed on 15 November 655 at the Battle of Winwaed, fighting Oswiu of Northumbria. Oswiu divided Mercia, keeping the north under his own control and giving the south to Penda's son Peada, who was murdered at Easter 656. Oswiu then ruled all Mercia himself. Bede describes Wulfhere as a youth at his accession, so he was probably in his middle teens. In 658 three Mercian leaders, Immin, Eafa and Eadbert, rebelled against the Northumbrians, and according to Bede they had kept Wulfhere in hiding; when the revolt succeeded he became king.

Wulfhere was the first Christian king of all Mercia, though the date and circumstances of his conversion are unknown. Bede says that, free under their own king, the Mercians gave willing allegiance to Christ. Wulfhere invited Bishop Wilfrid to Mercia in 667-69 when a bishop's services were needed, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he endowed the monastery at Medeshamstede, now Peterborough. He married Eormenhild, a daughter of King Eorcenberht of Kent.

In 661 he harried Ashdown in West Saxon territory and raided the Isle of Wight, which he gave, with the territory of the Meonware, to his godson King Æthelwealh of the South Saxons. He ordered the priest Eoppa to baptise the islanders. London, where Wulfhere sold the see to Wine between 665 and 668, lay in the lands of the East Saxons, whose kings Sigehere and Sæbbi ruled under him. A charter of 673-675 shows him confirming a grant in Surrey. By the early 660s he was the effective overlord of Britain south of the Humber, though not of Northumbria. The Tribal Hidage may date from his reign, though other origins have been suggested.

In 674 Wulfhere attacked Oswiu's son Ecgfrith of Northumbria. According to Stephen of Ripon's Life of Wilfrid, he had stirred up all the southern nations against the Northumbrians, but Ecgfrith defeated him, forced him to surrender Lindsey and made him pay tribute. In 675 Æscwine, one of the kings of the West Saxons, fought him at Biedanheafde; where the battle was and who won it are not known. Wulfhere died later in 675, probably of disease, in his mid-thirties.

His brother Æthelred succeeded him and reigned for nearly thirty years. Æthelred recovered Lindsey a few years after his accession but could not keep the domination of the south that Wulfhere had achieved. Modern historians consider that the rise of Mercia to primacy began in Wulfhere's reign. Eormenhild is thought to have become abbess of Ely. Stephen of Ripon described Wulfhere as a man of proud mind and insatiable will.
wulfred: Nothing is known of Wulfred before 803, when he attended a synod on the staff of Archbishop Æthelhard. He probably came from a wealthy noble family of Middlesex with lands at Hayes, Harrow and Twickenham, though earlier historians thought him Kentish. He was archdeacon of Christ Church, Canterbury, was named archbishop-elect at a synod on 26 July 805 and was consecrated on 3 August 805 or later that year. He may have owed his elevation to Mercia's dominance over Kent at the time.

Modelling his reform on that of Bishop Chrodegang of Metz, Wulfred required the cathedral clergy to eat together, hand their property to the chapter and keep the canonical hours, and by 813 he claimed to have rebuilt the community. Whether the clergy became canons or remained monks is unclear. He granted lands to the chapter on condition that it kept the new standards.

His dispute with King Coenwulf of Mercia turned on whether laymen could control monasteries, above all the Kentish houses of Reculver and Minster-in-Thanet. In 814 he travelled to Rome to see Pope Leo III. The king deprived him of authority for some years, six by Canterbury's own account of 825, though four is perhaps more likely, and Wulfred and his community answered with embassies to the pope and forged charters. Around 820 Coenwulf forced an unfavourable settlement on him. Relations improved under Ceolwulf, whom Wulfred consecrated king in September 822, and a council at Clofesho under King Beornwulf settled the matter in Wulfred's favour in 825.

Wulfred died in 832, probably on 24 March, leaving most of his wealth to his kinsman Werhard, who was to pass the lands to Christ Church. After Egbert of Wessex took Kent his relations with the new rulers were cold. The question of lordship over monasteries was finally settled at Kingston in 838. He was the first archbishop to put his portrait on his coins, which never named the Mercian king. The historian N. P. Brooks judged from the poor Latin of the charters of his time that the clergy of the cathedral were not very literate in Latin.
wunu-mountain: The mountain, whose name means mountain of Five Women, rises north of Huanren Town in Huanren Manchu Autonomous County, northwest of the Hun Jiang River. Its highest point, the Main Peak, reaches 821 metres and its summit measures 1,500 metres long and 300 metres wide. The site holds the elements of a defensive city: a wall, a temple, a palace, a barn, barracks and a water source, which allowed a garrison to stay on the mountain for long periods. The present name comes from a Chinese legend that five women of the Tang dynasty defended the mountain against foreign invaders.

People lived on the mountain long before Goguryeo: archaeologists have found remains dating to the late Neolithic, more than 4,500 years ago, among them weapons and tools. According to the Samguk Sagi, Goguryeo was founded on the mountain in 37 BCE, and the mountain city remained its capital until King Yuri moved the court to Gungnae Fortress in 3 CE. The Gwanggaeto Stele calls the city Holbon fortress and the Book of Wei Heulseunggol fortress; under Unified Shilla it was recorded as Jolbon fortress.

The identification is not accepted by everyone. Some scholars argue, from the description of the fortress in the time of King Daemusin, that Yuri's Gungnae was not the fortress at Ji'an, that the move to Ji'an came only under King Sansang, and that Jolbon was Nahap Fortress at the meeting of the Fu'er and Hun rivers. Others point out that the Samguk Sagi says Jumong first lived in a thatched house near the river, having no means to build a palace. In 1424 Li Manzhu, the third chief of the Jianzhou Jurchens, built defences on the southern side of the mountain.

The mountain was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2004, with the ancient cities of Gungnae and Hwando, as part of the Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom. It is also a national tourist site.
wupper: The Wupper rises near Marienheide in the western Sauerland and runs through the mountainous Bergisches Land before it enters the Rhine at Leverkusen, south of Düsseldorf. Its upper course is called the Wipper. Both names are related to the word for weave and refer to the river's twisting course. In Wuppertal, whose name means Wupper Valley, a suspension railway runs for 10 kilometres above the river. Near Müngsten, between Remscheid and Solingen, the river is crossed by the highest railway bridge in Germany, and a few kilometres further downstream Burg Castle stands on a hill above it.

From the 15th century the Wupper and its many streams gave rise to hundreds of workshops, mills and factories on their banks. Water was first used for dyeing, bleaching and washing canvas and cloth, and later to power machines or carry away waste. The river thus supported the early industrial growth of Wuppertal in the 18th, 19th and early 20th centuries. The Wupper Valley was one of the world's first industrialized regions and helped to empower the Ruhr valley as a coal-mining region.

On 21 July 1950 a young elephant named Tuffi, put on the suspension railway by her handler as an advertising stunt, panicked, burst out of the car and fell or jumped into the river, injuring herself only slightly. Marguerita Eckel and Ernst-Andreas Ziegler published a children's picture book about the incident in 1970, Tuffi und die Schwebebahn. The river also appears in German speech: the saying Über die Wupper gehen, literally to go over the Wupper, means going bankrupt, going to jail or dying. Else Lasker-Schüler wrote a drama titled Die Wupper.
wurzburg: Würzburg is the second-largest city in Franconia after Nuremberg and spans both banks of the Main river. A Bronze Age refuge castle, the Celtic Segodunum and later a Roman fort stood on the Leistenberg, where Fortress Marienberg now stands. Alamanni settled the area in the 4th or 5th century and Franks followed in the 6th and 7th. A Merovingian duke had his seat there from about 650, and Irish missionaries including Kilian Christianized it in 686. A donation of 1 May 704 mentions the place as Virteburch.

The bishops of Würzburg built a secular lordship that reached into Eastern Franconia in the 12th century, and the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg is dated 1168 to 1803. The city hosted several Imperial Diets, including that of 1180, which banned Henry the Lion. Charlemagne consecrated a first church on the cathedral's site in 788, and the present Romanesque cathedral was built from 1040 to 1225. The University of Würzburg was founded in 1402 and re-founded in 1582 by Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn. In 1400 the bishop's troops defeated the citizens at the Battle of Bergtheim, and the city stayed under his control. Jews were massacred in 1147 and 1298.

In the Peasants' War, about 8,000 peasants were killed outside the city on 4 June 1525. The council member Tilman Riemenschneider refused to fight them and was imprisoned and tortured at Marienberg with the entire council. Between 1626 and 1631, under Bishop Philip Adolf, an estimated 600 to 900 alleged witches were burnt, until King Gustaf Adolf of Sweden invaded. The Residence was begun in 1720. The city passed to Bavaria in 1803, became a grand duchy in 1805 and joined the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1814. In 1817 Friedrich Koenig and Andreas Bauer founded a maker of steam-driven printing presses there.

On 16 March 1945 about 90 per cent of the city was destroyed in 17 minutes by 225 British Lancaster bombers, and a firestorm killed some 5,000 people. Over the next twenty years the historic buildings were carefully reconstructed, at first largely by the women known as Trümmerfrauen. About 130,000 people live in the city, whose dialect is East Franconian. Its rebuilt old town and the Würzburger Residenz are cultural heritage, the Residence being a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wurzburg-residence: The Prince-Bishops of Würzburg lived in the Marienberg Fortress until the early 18th century. Johann Philipp Franz von Schönborn (1719–1724) moved the court to a palace built in 1701–1704, but thought it too small for an absolute monarch and wanted something comparable to Versailles or Schönbrunn. He financed a new building with 600,000 florins won in a court case in the year of his accession, and was supported by his uncle Lothar Franz von Schönborn, Archbishop of Mainz, and his brother Friedrich Carl von Schönborn, Imperial Vice-Chancellor in Vienna. The foundation stone was laid on 22 May 1720, and building began with the north block.

Balthasar Neumann, court architect of the Bishop, was the principal architect, working with Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt and Maximilian von Welsch and with Robert de Cotte and Germain Boffrand. Building stopped under Prince-Bishop Christoph Franz von Hutten once the north block was finished, and resumed in 1730 under Friedrich Carl von Schönborn. The whole shell was complete in December 1744. The Residence stands on a base of 92 by 167 metres, has almost 400 rooms and cost over 1.5 million guilders, at a time when a day labourer earned about one guilder a week.

Neumann built the staircase in 1737. It spans an area of 18 by 32 metres without pillars, beneath a vault 23 metres high. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, assisted by his sons, above all Giovanni Domenico, painted the ceiling above it between 1752 and 1753, the largest continuous ceiling fresco in the world at about 580 square metres. He also decorated the Imperial Hall. Neumann died in 1753.

Napoleon reportedly called the building the largest parsonage in Europe. He slept there on three visits between 1806 and 1813, and signed the declaration of war against Prussia there on 2 October 1806. The prince-bishopric was abolished in 1802–03, and the Residence was opened to the public in 1921. A British air raid on 16 March 1945 burnt it almost completely out; only the central building survived, without its roofs, and Neumann's stone vaults withstood the fire. Much furniture and panelling had been removed in time. Reconstruction lasted from 1945 to 1987 and cost about €20m. The Residence, with its Court Gardens and Residence Square, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981.
wurzen: Wurzen stands beside the river Mulde, which is crossed there by two bridges, 25 km east of Leipzig on the railway line to Riesa and Dresden. The town lies on the central German route of the pilgrim way to Santiago de Compostela, which follows the Via Regia, a designated Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.

Slavs founded Wurzen after 600. It is first mentioned in a donation of Otto I in 961 as a Burgward, civitas vurcine, in the Gau Neletici. Early in the twelfth century it was a town, and Herwig, bishop of Meissen, founded a collegiate church there. The castle was occasionally the residence of the bishop from 1497 to 1581, the year the town passed to the elector of Saxony. In 1637, during the Thirty Years' War, the Swedish army sacked Wurzen and burned it almost completely down.

In 1768 Goethe travelled through the town between Leipzig and Dresden, and the long wait for the ferry later inspired a passage in his first edition of Faust. On 31 July 1838 Wurzen was connected to the Leipzig-Dresden line, the first German long-distance railway, opened on 7 April 1839, and the first German railway bridge was built across the Mulde. American air raids between October 1943 and April 1945 killed over 40 people. On 24 April 1945 the mayor, Armin Graebert, together with members of the SPD and KPD and the pastors of the Protestant and Catholic churches, secured the surrender of the town to the 273rd US Infantry Regiment and saved it from destruction.

The collegiate church of St. Marien, consecrated in 1114, is Romanesque to late Gothic, with bronze sculptures by Georg Wrba of 1932. The late Gothic castle also survives. The writer and painter Joachim Ringelnatz was born in Wurzen, and the town styles itself Ringelnatz City; the fabulist Magnus Gottfried Lichtwer was also born there. The main commercial focus is the making of pastries and candies.
wushe-incident: Earlier armed resistance to Japanese rule in Taiwan, such as the Tapani Incident, had been met with harsh retaliation, and by the 1930s the younger Taiwanese generation had largely turned to organised political and social movements. The indigenous peoples, however, were still classed as seiban, raw barbarians, and treated as inferiors. They were disarmed and forced to settle as farmers, and Governor-General Sakuma Samata's five-year plan had sought to pacify or eradicate the groups living in areas marked for logging.

The Seediq of Musha were held up as a model of this policy, and Mona Rudao had been one of 43 indigenous leaders taken on a tour of Japan. Resentment remained over police misconduct, forced labour and disrespect for Seediq customs. Days before the attack, at the wedding of Mona Rudao's son Daho Mona, the police officer Katsuhiko Yoshimura refused a cup of wine and struck Daho Mona with his stick; a fight followed, and Mona Rudao's apology was turned away.

On 27 October 1930 hundreds of Japanese gathered at the elementary school for an athletics meet. Shortly before dawn Mona Rudao led over 300 warriors against police sub-stations to seize weapons and ammunition, then attacked the school, while other groups raided thirteen police stations, post offices, dormitories and shops and cut the telegraph lines and roads. The attackers killed 134 Japanese, among them women and children, and two Han Taiwanese mistaken for Japanese; most of the victims were beheaded.

Governor-General Ishizuka Eizō imposed a press blackout and sent two thousand troops. The Seediq withdrew into the mountains and fought by night, and the army air corps dropped mustard gas bombs, allegedly the first such use of chemical warfare in Asia. Mona Rudao killed himself on 28 November, and remaining resistance was suppressed by the third week of December. Of the 1,200 Seediq directly involved, 644 died, 290 of them by suicide.

Criticism forced Ishizuka and his chief civil administrator Hitomi Jirō to resign in January 1931. On 25 April 1931 indigenous groups working with the Japanese attacked the village where about 500 surrendered Seediq were confined and beheaded every male over 15, the Second Musha Incident. Policy then shifted: the indigenous peoples were recast as imperial subjects under the name takasagozoku, and part of the Seediq land went to their rivals the Truku and Toda. The uprising is the subject of the 2011 film Seediq Bale.
wusun: The Wusun were a semi-nomadic steppe people named in Chinese records from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. They first appear living near the Yuezhi between the Qilian Mountains and Dunhuang in Gansu. Chinese sources tell that the Yuezhi attacked them and killed their king Nandoumi. By legend his infant son Liejiaomi was left in the wild, suckled by a she-wolf and fed meat by ravens. The Xiongnu ruler adopted the child, made him leader of the Wusun and a general, and Liejiaomi won many victories for the Xiongnu.

The origin of the name is debated, and scholars have linked it to the Asmiraioi of Ptolemy's Geography, to words for horse and to a word for tent. Most scholars take the Wusun to have spoken an Indo-European language, probably Iranian, though Tocharian and Indo-Aryan have also been proposed.

With Xiongnu permission Liejiaomi attacked the Yuezhi in the Ili Valley in the 2nd century BCE, and the Yuezhi migrated to Sogdia and then Bactria. The Wusun took over the valley, and when the Xiongnu ruler died Liejiaomi refused to serve them. In 125 BCE the Han diplomat Zhang Qian was sent to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu and estimated the Wusun at 630,000 people. Their court was the walled city of Chigu, near Issyk Kul, whose exact site is unknown.

The Wusun at first hesitated from fear of the Xiongnu, but after Han blows against the Xiongnu and a threat of war, Liejiaomi sent horses and accepted the Han princess Xijun as a wife. A Xiongnu princess was declared his senior consort. After Xijun's early death, Princess Jieyou succeeded her and lived among the Wusun for fifty years. In 72 BCE the Wusun requested Han help against the Xiongnu, and a Han army of 160,000 inflicted a crushing defeat on them. Afterwards the Wusun gained significant influence over the city-states of the Tarim Basin. In the 5th century CE, pressed by the Rouran, they may have moved to the Pamir Mountains; they were last mentioned in Chinese sources in 436 CE.

The Wusun were governed by a hereditary Great Kunmi, assisted by a council of elders and an administration of sixteen officials, and every freeman counted as a warrior. Their society was highly stratified, by ownership of property; the wealthiest are believed to have owned 4,000 to 5,000 horses. Slaves, mostly prisoners of war, worked as servants and craftsmen.

Early Chinese descriptions record that they lived in felt tents, ate meat and drank fermented mare's milk. Cattle-raising was their main activity, but they also practised agriculture. The Kargali burial of a female shaman near Almaty held nearly 300 gold objects.
